Rephrase the request as a fact-check so a stricter standard is applied to the work
Ask Claude to search for supporting evidence for each of the figures in the summary
questions.why: Checking is relative to a source. Without one the model can only assess whether figures look plausible, which is a much weaker thing.
questions.traps: Confidence and stricter framing both operate without a reference. Searching introduces a source, but not the one the summary is supposed to match.

questions.stem: A team asks for advice on a decision and describes only the option they already favour.
options: Ask Claude to argue against the option that has already been described in the prompt
Ask for the risks of the favoured option in addition to the advice being requested
Describe the alternatives too, since advice is a comparison
Ask the question again in a more neutral tone so the preference is less apparent
questions.why: A single option leaves nothing to weigh. Supplying the alternatives makes advice a comparison rather than a justification of what was presented.
questions.traps: Devil's advocacy critiques one option without introducing another. Risks and neutral phrasing both stay inside a single-option frame.

questions.stem: A team needs consistent decimal places in generated figures and they drift inside tables while staying correct in prose.
options: State the precision required and check inside the tables specifically
Ask Claude to be consistent with number formatting throughout the whole document
Convert every figure to text so the model does not reformat any of them itself
Generate the tables separately with their own formatting instruction attached to them
questions.why: Local conventions inside structured elements are a known drift point, so an explicit rule plus a targeted check where drift concentrates is the reliable pattern.
questions.traps: A general consistency instruction has already implicitly failed. Text conversion fights the model, and separate generation adds steps for a formatting detail.

questions.stem: A team includes six examples for a binary classification. Accuracy is good and each call is slower and dearer than expected.
options: Keep all six, since accuracy matters more than the cost of each individual call
Test whether two or three examples hold the same accuracy
Move the examples into project configuration so they need not be sent every time
Combine several classifications into one call so the examples are amortised across them
questions.why: Example count has diminishing returns and a binary decision usually saturates within two or three. Measuring where accuracy plateaus finds the cheap point.
questions.traps: Assuming six are needed skips the test. Reuse and batching both lower cost per item without asking whether the examples earn their place.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to find problems in a process and design its replacement in one request, and the design addresses only the first two problems.
options: Ask for the design again and specify that every listed problem must be addressed
Ask for several designs so that between them all of the problems are covered
Request a table mapping each identified problem to the part of the design that solves it
Complete and review the problem list before asking for any design
questions.why: Diagnosis and design in one pass lets the design's momentum truncate the diagnosis. Separating them makes the problem list reviewable before it constrains a solution.
questions.traps: Insisting on coverage of a list generated in the same breath does not fix it. Multiple designs and mapping tables both organise an incomplete list.

questions.stem: A team asks for a summary "for the exec team" and it arrives at a length nobody will read before the meeting.
options: Say that the executives are busy so the model applies stronger compression to it
Give the length as a word count or a reading time
Ask for the shortest possible version and expand it again if too much has been lost
Provide the executives' job titles so the model can judge an appropriate length itself
questions.why: Brief is relative and the model has no anchor for yours. A number is checkable by both sides, which is what makes it a real constraint.
questions.traps: Busyness signals are another relative cue. Shortest-possible overshoots the other way, and job titles imply nothing reliable about reading time.

questions.stem: A researcher asks Claude to extract every mention of a concept from a long report, and it misses the passages that use a synonym.
options: List the synonyms that count as the same concept before asking
Ask for a second pass over the report to catch anything the first pass may have missed
Ask Claude to search for the concept itself rather than for the exact term used
Shorten the report so the model can attend to all of it within a single pass
questions.why: Extraction follows the definition it is given. Enumerating the variants converts a string match into a concept match with boundaries you control.
questions.traps: A second pass repeats the same definition. Asking for "the concept" leaves the boundary to the model, and shortening does not address vocabulary.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer keeps saying a section "doesn't feel right" and the resulting revisions swing unpredictably.
options: Pass the feedback through unchanged, since the model can interpret informal language well
Ask Claude to propose several readings of the feedback and pick one of them to act on
Translate the impression into a specific defect before prompting
Ask the reviewer to revise the section themselves rather than describing the problem
questions.why: Impressionistic feedback names a symptom without a cause. Interpreting it is the reviewer's job or yours; passing the ambiguity on makes the outcome a coin flip.
questions.traps: Model interpretation is exactly the unpredictability described. Multiple readings move the guess, and asking the reviewer to write it discards their role.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for "the main issue" with a plan and receives one, when three of comparable seriousness exist.
options: Ask for the main issue and then follow up asking whether there are any others as well
Ask for the top five issues so that a broader set is returned on every occasion
Ask Claude to rank every issue it can identify by how serious each of them is
Ask for issues meeting a stated severity threshold
questions.why: Asking for one forces a ranking the situation does not support. A threshold lets the true number surface, which is the finding that matters.
questions.traps: A follow-up recovers the others only if you think to ask. A fixed five over-collects, and ranking still starts from a singular framing.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt behaves differently in their own account than in a colleague's, and both are using identical wording.
options: Assume it is ordinary variation and use whichever of the two outputs is better
Ask the colleague to retype the prompt in case a copy-paste difference crept in
Compare the project settings and instructions on each account
Run the prompt several times in each account and compare the average of the results
questions.why: Account-level configuration is invisible in the prompt but present in every request. Comparing project instructions and settings is where identical wording diverges.
questions.traps: Attributing it to variance skips a systematic cause. Retyping tests a formatting theory, and averaging measures the difference without explaining it.

questions.stem: A team asks for a report with an executive summary and the summary describes the report's structure instead of its findings.
options: Ask for a longer executive summary so the findings have room to appear within it
Ask Claude to write the executive summary only after the report itself is complete
Say that the summary is written for an executive audience specifically and no other
Say the summary must state conclusions and what they imply
questions.why: Describing structure is the default reading of "summary" applied to a document. Naming conclusions and implications as required content is what changes it.
questions.traps: Length expands the description. Writing it last does not change what a summary is taken to mean, and an audience label does not specify content.

questions.stem: A prompt's two examples both happen to show the easy version of the task.
options: Add more examples of the easy version for clarity
Add an example of the difficult version as well
Describe the difficult version in words instead
Remove the examples, since they are unrepresentative
questions.why: Examples set the expected difficulty as well as the format, and a hard case is what shows the treatment it actually needs.
questions.traps: More easy examples reinforce the wrong level, a description is weaker than a demonstration, and removing them loses the format guidance.

questions.stem: A team pipes a classification into a drafting step. When the class is wrong, the draft is confidently written in the wrong register.
options: Surface the classification for a person to check before drafting
Ask the drafting step to check whether the classification looks right for the request
Combine the two steps so classification and drafting happen in a single response
Attach a confidence score to the classification and review the low-scoring cases
questions.why: Making the intermediate visible turns a silent pipeline error into a catchable one, because the classification determines everything downstream of it.
questions.traps: Self-checking downstream uses the same signal that produced the class. Merging hides the decision, and confidence catches only cases the model already doubts.

questions.stem: A team tells Claude to write "nothing that commits us" and the draft avoids commitments while also avoiding any useful specifics.
options: Ask for a more confident draft that still avoids making commitments on the company
Name the categories of statement that are off limits
Ask Claude what it understood the commitment restriction to mean before drafting
Have the legal team review each draft and remove anything that reads as a commitment
questions.why: A vague prohibition removes specificity along with the risk. Naming the prohibited categories lets the draft be concrete about everything else.
questions.traps: Asking for confidence fights the same vague ban. Asking the model to interpret it invites its own reading, and legal review is a control rather than an instruction.

questions.stem: An associate uploads meeting minutes and asks who owns an action, and the answer names whoever spoke most about the topic.
options: Ask the question again using the word accountable rather than the word responsible
Upload a document listing team roles so the assignment can be inferred correctly
Ask for explicit assignments and for a blank where none is recorded
Ask Claude to list everyone who discussed the topic so a choice can be made from it
questions.why: Prominence in a transcript is a strong but wrong signal for ownership. Asking for explicit assignment, and allowing a blank, stops inference filling the gap.
questions.traps: Synonyms do not change the inference. A roles document invites a different wrong inference, and a discussion list restates the conflation for you to resolve.

questions.stem: A team got an excellent result once and cannot reproduce it, because the prompt was typed mid-conversation in a thread since lost.
options: Try to recall the wording and reconstruct the prompt from what the team remembers
Ask Claude to reproduce the prompt that generated the earlier result from memory
Accept the variation, since good results are partly a matter of chance on any given run
Capture prompts that work as reusable text outside the thread
questions.why: A working prompt is an asset and a conversation is not durable storage. Capturing it outside the thread is what makes a good result repeatable.
questions.traps: Reconstruction from memory is lossy. The model cannot recover a prompt from a lost thread, and attributing it to chance discards a real technique.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to "make this clearer" and the rewrite is clearer and has lost a distinction the original drew deliberately.
options: Mark the distinctions that must be preserved before editing
Ask for a lighter rewrite so that fewer changes are made to the original wording
Ask Claude to list every change it made so unwanted edits can be reverted afterwards
Ask for the clearer version alongside the original so the two can be compared
questions.why: Clarifying is a form of simplifying, and deliberate distinctions are the first casualty. Marking them is what protects them through the edit.
questions.traps: A lighter edit lowers the rate without protecting the specific distinction. Change logs and comparisons both catch the loss after it happens.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to draft talking points for a difficult conversation and supplies only their own position.
options: Ask for more talking points so a wider range of possible responses is covered by them
Ask Claude to predict how the conversation is most likely to unfold in practice
Describe the other person's likely position as well
Ask for the points to be written in a more persuasive and confident style throughout
questions.why: Talking points for a difficult conversation are shaped by the resistance they meet. Supplying the other position makes them responsive rather than a monologue.
questions.traps: More points on one side is more monologue. Prediction without information is speculation, and persuasiveness assumes the objections are already known.

questions.stem: A team asks for three sections in a fixed order and receives all three with the conclusion moved to the front.
options: Ask Claude to reorder the sections after they have been generated in whatever order
Number the sections so their intended sequence is evident from the content itself
Generate each section separately and assemble them in the correct order afterwards
State the required order explicitly in the prompt
questions.why: Presentation order is a rhetorical choice the model makes unless it is specified. Stating the sequence removes the discretion.
questions.traps: A reordering pass is an extra call for something one clause supplies. Numbering is a hint rather than a requirement, and separate generation is heavier than needed.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to "sort out" a messy set of product descriptions and it rewrites them into a house style nobody specified.
options: Ask for a lighter touch so that fewer of the descriptions end up being altered
Name the fields to normalise, the style to hold, and what must not change
Provide one sample description written the way the team would like them to read
Ask Claude to list the changes it made to each of the descriptions afterwards
questions.why: "Sort out" is an outcome without a specification. Naming the operations, the target style and the untouchables makes it a job the model can do correctly first time.
questions.traps: A lighter touch reduces the rate without defining the target. One sample teaches style but not scope, and a change list arrives after the rewriting is done.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a briefing note and the result is accurate but pitched at someone who already knows the background.
options: Say what the reader knows and what they must be able to do after reading
Ask for a simpler version in a follow-up round once the first draft has arrived
Request that background material be added at the start of the briefing note
Ask for it to be written for a general reader rather than a specialist one
questions.why: Stating the knowledge boundary and the reader's task lets the model pitch correctly on the first attempt rather than converging through rounds.
questions.traps: Iterating to simplicity is slow and can overshoot. Added background and "general reader" both leave the actual starting point unspecified.

questions.stem: A team needs output that pastes cleanly into a spreadsheet and it keeps arriving with a sentence of commentary either side.
options: Copy the response and delete the surrounding sentences by hand each time
Ask for the data alone, naming the delimiter, with no preamble
Ask for a shorter response so that there is less room for the commentary
Ask for the data to be placed at the end so the extra text can be cut
questions.why: Conversational framing is the default register. It goes away when ruled out explicitly and the payload's shape is stated.
questions.traps: Manual cleanup repeats forever. Shortening and repositioning both accept the commentary rather than removing it.

questions.stem: A team's five examples all show the same category and the model now assigns that label to almost everything.
options: Add more examples until the total reaches twenty across all of the categories
Say that the other categories matter too and should not be overlooked by it
Balance the examples across categories rather than by frequency
Handle the rare labels with a separate prompt written just for those cases
questions.why: Example distribution reads as a prior. A skewed set pushes the model toward the majority label regardless of what the input actually says.
questions.traps: Padding the count keeps the skew. An importance instruction fights the demonstrated pattern, and a separate prompt needs the classification that is failing.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to draft a proposal, critique it, and produce a final version in one request. The critique is mild and the final barely differs.
options: Ask for a considerably harsher critique within the same combined request
Ask for the critique to be written before the proposal itself is drafted
Require the critique to list a minimum number of specific problems found
Run the critique as its own request without the drafting context
questions.why: Self-critique inside the same pass inherits a commitment to the draft. Separating it removes the authorship stake that makes the critique gentle.
questions.traps: Harshness and quotas force volume rather than independence. Critiquing before drafting has nothing to critique.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to avoid naming a competitor and the copy complies while describing them closely enough to identify.
options: Say that indirect identification is out of scope, not just the name
Ask Claude to avoid making comparisons entirely so nobody can be identified
Review each draft and remove any description that identifies the competitor
Replace the competitor's name with a generic placeholder throughout the copy
questions.why: Constraints are read literally. If the intent is that the competitor not be identifiable, that is the constraint to state, because a name ban only bans the name.
questions.traps: Removing comparisons discards useful content. Review is a check rather than an instruction, and a placeholder still carries the identifying description.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a 90-page manual and asks a narrow question. The answer is right and cites a section that discusses something else.
options: Ask Claude to double-check its own citation before the answer is finalised
Upload the manual a second time in case the file parsed badly on first read
Treat the locator as unverified and check the section against the manual
Reword the question so that the correct section is more easily located
questions.why: A correct answer with a wrong pointer is the characteristic failure here, which is why locators get checked separately from content.
questions.traps: Self-checking a citation uses the process that produced it. A parsing fault would corrupt content too, and rewording may move the error rather than reveal it.

questions.stem: A team's prompt has grown to two pages after twenty case-by-case fixes, and new instructions barely register.
options: Keep adding fixes as new cases arise, since each addresses a real problem
Split the two-page prompt into several shorter prompts run one after another
Move the newest instructions to the top so they carry the most weight
Rebuild it around the general rule that all the fixes share
questions.why: Case-by-case accretion produces a prompt where instructions compete and dilute. Consolidating around the underlying rule restores the leverage each one has.
questions.traps: Continuing accretion created the plateau. Splitting and reordering redistribute a bloated set without simplifying it.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for a risk register specifying ten risks, and the list pads to ten with near-duplicates.
options: Ask for the distinct risks that apply, with ten as a ceiling
Ask for twenty risks and then remove the duplicates from the longer list
Ask Claude to de-duplicate the finished list once it has been generated
Specify a different business category for each of the ten entries wanted
questions.why: A fixed count is a quota, and quotas get filled. Framing the number as a ceiling lets the honest answer be fewer, which is what stops the padding.
questions.traps: A longer list has proportionally more duplication. Self-checking applies after padding, and categories constrain shape without removing quota pressure.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to write a rejection email giving only the candidate's name and the role.
options: Ask for three separate drafts and pick whichever one seems safest to send
State the length, what may not be said, and the tone to use
Say that it is effectively a legal document so more caution gets applied
Supply the candidate's full interview notes so the draft is well grounded
questions.why: The model defaults to helpful and complete. Anything you cannot include has to be stated as an exclusion, because legal constraints cannot be inferred from a name.
questions.traps: More source material makes the feedback problem worse. Sampling leaves the gap to luck, and relabelling the register does not encode a prohibition.

questions.stem: A team asks for a comparison table and the model invents plausible values for cells the source leaves empty.
options: Ask for any invented entries to be marked in some distinguishable way
Drop the column that is most often empty in the underlying source data
State that unknown fields stay blank and are never inferred
Ask for a shorter table so there are fewer cells in which to invent
questions.why: A table's empty cell reads as an incomplete job, so explicit permission to leave a blank is what makes the honest output available to the model.
questions.traps: Self-marked invention is unreliable for the same reason the invention happened. Dropping the column loses real data and fewer rows keeps the proportion.

questions.stem: An associate's examples are excellent and each runs about a page, while real inputs run to thirty pages.
options: Add more one-page examples so that the pattern is reinforced more strongly
Chunk the real inputs into one-page pieces so each matches the examples
Note in the prompt that the real inputs are considerably longer than these
Use examples at the real input length, or state the difference
questions.why: Examples set expectations about scale, and a one-page example demonstrates a compression ratio that does not transfer to thirty pages.
questions.traps: Reinforcing a mismatched pattern strengthens the mismatch. Chunking changes the task, and a bare note is weaker than showing the real case.

questions.stem: A prompt asks for a decision and the reasoning behind it in a single response.
options: Ask for the reasoning first and the decision after
Ask for the decision first so that it is not buried
Ask for both in whichever order the model prefers
Ask for the decision only and infer the reasoning
questions.why: Reasoning that follows a stated decision tends to justify it, where reasoning that comes first can actually reach it.
questions.traps: Leading with the decision invites rationalisation, leaving the order open makes it unpredictable, and inferring reasoning is guesswork.

questions.stem: A team specifies a 400-word press release and receives 620 words, then 550 on a second attempt.
options: Ask for 300 words instead so that the overshoot lands nearer to the target
State the limit as hard, ask for the count, and verify before publishing
Give each section its own word budget so the total comes out about right
Accept the longer draft and trim it back by hand before it is published
questions.why: Length targets are approximate for a language model, so the reliable pattern is to state the constraint firmly and check the number yourself.
questions.traps: Deliberately under-asking misses in both directions. Sectioning still needs verification, and manual trimming abandons a constraint that matters for the channel.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to check a document against a criteria list. Every criterion is reported met, including one only partly addressed.
options: Ask Claude to be considerably stricter when assessing each of the criteria
Ask for a numeric score per criterion rather than a simple met-or-not call
Ask about each of the criteria in its own separate request to the model
Ask for the supporting evidence per criterion so partial coverage shows
questions.why: A binary judgement rounds partial evidence to the nearest verdict. Requiring the supporting text makes the strength of each match inspectable.
questions.traps: Strictness moves a threshold without exposing it. Scores are still unexplained judgements, and per-criterion requests repeat the same binary framing.

questions.stem: An associate is on the seventh revision. Each round fixes the stated problem and undoes something settled two rounds earlier.
options: Carry the settled requirements forward explicitly in every round
Ask Claude to remember the earlier corrections and not repeat those mistakes
Start over with a single prompt containing every requirement gathered so far
Accept the draft and fix the recurring issue by hand in the final version
questions.why: Constraints established conversationally compete for attention as a thread grows. Restating them is what keeps a settled decision settled.
questions.traps: Asking the model to remember relies on the fading attention that caused the regression. A restart discards progress and manual patching leaves the process broken.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to "analyse" churn data and receives an accurate description of the data with nothing about what drives the churn.
options: Ask for a considerably deeper analysis of the same churn data that was given
Supply more of the underlying dataset so the analysis has more to work with
Ask the specific question you need answered rather than naming an activity
Ask for a business perspective on the data rather than a statistical one
questions.why: Naming an activity leaves the model to choose the question, and description satisfies "analyse". Asking the actual question is the fix.
questions.traps: Depth and volume both extend a description. A business framing shifts vocabulary without specifying what is being asked.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to explain a delay to a customer and the honest draft reveals a supplier dispute the company will not disclose.
options: Ask for a vaguer explanation so the sensitive details are less likely to show
State what may not be disclosed before asking for the explanation
Remove the supplier information from the prompt before requesting a draft
Review each draft before sending and remove any sensitive content found
questions.why: Confidentiality is a constraint the model cannot infer. Naming the off-limits material lets it write candidly about everything else, which vagueness sacrifices.
questions.traps: Vagueness costs the clarity the message needs. Withholding context weakens the explanation, and review is a safety net rather than an instruction.

questions.stem: A team's downstream tool expects a strict structure and about three percent of responses arrive with an explanatory note attached.
options: Specify the structure alone and validate every response before use
Word the instruction considerably more strictly than it is worded at present
Ask for the explanatory note to come after the payload so it can be cut off
Use a simpler output structure so there is less about it to explain
questions.why: Prompt instructions reduce a failure rate rather than eliminating it. Anything feeding a downstream system needs validation, because the residual percent will break it.
questions.traps: Stronger wording chases an asymptote. Repositioning and simplifying both reduce the odds without protecting the consumer.

questions.stem: A team's two examples are well-shaped and one contains a factual error, which now appears in the model's output.
options: Two examples is an unstable number and the model averaged them together
Correct the examples, since they teach content as well as form
Later examples carry more weight, so the error came from the second one
Factual errors inside examples are ignored, so this came from elsewhere
questions.why: An example is a demonstration of a good answer in full. The model cannot know which parts you meant as structure and which as substance, so it copies both.
questions.traps: Count and position are not the mechanism. The claim that errors in examples are ignored is precisely backwards and is the misconception here.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to plan a project and estimate durations in one request, and every task lands on a round number of days.
options: Ask for considerably more precise estimates than the ones just produced
Ask Claude to show its working for each of the duration estimates given
Ask for the plan first, then estimate each task with its assumptions
Ask for a range rather than a single figure for each of the tasks
questions.why: Estimation generated alongside planning is filler that keeps the plan's rhythm. A separate pass with stated assumptions makes each number arguable.
questions.traps: Precision instructions produce less round filler. Explanations and ranges dress up numbers that were never derived from anything.

questions.stem: A team asks for onboarding docs with no jargon and gets vague phrasing that is harder to act on than the jargon was.
options: Drop the jargon constraint, since accuracy matters more than accessibility
Produce a jargon version and a plain version and let readers pick one
Define each technical term the first time that it appears in the document
Give a short list of terms that remain acceptable despite the ban
questions.why: A blanket ban removes vocabulary without supplying replacements, so the model reaches for imprecision. An allowed list keeps the words that carry meaning.
questions.traps: Dropping the constraint abandons the readers it was for. Two versions doubles maintenance, and inline definitions do not repair a ban already in force.

questions.stem: An associate uploads six papers and asks for the consensus. The synthesis is confident and two papers contradict it.
options: Ask for the consensus again and check whether the second answer matches
Upload the six papers one at a time so each gets the model's attention
Ask for each paper's position separately before asking what they support
Ask for page citations so the synthesis can be verified after the fact
questions.why: Synthesis flattens disagreement. Extracting each source's position first makes the contradiction visible as data you can inspect.
questions.traps: Repeat runs test stability, not accuracy. Sequential upload does not change the flattening, and citations help after a misleading synthesis exists.

questions.stem: An associate has spent forty minutes refining a prompt for a task that would take twenty minutes by hand, and it is a genuine one-off.
options: Finish this one manually, since refinement pays off on repeated tasks
Keep refining, since the prompt will be reusable for similar work in future
Ask Claude to write the prompt, since prompt writing is a task it handles
Lower the quality bar for this task so the current prompt is acceptable
questions.why: The economics of prompting depend on repetition. Refinement is an investment amortised over runs, and a genuine one-off has none to amortise against.
questions.traps: Assuming future reuse is what the scenario has disproven. Meta-prompting does not change the arithmetic, and lowering the bar trades quality for a sunk cost.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to shorten a proposal and the pricing table, which the client most needed, is what gets cut.
options: Specify a percentage reduction rather than a vague instruction to shorten
Say what must be preserved as well as the target length
Ask for only the narrative sections to be shortened and nothing else
Shorten the proposal by hand, since judging client priorities needs a person
questions.why: Cutting requires knowing what is load-bearing. A length target says how much to remove but nothing about what survives, so it trims by prose density.
questions.traps: A percentage is still only a size. Naming sections is closer but brittle across documents, and doing it by hand discards a task the model handles well.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works for the person who wrote it and produces poor results for a colleague on a different product line.
options: Add considerably more detail about the original product line to the prompt
Ask the colleague to write their own prompt, since prompts do not transfer
Ask Claude to rewrite the prompt more generally before the colleague reuses it
Make the product context an explicit input rather than assumed knowledge
questions.why: Prompts that rely on implicit shared context break when the context changes. Naming the variable and passing it in makes a prompt reusable across a team.
questions.traps: More detail about the wrong product entrenches the problem. Generalising strips the specificity, and abandoning reuse forfeits the point of sharing.

questions.stem: A team asks for meeting notes in a template with a decisions section, and when no decisions were made the section fills with discussion points.
options: Move the decisions section to the end where it is less likely to be padded
Say an empty section should read as none rather than being filled
Ask Claude to review its output and strip anything that is not a decision
Use a different word than decisions, since that term invites broad reading
questions.why: A blank looks like failure to a model trying to be complete. Naming the empty case and what to write in it makes "none" available and informative.
questions.traps: Reordering does not change the padding instinct. Self-review repeats the judgement that caused it, and renaming shifts the ambiguity.

questions.stem: A team wants scores from one to five and their examples show only one, three and five. Twos and fours almost never appear.
options: Instruct the model to use the whole scale including the middle values
Ask for one decimal place so intermediate judgements have somewhere to go
Reduce the scale to three points, since three is what is being used anyway
Add examples at the intermediate scores so the whole range shows
questions.why: Demonstrated values become the usable range. Unexemplified points read as unavailable, so the fix is showing what a two and a four look like.
questions.traps: An instruction to use the range does not say where the boundaries sit. Decimals and rescaling redesign the measurement rather than teaching the one you have.

questions.stem: A team chains three steps manually. Step two occasionally emits the wrong shape and step three then fails confusingly.
options: Validate step two's output against its expected shape first
Merge the three steps into one prompt so there are no handoffs to fail
Tell step three to handle unexpected input as gracefully as it can manage
Rerun the whole chain whenever step three produces a confusing failure
questions.why: Chains need contracts at their boundaries. Checking shape turns a confusing downstream failure into a clear, local one you can act on.
questions.traps: Merging hides the failure. Graceful handling masks bad input, and blind reruns treat a deterministic shape problem as noise.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for options to restructure a department and all three involve redundancies leadership has ruled out.
options: Ask for considerably more options so some avoid the redundancies entirely
Ask Claude to assess each option's feasibility after they are generated
State the ruled-out options up front so alternatives are available
Reframe the request around growth rather than around restructuring at all
questions.why: Exclusions shape generation only if stated. Ruling out the obvious answer pushes the model into the space of options you can actually consider.
questions.traps: More options resamples the same space. Post-hoc feasibility filters what should not have been generated, and reframing changes the question.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a dataset covering 2019 to 2024 and the answer describes a trend continuing into 2025.
options: Ask for the trend analysis again with an instruction to be more conservative
Add the 2025 data to the upload so that the projection can be verified
Ask for any projection to be labelled so it is distinguishable from data
Instruct the model to confine claims to the period the data covers
questions.why: Extrapolation reads as a natural completion of a trend. Stating the boundary of the data keeps described trends inside what was actually observed.
questions.traps: Conservatism is vague. Adding data moves the boundary without defining it, and labelling relies on the model recognising its own extrapolation.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer rejects drafts without saying why, and five rounds have produced five differently-wrong versions.
options: Ask the reviewer which aspect failed before prompting again
Try a completely different approach and see whether that one lands better
Ask for several drafts at once and let the reviewer choose between them
Ask Claude to guess what the reviewer is most likely to be objecting to
questions.why: Undirected rejection carries no gradient. Getting the specific defect from the reviewer is what turns a random walk into a correction.
questions.traps: A different approach is another blind guess. Batch drafting samples more widely without direction, and asking the model to guess compounds the ambiguity.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to "improve" a paragraph and dislikes what comes back.
options: Ask for it to be improved rather more carefully
Say which property of the paragraph should improve
Ask for several versions and pick the best one
Improve the paragraph by hand instead of asking
questions.why: "Improve" names no direction, so saying whether it is clarity, brevity or tone is what makes the request actionable.
questions.traps: More care has no target, generating options shifts the choice without stating the criterion, and doing it by hand abandons the task.

questions.stem: A team asks for a table and receives one whose columns differ from run to run.
options: Ask for the columns to stay consistent between runs
Reformat each table by hand after it is produced
Name each of the columns that the table must have
Accept it, since the content is right either way
questions.why: Columns that are not specified are chosen afresh each time, and naming them is what fixes the structure across runs.
questions.traps: Asking for consistency does not say consistent with what, hand-reformatting repeats forever, and varying columns break anything downstream.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to read fifty customer interviews and identify themes, and the themes lean on the interviews that came first.
options: Ask for considerably more themes so the later interviews get represented
Reverse the order of the interviews and run the whole analysis again
Ask Claude to weight all fifty of the interviews equally when finding themes
Extract points from each interview first, then find themes across them
questions.why: Two-stage analysis gives every source equal footing, because the second stage works on a uniform extract rather than fifty documents competing for attention.
questions.traps: Asking for equal weighting states the goal without the mechanism. Reversing reveals the bias, and more themes dilutes rather than rebalances.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for "a quick look" at a supplier contract and gets general commentary rather than the exposure they were worried about.
options: Ask for a considerably more detailed review covering the whole of the contract
Provide the supplier's previous contract so the two can be compared directly
Ask the specific question you are worried about, since a general look returns general commentary
Ask for the review to be structured under clear headings for readability
questions.why: A vague request returns a broad shallow sweep. Naming the exposure you care about directs the review to the clause that matters.
questions.traps: Depth and structure both improve a commentary still aimed at the wrong thing, and a comparison document widens the task rather than focusing it.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for a performance summary and it reads as though written for the employee rather than the panel who will read it.
options: Ask for a considerably more formal register in the next version produced
Name the reader and the decision the summary supports, since register follows from both
Provide the panel's terms of reference as background for the model to use
Ask for two versions and choose whichever of them suits the panel better
questions.why: Audience and purpose determine both register and content. Naming them lets the model pitch once, correctly, rather than defaulting to the subject's frame.
questions.traps: A register instruction narrows without grounding, terms of reference are background rather than direction, and sampling guesses at what a sentence would state.

questions.stem: A team asks for a summary in three fixed sections and roughly one response in six merges two of them together.
options: State that each section appears even when it would be empty in that case
Number the three sections so that their separateness is signalled more strongly
Ask for considerably longer summaries so that merging becomes less likely
Generate each of the three sections in its own separate request instead
questions.why: Sections merge when the model judges one to be thin. Stating that an empty section still gets its heading removes that judgement.
questions.traps: Numbering and length both nudge without deciding, and three separate calls guarantee the shape at three times the cost of one clause.

questions.stem: A team's examples all cover straightforward cases, so unusual inputs get forced into the same shape rather than handled properly.
options: Add an instruction about handling unusual inputs with particular care
Include an example covering an unusual case
Increase the number of straightforward examples that are supplied
Ask the model to flag any inputs that it considers to be unusual
questions.why: Examples teach the boundaries of the pattern as well as the pattern itself. Demonstrating the awkward case stops it being forced into the common shape.
questions.traps: An instruction competes with a demonstrated pattern, more of the same examples narrows it further, and flagging identifies the problem without resolving it.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to reconcile two datasets and explain the discrepancies at once, and the explanations do not match the differences found.
options: Ask for the explanations to be considerably more rigorous within one request
Ask for the explanation to be produced before the reconciliation is done
Reconcile first, review the differences, then ask for explanations of those
Request that the working be shown throughout the whole of the response
questions.why: Explanations generated alongside a reconciliation are written to fit the narrative rather than the data. Separating them anchors each to a verified difference.
questions.traps: Rigour instructions do not create the anchor, explaining before reconciling has nothing to explain, and shown working still sits inside one generation.

questions.stem: A team asks for social posts within a character limit and the posts fit until hashtags and links are added afterwards.
options: Ask for shorter posts to leave some headroom for the later additions
Add the hashtags and the links by hand once the posts are within limit
Ask Claude to report the character count for each of the posts produced
Say the limit includes hashtags and links
questions.why: Limits need their boundaries defined. Saying what counts toward the total makes the constraint match the platform's own measurement.
questions.traps: Headroom is guesswork, manual addition repeats forever, and a reported count measures the same wrongly-scoped total.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a policy and asks a question it does not address, receiving a confident answer drawn from general practice instead.
options: Instruct the model to answer only from the document and to say when it is silent
Ask a narrower question so the gap in the policy is less likely to be hit
Add more policy documents covering the adjacent areas of the subject
Ask for a citation to be attached to the answer that gets produced
questions.why: Grounding is an instruction, not an automatic consequence of attaching a file. Without it the model fills gaps from general knowledge, invisibly.
questions.traps: Narrowing avoids rather than detects the gap, more documents move the boundary without exposing it, and a citation may be attached to an unsupported claim.

questions.stem: A team's refinement improved results on their own examples and nobody has checked whether it helped on anything else.
options: Add considerably more examples to the refinement set being used
Refine for rather fewer rounds in any future work on this prompt
Ask a colleague to review the prompt and give their opinion on it
Hold back cases never used in refinement and measure against those
questions.why: Tuning against the cases you measure on inflates the measurement. A held-back set is the only way to see whether gains generalise.
questions.traps: A larger tuning set is still contaminated, fewer rounds leaves the same blind spot, and a colleague's read is opinion rather than measurement.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to "make the deck more persuasive" and it adds superlatives while leaving the argument structure untouched.
options: Ask for a considerably more substantial rewrite of the whole deck
Say which part is unpersuasive: the claims, the evidence, or their order
Provide a deck the team considers persuasive as a model to follow
Ask Claude to explain what makes a deck persuasive before it starts
questions.why: Persuasion spans claims, evidence and sequencing, and the model defaults to language when the layer is unnamed. Naming it directs the work.
questions.traps: A bigger rewrite operates at the same layer, an exemplar teaches style rather than diagnosis, and a general explanation never touches this deck.

questions.stem: An associate asks for an explanation aimed at "non-technical stakeholders" and it still assumes familiarity with the company's own systems.
options: Ask for a simpler explanation in a follow-up round after this one
Ask for every system name to be defined the first time it appears
State which systems the readers know and which they do not, since non-technical is relative
Request an analogy-based explanation instead of a technical one
questions.why: "Non-technical" is relative to a field and says nothing about internal system familiarity. Stating the actual boundary lets the model pitch it correctly.
questions.traps: Iterating to simplicity is slow, inline definitions patch symptoms, and analogy avoids the vocabulary without establishing what the reader knows.

questions.stem: A team needs machine-readable output and it is correct except that field values arrive with inconsistent capitalisation each run.
options: Specify the exact casing and validate values before the lookup runs
Ask Claude to be consistent with capitalisation across the whole output
Convert everything to lower case after the output has been received
Provide the list of permitted values so they can be matched exactly
questions.why: Machine-consumed values need an exact specification plus a check, because casing is presentation to the model and load-bearing to the consumer.
questions.traps: A consistency instruction has no defined target, blanket lower-casing may break valid values, and a permitted list helps matching without guaranteeing form.

questions.stem: A team's examples show the desired reasoning and the model reproduces it while reaching conclusions that do not follow from it.
options: Ask for the reasoning to be shown considerably more explicitly than now
Include an example where the reasoning leads to an unexpected conclusion
Add more examples demonstrating the same reasoning pattern as before
Ask Claude to check its conclusion against its own stated reasoning
questions.why: If every example's reasoning leads to a predictable conclusion, the model learns the conclusion rather than the reasoning. An unexpected case separates them.
questions.traps: Showing reasoning more explicitly reinforces the coupling, more examples deepen it, and self-checking uses the reasoning that produced the answer.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify problems and rank them by severity in one pass, and the ranking mirrors the order they were generated in.
options: Ask for the ranking step to be carried out considerably more carefully
Ask for numeric severity scores rather than a ranked ordering of them
Ask for the problems to be listed in reverse order of their severity
Generate the problems first, then rank the reviewed list separately
questions.why: A ranking produced alongside generation inherits generation order rather than assessing severity. Separating them makes ranking an actual judgement.
questions.traps: Care instructions do not change the coupling, scores inherit the same ordering effect, and reverse order presumes the ranking already works.

questions.stem: A team tells Claude the tone must stay positive and a material change affecting staff is quietly left out of the announcement.
options: Ask for an announcement that is both positive and complete at once
Ask Claude to list anything that it omitted from the announcement
Fix the required content first and ask for the framing separately
Switch to a neutral tone so nothing is dropped for tonal reasons
questions.why: A tone constraint over unbounded scope becomes an editorial filter. Fixing required content first keeps content and framing independent.
questions.traps: Stacking adjectives leaves the conflict unresolved, a post-hoc omissions list is unreliable, and going neutral abandons a legitimate goal.

questions.stem: A researcher uploads a paper and asks about its limitations, and the answer lists generic study limitations rather than the stated ones.
options: Ask for the limitations the authors stated, and for a blank if they stated none
Ask for a longer answer covering considerably more limitations
Ask for the paper's limitations section to be quoted in full
Ask a more specific question about the study's methodology
questions.why: Generic limitations are what a model produces when it treats the question as a topic rather than a lookup. Requiring the authors' own statement makes it retrieval.
questions.traps: Length produces more generic content, quoting avoids the problem rather than framing it, and method specificity narrows without redirecting to the source.

questions.stem: An associate has edited across nine messages and version nine has drifted well away from the version three the team approved.
options: Ask Claude to undo all the changes made since version three was approved
Ask for a summary of everything that has changed across the nine rounds
Continue with the current version and fix the drift at the very end
Return to the approved version and apply the outstanding edits to that
questions.why: Iteration is lossy and drift accumulates silently. Returning to the last approved state and reapplying edits recovers the intended document.
questions.traps: The model cannot reliably reconstruct an earlier state, a change summary describes drift without reversing it, and continuing compounds it.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to "validate" a calculation and it confirms the arithmetic without questioning whether the formula was right.
options: Ask for a considerably more thorough validation of the calculation
Supply the underlying data that the calculation was performed on
Say which layer to validate: the arithmetic, the formula, or the inputs
Ask for the validation to be shown step by step in the output
questions.why: "Validate" spans arithmetic, method and inputs, and arithmetic is the default reading. Naming the layer is what gets the formula questioned.
questions.traps: Thoroughness and step-by-step working both deepen the arithmetic check, and more data strengthens it further rather than redirecting it.

questions.stem: A team's prompt produces good drafts for one client and subtly wrong ones for another, and the only difference is the sector.
options: Add considerably more detail about the first client's own sector
Pass the sector and its conventions in as an explicit input
Ask the second client's team to adjust the drafts once produced
Ask Claude to write more generally so that both clients fit it
questions.why: Prompts relying on implicit context break when the context changes. Naming the variable and passing it in makes a prompt portable across clients.
questions.traps: More detail about the wrong sector entrenches the mismatch, local adjustment is manual rework, and generalising strips what made the drafts useful.

questions.stem: A team asks for a numbered list of steps and several entries reference decisions made in the surrounding prose.
options: State that each step must stand alone without reference to other text
Ask for considerably more steps so that each one of them is smaller
Remove the surrounding prose so only the numbered steps remain
Ask Claude to check that each step is independently actionable
questions.why: Independence is a property you have to require. A numbered list looks actionable while still leaning on context, so the constraint has to name it.
questions.traps: Granularity does not create self-containment, deleting prose leaves steps that referenced it, and self-review repeats the judgement that failed.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt includes examples written before a product rename, and outputs still use the old product name throughout.
options: Add a note to the prompt saying the product has since been renamed
Ask Claude to use the current product name rather than the old one
Update the examples when the underlying facts change
Reduce the number of examples that are supplied with the prompt
questions.why: Examples are supplied knowledge and go stale like any other. Reviewing them on change is maintenance the technique requires.
questions.traps: A correction note competes with a demonstrated pattern, an instruction fights the examples directly, and fewer stale examples are still stale.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise a policy and assess compliance against it at once, and the assessment covers only what the summary included.
options: Ask for a considerably longer summary so that more of it is covered
Assess compliance against the full policy rather than against a summary
Ask for the compliance assessment to be produced before the summary
Ask for the summary itself to be considerably more comprehensive
questions.why: An assessment built on a summary inherits the summary's omissions. Working from the full source is what makes the compliance check complete.
questions.traps: Length reduces the omissions without removing the dependency, reordering leaves the same coupling, and comprehensiveness is the property already failing.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to keep a document under two pages and it complies by removing the appendix containing the evidence.
options: Ask for a document that is allowed to run slightly longer than two pages
Ask Claude to list whatever it removed to meet the page limit
Move the appendix into a separate file of its own instead
Say what must be preserved as well as stating the page limit
questions.why: A size limit is a container, not its contents. Naming what must survive prevents the model choosing which section to sacrifice.
questions.traps: Loosening the limit invites the same choice at a larger size, a removals list arrives after the loss, and splitting is a workaround.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a contract and asks about termination, and the answer describes standard market practice rather than this contract.
options: Instruct the model to answer only from the uploaded contract
Ask the question again using considerably more specific wording
Upload the contract a second time in case it did not parse well
Ask for the termination clause to be quoted in full first
questions.why: Grounding is an instruction rather than an automatic consequence of attaching a file. Without it the model blends the document with what it knows.
questions.traps: Rewording helps retrieval but not the blending, re-uploading addresses a failure that did not occur, and a full quote lacks the crucial instruction.

questions.stem: An associate changes a prompt and the output improves on the case they were looking at.
options: Keep the change, since the output clearly improved
Check the change against all the other cases too
Keep the change and watch for problems later on
Revert the change, since one case proves nothing
questions.why: A fix aimed at one case can degrade others, and rerunning the rest is what shows whether it was an improvement overall.
questions.traps: One case is a sample of one, watching later means shipping the regression, and reverting discards a possible genuine gain.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for "options" and receives three variations on a single approach rather than genuinely different approaches.
options: Say the options must differ in approach, not only in their detail
Ask for considerably more options to be generated in the response
Ask Claude to make the three options rather more distinct from each other
Provide one example of a genuinely different approach to follow
questions.why: Without a stated axis of variation, "options" is satisfied by variations on one theme. Naming approach as the axis produces genuine alternatives.
questions.traps: More options resamples the same theme, a distinctness instruction is vague about the dimension, and one example anchors rather than broadens.

questions.stem: An associate gives Claude a role and the answers become more confident than the evidence allows.
options: Keep the role and add an instruction to be cautious
Keep the role but give it a rather more junior title
Keep the role, since it improves the answer's framing
Drop the role, since it is adding tone rather than knowledge
questions.why: A role shapes register, and a senior-sounding one can produce assurance the underlying answer does not actually support.
questions.traps: A caution instruction fights the role rather than removing it, a junior title is the same mechanism dialled down, and better framing is not better grounding.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for a structured summary and it is correct except that dates use three different formats across the document.
options: Ask for the dates to be kept consistent throughout the whole document
Convert every one of the dates to plain text before they are used
State the date format explicitly and check inside the tables
Generate the tables separately with their own formatting rule
questions.why: Local conventions inside structured elements are a known drift point, so an explicit format plus a targeted check where drift concentrates works.
questions.traps: A general consistency instruction has already implicitly failed, text conversion fights the model, and separate generation adds steps for a formatting detail.

questions.stem: A team's prompt has eight examples, and removing four of them makes no measurable difference to the accuracy of the results.
options: Keep the four, since the others cost tokens without earning their place
Restore all eight of them, since more examples are generally safer
Remove four more of them and keep testing further downward
Keep all eight but move them into the project configuration
questions.why: If removing examples does not change accuracy, they were not contributing. Keeping the smaller set is the measured conclusion rather than a guess.
questions.traps: Restoring them ignores the measurement, removing further without testing risks the plateau, and relocating them reduces cost without answering whether they help.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to review a document for five separate concerns at once, and the most serious concern gets a single sentence.
options: Ask for a considerably longer combined review of all five concerns
Run the serious concern as its own review
List the five concerns in priority order within the prompt itself
Ask Claude to weight the most serious concern more heavily than others
questions.why: Combined reviews split attention roughly evenly regardless of stakes. A dedicated pass gives a serious concern the depth it warrants.
questions.traps: Length raises the floor for all five, and ordering or weighting instructions nudge allocation inside a single pass without changing that it is shared.

questions.stem: A team asks for a plan with no external dependencies and it complies while taking twice as long, and the constraint was a preference.
options: State the dependency constraint rather more softly than at present
Ask for two plans, one with the constraint and one without it
Distinguish hard requirements from preferences in the prompt
Remove the constraint and rely on review to catch problems
questions.why: Everything stated as a constraint is treated as binding. Labelling the softer ones lets a plan spend a preference to buy something more valuable.
questions.traps: Softer phrasing is still undifferentiated, two plans is a workable fallback at double the cost, and removing it loses the signal entirely.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a report and asks for its recommendations, and the summary omits the conditions attached to each of them.
options: Ask for a considerably longer summary of the recommendations given
Ask for the supporting evidence for each recommendation as well
Read the recommendations section directly rather than summarising
Ask for the conditions attached to each recommendation to be preserved
questions.why: Conditions are the qualifying material that compression removes first, and they often determine whether a recommendation applies at all.
questions.traps: Length helps without targeting the category, supporting evidence is a different attachment, and reading it yourself forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: A team likes a draft, asks for one small change, and gets a version where two unrelated paragraphs have also been rewritten.
options: Ask for a considerably more conservative revision of the document
Mark the rest as fixed and name only the span that may change
Ask Claude to list everything that it changed in the document
Ask for the change to be supplied as a separate snippet
questions.why: Scope has to be marked or everything is in scope. Declaring the fixed text protects it while keeping the whole document available as context.
questions.traps: Conservatism is a degree rather than a boundary, a change list arrives after the edit, and a detached snippet loses the surrounding context.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify "any issues" with a supplier proposal and gets commercial points while the delivery risk goes unmentioned.
options: Ask for a considerably longer list of issues with the proposal
Ask for the issues to be ranked in order of their severity
Ask about the specific concern and what would most undermine delivery
Provide the supplier's past delivery record as background
questions.why: An open request returns a shallow sweep weighted to the most commonly discussed dimension. Naming the concern is what redirects it.
questions.traps: Length and ranking both operate on a list generated against the wrong emphasis, and a delivery record deepens one input without redirecting the question.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to draft a response to a complaint, supplying only the complaint, and the draft concedes a point the company disputes.
options: Ask for a considerably more neutral response to be drafted
Ask Claude to identify the disputed points before it drafts
Review each of the drafts and remove concessions found
Supply the company's position on the disputed points first
questions.why: The complaint is one side's account. Without the company's position the model treats every claim as established, and a responsive reply concedes them.
questions.traps: Neutrality avoids the positions you want to state, identifying disputes without your position is guesswork, and review is a net rather than an input.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to write a report and check its own figures in the same request, and the check confirms the figures it produced.
options: Separate drafting from checking so verification is independent
Ask for the checking step to be carried out considerably more rigorously
Ask Claude to show all of its calculations within the response
Ask for the figures to be checked before the report is drafted
questions.why: A check inside the same pass validates the model's own reasoning against itself, and independence is the property that makes verification meaningful.
questions.traps: Rigour instructions do not create independence, shown working helps a human reviewer, and reordering still leaves both steps inside one generation.

questions.stem: An associate is brainstorming options and keeps getting three polished recommendations instead.
options: Ask for more detail on each of the three it produced
Say that the task is divergent rather than a decision
Ask for breadth first and narrow down afterwards
Accept the three, since they are well reasoned options
Ask the same question again with more emphasis on ideas
questions.why: Brainstorming wants range before judgement, so the fix is to say the task is divergent and ask for breadth before any narrowing happens.
questions.traps: Emphasis does not change the task type, accepting three loses the breadth entirely, and more detail deepens a convergent answer rather than widening it.

questions.stem: An associate is drafting a document and an analysis prompt style is producing the wrong shape of output.
options: Drafting wants a voice, an audience and a format
Drafting always needs more context than analysis does
The two task types call for the same prompt structure
Analysis wants criteria and evidence rather than voice
Analysis is simply a more difficult form of drafting
questions.why: Different task types need different things stated: a draft needs audience and register, an analysis needs criteria and evidence.
questions.traps: The two are not interchangeable, context volume is not the distinction, and neither one is a harder version of the other.

questions.stem: A team is using Claude for research and wants prompts that suit that task type specifically.
options: Ask for a confident conclusion rather than caveats
State what would count as a sufficient answer
Say what question the research has to actually answer
Ask for the most comprehensive answer possible
Ask for sources to be named against each claim
questions.why: Research prompts need a question, traceable sources and a stopping condition, because those are what make the result both checkable and finite.
questions.traps: Comprehensiveness without a question produces volume, and demanding confidence suppresses the uncertainty that research is supposed to surface.

questions.stem: An associate uses one prompt template for analysis, drafting and brainstorming alike.
options: Lengthen it until it covers all three task types
Adapt the structure to what each task type needs
Keep it, since one template is easier to maintain
Expect it to serve one of the three well at best
Use it for analysis only, since that is the hardest
questions.why: A single template encodes one task's requirements, so it will fit one type and quietly misfit the others, which is why the structure has to follow the task.
questions.traps: Maintenance convenience is bought with output quality, a longer template dilutes every case, and difficulty is not what distinguishes the types.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt says to "keep it brief" and the answers now omit things the team needs.
options: Replace the vague direction with a concrete one
Add emphasis so the instruction is taken seriously
Accept the omissions as the cost of being brief
Ask for brevity twice so the point is not missed
Say what every answer must always include in it
questions.why: A minimising instruction with nothing to protect will cut whatever it likes, so naming the required content gives it something it must keep.
questions.traps: Emphasis and repetition restate the same vague direction, and accepting omissions gives up the content the team actually needs.

questions.stem: A prompt tells the model several things not to do and the output still does one of them.
options: Make the prohibitions considerably more forceful
A prohibition leaves the alternative unspecified
Remove them, since prohibitions never work at all
Repeat the prohibitions at the end of the prompt
State what to do instead of each prohibition given
questions.why: Negative instructions describe a space to avoid without naming a target, so replacing them with positive directions gives the model something to aim at.
questions.traps: Repetition and force restate the same negative, and abandoning prohibitions entirely overstates the point.

questions.stem: A team wants an answer bounded to a specific scope and keeps getting broader ones.
options: Ask for a shorter answer so that less can stray
Say what is out of scope as well as what is in
State the boundary explicitly in the prompt itself
Keep asking until a suitably narrow answer arrives
Accept the breadth and edit it down afterwards
questions.why: A scope that is not stated is inferred, so naming both what is included and what is excluded is what makes the boundary hold.
questions.traps: Length is not scope, repeated asking relies on chance, and editing afterwards repeats the work every time.

questions.stem: A team's prompt has accumulated constraints over months and the output has become rigid.
options: Accept the rigidity as the price of reliability
Remove the oldest ones, since they are least relevant
Keep them all, since each was added for a reason
Check which constraints still prevent a real failure
Remove the ones no observed failure depends on
questions.why: Constraints accumulate against failures that may no longer occur, so the test is which ones still earn their cost rather than how old they are.
questions.traps: Historic justification is not current need, age is not a measure of usefulness, and accepting rigidity forgoes a fixable problem.

questions.stem: An associate gives Claude a senior role and the answers become more assured than the evidence supports.
options: Give it a more junior role to lower the confidence
Keep it, since the framing improves readability
Keep it and add an instruction to be more cautious
Drop the role if it is adding confidence, not accuracy
A role shapes register rather than actual knowledge
questions.why: A role changes tone without changing what is known, so an unearned confidence is a reason to remove it rather than to counterbalance it.
questions.traps: A caution instruction fights the role instead of removing it, a junior title is the same mechanism dialled down, and readability is not the issue.

questions.stem: A team wants answers grounded in a document rather than in general knowledge.
options: Supply the document alongside the question itself
Ask the model to recall what the document says
Name the document and expect it to be found somehow
Assume general knowledge will be close enough
Say that the answer must come from that document
questions.why: Grounding requires both the text being present and an instruction that the answer must come from it, since either one alone leaves the model free to fall back.
questions.traps: Naming a document does not supply it, recall is not access, and general knowledge is exactly what grounding is meant to exclude.

questions.stem: An associate's grounded prompt produces an answer citing something the document does not contain.
options: Ask the model to point at the relevant passage again
Check whether the document was read as expected
Accept it, since the rest of the answer is accurate
Assume the model paraphrased it somewhat loosely
Treat the claim as ungrounded until it is located
questions.why: A claim that is not in the source is either a reading failure or a fabrication, so the document itself is what settles which before anything is relied on.
questions.traps: Assuming a loose paraphrase is charitable rather than evidenced, asking again produces another output, and partial accuracy does not license the rest.

questions.stem: A prompt's examples all share an incidental feature and outputs keep reproducing it.
options: Add more examples sharing that very same feature
Instruct the model not to copy that one feature
Reduce the number of examples down to just one
Vary the incidental feature across the examples
Examples teach whatever stays constant across them
questions.why: Examples transmit whatever is invariant among them, so varying the incidental property is what stops it being learned as the pattern.
questions.traps: An instruction fights the pattern instead of removing it, one example weakens the signal entirely, and more of the same reinforces it.

questions.stem: A team's examples show only easy cases and the model handles hard ones the same shallow way.
options: Examples set the expected depth as well as the format
Describe the hard cases in words instead of showing them
Add more easy examples to strengthen the pattern
Add an example of a genuinely difficult case too
Remove the examples, since they are unrepresentative
questions.why: Examples communicate how much effort a task deserves, so a worked hard case is what shows the treatment those inputs need.
questions.traps: A description is weaker than a demonstration, removing them loses the format guidance, and more easy cases reinforce the wrong depth.

questions.stem: An associate tweaks a prompt's wording, its examples and its format in a single edit.
options: Change one thing at a time to keep cause visible
Keep all three and adjust until it improves again
Undo the changes and reapply them one at a time
Revert everything and go back to the original
Ask the model which of the changes hurt the output
questions.why: Simultaneous changes make the cause unrecoverable, so reapplying them singly is what identifies which one did the damage.
questions.traps: A full revert loses whatever improved, blind adjustment compounds the confusion, and the model cannot see the prompt's history.

questions.stem: A team's prompt has plateaued and further rounds of refinement move it by under a point.
options: Look at the inputs and the task definition instead
Accept the plateau without investigating the cause
Keep refining, since improvement always continues
Rewrite the prompt completely from scratch again
Consider whether the limit is the prompt at all
questions.why: A plateau usually means the binding constraint has moved elsewhere, so the next place to look is the inputs and how the task is framed.
questions.traps: Endless refinement ignores diminishing returns, accepting it skips the diagnosis, and a rewrite re-tries the same variable.

questions.stem: A team needs output in a fixed structure that downstream work depends on.
options: Specify the structure explicitly in the prompt
Check each output against the structure required
Accept small structural variation between the runs
Ask for a consistent structure without defining it
Reformat every output by hand after it arrives
questions.why: A structure that something downstream depends on has to be both specified and verified, because generation varies between runs however carefully it is asked.
questions.traps: Asking for consistency does not say consistent with what, hand-reformatting repeats forever, and variation is exactly what breaks the downstream step.

questions.stem: An associate describes a desired format in three paragraphs and still gets the wrong shape.
options: Show the format as a small worked example instead
Describe the format in even greater detail again
Repeat the description at the end of the prompt
A format is easier to demonstrate than to describe
Accept the shape and reformat it all afterwards
questions.why: Format is a structural property that a short example conveys directly, where prose description leaves room for interpretation.
questions.traps: More description restates the same ambiguity, repetition lengthens the prompt, and reformatting repeats the work each time.

questions.stem: A prompt asks for four things in one paragraph and only the first is done properly.
options: Repeat the later parts at the end of the prompt
Send the four requests as four separate prompts
Multi-part tasks lose their later parts in prose
Write the paragraph in a much more forceful tone
Break the request into explicitly numbered steps
questions.why: Requests buried in prose lose their tail, and numbering makes each part a visible requirement rather than a clause.
questions.traps: Repetition lengthens without structuring, tone does not create structure, and four separate prompts lose the connection between the parts.

questions.stem: A team must decide whether to split a task into steps or keep it as one request.
options: Always split, since smaller steps are more reliable
Never split, since fewer steps means fewer failures
Split it where the parts fail for different reasons
Splitting lets each part be diagnosed on its own
Split it by length rather than by what each part does
questions.why: Decomposition pays where the parts have different failure modes, because that is what makes each one separately fixable.
questions.traps: Absolute rules in either direction ignore the task, and splitting by length divides the text rather than the work.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a summary and three specific answers in one request and the answers come back thin.
options: Ask the same question with more emphasis on detail
One request makes the parts compete for attention
Ask for the specific answers as their own request
Ask for a longer response covering everything
Accept the summary and work out the answers yourself
questions.why: Combining a broad task with specific ones makes them compete, and separating them gives each the attention it needs.
questions.traps: Length and emphasis do not resolve the competition, and doing the work yourself abandons what was delegated.

questions.stem: An associate receives a market summary from Claude citing a named consultancy's 2025 forecast with a specific growth percentage. The figure fits their expectations and the report is due in an hour.
options: Ask Claude whether it is confident the figure is accurate before including it
