questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to identify what could delay a project. The answer covers internal delays thoroughly and does not mention supplier lead times.
options: Ask for more delay factors so external ones eventually appear
Ask about dependencies on external parties as a named category of delay
Ask Claude whether external factors could also cause delays
Review the answer against the project's dependency list
questions.why: Delay analysis defaults to what the team controls. Naming external dependencies is what brings supplier and third-party timing into the assessment.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same default. A yes-or-no follow-up produces agreement without analysis, and dependency-list review arrives after the omission.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to rate how difficult it found a task. It reports the task was straightforward, and the output contains a significant error.
options: Accept the output, since the model found the task within its capability
Ask Claude to attempt the task again more carefully given the error found
Ask Claude to rate difficulty before each task and review the hard ones
Treat difficulty self-reports as uninformative about accuracy on that task
questions.why: Reported difficulty does not track where errors occur, because the errors the model makes are the ones it does not experience as difficult.
questions.traps: Reading ease as reliability is the trap. Retrying and difficulty-based routing both depend on a signal that does not correlate with accuracy.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for a summary of recent developments in a fast-moving area. The summary is coherent and describes developments the associate has not heard of.
options: Accept the summary, since the associate is not close enough to the area to judge it
Ask Claude for dates and sources for each development mentioned
Verify each of the developments individually before repeating them
Treat the summary as a starting point and read around the topic generally
questions.why: Unfamiliar specifics in a fast-moving area are exactly where fabrication is undetectable by the reader. Each development is a checkable factual claim.
questions.traps: Deferring to the model because you cannot judge inverts the caution. Requested dates and sources may be generated, and general reading does not confirm the specific claims.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output meets its quality bar but users have stopped reading it because it is longer than what it replaced.
options: Treat actual readership as part of quality, since unread output fails
Keep the current standard, since the output meets the defined quality bar
Ask users to read the output more carefully than they currently do
Reduce the length and accept a lower score against the quality bar
questions.why: An artefact that is not read has failed regardless of its internal quality. Incorporating actual use into the standard is what corrects a bar measuring the wrong thing.
questions.traps: Meeting a bar nobody benefits from is the failure. Asking users to change is not a fix, and cutting length without revising the bar treats a good change as a compromise.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude a question and it gives an answer while noting it is drawing on general knowledge rather than the uploaded documents.
options: Accept the answer, since the model was transparent about where it came from
Treat that as a useful signal and verify the answer against an appropriate source
Ask Claude to answer again using only the uploaded documents
Ask Claude to indicate how confident it is in the general knowledge answer
questions.why: Transparency about the basis is genuinely helpful and tells you which verification applies. It identifies the answer as unsourced rather than establishing it as correct.
questions.traps: Transparency is not verification. Re-asking within the documents may produce nothing, and confidence adds an unreliable second signal.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output goes through three review steps. Each reviewer assumes the others are checking accuracy, and none of them is.
options: Assign each of the checks to a single named step in the process
Ask all three reviewers to check accuracy as well as their own area
Add a fourth review step dedicated specifically to accuracy
Ask reviewers to confirm what they checked after each review
questions.why: Diffusion of responsibility across multiple reviewers is a recognised failure of layered controls. Explicit assignment is what closes it without adding steps.
questions.traps: Asking everyone to check everything recreates the diffusion. A fourth step adds cost, and after-the-fact confirmation records the gap rather than preventing it.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to assess whether a project should continue, mentioning that significant money has already been spent on it.
options: Accept the assessment, since past spending is relevant context for the decision
Ask Claude to weigh the sunk investment against the cost of stopping now
Ask for the assessment both with and without the spending mentioned
Ask whether the remaining investment is justified by the future benefit
questions.why: Money already spent is unrecoverable and should not affect a forward-looking decision. Framing the question around remaining cost and benefit is what keeps the sunk cost out of the reasoning.
questions.traps: Supplying prior spend invites it to be weighed, which is the fallacy. Explicitly weighing it is worse, and paired assessments leave you choosing between a biased and an unbiased answer.

questions.stem: An associate is verifying a Claude claim and finds a source that appears authoritative. The source is a page that aggregates content from elsewhere without attribution.
options: Accept the source, since the page presents the information authoritatively
Look for a second aggregator page that carries the same claim
Trace the claim back to an attributable original before using it
Cite the aggregator, since it is a stable and locatable web source
questions.why: An unattributed aggregator has no accountable origin and may itself be reproducing an error or generated content. Verification requires a source that can be held to the claim.
questions.traps: Authoritative presentation is a design choice, not provenance. A second aggregator may draw on the first, and citing one passes the problem to your reader.

questions.stem: An associate receives a Claude-drafted briefing containing a named statistic attributed to a government body, and the figure supports the case they were already making.
options: Ask Claude whether it is confident that the statistic is accurate as given
Locate the body's own publication and confirm the figure before it is used
Use the figure with a note saying it is approximate and subject to check
Look for a news article that reports a broadly similar figure instead
questions.why: Named source plus precise number is the shape a fabricated citation takes, and agreement with your existing view removes the friction that would prompt a check.
questions.traps: Self-reported confidence tracks fluency rather than truth, an approximate label still publishes the number, and a secondary article validates a different claim.

questions.stem: A team is checking a Claude-generated compliance summary and finds the first three claims accurate, with fourteen unchecked and a deadline in an hour.
options: Continue checking in document order until the hour runs out completely
Accept the summary, since the first three claims were all found accurate
Ask Claude to identify which of the remaining claims are most uncertain
Check the claims the decision actually rests on rather than continuing in order
questions.why: Under time pressure verification is risk management, so effort follows consequence. Checking in order spends the hour on whatever happened to come first.
questions.traps: Positional order is unrelated to importance, three clean checks say little about fourteen, and model-flagged uncertainty misses the confident errors.

questions.stem: An associate notices Claude has cited a British Standard by number in a technical note, and the number looks plausible for that subject area.
options: Accept it, since the number follows the correct format for that series
Ask Claude to confirm the standard number is current and still in force
Verify the standard number against the issuing body's own catalogue
Ask a colleague whether they recognise the standard being referenced
questions.why: Standard numbers are exactly the specific, checkable detail that generation constructs plausibly. Format correctness is what makes a fabricated one convincing.
questions.traps: Format is generated, self-confirmation is not independent, and colleague recognition is weak evidence about a specific identifier.

questions.stem: A team spot-checks six figures in a twenty-figure Claude analysis, finds all six correct, and concludes the analysis is sound.
options: Recognise six clean samples bound nothing about the other fourteen figures
Conclude the analysis is reliable, since a thirty percent sample was clean
Check six more figures and accept the analysis if those are clean too
Ask Claude to confirm the remaining fourteen figures are accurate
questions.why: A clean sample raises confidence slightly and bounds nothing. Recognising the limit of the inference is what keeps verification calibrated to evidence.
questions.traps: A thirty percent clean sample is weak evidence about the remainder, doubling it helps marginally, and model self-confirmation is not independent.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to grade its own analysis out of ten. It gives itself an eight and lists two weaknesses, both of which are real but minor.
options: Accept the two weaknesses as the complete set of issues with the analysis
Ask Claude to keep listing weaknesses until the serious one is identified
Treat the list as a starting point and review independently for what it missed
Ask Claude to grade the analysis again and see whether the score is stable
questions.why: Self-assessment surfaces the issues a model can see, which excludes its own blind spots by definition. It is a prompt for review, not a substitute.
questions.traps: Treating the list as complete is the error, iterating mines the same partial view, and score stability measures consistency rather than coverage.

questions.stem: Two reviewers disagree about whether a Claude-drafted policy note is fit to circulate, and both have read it carefully.
options: Agree what the note must achieve for its readers, then judge against that
Ask a third reviewer to read it and settle the matter by majority view
Ask Claude to assess the note's quality and use that as the tiebreaker
Circulate it with a request that readers flag anything unclear or wrong
questions.why: Disagreement about quality usually means the standard was never stated. Defining what the artefact must accomplish makes it a checkable question.
questions.traps: A third opinion adds a vote without a standard, model self-assessment is not independent, and circulating pushes the judgement onto readers.

questions.stem: An associate receives a Claude analysis of a supplier's financial position that is accurate throughout and never mentions the pending litigation.
options: Ask Claude whether it left anything important out of the analysis given
Check the output against what you know should be covered
Ask for a longer analysis so more relevant material gets included in it
Accept it, since everything the analysis does contain has been verified
questions.why: An omission leaves no mark in the text, so it can only be found by comparison against an external expectation. Verifying what is present says nothing about what is absent.
questions.traps: Asking the model about its own gaps assumes it knows them, length does not target the missing item, and accuracy of present content is a different property.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude summary table where each row is correct and the total at the foot does not equal the sum of the rows.
options: Ask Claude to recalculate the total and use whatever it returns
Ask Claude to show its working so the discrepancy can be traced
Accept the row figures and delete the total from the table entirely
Recompute the total yourself, since derived figures are generated as text
questions.why: Totals and other derived numbers are produced as text rather than computed, so they need an independent check that takes seconds and is conclusive.
questions.traps: Recalculation by the same means can repeat the error, shown working still needs checking, and deleting the total loses information the table should carry.

questions.stem: A team receives an analysis where one section reads as settled consensus, and nobody can tell whether it came from the uploaded reports or elsewhere.
options: Ask which claims came from the supplied reports and which did not
Ask Claude to add citations to the analysis that has already been written
Assume the claims came from the reports, since those were provided
Ask for the whole analysis again with an instruction to cite throughout
questions.why: Blended output is the default when documents are supplied alongside a model's own knowledge. Asking for the split makes the boundary visible and checkable.
questions.traps: Retrofitted citations may be attached to claims that did not come from the sources, assuming provenance is the error, and a rerun discards the analysis you have.

questions.stem: A team publishes Claude-drafted material after a copy-edit, and two factual errors have reached customers over three months, both well written.
options: Ask the copy-editor to read the drafted material considerably more carefully
Ask Claude to fact-check its own drafts before they reach the copy-editor
Reduce the volume of drafted material so each piece can be read slowly
Add a factual review step, since copy-editing checks prose rather than claims
questions.why: Copy-editing and fact-checking are different activities with different inputs. A well-written false statement passes a copy-edit by design.
questions.traps: Care does not supply the sources a copy-editor was never given, self-checking is not independent, and slowing down does not change what is being checked.

questions.stem: An associate describes a colleague's plan critically and then asks Claude to assess it.
options: Accept the assessment, since the criticisms were fair
Describe the plan neutrally and then ask again
Ask for the plan's strengths as a follow-up question
Have the colleague describe their own plan instead
questions.why: A critical description sets up a critical assessment, and a neutral description is what lets the plan be judged on its merits.
questions.traps: Fair criticisms in the prompt still frame the answer, a follow-up patches one output, and having the author describe it introduces the opposite tilt.

questions.stem: A team's literature review from Claude cites eleven sources. Nine are real and correctly described; two have real authors, real journals and titles that do not exist.
options: Verify the two that seem least familiar and accept the remaining nine
Ask Claude which of its citations it is least confident about first
Verify every citation individually, since a mostly-correct list is hardest to audit
Note that the review is largely accurate and flag it for later checking
questions.why: Fabricated citations are built from real components, so nothing distinguishes them at a glance. That is exactly why the check has to be exhaustive.
questions.traps: Familiarity is not a reliable filter, self-identified uncertainty misses confident fabrications, and deferring means publishing unverified claims.

questions.stem: An associate needs to confirm a regulatory deadline and Claude states it clearly, while a colleague recalls a different figure without certainty.
options: Ask Claude again in a fresh conversation and see whether it repeats itself
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning for the deadline that it gave
Go with Claude's figure, since a specific number implies a specific source
Check the regulation text, since two recollections do not settle a fact
questions.why: Two unreliable recollections do not average into a fact. The regulation is the authority and consulting it is faster than reasoning about which memory to trust.
questions.traps: Repetition tests consistency and a model can be consistently wrong, explanations rationalise the stated number, and specificity is not evidence of provenance.

questions.stem: A team compares two prompts by running each once on the same input, sees a clear difference, and adopts the better-looking one.
options: Run both several times, since one pair cannot separate prompt from variation
Adopt it, since a clearly better output on identical input is convincing
Run the winning prompt again to confirm the quality is reproducible
Ask Claude to compare the two prompts and say which should perform better
questions.why: Output varies run to run, so a single comparison can be decided entirely by that variation. Multiple runs are what distinguish a real difference from noise.
questions.traps: A clear single win is exactly what noise produces sometimes, re-running one arm tests its stability only, and model opinion is not output evidence.

questions.stem: A team judges Claude's output by how polished it reads, and three polished pieces have since turned out to contain significant errors.
options: Ask Claude to write in a plainer style so polish stops influencing judgement
Introduce a minimum length rule so short polished pieces are scrutinised
Separate the fluency of the writing from the accuracy of its claims
Ask Claude to flag its own factual claims so they are easier to spot
questions.why: Fluency is the property a language model optimises most directly and is uncorrelated with truth. Separating the two axes stops polish standing in for correctness.
questions.traps: Plainer prose does not make claims true, length rules measure the wrong thing, and self-flagging depends on the model recognising its own errors.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for the risks in an outsourcing plan and gets a thorough list covering cost and operations, with nothing on reputational exposure.
options: Ask for considerably more risks so that reputational ones eventually appear
Ask about specific risk categories by name rather than for risks in general
Ask Claude whether it has considered every category of risk that applies
Rank the risks and investigate whichever category is least represented
questions.why: An open request returns the categories most represented in ordinary discussion. Naming the categories guarantees each one gets considered.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same distribution, a self-check on coverage is unreliable, and ranking works on a list that already omits the category.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to convert a set of costs between currencies, and the conversions are internally consistent using an unstated rate.
options: Supply the rate you want used, since an unstated one makes every figure unverifiable
Ask Claude which exchange rate it applied and record that alongside
Ask Claude to use the current exchange rate for all the conversions
Convert the figures yourself, since the arithmetic is straightforward
questions.why: Conversion is only meaningful relative to a stated rate. Supplying it makes every output figure reproducible and puts the rate choice where it belongs.
questions.traps: Asking afterwards may get an invented rate, requesting the current rate assumes live data access, and doing it manually forfeits the task unnecessarily.

questions.stem: A team routes every Claude output to the same reviewer, who is a strong writer with no background in the subject matter being reviewed.
options: Give the reviewer more time so they can research the technical claims
Ask Claude to explain the technical claims so the reviewer can follow
Reduce the technical content so the existing reviewer can assess it all
Match the reviewer to what actually needs checking in each case
questions.why: Review is only as good as the reviewer's ability to detect the relevant errors. Matching expertise to content makes the step a control rather than a formality.
questions.traps: Research time does not create domain expertise, model explanations of its own claims are not independent, and stripping technical content damages the work.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to confirm it used only the documents provided and it says it did.
options: Accept it, since the question it answered was factual
Accept it, since the model has the documents in view
Check the claims against the documents yourself
Ask it to confirm a second time to be certain
questions.why: A self-report about sourcing comes from the same process as the output, so only a comparison against the documents settles it.
questions.traps: Factual phrasing does not make a self-report reliable, having documents available does not mean they were used, and a repeat is another self-report.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to evaluate two suppliers, and the evaluation is structurally balanced while describing the better-known supplier's weaknesses more gently.
options: Ask for a considerably more critical evaluation of the better-known one
Apply the same specific criteria to both and compare the assessments
Ask Claude to evaluate them without being told which is better known
Run the evaluation twice with the supplier order reversed and compare
questions.why: Asymmetric treatment is corrected by imposing symmetric criteria. The same checklist applied to both makes any remaining difference attributable to the suppliers.
questions.traps: Extra criticism of one side overcorrects, withholding identity is impractical, and order reversal detects the asymmetry without fixing the evaluation.

questions.stem: An associate checks a Claude-generated figure by asking the same question in a second conversation, and receives the same figure.
options: Recognise that two runs of the same model are not independent sources
Accept the figure, since it was confirmed by a separate check
Run a third conversation and accept it if all three now agree
Ask Claude in the second conversation to be especially careful
questions.why: Independence is the property that makes corroboration meaningful, and two runs of the same model share the same tendencies. Agreement between them is close to no evidence.
questions.traps: Treating a second run as independent is the core error, a third run compounds it, and instructions about care do not create independence.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude about a niche accounting treatment and receives a detailed, confident answer that nobody on the team can assess.
options: Accept it, since the level of detail indicates real familiarity with the topic
Ask Claude how well documented the treatment is before relying on it
Treat confidence as uninformative on obscure topics and verify against the standard
Ask the question again and compare the two answers for consistency
questions.why: Fluency does not degrade gracefully on thin topics, so a confident detailed answer about something obscure is exactly where verification matters most.
questions.traps: Detail is generated rather than evidence of familiarity, self-assessment of coverage is unreliable, and consistency between runs is not accuracy.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise the findings of an internal review, and the summary covers the significant findings while omitting the areas found satisfactory.
options: Ask for a longer summary so more of the review's content survives
Ask Claude whether the review found anything that was satisfactory
Read the findings section directly rather than relying on a summary
Ask for the negative and null findings specifically
questions.why: Absence of a problem is a finding that summarisation systematically drops as uninformative. Asking for it explicitly brings it into scope.
questions.traps: Length does not restore a category treated as non-content, a yes-or-no follow-up may be answered from the same compressed view, and reading it yourself forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude forecast quoted to two decimal places, built from inputs the team had rounded to the nearest hundred thousand.
options: Keep the decimals, since more precise figures are more useful for planning
Round the output to reflect the precision of the inputs it came from
Ask Claude to recalculate using more precise inputs where available
Present the figures with a note explaining they rest on estimates
questions.why: Precision in an output cannot exceed the precision of its inputs. Two decimals from rounded hundreds of thousands communicates confidence the numbers do not support.
questions.traps: Spurious precision misleads regardless of usefulness, better inputs would change the analysis, and a caveat does not undo the visual claim the decimals make.

questions.stem: An associate's slide credits a chart to internal analysis and that analysis was Claude's.
options: Credit it to internal analysis, since the team ran it
Credit it to Claude, since Claude produced the chart
Remove the credit line from the slide entirely
Name the data that the analysis was performed on
questions.why: A credit tells a reader what the chart rests on, and the underlying data is what they would need in order to check it.
questions.traps: "Internal analysis" hides the basis, naming the tool describes production rather than evidence, and removing the line leaves the chart unsourced.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers record that they checked an item without recording what they found.
options: Record what was checked and what was actually found
Record only the items that failed the review step
Record the time that each review took to complete
Accept it, since the approval itself is the record
questions.why: A review log is useful when it shows what the review is catching, which is what tells you whether the step is working at all.
questions.traps: Failures alone hide how much was examined, duration measures effort rather than findings, and an approval records a verdict without its basis.

questions.stem: A team defines good output as output needing no edits, and an associate accepts a thinner summary because it required no changes.
options: Keep the rule and add a minimum length requirement alongside it
Measure editing time instead of counting the number of edits made
Define quality by fitness for purpose rather than by editing effort saved
Ask reviewers to record why they edited so the rule can be refined
questions.why: Edit count measures convenience rather than value, and optimising it selects for output that is easy to accept rather than useful.
questions.traps: A length floor patches one symptom, editing time is the same proxy in different units, and logging reasons improves a metric measuring the wrong thing.

questions.stem: An associate tests a new prompt on the four examples they have to hand, all four work, and they roll it out to the team.
options: Roll it out and rely on colleagues to report problems as they hit them
Gather harder and more varied cases before rolling it out to anyone
Test the same four examples several times each to confirm stability
Roll out to a small group first and expand if nothing is reported
questions.why: Four cases cannot represent the variety a team encounters. Building a varied test set before rollout is what surfaces failures before other people meet them.
questions.traps: Relying on reports discovers failures through users, repeating the same tests measures stability rather than coverage, and a staged rollout still ships an undertested prompt.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise arguments for and against a merger, and the against section is shorter, which the team reads as the case being weaker.
options: Recognise that section length reflects how arguments were expressed
Accept the reading, since a balanced summary would produce equal sections
Ask for both sections to be rewritten at equal length and compare again
Ask Claude to state which side it considers stronger and explain why
questions.why: Length in a summary tracks the volume and articulacy of the source material rather than the merit of a position. Reading it as strength imports an artefact of the writing.
questions.traps: Assuming balance means equal length inverts the relationship, equalising length is cosmetic, and asking for a verdict substitutes the model's judgement for yours.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude how confident it is in six claims. It reports high confidence in five, and one of those five turns out to be wrong.
options: Verify only the claim flagged as less confident by the model
Treat stated confidence as weakly informative and verify by consequence
Ask for numerical confidence scores so the ranking becomes finer
Ask Claude to explain the basis for each confidence assessment given
questions.why: Self-reported confidence correlates loosely with accuracy and cannot direct verification. Consequence is the better guide to where checking time goes.
questions.traps: Trusting the flags is what failed here, numerical scores add precision to an unreliable signal, and explanations rationalise the assessment.

questions.stem: A team finds Claude has described a feature of their own procurement system that does not exist, in an otherwise accurate process note.
options: Ask Claude where it obtained its information about the internal system
Correct the note and ask Claude to remember the actual process
Recognise the model has no access to internal systems and is describing a typical one
Assume the description matches an earlier version of the system
questions.why: Questions about private internal facts have no source in what the model can draw on, so the answer is a plausible generic construction.
questions.traps: Asking for a source invites invention, assuming an old version rationalises a fabrication, and a correction addresses one instance.

questions.stem: An associate has ten claims to verify, time for three, and the claims vary in how much of the argument rests on them.
options: Verify the first three claims, since early claims often set up later ones
Verify the three claims that seem least plausible on their face
Verify three claims chosen at random to get an unbiased sample
Verify the claims the conclusion depends on, since effort follows consequence
questions.why: Under a time constraint verification is risk management. Checking what carries the conclusion protects the most, which random or positional sampling does not.
questions.traps: Position is unrelated to importance, implausibility catches obvious errors but misses plausible ones, and randomness ignores stakes entirely.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to compute a compound figure over six years and cannot reproduce the result with a spreadsheet.
options: Trust the spreadsheet, since arithmetic done as text generation is unreliable
Ask Claude to recalculate and accept the figure if the second attempt agrees
Ask Claude to show the formula so the discrepancy can be located
Use the model's figure, since it may account for factors the sheet omits
questions.why: A deterministic calculation has one right answer and a spreadsheet produces it. Where the two disagree the arithmetic tool wins without further investigation.
questions.traps: Repetition can reproduce the same error, the formula is worth seeing for learning but does not change which result is correct, and there are no hidden factors here.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify the dependencies for a project, and the list covers technical dependencies while omitting the board approval required first.
options: Ask for a longer list so non-technical dependencies eventually appear
Ask about dependency types by name, including approvals and external parties
Ask Claude whether it has missed any dependencies from the plan
Review the list against the project charter to find what is missing
questions.why: Enumerating the categories stops a generic request returning only the most commonly discussed type. Approvals are the dependency people forget to ask about.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same skew, self-checking is unreliable, and charter review is good practice arriving after the omission.

questions.stem: A team's review is done at the end of the week on everything produced that week.
options: Keep the weekly review, since it is efficient to batch
Move the review to the start of the following week
Review closer to production, since errors travel
Accept it, since everything does eventually get reviewed
questions.why: Output that has already been sent cannot be corrected by a later review, so the timing determines whether the check protects anything.
questions.traps: Batching is efficient for the reviewer and not for the risk, moving it later is worse, and eventual review does not undo what has already left.

questions.stem: A team's briefing quotes a figure that appears in two uploaded documents with different values.
options: Use the figure from the longer of the two documents
Use whichever of the figures appears more often
Average the two figures and cite both documents
Say which of the documents the figure came from
questions.why: Two sources with different values means the citation has to name which one was used before the figure means anything at all.
questions.traps: Length and frequency are arbitrary tie-breaks, and averaging invents a figure that neither of the documents actually contains.

questions.stem: An associate has to decide whether a Claude-drafted email is ready to send and keeps rereading it, finding small improvements each time.
options: Keep refining until no further improvements can be identified at all
Judge it against whether it achieves its purpose for the reader and send it
Ask Claude to assess whether the email is ready to be sent out
Ask a colleague to read it and send once they have no suggestions
questions.why: Every draft admits further tweaks, so a purpose-based stopping rule is what prevents refinement running indefinitely. Fitness for purpose is a threshold rather than a maximum.
questions.traps: Refining to exhaustion has no endpoint, model self-assessment is not independent, and a colleague without the standard faces the same open-ended question.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise feedback from thirty customers, and the summary foregrounds the two most articulate complaints as though representative.
options: Ask for a longer summary so the less articulate feedback also appears
Ask Claude to weight all thirty of the responses equally in the summary
Ask how many customers raised each theme, so prominence reflects frequency
Read the individual responses rather than relying on any summary
questions.why: Articulacy translates into salience during summarisation. Requesting counts grounds emphasis in how many people said something rather than how well they said it.
questions.traps: Length does not rebalance emphasis, an equal-weighting instruction states a goal without a mechanism, and reading everything forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for examples of organisations that have adopted a practice. Four of six are real and correctly described; two exist but never did this.
options: Accept the examples, since all six organisations are real bodies
Ask Claude for a source for each of the six examples it gave
Use only the four examples the team already recognises as accurate
Verify each example against the organisation's own account of what it did
questions.why: Attributing a real practice to a real organisation is a factual claim about that organisation. The components being real is what makes the composite persuasive.
questions.traps: Existence of the organisation is not evidence about its actions, requested sources may be generated, and recognition is a weak filter.

questions.stem: An associate receives a Claude analysis where the ranking of five options by cost is right, and two of the underlying cost figures do not match the source.
options: Verify the figures separately from the ranking
Accept the ranking, since the ordering was what the analysis was needed for
Ask Claude to recheck the figures that were used to build the ranking
Present the ranking without showing the underlying cost figures at all
questions.why: Ordering and magnitude are different claims that can fail independently. A correct ranking is not evidence that the values behind it are right.
questions.traps: Accepting the ranking ignores that the figures will be quoted, self-rechecking is not independent, and hiding the figures conceals rather than corrects.

questions.stem: A team measures a prompt at 90% accuracy across twenty test cases and reports that as the accuracy to expect in production.
options: Report ninety percent, since it was measured on genuine test cases
Round the figure down to eighty-five percent to be conservative
Test twenty more cases and report the average of the two runs
Note that twenty cases give a wide margin and production inputs differ
questions.why: A small sample gives an imprecise estimate, and test cases are usually easier and less varied than production traffic. Both caveats matter to anyone acting on the number.
questions.traps: Reporting the point estimate hides both problems, rounding down is arbitrary, and a second small sample narrows the interval slightly without addressing the distribution difference.

questions.stem: A team's process asks Claude to rate each output's quality and routes anything below four out of five to a human, and errors still reach customers in fives.
options: Lower the threshold so outputs rated four also go to human review
Route by the consequence of the content rather than by the model's self-rating
Ask Claude to be considerably stricter when rating its own output
Add a second rating pass and route anything either pass rates low
questions.why: Self-rating cannot detect the errors the model is blind to, so no threshold on that scale catches them. Routing on stakes does not depend on the model's self-knowledge.
questions.traps: Every threshold-based fix assumes the rating carries signal about the errors that matter, and a second pass shares the same blind spot.

questions.stem: An associate checks a claim and the first three search results all cite the same original article.
options: Treat the agreement as strong confirmation of the claim
Look for a fourth result to strengthen the evidence
Treat the three as one source rather than as three
Accept the claim, since the original article exists
questions.why: Repetition of one source is not corroboration, so the count of results says nothing about how well supported the claim is.
questions.traps: Agreement among copies is not agreement among sources, a fourth copy adds nothing, and the original's existence is not its correctness.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to check a tender response against a scoring rubric, and it reports on every rubric item while missing a disqualifying omission outside it.
options: Recognise a rubric review is bounded by the rubric and run a separate open review
Ask Claude to check for problems generally as well as against the rubric
Expand the rubric so it covers the item that was missed this time
Ask Claude whether it noticed anything concerning beyond the rubric
questions.why: A rubric defines scope, and anything outside it is out of scope by construction. Knowing that limitation is what tells you a second, open-ended pass is needed.
questions.traps: A general instruction bolted onto a rubric review muddles both, expanding the rubric fixes one gap, and a follow-up question is weaker than a dedicated pass.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers see Claude output only after it has been formatted into the final template, and catch rate has fallen since that change.
options: Ask reviewers to read the formatted version considerably more carefully
Review before formatting, since polished presentation reduces scrutiny
Add a second review pass after the formatting has been applied
Format the drafts more plainly so they look less finished at review
questions.why: Finished-looking artefacts attract less scrutiny, so review is better placed before presentation is applied. This is a sequencing fix rather than an effort one.
questions.traps: Asking for more care fights a well-documented effect, a second pass costs more for the same bias, and degrading formatting is a workaround for the sequencing.

questions.stem: A team's standard for Claude output is that it must be at least as good as a capable junior would produce, and two reviewers disagree constantly.
options: Have both reviewers calibrate by reviewing the same junior's work
Lower the standard so borderline cases are more likely to be accepted
Have a junior produce a version for direct comparison each time
Replace the comparison with concrete checks the output must pass
questions.why: A comparative benchmark living in each reviewer's head is not a standard. Concrete checks are what make two reviewers reach the same verdict on the same artefact.
questions.traps: Calibration helps but leaves the standard implicit, lowering the bar dodges the disagreement, and parallel production defeats the point of drafting.

questions.stem: An associate asks which of two suppliers is better and names one of them first.
options: Accept the answer, since the named order is incidental
Ask for both suppliers to be assessed separately
Ask again with the order of the two names reversed
Ask a colleague to run the same comparison instead
questions.why: Order effects are real and cheap to test, and reversing the sequence is what shows whether the answer depended on it.
questions.traps: Assuming order is incidental is exactly what needs testing, separate assessments answer a different question, and a colleague running the same prompt reproduces the effect.

questions.stem: A team receives a percentage change from Claude and the base figure it was calculated from appears nowhere in the output.
options: Ask for the base figure, since a percentage change is uninterpretable without it
Accept the percentage, since the calculation was requested and performed
Ask Claude to recalculate and include considerably more detail this time
Compare the percentage against last quarter's figure for plausibility
questions.why: A relative figure without its base is not a number you can act on, and stating the base also makes the calculation checkable. Both problems are solved by asking for it.
questions.traps: Accepting it leaves the figure uninterpretable, a vaguer request for detail may not surface the base, and plausibility comparison does not supply it.

questions.stem: An associate reads a Claude answer containing a quotation attributed to a named regulator, and the quotation captures the regulator's known position closely.
options: Accept it, since it is consistent with the regulator's documented positions
Ask Claude for the date and venue of the quotation to establish provenance
Paraphrase the quotation so exact attribution matters less in the text
Treat the quotation as unverified until located in a primary source
questions.why: Quotations are generated to fit context, and fitting well is what makes a fabricated one persuasive. Only locating it in a source establishes that it was said.
questions.traps: Consistency with known views is what a plausible fabrication has, asking for date and venue invites more invented detail, and a paraphrase still attributes a position.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output cites a real report by name, and the specific page cited discusses an unrelated topic.
options: Accept it, since the report itself is real and relevant to the subject
Check citations at the page level, since a real document does not make a locator correct
Ask Claude to correct the page number in the citation it provided
Cite the report without a page number to avoid the specificity problem
questions.why: Document, page and content are separately checkable, and a correct document with a wrong locator is a common pattern. Verification has to reach the level of the claim.
questions.traps: A real document is not evidence about the page, self-correction is not independent, and removing the locator hides the problem rather than resolving it.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for lessons learned from a failed project, and every item on the thoughtful list concerns something the team did wrong.
options: Ask for more lessons so that the positive ones eventually appear
Ask Claude to balance the list between positive and negative lessons
Ask what went well too, since a lessons request is read as a request for problems
Accept the list, since lessons learned conventionally focus on improvement
questions.why: The framing of "lessons learned" selects for failure. Asking about what worked surfaces practices worth repeating, which is half the value of the exercise.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same framing, a balance instruction manufactures symmetry, and accepting the convention keeps the gap.

questions.stem: A team introduces a review step and reviewers approve nearly everything, because the drafts read well and they were given no time.
options: Give reviewers the time and the specific checks the review should perform
Ask reviewers to reject a minimum proportion of drafts each week
Ask Claude to make the drafts less polished so they get scrutinised
Remove the review step, since it is not currently catching anything
questions.why: A review with no defined checks and no time becomes a rubber stamp. Specifying what to look for and resourcing it turns the step into a control.
questions.traps: A rejection quota manufactures rejections, degrading drafts is perverse, and removing the step abandons the control rather than repairing it.

questions.stem: An associate needs to confirm a figure and the only source they have is the output itself.
options: Ask Claude to confirm the figure a second time
Find an independent source before using the figure
Use the figure, since nothing contradicts it yet
Ask Claude how confident it is in the figure given
questions.why: Verification requires a source outside the thing being verified, which is exactly what makes it independent.
questions.traps: Re-asking produces another output from the same source, absence of contradiction is not evidence, and a confidence statement is one more generated claim.

questions.stem: A team receives a total that does not match the sum of the figures printed above it.
options: Ask Claude to check over its own arithmetic again
Use the total, since the individual figures are right
Recompute the total from the individual figures
Report both the total and the individual figures
questions.why: Arithmetic is verifiable directly, so recomputing settles which number is wrong without any further generation.
questions.traps: Asking for a self-check produces another output, using an inconsistent total publishes the error, and reporting both passes the contradiction on.

questions.stem: An output names a report that an associate cannot find anywhere at all.
options: Treat the citation as unverified until it is located
Assume the report exists and is hard to search for
Ask Claude for the report's publication details
Remove the citation and keep the claim it supports
questions.why: A citation nobody can find may simply not exist, and treating it as unverified is what stops it being relied on.
questions.traps: Assuming it exists is the failure, asking for more details generates more unverifiable text, and keeping the claim without a source leaves it unsupported.

questions.stem: An associate asks "why is this the best option" and gets reasons why it is.
options: Ask the same question about each of the options
Ask for the drawbacks as a follow-up question
Accept the answer, since the reasons given are sound
Ask an open question that does not assume the answer
questions.why: A question that presupposes its conclusion gets an answer built on that presupposition, and removing the assumption is the fix.
questions.traps: Repeating the leading question per option repeats the bias, a follow-up patches one answer, and sound reasons for a presupposed conclusion are still one-sided.

questions.stem: A team asks how they should decide whether a given output is good enough.
options: By whether it reads well and looks professional
By whether it needed fewer edits than last time
By what the output has to achieve for its reader
By whether the team is satisfied with it overall
questions.why: Quality is fitness for a purpose, so the reader's need is what any standard has to be built from.
questions.traps: Polish, edit count and satisfaction are all proxies that can move independently of whether the output actually works.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer reads the output once from beginning to end and approves it.
options: Read it through twice so that nothing gets missed
Check against specific criteria rather than reading through
Have a second person also read it from start to finish
Read it more slowly to catch more of the issues
questions.why: Reading fluent text tends to confirm it, and checking against named criteria is what turns reading into reviewing.
questions.traps: Reading twice, adding a reader and slowing down all repeat the same vulnerable process.

questions.stem: An associate asks for the risks of a plan and gets a list that feels thorough.
options: Ask for more risks until the list stops growing
Accept the list, since it appears comprehensive
Ask Claude whether the list is complete or not
Ask what kinds of risk the list does not cover
questions.why: A thorough-feeling list can be systematically missing a whole category, and asking about categories is what surfaces that.
questions.traps: Asking for more produces more of the same kind, apparent comprehensiveness is what the gap hides behind, and a completeness self-check is unreliable.

questions.stem: A team's output says "studies show" without naming any study at all.
options: Ask which studies, and check that they really exist
Accept it, since the claim itself sounds plausible
Remove the phrase and keep the underlying claim
Add a general reference to the research literature
questions.why: An unnamed source cannot be checked, and naming it is the step that makes the claim either verifiable or visibly unsupported.
questions.traps: Plausibility is not evidence, removing the phrase leaves an unsupported claim, and a general reference is no more checkable than the original.

questions.stem: A team tests a prompt on three examples and it works correctly on all three.
options: Conclude the prompt works, since all three passed
Test on more cases before drawing a conclusion
Conclude nothing, since three cases prove nothing
Test the same three examples over a second time
questions.why: Three successes are consistent with a wide range of true accuracies, so more cases are what narrow the estimate down.
questions.traps: Concluding from three overstates the evidence, dismissing them entirely ignores real information, and repeating them adds nothing new.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude whether its own answer contains any errors in it.
options: Treat the reply as a reliable report of the errors
Ask again in different words in order to confirm it
Accept the reply if it identifies at least one error
Treat the reply as another output, not as a check
questions.why: A self-assessment is generated by the same process that produced the answer, so it cannot serve as an independent check.
questions.traps: Trusting it is the misconception, rephrasing produces another self-report, and finding one error does not validate the rest.

questions.stem: An output gives a percentage change without stating what it is a percentage of.
options: Assume the base is the earlier of the two figures
Use the percentage, since the direction is clear
Ask for the base figure the percentage is taken from
Recalculate the percentage from your own figures
questions.why: A percentage change is meaningless without its base, and asking for it is what makes the number interpretable at all.
questions.traps: Assuming a base can invert the meaning, direction is not magnitude, and recalculating from different figures answers a different question.

questions.stem: A team must verify a claim and finds a source that repeats the same wording.
options: Look for whether the source is independent of the claim
Treat the match as confirmation of the whole claim
Treat the match as evidence the claim was copied
Look for a second source that says the same thing
questions.why: Identical wording often means one source copied the other, so independence is what determines whether it confirms anything.
questions.traps: Treating a match as confirmation is the trap, assuming copying is the same guess reversed, and a third repeating source adds no independence.

questions.stem: A team asks about their own internal process and gets a confident, plausible answer.
options: Accept it, since the answer describes their process well
Ask the model where it got the information from
Accept it if it matches what the team remembers
Check it against their own internal documentation
questions.why: The model has no access to a team's internal process, so a confident answer about it is generated rather than known.
questions.traps: Plausibility is the failure mode, asking for a source produces an invented one, and memory is not the documentation.

questions.stem: An associate mentions in the prompt that they favour one of the two options.
options: Keep the preference, since context helps the answer
Mention the other option's merits in the prompt too
Remove the preference and ask the question again
Ask a colleague to run the same question instead
questions.why: A stated preference shapes what comes back, so removing it is what lets the answer be about the options rather than the asker.
questions.traps: Preference is not the kind of context that helps, balancing the framing still frames it, and a colleague running a biased prompt gets a biased answer.

questions.stem: A team wants to know how much of their Claude output should be reviewed.
options: As much as the consequence of an error justifies
All of it, since any output could contain an error
A fixed percentage chosen for the sake of consistency
Whatever the team happens to have capacity to review
questions.why: Review is a cost paid against risk, so the consequence of a missed error is what sets the amount worth doing.
questions.traps: Reviewing everything spends most effort where it matters least, a fixed rate ignores which work is consequential, and capacity is a constraint rather than a criterion.

questions.stem: A summary of a document is accurate and omits its section on exceptions.
options: Accept the summary, since what it says is accurate
Ask specifically about the exceptions section
Ask for a longer summary covering more ground
Read the document instead of using the summary
questions.why: Accuracy and completeness are different properties, and naming the missing section is what recovers it.
questions.traps: Accuracy does not imply coverage, a longer summary may still omit the same section, and abandoning the summary discards its value.

questions.stem: A team defines good output as output that needs no editing at all.
options: A good standard, since editing costs the team time
A good standard, since it is very easy to measure
A poor standard, since it rewards unchallenged text
A poor standard, since some editing is always needed
questions.why: Text that needs no editing may simply be text nobody examined closely, which is the opposite of what the standard intends.
questions.traps: Time saved and measurability are real but do not make it a quality measure, and "some editing is always needed" objects to the threshold rather than the measure.

questions.stem: A forecast is given to two decimal places from figures rounded to the nearest thousand.
options: Report the forecast exactly as it was produced
Round the forecast to match its least precise input
Recompute the forecast using unrounded inputs
Report the forecast with a note about the inputs
questions.why: Precision cannot exceed that of the inputs, and reporting two decimals implies a certainty the underlying data does not support.
questions.traps: Reporting it unchanged conveys false precision, unrounded inputs may not exist, and a note leaves the misleading figure in place.

questions.stem: A team's output is reliably correct on a topic and then wrong on an adjacent one.
options: Conclude the model has become less reliable overall
Assume the question was worded unusually this time
Continue, since one error among many is acceptable
Treat reliability as topic-specific rather than general
questions.why: Accuracy varies by how well-covered a topic is, so a record on one subject does not transfer to a neighbouring one.
questions.traps: A general decline is not supported by one case, blaming the wording is unevidenced, and the error rate is not what is at issue.

questions.stem: An analysis of why a project failed attributes every cause to the same department.
options: Ask what the other departments contributed to it
Accept it, since the analysis is internally coherent
Ask for the analysis to be rewritten more fairly
Share it with that department for their response
questions.why: A single-cause explanation of a complex failure is usually incomplete, and asking about the others is what tests it.
questions.traps: Coherence is not completeness, asking for fairness treats a symptom, and circulating it starts an argument rather than an inquiry.

questions.stem: An associate has ten claims to check and time enough to check three of them.
options: Check the first three claims in the document itself
Check three claims chosen at random from the ten
Check the three the conclusion most depends on
Check the three that look least likely to be true
questions.why: Verification effort belongs where an error would change the conclusion, since that is what the checking is for.
questions.traps: Position is arbitrary, random selection ignores importance, and implausibility is a weak proxy for consequence.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers approve almost everything and the team is unsure the step works.
options: Look at what has slipped through the review so far
Trust the reviewers, since approval rates are high
Add a second reviewer to increase the scrutiny
Replace the reviewers with different colleagues
questions.why: A review's value shows in what it catches and what it misses, and the escapes are the evidence about which is happening.
questions.traps: High approval is consistent with both a good process and a useless one, and adding or swapping reviewers changes the process before diagnosing it.

questions.stem: A team measures 88% accuracy once and 79% when they repeat the measurement.
options: Take the higher figure, since it was measured first
Take the average of the two separate measurements
Take the lower figure in order to be conservative
Treat both as estimates with real uncertainty
questions.why: Two different results from the same task mean the sample is too small to pin the number down, which is itself the finding.
questions.traps: Order, averaging and conservatism all produce a single number from data that does not support one.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to rate its confidence in each of six separate claims.
options: Verify only the claims rated as low confidence
Use the ratings to prioritise, and not to decide
Accept the high-confidence claims without checking
Ignore the ratings, since they carry no information
questions.why: Stated confidence correlates loosely with correctness, which makes it useful for ordering work and unsafe as a substitute for checking.
questions.traps: Verifying only the low ones trusts the high ones, accepting them outright is the same error, and discarding the signal wastes a weak but real one.

questions.stem: A list of stakeholders covers everyone who benefits and nobody who loses out.
options: Accept it, since the beneficiaries are the priority
Ask for a longer stakeholder list to be produced
Add the obvious opponents to the list by hand
Ask who would be disadvantaged by the proposed change
questions.why: A systematic omission is best surfaced by asking directly for the missing category rather than by asking for more of the same.
questions.traps: Prioritising beneficiaries is what produced the gap, a longer list extends the same pattern, and adding names by hand fixes one instance.

questions.stem: A team's quality bar is that a reviewer would not be embarrassed to send the output.
options: Adequate, since it captures professional judgement
Too vague, since embarrassment varies by reviewer
Too strict, since it rules out anything imperfect
Adequate, provided reviewers are experienced enough
questions.why: A standard has to mean the same thing to different people, and a feeling does not.
questions.traps: Calling it judgement does not make it consistent, it is not obviously strict, and experience does not align two people's discomfort.

questions.stem: A quotation is attributed to a named person who did say similar things elsewhere.
options: Verify the exact wording before using the quotation
Use it, since the person holds that view anyway
Paraphrase it instead of quoting it directly there
Attribute it more loosely to avoid the problem
questions.why: A quotation asserts specific words, and similar views do not license attributing a sentence someone did not actually say.
questions.traps: Holding the view is not saying the words, paraphrasing still attributes it, and vague attribution obscures rather than fixes the problem.

questions.stem: An output reports both a 40% growth and a change from fifty to sixty-eight.
options: Use the percentage, since it is stated directly
Use the raw figures, since they are more concrete
Recompute, since the two statements plainly disagree
Report both and let the reader reconcile them
questions.why: Fifty to sixty-eight is thirty-six per cent, so the two statements cannot both be right and the arithmetic settles which is.
questions.traps: Preferring either form picks without checking, and publishing both passes an internal contradiction to the reader.

questions.stem: An output describes a feature of the team's own software that does not exist.
options: Check whether other claims about the software are invented
Correct the feature description and use the rest
Ask the model where it learned about the feature
Assume the feature was renamed rather than invented
questions.why: One invented detail about a system the model cannot see suggests the rest may be equally ungrounded.
questions.traps: Fixing one detail assumes the rest is sound, asking for a source generates one, and a renaming theory is a charitable guess.

questions.stem: A comparison of two vendors is balanced in structure and consistently warmer about one.
options: Accept it, since the structure gives equal space
Compare the two sets of wording directly side by side
Ask for the comparison to be rewritten neutrally
Add the missing criticisms of the favoured vendor
questions.why: Equal structure can carry unequal language, and reading the two descriptions against each other is what exposes it.
questions.traps: Structural balance is what hides it, a rewrite treats the symptom, and adding criticisms edits the output without diagnosing the tilt.

questions.stem: A team's three reviewers each assume the previous one checked the facts.
options: Ask all three of the reviewers to check the facts
Reduce the review to a single thorough reviewer
Add a fourth reviewer dedicated to fact checking
State which reviewer checks what, and record it
questions.why: Diffused responsibility is what produced the gap, and assigning it explicitly is what closes it without adding more work.
questions.traps: Triplicating the check wastes effort, one reviewer loses the other perspectives, and a fourth adds cost to a still-unassigned process.

questions.stem: A team compares two prompts by running each once and picking the better result.
options: Pick the better result, since the comparison was fair
Run each once more and take the best of the two
Run each several times before choosing between them
Pick whichever of the prompts is shorter and clearer
questions.why: Single runs vary enough that the difference observed may be noise rather than a real difference between the prompts.
questions.traps: One run each is not a fair comparison, best-of-two amplifies the noise, and prompt length is not performance.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to flag anything a reviewer should look at closely.
options: Useful as a starting point, and not as a filter
Useful as a filter, since it saves reviewer time
Not useful, since the model cannot assess itself
Useful only if the flags are usually accurate
questions.why: Self-flagging surfaces some real issues and misses others, which makes it an addition to review rather than a replacement for it.
questions.traps: Using it as a filter trusts what it misses, dismissing it discards a real signal, and accuracy of the flags says nothing about the unflagged.

questions.stem: An associate verifies a claim by asking Claude to find supporting sources for it.
options: Accept the sources it returns as verification
Check that the returned sources actually exist
Ask for more sources to increase the confidence
Find the sources independently rather than through it
questions.why: Sources produced by the thing being checked are not independent, and finding them yourself is what makes the check real.
questions.traps: Accepting them is circular, checking they exist does not check they say it, and more of the same adds no independence.

questions.stem: A summary of thirty customer comments reflects the twenty-eight that were detailed.
options: Accept it, since twenty-eight of thirty is most of them
Ask what the two briefest comments actually said
Ask for a summary that weights all comments equally
Read all thirty comments rather than the summary
questions.why: Short comments are systematically under-represented in summaries, and they can carry the sharpest signal in the set.
questions.traps: A majority is not the whole picture, an equal-weighting request does not say what was missed, and reading everything discards the summary's value.

questions.stem: A team measures output quality by counting how many edits a reviewer makes.
options: A good measure, since it is objective and countable
A good measure, provided one reviewer does them all
A poor measure, since edits vary with the reviewer
A poor measure, since some edits are improvements
questions.why: Edit counts measure reviewer behaviour rather than output quality, and two reviewers will produce different counts on identical text.
questions.traps: Countability is not validity, a single reviewer makes it consistent rather than meaningful, and the improvement objection misses the reviewer variance.

questions.stem: An output's figures are individually correct and the conclusion drawn from them is wrong.
options: Recheck the figures, since the conclusion is wrong
Check the reasoning, since the arithmetic already passed
Accept the conclusion, since the figures support it
Ask for the conclusion to be restated more carefully
questions.why: Correct inputs with a wrong conclusion isolates the fault to the step between them, which is where to look first.
questions.traps: Rechecking verified figures repeats work, assuming support is the error, and restating a wrong conclusion does not correct it.

questions.stem: A team finds one fabricated citation in a document that contains forty others.
options: Correct the one citation and use the rest as they are
Check a sample of the remaining forty citations
Remove all the citations rather than checking them
Check all forty, since one fabrication changes the prior
questions.why: A single fabrication is evidence about how the document was produced, which makes every other citation newly uncertain.
questions.traps: Fixing one assumes it was isolated, a sample may miss the others, and removing citations destroys the document's grounding.

questions.stem: An associate lists three options in order of preference and the analysis favours the first.
options: Reorder the options and see whether the answer moves
Accept the answer, since the first option may be best
Ask for the options to be assessed independently
Remove the ordering and ask the question again
questions.why: Reordering is a direct test of whether the position influenced the answer, which neither accepting nor neutralising establishes.
questions.traps: The first option may be best or may simply be first, an independence instruction is not a test, and removing the order fixes it without confirming the effect.

questions.stem: A team's review catches every formatting error and has never caught a factual one.
options: Formatting errors are more common than factual ones
The output has no factual errors to be caught
The review is checking form rather than substance
Reviewers should be asked to look more carefully
questions.why: A perfect record on one class and none on another describes what the review is actually looking at.
questions.traps: Relative frequency does not explain a total absence, assuming no errors exist is unwarranted, and asking for care does not change what is being checked.

questions.stem: A claim is expensive to verify and the decision it supports is easy to reverse.
options: Verify it, since unverified claims should not be used
Verify it, since the cost of checking is fixed
Proceed and verify it at some point afterwards
Proceed without verifying, given the reversal is cheap
questions.why: Verification is worth its cost against the cost of being wrong, and an easily reversed decision makes that cost low.
questions.traps: A blanket verification rule ignores the economics, fixed cost is not the comparison, and deferred verification is a commitment rarely kept.

questions.stem: A team's prompt scores 92% on the twenty cases they used to build the prompt.
options: The score is a fair estimate of real performance
The score is pessimistic, since twenty cases is few
The score is optimistic, since the cases shaped the prompt
The score is meaningless without a confidence interval
questions.why: A prompt tuned against particular cases performs better on those cases than on cases it has never seen.
questions.traps: Treating it as unbiased is the error, small samples are noisy rather than pessimistic, and an interval on a biased estimate is still biased.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to grade its own output and it consistently gives itself high marks.
options: The output is probably good, since it grades itself well
The grades carry little information about quality
The grading prompt should be made more demanding
The model should be asked to grade itself more harshly
questions.why: A self-grade produced by the same process reflects that process rather than the result, which is why it clusters high.
questions.traps: Treating the grade as evidence is the error, and adjusting the grading prompt changes the number without adding any information.

questions.stem: A risk list covers what could go wrong and omits what happens if nothing does.
options: Ask about the case where the plan simply succeeds
Accept it, since a risk list should cover the risks
Ask for a longer and more thorough risk list again
Add the success case to the list by hand afterwards
questions.why: The scenario where a plan succeeds and turns out to have been unnecessary is a real risk that a failure-focused list will not produce.
questions.traps: A narrow reading of "risk" is what created the gap, a longer list extends the same frame, and adding it manually fixes one document.

questions.stem: Two associates disagree about whether a Claude output is fit to be sent.
options: Send it, since one of them considers it acceptable
Revise it until both are satisfied with the result
Establish what it has to do before judging it
Escalate the disagreement to their line manager
questions.why: Disagreement about quality is usually disagreement about the standard, and naming the standard is what makes the judgement shared.
questions.traps: Deferring to the permissive view sets no bar, revising to satisfy both may over-polish, and escalation adds a decider rather than a criterion.

questions.stem: A team's submission must show where each factual claim in it came from.
options: Reconstruct the sources once the submission is drafted
Cite the model itself as the source of the claims
Remove any claim whose source cannot be recalled
Record the source at the point each claim is written
questions.why: Provenance is cheap to capture as you go and expensive to reconstruct afterwards, which is what makes recording it the workable answer.
questions.traps: Reconstruction is slow and error-prone, the model is not a source, and removing unattributable claims discards work that was probably sound.

questions.stem: A team receives figures that are internally consistent and disagree with their own records.
options: Use their own records, since those are authoritative
Find which set is wrong before using either of them
Use the output's figures, since they are consistent
Report both sets and note the discrepancy found
questions.why: Internal consistency is not correctness, and a disagreement with the records is a question about which source is wrong.
questions.traps: Assuming the records are right skips the check, consistency proves nothing about accuracy, and publishing both hands the problem on.

questions.stem: Claims about a public topic are correct and claims about the team's own work are not.
options: The model has access to one and not to the other
The model is less reliable than it used to be
The prompt described the team's work rather poorly
The team's work is unusually complex to describe
questions.why: Accuracy tracks what the model has actually seen, which is why public material holds up and private material does not.
questions.traps: A general decline does not explain the split, prompt quality would affect both, and complexity is not what distinguishes them.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to review a document and mentions that they wrote it.
options: The context helps the review by explaining intent
The authorship makes no difference to the review
The review will be harsher to prove independence
The review is likely to be gentler than a blind one
questions.why: Stated authorship is context that tends to soften criticism, so withholding it is what gets a franker read.
questions.traps: Intent is rarely what a review needs, assuming no effect ignores a known one, and over-correction is not the observed pattern.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer is the same person who wrote the prompt that produced the output.
options: Have someone else review it, since they are invested
Keep them, since they best understand the intent
Keep them and ask them to be rather more critical
Have them review it after a full day has passed
questions.why: The prompt's author has an interest in the output being good, which is exactly the position independent review exists to avoid.
questions.traps: Understanding intent is not independence, self-directed criticism does not remove the investment, and a delay does not change who they are.

questions.stem: A team's accuracy fell from 94% to 89% across two consecutive months.
options: Investigate the cause, since performance has declined
Check whether the difference is larger than the noise
Accept it, since five points is within normal variation
Average the two months and report the combined figure
questions.why: Whether five points is a real change depends on how many cases each figure rests on, and that is the first thing to establish.
questions.traps: Investigating assumes a real change, dismissing it assumes noise, and averaging discards the question entirely.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether the answer would change if more information were given.
options: The reply usefully identifies what information is missing
The reply is reliable, since it concerns its own reasoning
The reply describes a hypothetical it cannot test
The reply should be checked against a second answer
questions.why: The model cannot run the counterfactual, so its account of how a different input would change things is generated rather than observed.
questions.traps: It may name plausible gaps without those being the operative ones, self-knowledge of reasoning is exactly what is unavailable, and a second answer is another guess.

questions.stem: An output converts costs between currencies without stating the rate that it used.
options: Ask which exchange rate was applied, and when
Accept the figures, since the conversion looks right
Convert one figure yourself to check the others
Ask for the figures in the original currency only
questions.why: A conversion depends entirely on the rate and its date, and without those the figures cannot be reproduced or checked.
questions.traps: Appearance is not verification, spot-checking one figure does not reveal the rate, and dropping the conversion abandons what was asked for.

questions.stem: An associate needs to check a claim and their team has nobody with that expertise.
options: Accept the claim, since nobody can dispute it here
Ask the most senior person to make a judgement
Ask Claude to explain the claim in simpler terms
Find an external source rather than judging it internally
questions.why: Absence of internal expertise is a reason to go outside, not a reason to lower the standard of checking.
questions.traps: Undisputed is not verified, seniority is not subject knowledge, and a clearer explanation is still an unverified one.

questions.stem: An output gives a precise statistic with no source and no date attached to it.
options: Accept it, since precise figures are rarely invented
Round it, since the precision may be overstated
Treat the precision as no evidence of accuracy
Ask for the same statistic a second time to confirm
questions.why: Fabricated figures are produced with the same precision as real ones, so the decimal places carry no information about truth.
questions.traps: Precision is a stylistic feature, rounding an unsourced figure keeps it unsourced, and a repeat is not independent.

questions.stem: A summary of a debate gives more space to the side the prompt mentioned first.
options: Accept it, since the first side may have more to say
Check whether the space matches the actual balance
Ask for the two sides to be given equal space
Reverse the order and use the second summary instead
questions.why: Space in a summary should follow the material rather than the order of the prompt, and comparing the two is what tests it.
questions.traps: The imbalance may be real or positional, forcing equal space misrepresents an unequal debate, and swapping produces a second untested output.

questions.stem: A team wants one single number that represents the quality of their output.
options: Use accuracy, since it is the most important one
Combine the dimensions into one weighted score
Use whichever number stakeholders find clearest
No single number captures more than one dimension
questions.why: Quality has several dimensions that move independently, so one number necessarily hides the trade-offs between them.
questions.traps: Elevating accuracy discards the rest, a weighted score buries the weights inside it, and clarity to stakeholders is not validity.
