questions.stem: A team's reviewer checks accuracy, tone, compliance and formatting all in one pass.
options: Keep one pass, since it is faster for the reviewer
Separate the checks, since they need different attention
Keep one pass and give the reviewer a checklist
Keep one pass and lengthen the time allowed for it
questions.why: Scanning for form and verifying substance are different activities, and one pass over four reliably does the easiest of them.
questions.traps: Speed is the cost being paid, a checklist orders the work without separating the modes, and more time does not change the interference.

questions.stem: An answer lists what a change will cost and does not list what it will save.
options: Accept it, since the costs were what was asked for
Estimate the savings yourself from the cost figures
Ask for the savings as well as the costs involved
Ask for a more complete answer about the change
questions.why: A one-sided answer to a two-sided question is completed by asking for the missing side directly rather than indirectly.
questions.traps: Literal compliance produces a misleading picture, savings cannot be derived from costs, and a vague completeness request does not name what is missing.

questions.stem: A team needs to show a regulator where a figure in their submission came from.
options: Name the document and location the figure came from
Say the figure was produced with Claude's assistance
Say the figure was checked before it was submitted
Provide the conversation in which the figure appeared
questions.why: Provenance means the underlying source, since that is what a regulator can independently go and examine.
questions.traps: Naming the tool describes production, a checking assertion is not a source, and a conversation shows generation rather than origin.

questions.stem: A team reports that their prompt is 90% accurate, based on twenty test cases.
options: Report 90%, since that is what the test produced
Round it to "about 90%" to avoid false precision
Report the figure with the sample size alongside it
Test more cases before reporting any figure at all
questions.why: Twenty cases give a wide range around ninety per cent, and stating the sample size is what lets a reader judge the figure.
questions.traps: A bare percentage implies more certainty than twenty cases give, rounding is cosmetic, and withholding it discards real information.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to identify the weakest part of its own analysis.
options: Treat the identified part as the only weak point
Treat everything else as sound by implication
Ignore it, since self-criticism carries no weight
Treat the answer as a hint rather than a finding
questions.why: A self-identified weakness may well be real and is certainly not exhaustive, which makes it a place to start looking.
questions.traps: Treating it as the only weakness is the error, inferring soundness elsewhere is worse, and dismissing it wastes a usable pointer.

questions.stem: A table's rows are each correct and the column totals do not add up properly.
options: Trust the totals, since the rows are all correct
Recompute the totals from the rows that are shown
Trust the rows and remove the totals entirely
Ask for the table to be regenerated from scratch
questions.why: Rows and totals are separately produced, so a mismatch is resolved by doing the arithmetic rather than by choosing a side.
questions.traps: Correct rows do not validate totals, deleting the totals loses information, and regenerating may simply reproduce the error.

questions.stem: An associate checks a Claude figure by asking Claude the very same question again.
options: Not a check, since both answers share one source
A valid check, since two answers agreeing is evidence
A valid check if the question is worded differently
Not a check, but useful for testing consistency
questions.why: Two answers from the same system are not independent, so agreement between them says nothing about correctness.
questions.traps: Agreement between dependent sources is not evidence, rewording does not create independence, and consistency is a different property being confused with truth.

questions.stem: An output about a fast-moving topic is confident and describes last year's position.
options: Accept it, since the description is internally coherent
Check the current position against a live source
Ask the model whether its information is current
Adjust the answer for what has changed since then
questions.why: A model describes what it was trained on, so currency has to come from a source that is itself actually current.
questions.traps: Coherence is not currency, asking about its own recency is unreliable, and adjusting assumes you already know what changed.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to help defend a decision they have already made.
options: Treat the arguments as an evaluation of the decision
Ask for the arguments and the counter-arguments
Accept the arguments, since they are sound in themselves
Expect supporting arguments rather than an assessment
questions.why: A request to defend produces a defence, which is a different thing from a judgement about whether the decision was right.
questions.traps: Reading a defence as an evaluation is the error, adding counter-arguments patches one output, and soundness does not make it balanced.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers see the output only after it has been formatted for publication.
options: Keep the order, since formatted output is easier to read
Keep the order and ask reviewers to ignore the styling
Review before formatting, since polish suppresses scrutiny
Format it twice, once plainly and once for publication
questions.why: Polished presentation makes text read as finished, which reduces the scrutiny a reviewer applies to its content.
questions.traps: Readability is what causes the problem, asking reviewers to ignore styling relies on resisting a strong effect, and double formatting adds work.

questions.stem: A list of process steps covers the normal path and omits what happens on failure.
options: Ask what happens when a step does not succeed
Accept it, since the normal path is the common case
Ask for a longer and more detailed list of steps
Write the failure paths in yourself afterwards
questions.why: Exception handling is a category that a description of the normal path will not produce, and asking for it directly recovers it.
questions.traps: Frequency does not make the exceptions unimportant, more detail extends the same path, and writing them yourself fixes one document.

questions.stem: A team judges output by whether anybody objects to it after it has been sent.
options: A reasonable standard, since objections reveal problems
A weak standard, since objections arrive far too late
A reasonable standard if the audience is engaged
A weak standard, since silence is not approval
questions.why: Most readers of most documents say nothing regardless of quality, which makes the absence of objection almost uninformative.
questions.traps: Objections reveal only the loudest problems, lateness is a secondary objection, and audience engagement does not make silence a signal.

questions.stem: An output states a growth rate that is correct and a base year that is wrong.
options: Recompute the rate against the correct base year
Correct the base year and keep the growth rate
Keep both, since the growth rate itself is right
Ask for the figures to be produced again entirely
questions.why: A growth rate is defined relative to its base, so changing the base changes the rate that was correct against the old one.
questions.traps: Fixing the year alone leaves an inconsistent pair, keeping both publishes a contradiction, and regenerating discards the correct work.

questions.stem: An associate finds two authoritative sources that give different figures for the same thing.
options: Use the figure from the more recent of the two
Use the figure from the more authoritative source
Find out what each source is actually measuring
Report both figures and let the reader choose
questions.why: Two credible sources usually differ because they are measuring different things, and identifying that is what resolves the conflict.
questions.traps: Recency and authority both pick a side without understanding the difference, and reporting both hands the problem to the reader.

questions.stem: An account of a meeting includes a decision that nobody remembers being taken.
options: Accept it, since memories of meetings are unreliable
Check it against the meeting's own written record
Remove the decision and keep the rest of the account
Ask attendees whether the decision was in fact taken
questions.why: A written record is what settles whether a decision was taken, and it is available where recollection is not.
questions.traps: Unreliable memory is a reason to consult the record rather than accept the output, removing it assumes it is wrong, and canvassing attendees polls the same memories.

questions.stem: An analysis of a competitor is entirely negative and the competitor is doing well.
options: Accept it, since the criticisms are individually valid
Ask for the analysis to be more balanced overall
Ask what the competitor is actually doing effectively
Discount the analysis, since it is clearly one-sided
questions.why: Commercial success is evidence something is working, and asking what that is recovers the half the analysis omitted.
questions.traps: Valid criticisms can still be a partial picture, a request for balance does not name what is missing, and discarding it loses valid observations.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer catches far more issues than the other three reviewers do.
options: Route all of the output through that one reviewer
Accept it, since the strong reviewer covers the gap
Replace the other three reviewers with new people
Find out what that one reviewer does differently
questions.why: One reviewer outperforming the rest is a method worth extracting, which is what raises everyone rather than concentrating the work.
questions.traps: Routing everything creates a bottleneck, relying on one person is fragile, and replacing reviewers assumes the people rather than the method.

questions.stem: A compliance check reports on every checklist item and mentions nothing outside it.
options: Recognise the checklist as a floor rather than the scope
Accept it, since the checklist defines what matters
Ask for a longer checklist covering more items
Run the check again with a different checklist
questions.why: A checklist covers known requirements, and issues outside it are exactly what a checklist-driven check will never raise.
questions.traps: Treating the checklist as complete is the error, a longer checklist has the same boundary, and a second checklist has a different one.

questions.stem: A team spot-checks six of twenty figures, finds them correct, and signs off.
options: Sign off, since the sample was correct throughout
Note that fourteen of the figures remain unchecked
Check six more of the figures and then sign off
Check every figure before signing anything off
questions.why: A clean sample supports a claim about the sample, and saying what was not checked is what makes the sign-off honest.
questions.traps: Generalising from six overstates it, a bigger sample has the same issue at a different size, and full checking may not be warranted.

questions.stem: A team includes an instruction telling Claude to say when it is unsure.
options: Useful, though absence of a caveat is not confidence
Useful, since caveats now mark the uncertain claims
Not useful, since the model cannot judge uncertainty
Useful only if the caveats appear frequently enough
questions.why: The instruction increases how often uncertainty is flagged without making the unflagged claims reliably certain.
questions.traps: Treating the absence of a caveat as a signal is the trap, dismissing it discards a real improvement, and frequency is not the test.

questions.stem: A team's output meets every quality criterion and users have stopped reading it.
options: The users are at fault for not reading the output
The output should be made shorter to encourage reading
The criteria should be applied more strictly still
The criteria are missing something users care about
questions.why: A gap between passing the criteria and being read means the criteria do not capture what makes it worth reading.
questions.traps: Blaming users ignores the evidence, shortening guesses at the cause, and stricter application of the wrong criteria does not help.

questions.stem: An associate's claim came from a Claude answer that drew on a document they hold.
options: Cite Claude, since that is where they encountered it
Cite the document, since that is where the claim originates
Cite both the document and the conversation itself
Cite neither, since the claim is now their own
questions.why: The document is the source of the fact and the conversation is only how it was found, which is not what a citation records.
questions.traps: Citing the tool records the route, citing both adds noise, and citing nothing removes the provenance entirely.

questions.stem: An output describes two variables as related in wording that implies one caused the other.
options: Accept it, since the relationship is real in the data
Rewrite it to describe the relationship as a correlation
Check whether the source supports a causal claim
Remove the relationship from the output entirely
questions.why: A correlation in the data does not establish causation, and whether the source claims it is what determines the right wording.
questions.traps: A real relationship is not a causal one, rewriting without checking may understate a supported claim, and removal discards a genuine finding.

questions.stem: An output names a standard by number and that number belongs to something else.
options: Verify standard numbers against the issuing body
Correct the number and leave the description alone
Remove the number and keep the standard's name
Accept it, since the description of the standard is right
questions.why: A number and a description that do not match means at least one is wrong, and the issuing body is what settles which.
questions.traps: Correcting the number assumes the description is right, removing it loses the identifier, and accepting the description ignores the mismatch.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to assess a risk and states in the prompt that it is low.
options: Accept the assessment, since it may still be accurate
Ask for the assessment to be more sceptical instead
Have someone else assess the risk independently
Ask again without stating a view about the risk
questions.why: An anchor in the prompt pulls the assessment towards it, and removing the anchor is what tests whether the conclusion survives.
questions.traps: The answer may be right or may be anchored, asking for scepticism substitutes one nudge for another, and a second person answers a different question.

questions.stem: A team reviews output thoroughly on Monday and less carefully as the week goes on.
options: Ask reviewers to maintain their standard all week
Spread the review out or rotate who performs it
Do all of the reviewing on a Monday each week
Accept it, since some variation is unavoidable
questions.why: Declining attention across a week is a workload pattern, and changing how the work is distributed is what addresses it.
questions.traps: Asking for consistency ignores the cause, concentrating everything on Monday creates its own fatigue, and accepting it leaves later work under-reviewed.

questions.stem: A summary of a study reports its findings and omits the limitations the study states.
options: Accept it, since the findings are what matter
Ask for a longer summary of the whole study instead
Ask what the study says about its own limitations
Read the study's limitations section yourself
questions.why: Limitations determine how far findings can be relied on, and asking for them directly recovers a systematically dropped section.
questions.traps: Findings without limitations can be badly misapplied, a longer summary may still drop them, and reading it yourself discards the summary's value.

questions.stem: A team tests a workflow on cases from the past month and it performs well.
options: Deploy it, since a month of cases is a good sample
Test it on cases from the previous year as well
Deploy it and monitor performance from then on
Check whether last month's cases are typical ones
questions.why: A month can be seasonal or unusual, and knowing whether it represents ordinary work is what makes the result generalisable.
questions.traps: Sample size does not address representativeness, a longer window is a fix chosen before the question, and monitoring finds problems in production.

questions.stem: A process asks Claude to rate each output and routes the low ratings to a reviewer.
options: Keep the process, since it directs effort sensibly
Route by consequence as well as by the rating
Remove the ratings and review everything equally
Lower the threshold so more outputs are reviewed
questions.why: The rating is a weak signal, so consequential work needs review whether or not the model happened to flag it.
questions.traps: Trusting the rating alone leaves high-rated consequential work unchecked, reviewing everything discards a useful signal, and a lower threshold keeps the blind spot.

questions.stem: An associate must verify a translated quotation and does not read the original language.
options: Have someone who reads the language check it over
Verify the translation by translating it back again
Accept the translation, since the meaning is clear
Use the translated quotation with a note about it
questions.why: Only someone who can read the original can confirm that the translation actually says what the original says.
questions.traps: Back-translation can round-trip an error, clarity is not fidelity, and a note flags a risk without resolving it.

questions.stem: A team wants their output to be at least as good as a human would produce.
options: Use the team's average performance as the bar
Use the team's best performer as the standard bar
Name which human, and on which particular dimension
Accept the standard, since it is intuitively clear
questions.why: Human performance varies widely by person and by dimension, so the comparison has to be made specific before it can be applied.
questions.traps: Average and best are two of many possible readings, and intuitive clarity is what allows two people to apply it differently.

questions.stem: Figures are correct and the denominator changed between the two periods compared.
options: The comparison is valid, since both figures are correct
The comparison should be reported with a caveat
The later denominator should be used for both periods
The comparison is invalid until the denominators match
questions.why: A ratio computed on different bases is not comparable, so the arithmetic being right does not make the comparison meaningful.
questions.traps: Correct components do not make a valid comparison, a caveat publishes a misleading figure, and reusing one denominator changes what the earlier figure means.

questions.stem: An output is accurate on everything the team can check and they cannot check the rest.
options: Say which parts were checked when passing it on
Treat the whole output as reliable, since checks passed
Treat the whole output as unreliable, since gaps remain
Check the remaining parts however long it takes
questions.why: A reader can weigh checked and unchecked material differently if they are told which is which, and that is what makes it honest.
questions.traps: Generalising from the checked part is the error, discarding it all wastes verified work, and exhaustive checking may not be proportionate.

questions.stem: A team's output is balanced and every example it chooses supports the same conclusion.
options: The output is balanced, since the argument is even
The examples are chosen because they are the clearest
Selection of the examples is where the framing sits
More examples should be added to restore the balance
questions.why: A balanced argument illustrated only by supportive cases still leads the reader, and the example set is where that happens.
questions.traps: Argumentative balance is what disguises it, clarity is an unevidenced explanation, and adding examples without examining the selection repeats it.

questions.stem: A team's review takes longer than writing the output from scratch would take.
options: Speed up the review so the workflow stays worthwhile
Ask whether the workflow is worth keeping at all
Keep it, since the review is catching real errors
Reduce the review until the total time is acceptable
questions.why: When verification costs more than doing the work, the arrangement has stopped paying, and that is the question to put.
questions.traps: Speeding up the review assumes it should continue, catching errors does not settle the economics, and cutting review to fit a time budget trades safety for arithmetic.

questions.stem: A team's output answers the question asked and the question asked was the wrong one.
options: Fix the question, since the answer is only as good as it
Accept the answer, since it addressed the question
Ask a supplementary question to cover the gap
Ask for a broader answer to the original question
questions.why: An output cannot be better than the question behind it, so a wrong question makes even a correct answer useless.
questions.traps: Literal correctness is what hides the problem, a supplement bolts onto a wrong frame, and breadth does not correct direction.

questions.stem: An associate verifies six of seven claims and the seventh is what the decision rests on.
options: Accept the document, since six of seven were correct
Verify the seventh claim only if there is time for it
Verify the seventh, since the others were not the point
Report that six of the seven claims were verified
questions.why: Verification effort should follow what the conclusion depends on, and a clean record on six irrelevant claims does not transfer.
questions.traps: A high pass rate on the wrong claims is not reassurance, treating the key claim as optional inverts the priority, and the count omits which one matters.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has been correct on every case that they have tried so far.
options: Report it as a perfect record on the workflow so far
Report it as evidence that the workflow is reliable
Keep testing until an error eventually appears
Say how many cases that is, since the number is the evidence
questions.why: Ten clean cases and a thousand support very different conclusions, so the count is the whole of what the record means.
questions.traps: A perfect record without a denominator is uninterpretable, calling it reliable overstates it, and testing to failure is not a reporting standard.

questions.stem: A team notices the model sometimes says it is unsure and starts trusting unhedged answers.
options: Unhedged answers are more likely to be correct ones
The absence of a hedge is not a claim of certainty
The hedging is reliable enough to act on this way
Hedges should be removed so the output reads better
questions.why: Hedges appear inconsistently, so their absence reflects how the text was generated rather than a judgement of confidence.
questions.traps: Treating absence as a signal is the misconception, partial reliability does not support the inference, and removing hedges destroys the weak signal there is.

questions.stem: A team's output is consistently accurate and consistently later than the deadline.
options: Accuracy matters more, so the lateness is acceptable
The deadline should be moved to match the process
The accuracy should be reduced to meet the deadline
Accuracy and timeliness are both part of the standard
questions.why: An output that arrives after it is needed has failed regardless of how accurate it is, which makes timeliness a criterion rather than a preference.
questions.traps: Ranking accuracy above everything ignores the purpose, moving deadlines is not always available, and lowering accuracy is not the only alternative.

questions.stem: A paraphrase in an output says slightly more than the source it came from says.
options: Keep it, since the paraphrase captures the general point
Tighten the paraphrase to what the source supports
Quote the source directly instead of paraphrasing it
Cite the source and keep the stronger wording
questions.why: A paraphrase that strengthens a claim attributes to the source something it did not say, and pulling it back is the fix.
questions.traps: The general point is not what a citation asserts, direct quotation is heavier than needed, and citing a source for a stronger claim misrepresents it.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce review as their confidence in the output grows over time.
options: Reduce it uniformly, since confidence has grown overall
Keep it as it is, since confidence is not evidence
Reduce it where the record supports it, not everywhere
Reduce it and reinstate it if problems appear
questions.why: A track record is task-specific, so the reduction belongs on the work the record actually covers rather than on everything.
questions.traps: Uniform reduction extends a record beyond its scope, refusing any reduction ignores real evidence, and reinstating after problems means the problems land first.

questions.stem: An output's percentages are each correct and sum to 103% because of rounding.
options: Say the figures are rounded and do not sum exactly
Adjust one figure so that the total comes to 100%
Report the figures unchanged without any explanation
Report them to more decimal places so they sum
questions.why: Rounded components genuinely do not sum, and saying so is more honest than adjusting a figure to make the arithmetic look tidy.
questions.traps: Adjusting a figure makes it wrong, an unexplained 103% looks like an error, and more decimals conveys precision that was not there.

questions.stem: An output cites a real report and the page it gives does not contain the claim.
options: Correct the page number and keep the citation
Accept it, since the report itself certainly exists
Treat the citation as unverified despite the real report
Remove the page number and cite the report generally
questions.why: A real document with a wrong location suggests the claim was not read from it, which makes the whole citation uncertain.
questions.traps: Correcting the page assumes the claim is in there somewhere, the report's existence is not the question, and a vague citation hides the problem.

questions.stem: An associate reviews output in a subject they know well and finds it excellent.
options: Their expertise may be filling gaps as they read
Their expertise makes them the ideal reviewer for it
Their assessment is reliable, since they know the field
They should have a non-expert review it as well
questions.why: An expert reader supplies missing context automatically, which can make an incomplete output read as complete.
questions.traps: Expertise helps and also hides gaps, reliability does not follow from knowledge, and a non-expert reviewer has the opposite problem.

questions.stem: A team's output covers everything in the brief and the brief omitted a key constraint.
options: The output should have identified the missing constraint
The gap is in the brief rather than in the output
The output is complete, since it matched the brief
The brief should be rewritten and the output redone
questions.why: An output is bounded by what it was asked for, so a missing constraint is a failure of the brief that the output could not fix.
questions.traps: Expecting the output to supply what it was not told is unrealistic, matching the brief is not being useful, and redoing everything skips the diagnosis.

questions.stem: An associate is asked whether a document is verified and only part of it was checked.
options: Say it is verified, since the checked parts were correct
Say it is not verified, since the check was partial
Verify the remainder before answering the question
Say which parts were verified and which were not
questions.why: "Verified" is a claim about the whole document, and describing the actual coverage is what makes the answer accurate.
questions.traps: A blanket yes overstates it, a blanket no discards real verification, and completing the check may not be proportionate or even possible.

questions.stem: An associate cites a webpage and the page has changed since they read it.
options: Cite it without a date, since the page still exists
Re-read the page and cite whatever it says now
Record the date they accessed it alongside the citation
Remove the citation, since the page is unstable
questions.why: A dated access records what was seen and when, which is what makes a changing source citable at all.
questions.traps: An undated citation to changed content misleads, re-reading changes what the claim rests on, and removing it loses the provenance.

questions.stem: A team asks whether their output needs to be perfect before it is sent out.
options: It needs to be good enough for what it is used for
Yes, since errors damage the team's credibility
No, since perfection is never actually achievable
Yes for external work and no for internal work
questions.why: The standard is set by the use, since that determines what an error would cost and therefore how much checking is warranted.
questions.traps: A perfection rule is unachievable and unaffordable, its impossibility is not the argument, and the internal-external split is a proxy for consequence.

questions.stem: An associate needs to check a claim and the only available source is behind a paywall.
options: Use a secondary source that describes the paywalled one
Get access to the source rather than working around it
Accept the claim, since the source is inaccessible
Ask Claude to summarise what the source likely says
questions.why: Verification means reading what the source actually says, and access is the obstacle to remove rather than to route around.
questions.traps: A secondary description may itself be wrong, inaccessibility is not evidence, and a summary of an unread source is generated rather than read.

questions.stem: An output reports a figure in thousands where the source reports it in millions.
options: Use the output's figure, since it is more specific
Use the source's figure, since it is authoritative
Report the figure without stating any units at all
Check the units before using either of the figures
questions.why: A unit mismatch means one of them has been converted or misread, and establishing which is what makes the figure usable.
questions.traps: Specificity and authority both pick a side without checking, and omitting units makes the figure meaningless.

questions.stem: A team asks whether Claude can tell them when it has made something up.
options: Yes — it flags uncertain claims when asked to
Yes — provided the instruction is clearly worded
No — it does not know which parts are invented
No — but a second model can detect it reliably
questions.why: Fabricated content is produced by the same process as accurate content, so there is no internal marker available to report.
questions.traps: Flagging is inconsistent rather than reliable, wording does not create the capability, and a second model has exactly the same limitation.

questions.stem: An associate asks for "the problems with" an approach and gets a list of problems.
options: The list is a balanced assessment of the approach
The list shows the approach is a poor one overall
The list should be longer to be properly complete
The question asked for problems, so the list is one-sided
questions.why: The answer reflects what was asked, so a list of problems is a response to the question rather than a verdict on the approach.
questions.traps: Reading it as balanced misreads the question, treating it as a verdict is worse, and length does not address one-sidedness.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to check whether its output followed all the instructions given.
options: Accept the check, since the instructions are explicit
Check the output against the instructions yourself
Ask for the check to be repeated more carefully
Accept the check if it reports at least one miss
questions.why: Comparing text to a list is something a person can do directly, and doing it yourself removes the dependence on a self-report.
questions.traps: Explicit instructions do not guarantee a reliable self-check, repetition produces another self-report, and finding one miss does not validate the rest.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether one of their prompts is better than another.
options: Run both on the same inputs and compare the outputs
Run each on its own inputs and compare the results
Ask the team which prompt they prefer working with
Use whichever prompt produced the better last output
questions.why: Holding the inputs constant is what makes the difference attributable to the prompt rather than to the material it was given.
questions.traps: Different inputs confound the comparison, preference is not performance, and a single output is one sample of a noisy process.

questions.stem: A team's document quotes a figure from a summary of a report rather than the report.
options: Cite the summary, since that is where they read it
Cite the report, since that is where it originated
Cite both of them without checking either one
Cite the report, and check the summary quoted it right
questions.why: The report is the source and the summary is a route to it, so the citation names the report once the figure has been confirmed.
questions.traps: Citing the summary records the route, citing the report without checking assumes the summary transcribed it correctly, and citing both skips the check.

questions.stem: A team's review process is documented and nobody actually follows it in practice.
options: Enforce the documented process across the whole team
Find out why it is not followed before enforcing it
Rewrite the documentation to match what people do
Remove the documentation, since it is not being used
questions.why: A process nobody follows usually does not fit the work, and finding out is what determines whether to change the process or the practice.
questions.traps: Enforcement assumes the document is right, updating it assumes practice is right, and removing it abandons the standard entirely.

questions.stem: An answer covers what a policy requires and not when the policy actually applies.
options: Accept it, since the requirements were the question
Assume the policy applies to the current situation
Ask what the policy's scope of application is
Ask for a fuller answer about the whole policy
questions.why: Requirements without scope can be applied where they do not belong, and asking about scope directly recovers it.
questions.traps: Literal compliance leaves the risk in place, assuming applicability is the error, and a vague request for fullness does not name the gap.

questions.stem: A team defines good output as output that matches what they would have written.
options: A poor standard, since it rules out better answers
A good standard, since the team knows their own work
A good standard, since it is very easy to apply
A poor standard, since the team cannot write it all
questions.why: A standard defined as similarity to your own draft cannot recognise an output that is better than what you would have produced.
questions.traps: Familiarity with the work is not a quality criterion, ease of application is not validity, and capacity is a different objection.

questions.stem: An output rounds a figure and then uses the rounded figure in a further calculation.
options: Accept it, since the rounding error is a small one
Recalculate from the unrounded figure where possible
Round the final result to hide the discrepancy
Report both the rounded and unrounded versions
questions.why: Rounding errors compound through a calculation, so the unrounded value is what the later steps should be using.
questions.traps: Small errors accumulate, rounding the result conceals rather than corrects, and reporting both passes the problem on to the reader.

questions.stem: An output attributes a policy position to a government department without naming a document.
options: Find the document, or do not attribute the position
Attribute it, since the position sounds like theirs
Attribute it more vaguely to avoid being specific
Remove the attribution and keep the position stated
questions.why: Attributing a position to a named body is a factual claim about that body, which requires something concrete to point at.
questions.traps: Plausibility is not evidence, vagueness obscures an unsupported claim, and stating the position without attribution changes what is being asserted.

questions.stem: An output about a decision the team made praises the reasoning behind that decision.
options: Accept the praise, since the reasoning may be sound
Ask for the weaknesses in the reasoning as well
Note that the prompt told it whose decision it was
Discount it entirely, since it is clearly flattering
questions.why: Knowing whose decision it is changes how it is described, and recognising that is what puts the assessment into context.
questions.traps: The reasoning may be sound and the assessment still tilted, a follow-up patches one output, and discarding it loses valid observations.

questions.stem: An associate needs to confirm a date and the output gives one quite confidently.
options: Accept it, since the date is stated without hedging
Ask the model to confirm the date one more time
Accept it if it fits the surrounding timeline
Check the date against a source that records it
questions.why: Dates are precisely the kind of detail that is generated fluently and wrongly, and a record is what settles them.
questions.traps: Confidence is not accuracy, re-asking is not independent, and internal consistency can be consistently wrong.

questions.stem: An output lists eight sources and two of them cannot be found anywhere.
options: Check the other six, since two failures change the picture
Remove the two and use the other six as they are
Ask for two replacement sources to be supplied
Accept the six, since most of the list was genuine
questions.why: Two fabrications in eight is evidence about how the list was produced, which makes the remaining six newly uncertain.
questions.traps: Removing the two assumes the rest are sound, replacements come from the same process, and a majority being real is not reassurance.

questions.stem: A team's internal document has no author and is cited in an external submission.
options: Cite it as an internal document without an author
Cite the team itself as the author of the document
Remove the citation and state the claim directly
Establish who owns it before citing it externally
questions.why: An external citation asserts that a named body stands behind the content, which requires knowing who that body is.
questions.traps: An authorless citation cannot be followed up, naming the team may misattribute it, and stating it unattributed removes the support.

questions.stem: A team's threshold is met by 80% of outputs and the other 20% are sent anyway.
options: The threshold is set too high for the team's work
The threshold is not functioning as a threshold
The failing 20% should be improved until they pass
The threshold should be lowered to match reality
questions.why: A standard that does not change what gets sent is a description rather than a control.
questions.traps: Height is one hypothesis among several, improving the failures assumes the bar is right, and lowering it assumes the opposite.

questions.stem: An output's figures are drawn from a spreadsheet the associate has not opened.
options: Accept them, since the spreadsheet was the source given
Ask the model to quote the cells it took them from
Open the spreadsheet and check the figures against it
Check the figures against a different source instead
questions.why: A file being supplied does not guarantee it was read correctly, and the file itself is the cheapest place to check.
questions.traps: Provision is not verification, quoted cell references can be invented, and a different source answers a different question.

questions.stem: An output about a niche standard is detailed and the team cannot check any of it.
options: Accept it, since the level of detail suggests knowledge
Treat detail on a niche topic as a reason for caution
Accept it, since nothing in it appears contradictory
Ask the model how confident it is in the detail
questions.why: Sparse topics are where fabrication is most likely and detail is produced regardless, so richness is not reassurance.
questions.traps: Detail is a stylistic property, internal consistency is easy to generate, and a confidence report is another generated claim.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to evaluate a proposal and mentions the deadline is tomorrow.
options: Accept it, since the deadline is genuinely relevant
Note the possible effect and use the evaluation anyway
Ask for the evaluation again without the deadline
Ignore the evaluation, since the framing rushed it
questions.why: Removing the pressure from the prompt is what shows whether the assessment depended on it.
questions.traps: Relevance to the situation does not make it neutral context, noticing an effect without testing it changes nothing, and discarding the output overreacts.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to rate how difficult it found a task and it says it was easy.
options: Easy tasks are more likely to be done correctly
The rating is useful for prioritising review effort
The rating should be checked against the output quality
The rating describes the text, not the difficulty
questions.why: There is no internal experience of difficulty to report, so the rating is generated in the same way as the answer itself.
questions.traps: Inferring accuracy from a self-rating is the error, using it to prioritise trusts it, and checking it against quality treats it as a measurement.

questions.stem: A team notices worse performance on Fridays across four weeks of their data.
options: Four Fridays is too few to establish any pattern
Investigate what is different about their Fridays
Avoid running the workflow on Fridays for now
Accept it, since four weeks is a reasonable window
questions.why: Four observations of one weekday cannot separate a real effect from ordinary variation, which makes the pattern unestablished.
questions.traps: Investigating assumes the effect is real, avoiding Fridays acts on it, and calling four weeks reasonable ignores that it is four Fridays.

questions.stem: A team's two required reviewers both approve without either knowing the other did.
options: Keep both, since two approvals are safer than one
Have them review different aspects rather than the same
Reduce it to one reviewer, since the second adds nothing
Have the second reviewer see the first one's comments
questions.why: Two people doing the same read catch the same things, and splitting the aspects is what makes the second reviewer additive.
questions.traps: Two identical reviews are not twice the coverage, dropping one loses capacity that could be redirected, and sharing comments anchors the second reviewer.

questions.stem: A summary of three documents notes where they agree and not where they differ.
options: Accept it, since the agreements are the useful part
Ask for a longer summary covering all three fully
Ask specifically where the three documents disagree
Read the three documents and compare them yourself
questions.why: Disagreements are usually the informative part of a document set and are exactly what a summary tends to smooth over.
questions.traps: Agreement is the easy half, a longer summary may smooth the same way, and reading everything discards the summary's purpose.

questions.stem: An output gives a statistic and attributes it to "a recent survey" and no more.
options: Accept it, since the statistic is plausible enough
Use the statistic without the attribution phrase
Attribute it to "industry sources" more generally
Ask which survey, and check the figure inside it
questions.why: An unnamed survey cannot be checked, and naming it is what turns the statistic into something verifiable.
questions.traps: Plausibility is not evidence, dropping the attribution leaves an unsupported figure, and a vaguer attribution is less checkable still.

questions.stem: An associate finds a supporting source published by the organisation that made the claim.
options: Look for a source outside that organisation as well
Accept it, since the source directly supports the claim
Accept it, since the organisation is a credible one
Reject it, since the source cannot be independent
questions.why: An organisation confirming its own claim is not independent confirmation, so an outside source is what adds evidence.
questions.traps: Direct support from a related source is what the check is testing, credibility is not independence, and rejecting it discards a relevant source.

questions.stem: A team's output is judged good by its authors and poor by the people reading it.
options: The authors' judgement is better informed about intent
The two judgements should be averaged into one view
The readers' judgement is the one that matters here
The readers should be told what the output is for
questions.why: Output exists to serve its readers, so their assessment is the one that determines whether it works.
questions.traps: Knowing the intent is not knowing the effect, averaging incommensurable views decides nothing, and explaining the purpose argues rather than listens.

questions.stem: An output's calculation is correct and it uses a figure that is now out of date.
options: Accept it, since the calculation itself is correct
Redo it with the current figure, since the method is sound
Adjust the result for the change in the figure
Report the result with the date of the figure used
questions.why: A correct method applied to a stale input gives a stale answer, and rerunning it is what makes the result current.
questions.traps: Method correctness is not answer correctness, adjusting the result approximates rather than recomputes, and dating a stale figure leaves it stale.

questions.stem: An output about a competitor's pricing is specific and that pricing is not published.
options: Accept it, since the figures are specific and plausible
Ask the model where it obtained the pricing from
Use the figures as an estimate rather than as facts
Treat unpublished specifics as very likely invented
questions.why: Specific figures about information that is not public have no available source, which makes them generated rather than known.
questions.traps: Specificity is the tell rather than the reassurance, a source request produces an invented one, and relabelling them as estimates keeps using them.

questions.stem: A team's outputs consistently favour the option their prompt happens to describe first.
options: Vary the order across a set of cases and compare
Always list the preferred option second from now on
Accept it, since the first option is often the best one
Ask the model to ignore the order of the options
questions.why: Testing the effect across several cases is what establishes whether the order is driving the outcome or merely coinciding with it.
questions.traps: Reversing the order exploits the effect rather than testing it, coincidence is the hypothesis, and an instruction to ignore order is not a test.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to list what it does not know about a particular topic.
options: The list is a reliable map of the topic's gaps
The list should be treated as an exhaustive one
The list names known gaps, not the unknown ones
The list carries no information about the topic
questions.why: What is missing from an answer cannot be reported by the process that produced the answer, so the list covers only what it can articulate.
questions.traps: Treating it as a map or as exhaustive is the error, and dismissing it entirely discards a partially useful prompt.

questions.stem: An associate tests a new prompt on the four examples they happen to have available.
options: Note that four convenient cases are not a sample
Report the result as a measure of the prompt's accuracy
Test the same four examples using the old prompt too
Conclude nothing, since four cases are worthless
questions.why: Cases chosen for availability may not represent the work, so the result describes those four rather than the task.
questions.traps: Reporting it as accuracy overstates it, a comparison on four convenient cases inherits the same problem, and dismissing them discards real information.

questions.stem: A team wants a reviewer to check output in a format that hides its structure.
options: Keep the format, since it is what readers will see
Ask the reviewer to reconstruct the structure themselves
Have a second reviewer check the structure separately
Give the reviewer the format that makes errors visible
questions.why: A review finds what the presentation lets it find, so the reviewing format should be chosen for detection rather than for reading.
questions.traps: The reader's format is not the reviewer's tool, reconstruction wastes the reviewer's effort, and a second reviewer duplicates a fixable problem.

questions.stem: An output identifies who must approve a change and omits a conditional approver.
options: Accept it, since the main approvers were identified
Ask which approvals depend on the circumstances
Ask for the approver list to be produced again
Add the conditional approver from your own knowledge
questions.why: Conditional requirements are a category that a straightforward list will not surface, and asking about conditions is what recovers them.
questions.traps: The main approvers are what a list produces, regenerating repeats the same omission, and filling it in yourself fixes one document.

questions.stem: A team must show the chain from a claim in their report back to its original source.
options: Reconstruct the chain from the documents afterwards
Cite only the final source and omit the intermediate ones
Record each step at the time, since chains cannot be rebuilt
Cite the conversation as the link in the chain
questions.why: A provenance chain is cheap to record as it forms and effectively impossible to reconstruct once the intermediate steps are forgotten.
questions.traps: Reconstruction misses steps nobody remembers, omitting intermediates hides where an error entered, and a conversation is not part of the chain.

questions.stem: A team's output quality has improved and their stakeholders have not noticed at all.
options: Publicise the improvement so that stakeholders notice it
Ask what stakeholders judge that the team is not improving
Accept it, since the improvement is real regardless
Keep improving until the difference becomes obvious
questions.why: An unnoticed improvement usually means the effort went into a dimension stakeholders do not weigh, and asking is what finds the one they do.
questions.traps: Publicising argues rather than investigates, real-but-unvalued improvement is the problem, and more of the same compounds the misdirection.

questions.stem: An associate has verified a document and is asked how long that verification holds.
options: Only as long as the facts it rests on stay unchanged
Indefinitely, since the document was checked properly
Until the document itself is next edited by someone
For a fixed period agreed by the team in advance
questions.why: Verification is a statement about facts at a moment, so it expires when those facts move rather than on any schedule.
questions.traps: Permanence ignores changing facts, editing is one trigger among several, and a fixed period is arbitrary relative to the facts.

questions.stem: An output's figures are right and presented in a way that overstates the trend.
options: Accept it, since every figure in it is correct
Add a caveat about how the trend is presented
Remove the trend and present the figures alone
Change the presentation, since the framing is the error
questions.why: Correct numbers can be arranged to mislead, and the arrangement is where the fix belongs once the figures themselves check out.
questions.traps: Correct components do not make an honest presentation, a caveat leaves the misleading display in place, and removing the trend discards a real finding.

questions.stem: A team's checks find no fabrications and they only checked the checkable claims.
options: Say that the unverifiable claims remain unverified
Report that no fabrications were found in the document
Report the document as verified, since the checks passed
Treat the unverifiable claims as probably accurate
questions.why: A clean result on the checkable subset says nothing about the claims that could not be checked, and saying so keeps the report accurate.
questions.traps: A bare "no fabrications found" implies coverage it does not have, calling it verified overstates it, and inferring accuracy from the subset is the error.

questions.stem: A team's analysis is even-handed and its recommendation follows only one side of it.
options: The analysis is balanced, so the output is balanced
The recommendation follows from the stronger arguments
The recommendation should be removed from the output
The recommendation is where the framing actually sits
questions.why: A balanced analysis can carry a one-sided conclusion, and the step from analysis to recommendation is exactly where that happens.
questions.traps: Analytical balance is what makes it persuasive, assuming the arguments were stronger is untested, and deleting the recommendation avoids rather than examines it.

questions.stem: A team's review catches errors reliably and the errors keep recurring in new output.
options: Keep reviewing, since the errors are being caught
Increase the review effort to catch them faster
Feed what the review catches back into the prompt
Accept the recurrence, since the review is working
questions.why: A review that catches the same error repeatedly is describing a fixable upstream problem, and closing that loop is what stops the recurrence.
questions.traps: Catching them forever pays the cost forever, more review scales the symptom, and calling it working ignores the waste.

questions.stem: An answer is complete for the question asked and the reader needed a different one answered.
options: Accept it, since the question asked was answered
Find out what the reader actually needed to know
Answer the reader's question as a supplement to it
Ask the reader to phrase their question more precisely
questions.why: A complete answer to the wrong question is a failure of understanding rather than of execution, and finding the real need is the fix.
questions.traps: Literal completeness is what hides it, a supplement patches this instance, and asking the reader to be more precise shifts the work to them.

questions.stem: A process routes every output the model marks high-confidence straight to a customer.
options: The process is sound, since confidence tracks accuracy
The threshold for high confidence should be raised
Consequence should decide the routing, not the marking
All outputs should be reviewed before reaching a customer
questions.why: A weak internal signal is not a basis for skipping review on work that reaches a customer, where the consequence of an error is real.
questions.traps: A loose correlation does not support the inference, raising the threshold keeps the same dependence, and reviewing everything ignores which work is consequential.

questions.stem: A team measures accuracy on the cases their reviewers flagged as worth checking.
options: The sample is not representative of all the output
The sample is the most informative one available
The measurement understates the true accuracy
The measurement is reliable, since reviewers chose well
questions.why: Cases selected because they looked worth checking differ systematically from the output as a whole, so the figure does not generalise.
questions.traps: Informativeness for review is not representativeness, the direction of the bias is not obvious, and reviewer judgement is what creates the selection.

questions.stem: A team's report cites a figure to Claude on the grounds that Claude produced it.
options: Acceptable, since it records where the figure came from
Acceptable, since it is transparent about the method
Not acceptable, since assistance should not be disclosed
A tool is not a source, so the underlying source is needed
questions.why: A citation tells a reader where to check a claim, and naming the tool that generated it gives them nothing they can check.
questions.traps: Recording the route is not recording the source, transparency about method is a different obligation, and there is no rule against disclosing assistance.

questions.stem: A team applies the same quality bar to internal notes and to regulatory filings.
options: Keep one bar, since a single standard is easier to apply
Set the bar by what an error would cost in each case
Keep one bar set at the regulatory level throughout
Keep one bar set at the internal level for speed
questions.why: The cost of being wrong differs enormously between those two, and a standard that ignores that either overspends or underprotects.
questions.traps: Ease of application is what a single bar buys, the regulatory level overspends on notes, and the internal level underprotects the filing.

questions.stem: An associate finds a source supporting a claim that was itself written with AI assistance.
options: Reject it, since AI-assisted text may be unreliable
Accept it, since it is a published source either way
Judge it by whether it cites something checkable
Look for a source written without any assistance
questions.why: What matters is whether the source can be traced to something verifiable, which is the same test applied to any source at all.
questions.traps: A blanket rejection discards legitimate sources, publication is not verification, and screening by production method is neither practical nor the point.

questions.stem: A team's model and their spreadsheet disagree and both are internally consistent.
options: Trust the spreadsheet, since the team built it
Trust the model, since it shows all of its working
Average the two answers to split the difference
Find the assumption where the two of them diverge
questions.why: Two consistent methods disagreeing means they encode different assumptions, and locating that difference is what resolves it.
questions.traps: Provenance and visible working are both weak grounds for choosing, and averaging produces a number that neither method supports.

questions.stem: A team's output has been accurate for months and today contains an obvious fabrication.
options: Treat the record as topic-dependent rather than broken
Conclude the model's reliability has suddenly dropped
Treat the fabrication as a one-off and simply continue
Stop using the workflow until the cause has been found
questions.why: A long clean record on familiar material tells you little about a question that strays outside it, which is usually what has happened.
questions.traps: A sudden decline is the least likely explanation, dismissing it as a one-off ignores what it reveals, and halting everything overreacts to a scoped problem.

questions.stem: A team asks for a summary of feedback and the summary matches what they expected.
options: Accept it, since it confirms what the team already knew
Check the feedback for what the summary left out
Accept it, since expectation and reality often align
Ask for a summary that challenges their expectations
questions.why: A summary that confirms expectations is exactly when the omissions are least likely to be noticed, which makes checking most valuable.
questions.traps: Confirmation feels like validation, alignment is possible but untested, and asking for a contrarian summary substitutes one bias for another.

questions.stem: An associate has an accurate draft written for specialists and the readers are non-specialists.
options: Send it as it is, since the content is entirely accurate
Add a glossary at the end and leave the text unchanged
Ask the readers to look up the terms they do not know
Rewrite it for the audience who will actually read it
Say who the audience is when asking for the revision
questions.why: Accuracy and fitness for an audience are different properties, so naming the real reader is what gets a draft that lands with them.
questions.traps: Accuracy does not make it usable, a glossary bolts onto the problem, and pushing the work to readers is how documents go unread.

questions.stem: A team must adapt one analysis for an executive summary and for a technical appendix.
options: Shorten the same text for one and lengthen it for the other
Let each version carry what its own reader needs
Use identical content and vary only the tone between them
Produce one version and let each reader skim what they need
Change what is included, not only how it is worded
questions.why: Adapting for an audience changes the selection of content, not just its register, because different readers need different facts rather than the same facts styled differently.
questions.traps: Length and tone are surface changes, and one version for both leaves each reader filtering material meant for the other.

questions.stem: An associate is comparing two drafts of the same message and cannot decide between them.
options: Combine them into a single longer third version
Ask which one the intended reader would act on
Pick the longer one, since it covers more ground
Judge them against what the message has to achieve
Pick whichever one reads more fluently overall
questions.why: Comparison needs a criterion, and for a message that criterion is the effect on its reader rather than how it reads to the writer.
questions.traps: Fluency and length are properties of the text rather than of its effect, and merging two drafts usually produces a worse third.

questions.stem: A team's output is technically correct and consistently ignored by the people it is written for.
options: Shorten it, since length is the most likely problem
Insist the readers engage with what has been produced
Treat readability for that audience as part of quality
Ask those readers what would make it worth reading
Accept it, since correctness is what the team controls
questions.why: Output that goes unread has failed at its purpose, so the readers' account of why is the information the quality standard is missing.
questions.traps: Insisting ignores evidence, shortening guesses at the cause, and treating correctness as the whole of quality is what produced the gap.

questions.stem: An associate must choose how to deliver a result that a colleague needs to work with directly.
options: Whichever format the associate finds quickest to produce
Always inline, since it needs no extra step to open
Always an artifact, since it looks more considered
Inline text, if they only need to read the conclusion
An artifact, if the colleague will interact with the result
questions.why: Format follows what the receiver will do with the output, which is what separates something to read from something to use.
questions.traps: Producer convenience is not the criterion, and both absolute rules ignore what the colleague actually needs.

questions.stem: A team needs output that another system will consume automatically rather than a person.
options: Ask for prose and let the receiving system parse it
Ask for structured data in an agreed fixed shape
Fix the structure with a deterministic step after generation
Have a person retype the values into the other system
Ask for a nicely formatted document for readability
questions.why: A machine consumer needs a stable structure, and generated text varies, so the shape has to be both specified and enforced after the fact.
questions.traps: Parsing prose is fragile, human readability is the wrong goal here, and retyping puts a person inside an automated path.

questions.stem: A team asks when curating information matters more than producing more of it.
options: When the volume produced already exceeds what is read
When the subject is technically complex to describe
When the reader has to act on a decision quickly
When the output will be stored rather than circulated
When the audience is more senior than the author is
questions.why: Curation earns its place where attention is the scarce resource, which is exactly the case for a decision under time pressure and for output nobody finishes reading.
questions.traps: Complexity, seniority and storage describe the material and its route rather than the reader's capacity to absorb it.

questions.stem: An associate's structured output is correct and the receiving team keeps reworking it by hand.
options: Tell them the output already meets the agreed format
Ask what they rework and build that into the format
Accept it, since reworking is their own choice to make
Treat the rework as an unmet requirement in the spec
Add a review step before the output reaches them
questions.why: Silent rework is a requirement nobody wrote down, so collecting what they change is what turns the effort into a fixable specification.
questions.traps: Asserting compliance answers a question they did not ask, treating it as their choice hides a real cost, and another review checks against the wrong standard.

questions.stem: An associate needs to verify a claim and has only the output that made the claim.
options: Find a source independent of the thing being checked
Treat the claim as unverified until such a source is found
Ask the model to confirm the claim a second time
Ask the model how confident it is about the claim
Accept it, since nothing so far contradicts the claim
questions.why: Verification requires evidence from outside the thing being verified, which is what makes independence the whole point rather than a refinement.
questions.traps: Re-asking produces another output from the same source, absence of contradiction is not evidence, and self-reported confidence is one more generated claim.

questions.stem: An associate has limited time and ten claims to check in a document.
options: Say which claims were checked when passing it on
Check the claims the conclusion actually rests on
Check the ones that look least plausible on the face of it
Check them in the order that they appear in the text
Check anything that would be expensive to get wrong
questions.why: Limited verification is allocated by consequence and reported honestly, so the reader knows which parts carry evidence and which do not.
questions.traps: Document order is arbitrary, and implausibility is a weak proxy for whether an error would actually matter.

questions.stem: An associate spots that one figure in a briefing was invented and the briefing holds many more.
options: Recognise that one fabrication is evidence about the process
Check a small random sample of the remaining citations
Treat every other citation as newly uncertain
Correct that citation and rely on the rest as they are
Remove all the citations rather than checking any of them
questions.why: A fabrication says something about how the document was produced, which changes the prior on everything produced the same way.
questions.traps: Fixing one assumes it was isolated, removing citations destroys the grounding, and a small sample can easily miss the others.

questions.stem: A team receives a confident, detailed answer about their own internal process.
options: Accept it, since the description matches what they expected
Ask the model where it obtained the information from
Accept it if nothing in it appears self-contradictory
Check it against the team's own documentation
Recognise the model has no access to that process
questions.why: A model cannot know an organisation's internal process, so a confident answer about one is generated, and the documentation is what settles it.
questions.traps: Matching expectations is exactly how a plausible fabrication passes, a source request produces an invented source, and internal consistency is easy to generate.

questions.stem: A market summary quotes a share figure to one decimal place and names no source for it.
options: Round it, since the precision is probably overstated
Ask for the same figure again to see if it matches
Accept it, since precise figures are rarely invented
Treat the figure as unsupported until it is sourced
Precision is not itself evidence of accuracy here
questions.why: Fabricated numbers are produced with the same precision as real ones, so the decimal places carry no information about whether it is true.
questions.traps: Rounding an unsourced figure leaves it unsourced, and asking again is not an independent check.

questions.stem: A team's output is accurate on everything checkable and much of it cannot be checked.
options: Discard the whole output, since gaps remain in it
Report the document as verified, since checks all passed
Treat the unverifiable parts as probably accurate too
Say which parts were verified when passing it on
Avoid generalising from the checked part to the rest
questions.why: A clean result on the checkable subset says nothing about the rest, so the honest report distinguishes the two rather than extending one verdict over both.
questions.traps: Calling it verified overstates the coverage, inferring accuracy is the error itself, and discarding verified work overreacts.

questions.stem: An associate asks why an approach is better than the alternative and gets a strong case for it.
options: Ask for the drawbacks as a separate follow-up
Accept it, since the reasoning given is sound
The question itself presupposed its own conclusion
Ask the same question about the other approach too
Ask an open question that does not assume an answer
questions.why: A question built on a conclusion returns an answer built on it, so removing the presupposition is what makes the comparison real.
questions.traps: Sound reasoning for a presupposed conclusion is still one-sided, and a follow-up patches one output rather than the question.

questions.stem: A team notices their outputs consistently favour whichever option the prompt lists first.
options: Always list the preferred option second from now on
Vary the order across several cases and compare
Establish whether order is driving the outcome at all
Instruct the model to disregard the order given
Accept it, since the first option is often the best one
questions.why: An order effect is cheap to test by reordering across cases, which is what distinguishes a real effect from a coincidence.
questions.traps: Exploiting the effect is not correcting it, coincidence is the hypothesis being tested, and an instruction to ignore order is not a test.

questions.stem: A team's analysis is even-handed and every example it uses supports one side.
options: Accept it, since the argument itself is balanced
Remove the examples so the argument stands alone
A balanced argument can still lead the reader
Selection of examples is where the framing sits
Add more examples until the balance is restored
questions.why: Illustration carries as much persuasive weight as argument, so an evenly argued piece with one-sided examples still steers its reader.
questions.traps: Argumentative balance is what disguises it, adding examples without examining the selection repeats it, and removing them loses the illustration.

questions.stem: A summary of a policy is accurate and leaves out the section on exceptions.
options: Accept it, since everything it does say is accurate
Ask for a longer summary covering more of the document
Read the whole policy instead of using any summary
Recognise accuracy and completeness as different properties
Ask specifically about the exceptions that were omitted
questions.why: A summary can be entirely accurate and still omit the part that changes the answer, so the missing category has to be asked for by name.
questions.traps: A longer summary may omit the same section, and abandoning summarisation discards its value entirely.

questions.stem: A team asks for the downsides of a proposal and every item listed is a way it could fail.
options: Add the success case to the list by hand afterwards
Ask for a longer and more thorough list of risks
Accept it, since a risk list should cover risks
Ask about the case where the plan simply succeeds
A failure-focused frame will not produce that case
questions.why: Some real risks are not failures — a plan succeeding and proving unnecessary is one — and a list framed around failure will never surface them.
questions.traps: A longer list extends the same frame, and adding it manually fixes one document rather than the prompt.

questions.stem: A team's answer is complete for the question asked and the question asked was wrong.
options: Recognise this as a failure of framing, not execution
Accept the answer, since it did address the question
Ask a supplementary question to cover the difference
Fix the question, since the answer cannot exceed it
Ask for a broader answer to the original question
questions.why: An output is bounded by the question behind it, so a well-executed answer to the wrong question is a framing problem.
questions.traps: Literal correctness is what hides the failure, a supplement bolts onto a wrong frame, and breadth does not correct direction.

questions.stem: A report says a metric improved by a third and does not say what it improved from.
options: Ask for the base figure the percentage is taken from
Use it, since the direction of change is clear enough
A percentage change is uninterpretable without its base
Assume the base is the earlier of the two figures
Recalculate the percentage from the team's own figures
questions.why: The base defines what the percentage means, so without it the number cannot be interpreted, let alone checked.
questions.traps: Direction is not magnitude, an assumed base can invert the meaning, and recalculating from other figures answers a different question.

questions.stem: A supplier summary's totals all reconcile with each other and none match the team's ledger.
options: Find which of the two sets is wrong before using either
Internal consistency is not the same as correctness
Use the team's records, since those are authoritative
Use the output's figures, since they are self-consistent
Report both sets and note that the two disagree
questions.why: A self-consistent set of numbers can be uniformly wrong, so the disagreement is a question to resolve rather than a preference to exercise.
questions.traps: Assuming the records are right skips the check, and publishing both hands an unresolved contradiction to the reader.

questions.stem: Every number in a recommendation checks out and the recommendation itself does not follow.
options: Check the reasoning, since the arithmetic already passed
Accept the conclusion, since the figures support it
Ask for the conclusion to be restated more carefully
Recheck the figures, since the conclusion is wrong
The fault lies between the figures and the conclusion
questions.why: Correct inputs with a wrong output isolate the fault to the step between them, which is where the checking effort belongs.
questions.traps: Rechecking verified figures repeats work, assuming support is the error, and restating a wrong conclusion does not correct it.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer reads each output from start to finish and approves nearly all of them.
options: Look at what has slipped past the review so far
Add a second reviewer to increase the scrutiny
Accept it, since a high approval rate is reassuring
Check against named criteria rather than reading through
Read each output twice so that less is missed
questions.why: Fluent text invites confirmation, so a review becomes a control when it checks specific things and when its escapes are examined.
questions.traps: Reading twice and adding readers repeat the same vulnerable process, and a high approval rate is consistent with a useless check.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce review effort without losing the protection it provides.
options: Reduce it uniformly across all of the team's work
Keep it where a missed error would reach a customer
Keep reviewing everything at exactly the same depth
Reduce it where an error would be caught downstream
Replace review with a check the model performs itself
questions.why: Review is a cost paid against consequence, so it is relaxed where something else would catch the error and kept where nothing would.
questions.traps: Uniform reduction ignores which work is consequential, reviewing everything equally spends most effort where it matters least, and self-review is not independent.

questions.stem: A team's review catches the same category of error month after month.
options: Increase review effort so they are caught sooner
Feed what the review catches back into the prompt
Treat a recurring catch as a fixable upstream problem
Keep reviewing, since the errors are being caught
Accept the recurrence as the cost of using the tool
questions.why: A review that repeatedly catches one thing is describing a defect upstream, and closing that loop is what stops paying for the catch forever.
questions.traps: Catching them indefinitely pays the cost indefinitely, more review scales the symptom, and acceptance normalises avoidable waste.

questions.stem: A team reports a 90% accuracy figure measured on twenty test cases.
options: Withhold the figure until far more cases are tested
Report 90%, since that is what the test produced
Recognise that twenty cases give a wide margin
Report the sample size alongside the percentage
Round it to "about 90%" to avoid false precision
questions.why: A percentage from a small sample carries a wide interval, so the sample size is part of the finding rather than a footnote.
questions.traps: A bare percentage implies certainty it does not have, rounding is cosmetic, and withholding discards real information.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude whether its own output followed every instruction in the prompt.
options: Treat the reply as another output, not as a check
Check the output against the instructions yourself
Accept it if the reply identifies at least one miss
Accept the reply, since the instructions were explicit
Ask for the self-check to be repeated more carefully
questions.why: A self-assessment comes from the same process as the output, so it cannot serve as independent verification of that output.
questions.traps: Explicit instructions do not make a self-report reliable, repetition produces another self-report, and finding one miss does not validate the rest.

questions.stem: An associate's claim came from Claude, which drew it from a document the team holds.
options: Cite Claude, since that is where they encountered it
Recognise the conversation as a route, not a source
Cite both the document and the conversation together
Cite the document, since the claim originates there
Cite nothing, since the claim is now the team's own
questions.why: A citation points a reader at something they can check, which is the document rather than the conversation that surfaced it.
questions.traps: Citing the tool records the route, citing both adds noise, and citing nothing removes the provenance entirely.

questions.stem: A support team must classify roughly 50,000 tickets a day into twelve well-documented categories. Cost per ticket and response latency are both hard limits.
options: Opus, because classification accuracy is the highest-stakes property of this workflow
Sonnet, as a mid-tier model is the safe default whenever the requirements are not yet clear
