Expect input variety, error handling and review capacity to change, not just cost
Expect nothing to change until the volume is reached
questions.why: A hundredfold increase surfaces input variety the pilot never saw and outstrips any review process built for 500. Cost is the most visible change, not the only one.
questions.traps: Assuming only cost scales is the misconception. Unit pricing is a separate question, and waiting to find out defers the planning that matters.

questions.stem: An associate needs the same five checks applied to every document the team produces, and people currently remember them inconsistently.
options: Circulate a checklist so each person applies the five checks themselves before submitting their work
Encode the checks in project instructions so they are applied to every response
Ask Claude to recall the checks at the start of each conversation
Audit a sample of finished documents against the five checks
questions.why: Standing checks belong in configuration, which is what makes them automatic rather than dependent on individual memory that has already proven inconsistent.
questions.traps: A circulated checklist relies on the consistency that is already failing. Per-conversation recall is manual, and sampling accepts inconsistency by design.

questions.stem: A team discovers that most of their cost comes from a small number of very long documents rather than from request volume.
options: Reduce the overall number of requests across the whole team so the total cost falls proportionally
Move every request to a cheaper tier so the total spend falls
Ask people to submit shorter documents so each one costs less
Handle the long documents differently, since they are where the cost concentrates
questions.why: Cost concentrated in a few large inputs is addressed by treating those inputs differently, not by uniform reductions that mostly affect the cheap majority.
questions.traps: Cutting overall volume mostly reduces inexpensive requests. A cheaper tier pays less for the same skew, and shorter submissions may not be possible.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to act on a schedule without anyone triggering it, producing a report every Monday at 6am.
options: A scheduled automation, since unattended execution needs something that runs on its own
A Project with instructions saying the report should be produced every Monday morning at six, so the schedule is recorded alongside the rest of the configuration
A calendar reminder for someone to run it manually
A conversation left open over the weekend so it is ready Monday
questions.why: Unattended scheduled execution requires a scheduler. Configuration describing a schedule does not cause anything to run.
questions.traps: Instructions describe intent without triggering execution. A reminder makes it manual, and an open conversation does nothing on its own.

questions.stem: A team is choosing between spending on a stronger tier and spending the same amount on better source documents.
options: Spend on the stronger tier, since model capability affects every task the team runs
Spend on better documents, since inputs constrain everything downstream
Split the available budget evenly between the two options
Test which change moves the result more, since both are plausible and only one is measured
questions.why: Two competing hypotheses with a fixed budget is an empirical question. Testing which lever moves the outcome is what makes the spend defensible.
questions.traps: Both assertions are plausible and untested. Splitting the budget buys half of each without learning which mattered.

questions.stem: An associate wants their Project to behave differently for two distinct kinds of question, but a single instruction set applies to both.
options: Write conditional instructions describing which behaviour applies to which kind of question, so a single Project can serve both purposes
Ask people to specify which mode they want in each question
Use two Projects, since standing instructions apply to everything in one of them
Alternate the instructions from one week to the next
questions.why: Standing instructions apply to every response in a Project. When two behaviours are genuinely different, separate Projects is the structural answer.
questions.traps: Conditional instructions ask the model to classify correctly every time. Per-question mode selection puts the burden on users, and alternating serves neither well.

questions.stem: A team notices their cheapest-tier workflow fails specifically on inputs longer than about ten pages.
options: Move everything to a stronger tier, since the team cannot always predict in advance which inputs will exceed the length where the cheaper tier begins to fail
Route long inputs to a stronger tier and keep the cheap one for the rest
Truncate inputs to ten pages before processing them
Accept that long inputs will sometimes fail and move on
questions.why: A clean, observable predictor of failure is exactly what makes routing work. Input length is known before the request, so the split is reliable.
questions.traps: Upgrading everything ignores a usable signal that is trivially available. Truncation discards content, and accepting failures on long inputs abandons those cases.

questions.stem: A team's manual review process handles 50 items a day comfortably. The workflow they are scaling will produce 800 a day.
options: Redesign the review approach, since a process built for 50 will not stretch to 800
Hire additional reviewers so the existing review process can be applied to the full volume at the same depth it is currently applied to the fifty daily items
Keep the same review process and let the backlog grow
Ask reviewers to work faster so the whole volume is covered
questions.why: A sixteenfold increase breaks a process designed for the smaller volume. Redesigning around risk-weighted review is what makes the control survive the scale.
questions.traps: Linear hiring is expensive and may not be available. A growing backlog is a failing control, and asking for speed degrades the check.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to work from a document but is not allowed to upload it because of a data classification rule.
options: Upload the document anyway, since the analysis is internal and the resulting output will not be shared outside the organisation or retained beyond the current task
Paste the document's text rather than uploading the file
Summarise the document by hand and work from the summary
Confirm what the classification permits before choosing any technical approach
questions.why: A classification rule is a governance constraint, and the permitted approaches follow from what it actually says. Establishing that comes before any technical choice.
questions.traps: Uploading against the rule is a policy breach regardless of intent. Pasting is the same disclosure by another route, and hand-summarising may also be prohibited.

questions.stem: A team's workflow runs a second verification call on every output, doubling the cost. Verification catches an error roughly once in eighty runs.
options: Remove the verification step, since catching one error in eighty runs does not justify doubling the cost of every single request the workflow makes
Keep the verification, since any error caught is worth the cost
Weigh the doubled cost against what one error in eighty would cost if it escaped
Run the verification call on a random tenth of outputs
questions.why: The decision needs both numbers: the doubled cost and the cost of an escaped error. One in eighty may be cheap or catastrophic depending on what the error does.
questions.traps: Both blanket answers decide without the consequence figure. Random sampling reduces cost and catch rate together without reasoning about either.

questions.stem: A team's task involves both simple extraction and difficult judgement, currently handled in a single request on an expensive tier.
options: Keep the single request, since splitting introduces a handoff between steps where information can be lost and adds complexity to a workflow that currently works reliably
Split the task so the simple part runs cheaply and only the judgement uses the strong tier
Move the whole combined task to a cheaper model tier
Run the task twice on different tiers and compare
questions.why: Mixed-difficulty work in one request pays the top rate for the easy portion. Splitting lets each part run on the tier it needs.
questions.traps: Keeping it whole overpays for the extraction. Downgrading everything under-serves the judgement, and duplicate runs double the cost.

questions.stem: A team's shared Project is used by twelve people, and one of them keeps changing the instructions to suit their own workflow.
options: Ask that person to stop making changes to the shared instructions
Give that person a separate Project of their own to configure
Revert the shared instructions whenever they are changed
Establish who owns the configuration and how changes are agreed
questions.why: Shared configuration needs an ownership model, otherwise every user is an editor and the behaviour drifts. That is a governance fix rather than an interpersonal one.
questions.traps: A request without a rule relies on goodwill. A separate Project addresses one person, and reverting is an ongoing conflict rather than a resolution.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know if the newest model is automatically the right choice for their existing, well-tuned workflow.
options: Test it against the current setup, since a newer model is not automatically better for a tuned workflow
Adopt it, since newer models are generally more capable and the workflow will benefit from the improvement
Stay on the current model indefinitely to avoid any disruption
Adopt the newer model for new workflows only, not existing ones
questions.why: A prompt tuned against one model may not transfer cleanly. Testing is what establishes whether the change helps this particular workflow.
questions.traps: Assuming newer is better for a tuned setup skips the test. Never changing forgoes real improvements, and a new-work-only rule avoids the question.

questions.stem: A team wants non-technical staff to run a workflow that currently requires someone to assemble three documents and write a careful prompt each time.
options: Write a detailed instruction document explaining how to assemble the three documents and construct the prompt, so any staff member can follow the same procedure reliably
Have the technical person run the workflow whenever it is needed
Package it as a Project so the documents and prompt are already in place
Train all the staff to assemble and write the prompt themselves
questions.why: Packaging the assembly into configuration removes the expertise requirement entirely. Staff supply only what actually varies.
questions.traps: A procedure document leaves the assembly manual and error-prone. A single operator is a bottleneck, and training everyone is disproportionate.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to explain a decision it made three weeks ago in a conversation that has since been deleted.
options: Ask Claude to recall the conversation and explain the reasoning it used at the time
Recognise the reasoning is not recoverable and rebuild the analysis from the inputs
Ask Claude to reconstruct what it probably said three weeks ago
Check whether a colleague remembers the explanation
questions.why: A deleted conversation is gone, and asking for a reconstruction produces a plausible account rather than a record. Rebuilding from the inputs is honest.
questions.traps: Both recall options invite fabrication presented as memory. A colleague's recollection is weak evidence about a specific analysis.

questions.stem: A team's costs spiked in one week with no change in usage volume. They have per-request logs available.
options: Move to a cheaper tier to bring the cost back down to its previous level before investigating what caused the increase, so the budget impact is contained immediately
Assume it was a pricing change and query the invoice
Examine the logs to find which requests changed in size or shape that week
Average the cost over the quarter so the spike is less visible
questions.why: Per-request logs make the cause directly findable. Diagnosing before acting is what prevents an unnecessary change to a workflow that may be fine.
questions.traps: Downgrading treats a symptom of an unknown cause. Assuming a pricing change skips available evidence, and averaging conceals the signal.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works on the strongest tier and fails on every cheaper one, and they have not examined why it fails.
options: Accept that the task requires the strongest tier and budget accordingly
Retest the cheaper tiers using a longer and fuller prompt
Use the strongest tier and revisit the question next year
Look at how the cheaper tiers fail, since the pattern may point at a fixable prompt issue
questions.why: The failure mode carries diagnostic information. A consistent structural failure often reflects under-specification that a capable model absorbs and a cheaper one does not.
questions.traps: Accepting the result without examining it forgoes a likely saving. A longer prompt is an untargeted change, and deferring keeps paying meanwhile.

questions.stem: An associate is asked whether a workflow should be rolled out to a team that works in a language the pilot never tested.
options: Roll out, since the workflow logic is language-independent and the model handles many languages capably enough for the same process to produce comparable results
Test in that language before rolling out, since performance varies across languages
Roll out with an instruction to work in the new language
Roll out and have the outputs translated after they are produced
questions.why: Model performance varies by language, so an untested language is an untested workload. Testing is what turns the assumption into knowledge.
questions.traps: Assuming language independence is the misconception. An instruction does not establish quality, and translating afterwards adds a step and a new error source.

questions.stem: A team wants to preserve a particularly good conversation so its approach can be reused, but conversations are not a durable store.
options: Extract what made it work into reusable configuration rather than keeping the thread
Keep the conversation open and return to it whenever similar work comes up, continuing from the point where the good result was originally produced by the team
Export the conversation as a text file for reference
Ask Claude to summarise what made the conversation effective
questions.why: The reusable asset is the prompt and context that produced the result, not the transcript. Extracting it into configuration is what makes it repeatable.
questions.traps: A long-running thread degrades and cannot be shared cleanly. An export is a record rather than a working setup, and a summary is commentary rather than configuration.

questions.stem: An associate needs a quick answer about a topic requiring no documents or history.
options: Create a Project so the answer is kept for later
Just ask in a plain conversation and then move on
Attach related documents so the answer is grounded
Use a scheduled task so it can be repeated later
questions.why: A one-off question with no context needs no structure around it, and the setup would cost more than the answer is worth.
questions.traps: A Project, attachments and scheduling all add machinery for a question that will not recur.

questions.stem: A team asks the same kinds of question about the same five documents every week.
options: Attach the five documents to each conversation
Paste the relevant passages into each question
Keep one long conversation and add to it weekly
Put the documents in a Project the team shares
questions.why: Recurring questions against stable documents is exactly what a Project is for, since the material is then always present.
questions.traps: Re-attaching and pasting repeat work every week, and one long conversation grows until earlier material falls out of reach.

questions.stem: An associate asks what ought to decide which model tier a particular task uses.
options: The tier the rest of the team is already using
The newest tier that is currently available to them
What the task actually demands of the model itself
The tier that costs the least to run at volume
questions.why: Tier choice is a fit question, so the difficulty of the task is what settles it rather than habit, novelty or price alone.
questions.traps: Team habit, recency and cost are all inputs to the decision rather than the thing being matched.

questions.stem: A team's overnight batch finishes at three in the morning and is needed by eight.
options: Latency is not the constraint here, so optimise cost
Optimise latency, since faster is always better
Optimise both equally, since both always matter
Leave it alone, since the job already completes
questions.why: With five hours of slack, speed buys nothing, which makes cost the dimension worth working on.
questions.traps: "Faster is better" ignores that the deadline is already met, splitting effort spends on a non-constraint, and leaving it alone forgoes an available saving.

questions.stem: A team needs a model to extract three fixed fields from a standard printed form.
options: The strongest tier, since accuracy matters most
The strongest tier, since forms vary in practice
A cheaper tier is likely to be sufficient here
Whichever tier the team already has configured
questions.why: A narrow, well-defined extraction is the kind of task cheaper tiers handle reliably, so paying for more capability buys little.
questions.traps: Accuracy concerns are addressed by testing rather than by always buying the top tier, and existing configuration is not a fit argument.

questions.stem: An associate wants a colleague to interact with a result rather than just read about it.
options: Write a rather longer explanation of the result
Produce it as something the colleague can use
Send the conversation that produced the result
Summarise the result in a short written message
questions.why: When the point is for someone to explore a result, a thing they can interact with does what prose cannot.
questions.traps: More prose, the source conversation and a summary are all still reading rather than using.

questions.stem: A pilot ran on fifty items and the team now wants to run five thousand a week.
options: Check what changes at that volume before scaling
Scale up, since the pilot worked at fifty items
Scale up gradually and watch for any problems
Rerun the pilot on a hundred items to be sure
questions.why: A hundredfold increase changes cost, latency and the range of inputs met, and checking those is what makes the scale-up informed.
questions.traps: Assuming the pilot generalises is the risk, gradual scaling discovers problems in production, and doubling the pilot tests none of the volume effects.

questions.stem: An associate has a document they will use once and never look at again afterwards.
options: Add it to a Project so it is available later on
Create a new Project just for that one document
Paste its full text into the conversation instead
Attach it to the conversation rather than a Project
questions.why: A Project is for material that recurs, and a single-use document belongs with the single conversation that uses it.
questions.traps: Adding it to a Project or creating one clutters the knowledge base, and pasting a full document wastes the room it occupies.

questions.stem: A team's costs are driven by one workflow and they do not know which one it is.
options: Break the spend down by workflow before acting
Reduce usage across every workflow proportionally
Move every workflow to a cheaper tier all at once
Cap the total spend and let the workflows compete
questions.why: An undiagnosed bill is fixed by finding where the money goes, since one workflow usually dominates and the rest are noise.
questions.traps: Across-the-board cuts penalise workflows that cost little, a blanket tier move risks quality everywhere, and a cap defers the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A task requires holding several conditions in mind at once and applying them together.
options: A cheaper tier, since the conditions are written down
A stronger tier, since the reasoning is the demand
A cheaper tier with a longer, more detailed prompt
Whichever tier is fastest, since the task is short
questions.why: Combining several conditions is reasoning work, and that is the dimension stronger tiers actually differ on.
questions.traps: Written conditions still have to be held together, prompt length does not supply reasoning, and speed is not the constraint here.

questions.stem: A team wants staff to reach Claude without leaving the tool they work in all day.
options: Ask staff to keep a second window open alongside
Train staff to switch tools when they need it
Put it inside the tool they are already using daily
Send staff a link they can open when required
questions.why: Adoption follows the path of least friction, and the tool people already have open is the shortest path there is.
questions.traps: A second window, switching and links all ask the user to leave what they are doing.

questions.stem: A new model tier is released and a team's current workflow is already performing well.
options: Switch to it, since newer models are generally better
Stay put, since the current workflow already works
Switch and keep the old one running as a fallback
Test it before deciding, since new is not automatically better
questions.why: A tuned workflow is tuned to a particular model, so the only way to know whether a new one helps is to run the comparison.
questions.traps: Switching on release assumes an improvement, staying put forgoes one, and running both doubles the cost without deciding.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to work with the figures inside a large spreadsheet.
options: Describe the spreadsheet's contents in the prompt
Give it the spreadsheet rather than describing it
Paste the rows that seem most relevant to the task
Convert the spreadsheet into prose before sending it
questions.why: The file itself carries the structure and the values, which is what any analysis of it depends on.
questions.traps: A description loses the data, a selected subset assumes the answer's location, and prose destroys the structure.

questions.stem: A team's per-request cost is dominated by a style guide sent with every request.
options: Move the style guide somewhere it is not resent
Shorten the style guide until the cost is acceptable
Send the style guide only on the first request
Accept the cost, since the guide improves the output
questions.why: Material that is identical on every request is exactly what should live outside the request rather than being paid for repeatedly.
questions.traps: Shortening loses guidance, first-request-only means later requests lack it, and accepting the cost forgoes an easy saving.

questions.stem: A team's task is mostly simple with roughly one case in twenty needing real judgement.
options: Use the stronger tier for everything, just to be safe
Use the cheaper tier and accept the hard cases failing
Route by case rather than choosing one tier for all
Use the cheaper tier and review every output by hand
questions.why: A mixed workload does not have one right tier, and separating the cases is what lets each be handled at its own cost.
questions.traps: One strong tier overpays on nineteen cases in twenty, accepting failures is choosing to be wrong, and reviewing everything is expensive.

questions.stem: A team measures three tiers at 91%, 93% and 94% accuracy with costs rising steeply.
options: Take the 94%, since accuracy is what matters most
Take the 91%, since the difference is only three points
Take the middle tier as a reasonable compromise
Ask what the extra points are worth in this use
questions.why: Three points of accuracy is worth a lot in some uses and nothing in others, and only the use can say which this is.
questions.traps: Maximising accuracy ignores the price, dismissing three points ignores what they might cost, and splitting the difference decides without a reason.

questions.stem: A team's Project has grown to forty documents and answers have become less precise.
options: Reduce it to what the questions actually reach for
Split it into two Projects of twenty documents each
Add instructions telling the model which to prefer
Accept it, since more material means more coverage
questions.why: Precision falls when retrieval has to choose among material that no question uses, and curation is what restores it.
questions.traps: An arbitrary split keeps the bloat in two places, preference instructions do not reduce what is present, and coverage is causing the problem.

questions.stem: A team wants a report produced every Monday without anyone remembering to ask for it.
options: Put a recurring reminder in the team's calendar
Ask one named person to run it each Monday morning
Run it whenever someone notices it is missing
Use a surface that is able to run on a schedule
questions.why: A task that should happen without prompting needs something that triggers itself rather than a person who remembers.
questions.traps: Reminders, an assigned person and ad-hoc running all depend on a human not forgetting.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to check figures in a PDF against those in a spreadsheet.
options: Provide the PDF and type the spreadsheet figures in
Provide both of the files and ask for the comparison
Compare them by hand and ask about the differences
Convert both into a single document before asking
questions.why: Giving both sources lets the comparison be made against what each actually says rather than against a transcription.
questions.traps: Typing figures in introduces errors, comparing by hand is the work being delegated, and merging them first is unnecessary effort.

questions.stem: A pilot's benefit came from two enthusiastic volunteers and the rollout covers forty people.
options: Project the pilot's benefit across all forty people
Cancel the rollout, since the pilot was unrepresentative
Expect a smaller benefit and plan for the difference
Roll out only to the people who volunteer for it
questions.why: Volunteers are not typical users, so the pilot's figure is an upper bound rather than a forecast.
questions.traps: Multiplying up assumes everyone behaves like a volunteer, cancelling discards a real result, and restricting to volunteers never reaches the team.

questions.stem: A team's chatbot must answer within three seconds and currently takes four.
options: Move to a faster tier and see whether that helps
Find where the four seconds is actually being spent
Shorten the prompt to reduce the processing time
Raise the response budget from three seconds to five
questions.why: A second has to come from somewhere specific, and knowing where the time goes is what makes the fix land.
questions.traps: Changing tier or prompt are guesses at the cause, and moving the budget changes the requirement rather than meeting it.

questions.stem: A team's workflow fails on the cheaper tier and they have not tried improving the prompt.
options: Improve the prompt before concluding the tier is the limit
Move to the stronger tier, since the cheaper one fails
Stay on the cheaper tier and accept the failures
Alternate tiers depending on how the input looks
questions.why: Prompt quality and model capability produce the same symptom, and the cheaper variable is the one to test first.
questions.traps: Upgrading treats an untested hypothesis, accepting failures gives up, and alternating adds complexity without a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A team wants to standardise on one tier across every workflow for administrative simplicity.
options: Standardise, since one tier is much easier to manage
Do not standardise, since each task differs in demand
Weigh the simplicity against what it costs per workflow
Standardise on the strongest tier so nothing underperforms
questions.why: Uniformity has real administrative value and a real cost in over- or under-provisioning, and the comparison is the decision.
questions.traps: Both absolute positions skip the arithmetic, and standardising on the top tier pays the maximum everywhere.

questions.stem: A team's Project instructions have grown to two pages as people kept adding rules.
options: Reorganise the two pages so they read more clearly
Split the rules across two Projects used in turn
Keep them, since each rule was added for a reason
Cut them to the rules the work actually needs
questions.why: Long instructions dilute one another, and deciding which rules genuinely matter is what makes the remaining ones effective.
questions.traps: Reorganising changes presentation rather than volume, splitting means neither Project has the full set, and historic reasons do not prove current need.

questions.stem: An associate must choose between a shareable page and a document for a set of numbers.
options: Choose the page, since it looks more professional
Choose the document, since it can be edited later
Choose by whether the reader needs to explore them
Produce both so the reader can pick what they prefer
questions.why: An interactive page earns its cost when the reader wants to slice the numbers, and a document is right when they will read a fixed view.
questions.traps: Appearance and editability are secondary to what the reader will do, and producing both doubles the work and the maintenance.

questions.stem: A team needs answers grounded in prices that change several times every week.
options: Put the price list in a Project and update it weekly
Give it the current prices at the time of asking
Ask the model to use the most recent prices it knows
Accept small errors, since prices change constantly
questions.why: Data that moves faster than any stored copy has to arrive with the question, which is what keeps the answer current.
questions.traps: A weekly update is already stale by mid-week, the model has no live access, and accepting errors on prices is a business problem.

questions.stem: A team's requests are slow because each one carries the entire conversation history.
options: Ask shorter questions so the requests are smaller
Move to a faster tier to absorb the extra length
Accept it, since the history improves the answers
Start fresh conversations when the history stops mattering
questions.why: Accumulated history is paid for on every subsequent request, and dropping it when it is no longer needed removes the cost.
questions.traps: Shorter questions do not shrink the history, a faster tier pays to carry the same weight, and history often stops being useful long before it stops being sent.

questions.stem: A team's task gets 78% from the cheapest tier and a person achieves roughly 85%.
options: Ask what the remaining errors cost before choosing
Use the model, since 78% at scale beats 85% by hand
Use people, since 85% is clearly the better accuracy
Use the model and have people check every output
questions.why: Seven points of accuracy matters enormously in some uses and not at all in others, and the cost of an error is what decides.
questions.traps: Volume and accuracy arguments each ignore the other, and checking everything gives up the throughput the model was for.

questions.stem: A team can halve their spend at the cost of roughly ten extra errors each month.
options: Take the saving, since the cost reduction is certain
Compare the saving against what those errors cost
Refuse, since introducing errors deliberately is wrong
Take the saving and add a review step to catch them
questions.why: The trade is money against errors, and it can only be settled by pricing both sides rather than preferring one of them.
questions.traps: Certainty of saving says nothing about the cost, a principled refusal ignores that all tiers make errors, and a review step has its own cost.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works reliably on the strongest tier and is unstable on the cheaper ones.
options: Find what the prompt leaves to the model's judgement
Stay on the strongest tier, since it works reliably
Use the cheaper tier and post-process the output
Conclude the task requires the strongest tier available
questions.why: Instability on cheaper tiers usually marks the places a prompt is under-specified, and tightening those often makes the cheaper tier viable.
questions.traps: Staying put pays for a possibly avoidable gap, post-processing patches symptoms, and concluding a capability requirement skips the test.

questions.stem: An associate wants a Project to behave differently for two distinct kinds of question.
options: Use one Project with instructions covering both kinds
Use one Project and state the kind in each question
Use one Project and switch the instructions as needed
Use two Projects, since instructions apply to everything
questions.why: Instructions apply to every conversation in a Project, so two behaviours means two Projects rather than one with conditional rules.
questions.traps: Dual instructions fire on both kinds, per-question labelling depends on the asker, and switching invites an error at every change.

questions.stem: A workflow works on the 200 cases a team has tried and is proposed for a new department.
options: Extend it, since 200 cases is a substantial sample
Do not extend it, since it was built for one team
Test it on that department's cases before extending it
Extend it and monitor the results as they come in
questions.why: Two hundred cases from one team says nothing about a different team's inputs, and a test on those makes the extension informed.
questions.traps: Sample size within one team does not transfer, refusing forgoes real reuse, and monitoring in production lets the department meet the failures.

questions.stem: A team must choose between a custom integration and the standard interface for a stable task.
options: Build the integration, since it fits the task exactly
Stay standard, since integrations are costly to maintain
Build the integration and keep the standard route too
Stay standard unless the integration removes real friction
questions.why: A custom integration earns its build and maintenance cost only where it removes friction people actually feel, which has to be shown.
questions.traps: Fit alone does not justify the cost, blanket avoidance forgoes real gains, and running both doubles what has to be kept working.

questions.stem: A team needs the model to say when it cannot answer, and cheaper tiers tend to guess.
options: Use a cheaper tier and instruct it not to guess
Treat willingness to decline as a capability requirement
Use a cheaper tier and check every answer instead
Accept the guessing, since most answers are correct
questions.why: Reliable abstention is a real capability difference between tiers, which makes it part of the fit rather than something a prompt fixes.
questions.traps: An instruction does not confer the ability, checking everything is the cost being avoided, and accepting guesses is the failure itself.

questions.stem: A team's workflow runs a second verification call on every output, doubling the cost.
options: Keep verifying everything, since errors are expensive
Stop verifying, since the first call is usually right
Verify only where an error would actually matter
Verify a random sample of the outputs each day
questions.why: Verification is worth its cost where an error is consequential, and targeting it there keeps the protection at half the price.
questions.traps: Verifying everything pays the maximum, stopping removes the protection, and random sampling may miss the cases that matter.

questions.stem: A team's task is simple and a rare error would be severe and hard to notice.
options: Choose the tier by the severity, not by the difficulty
Choose a cheap tier, since the task is genuinely simple
Choose a cheap tier and add a human review step
Choose the strongest tier and skip any review entirely
questions.why: Task difficulty sets what is needed to succeed and consequence sets what is needed to fail safely, and the second dominates here.
questions.traps: Simplicity is the wrong dimension when the downside is severe, review may not catch what is hard to notice, and no tier removes the need for care.

questions.stem: A team's disappointing results could be the model or could be half their inputs being poor.
options: Move to a stronger tier and see whether results improve
Fix the inputs and change the tier at the same time
Conclude the model is the limit, since the prompt is fine
Fix the inputs first, since that is the cheaper test
questions.why: Two candidate causes are separated by changing one, and input quality is both the cheaper change and the more likely culprit.
questions.traps: A tier change tests the expensive hypothesis first, changing both leaves the cause unknown, and concluding from prompt quality alone skips the inputs.

questions.stem: A team is moving from eight hundred to eighty thousand monthly requests.
options: Expect only the bill to change proportionally with it
Expect nothing to change beyond the volume itself
Expect rate limits, cost and error handling all to change
Expect quality to fall as the volume increases
questions.why: A hundredfold increase crosses thresholds that a small volume never meets, and each of those is a design question rather than a bigger bill.
questions.traps: Treating it as arithmetic misses the thresholds, expecting nothing is the same error, and quality does not degrade with volume by itself.

questions.stem: A team member leaves and their Projects held the only copy of several careful prompts.
options: Recover them from the departing member before they go
Keep prompts somewhere outside any individual's Projects
Rebuild the prompts as and when they are next needed
Share every Project with the whole team by default
questions.why: A prompt stored only inside one person's Project is a single point of failure, and keeping the source elsewhere is what survives any departure.
questions.traps: A one-off recovery fixes this instance rather than the pattern, rebuilding discards work, and sharing everything spreads access without preserving anything.

questions.stem: An associate must decide whether extended reasoning is worth enabling on a high-volume task.
options: Enable it only where the task's difficulty warrants it
Enable it, since more reasoning improves any output
Leave it off, since high volume makes the cost prohibitive
Enable it and reduce the volume to keep costs level
questions.why: Extra reasoning helps on genuinely hard steps and adds cost everywhere else, so it belongs where the difficulty is.
questions.traps: Universal enablement pays on easy work, a blanket refusal forgoes it where it helps, and cutting volume changes the task to fit the setting.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to read text from photographs of handwritten forms.
options: Assume it can, since reading text is a basic capability
Type the forms up first so that the text is clean
Use the strongest tier, since handwriting is difficult
Check whether it reads that handwriting reliably first
questions.why: Handwriting quality varies enormously, so a test on the actual forms is what establishes whether the task is feasible at all.
questions.traps: Assuming it works skips the question, typing up is the work being avoided, and a stronger tier does not guarantee legibility.

questions.stem: A team wants to try Claude on a task before committing any real effort to it.
options: Build the full workflow and evaluate it afterwards
Run it manually on a handful of their real cases
Read about what others have done with similar tasks
Ask the team whether they think it would work
questions.why: A few real cases run by hand answers the feasibility question at almost no cost, and it uses the team's actual inputs.
questions.traps: Building first spends the effort being tested, reading about others uses their inputs, and asking the team collects opinion rather than evidence.

questions.stem: An associate's outputs are long and the readers only skim the first few lines.
options: Keep the length, since more detail is always safer
Keep the length and summarise it for the readers
Ask for shorter output, since length is being paid for
Move to a cheaper tier to offset the output length
questions.why: Output length costs money and reader attention, and neither is being repaid when the text is skimmed.
questions.traps: Unread detail is not safety, summarising adds a second step, and a cheaper tier pays less for exactly the same waste.

questions.stem: An associate wants a colleague to run a carefully built prompt without rebuilding it.
options: Share it in a form the colleague can run directly
Send the colleague the prompt text to paste in
Explain to the colleague how to write it themselves
Run it for the colleague whenever they need it
questions.why: Sharing the working thing is what transfers the capability rather than the instructions for recreating it.
questions.traps: Pasted text drifts as it is edited, teaching them to rebuild it repeats the work, and running it for them makes you the bottleneck.

questions.stem: A team asks whether the strongest tier is the safe default for absolutely everything.
options: Yes — capability is never a disadvantage in itself
Yes — provided the budget can absorb the cost
No — the strongest tier is slower on every task
No — it costs more without helping on easy tasks
questions.why: Paying top rates for work a cheaper tier does equally well is waste, which is why the default should follow the task.
questions.traps: Capability without benefit is cost, budget headroom is not a reason to spend, and speed is not the general objection.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to produce output in an identical structure every single week.
options: Ask for a consistent structure in the prompt text
Reformat each week's output into the structure
Specify the structure and check it on each run
Accept small variations between the weekly runs
questions.why: A structure that downstream work depends on has to be both specified and verified, since generation varies between runs.
questions.traps: Asking for consistency does not define it, weekly reformatting is manual work, and accepting variation is what breaks the downstream use.

questions.stem: Several people each keep their own conversation with the same set of policy documents.
options: Have each person keep their own conversation going
Move to one shared Project everyone works from
Have one person answer everyone else's questions
Circulate the documents so everyone has a copy
questions.why: One shared Project gives everyone the same grounding and one place to maintain, rather than five diverging copies.
questions.traps: Separate conversations drift apart, a single answerer is a bottleneck, and circulating copies multiplies what has to be kept current.

questions.stem: A task needs twelve steps followed exactly, where skipping one invalidates the result.
options: A tier that follows instructions reliably, then verify
Any tier, since the steps are written down clearly
The cheapest tier, since each step is individually simple
The strongest tier, and no verification is then needed
questions.why: Reliable instruction-following differs by tier, and where omission invalidates the result the check has to exist regardless.
questions.traps: Written steps are not self-enforcing, individually simple steps still get skipped, and no tier removes the need to verify a strict sequence.

questions.stem: A manual review handles fifty items a day and the new workflow will produce five hundred.
options: Keep the review and let the backlog simply build up
Remove the review, since the volume is too high
Redesign the review before the volume arrives
Hire more reviewers to match the new higher volume
questions.why: A tenfold increase makes the existing review physically impossible, so it has to change shape before the work arrives.
questions.traps: A backlog defers the failure, removing the review discards the control, and hiring at ten times scale is rarely the cheapest answer.

questions.stem: An associate is choosing between one request covering ten documents and ten separate ones.
options: One request, since fewer requests always costs less
Ten requests, since each document gets full attention
Whichever of the two is faster to write as a prompt
It depends on whether the documents interact at all
questions.why: Documents that must be compared belong together and independent ones do not, and that is what settles the batching.
questions.traps: Cost and attention arguments each hold in only one case, and ease of writing is not the criterion.

questions.stem: A team needs the model to work from a document they are not permitted to upload.
options: Upload it anyway, since the task requires the content
Check what the restriction actually covers first
Describe the document from memory in the prompt
Abandon the task, since the document cannot be used
questions.why: A restriction may cover the file, the data or the whole subject, and knowing which determines whether any route exists.
questions.traps: Uploading breaches it, memory is unreliable and may breach it anyway, and abandoning assumes the broadest reading without checking.

questions.stem: A team wants stakeholders to see quarterly numbers without installing anything at all.
options: Give them something that opens in any web browser
Send a spreadsheet they can open in their own tools
Present the numbers to them in a meeting instead
Send a document with all the numbers written out
questions.why: A browser is the one thing every stakeholder already has, which makes it the lowest-friction way to reach all of them.
questions.traps: A spreadsheet assumes a tool and a version, a meeting requires everyone at once, and a static document cannot be explored.

questions.stem: An associate is asked why their workflow uses an expensive tier and does not know.
options: Keep the expensive tier, since the workflow works
Test the cheaper tiers and choose on the evidence
Move to the cheapest tier and watch for problems
Explain that the tier was chosen when it was built
questions.why: An unjustified choice becomes a justified one by measuring the alternatives on the actual task.
questions.traps: Working is not the same as being right-sized, moving to the cheapest is the same guess reversed, and explaining the history does not answer the question.

questions.stem: A pilot saved twelve hours a week across four people and forty people are next.
options: Multiply the saving by ten for the forty people
Expect the same saving per person as the pilot had
Expect the per-person saving to fall as it widens
Expect no saving at all until everyone is trained
questions.why: Pilot participants are self-selected and better supported, so the average saving typically falls as the population widens.
questions.traps: Straight multiplication assumes the pilot is representative, per-person parity is the same assumption, and expecting nothing ignores a real effect.

questions.stem: A team's task produces occasional badly wrong answers on every tier they have tested.
options: Try a tier they have not yet tested on the task
Accept the failures as inherent to the task itself
Add a verification pass over every single output
Look at the task itself rather than at the tiers
questions.why: A failure that survives every tier is usually about how the task is posed rather than about capability.
questions.traps: Another tier tests the same hypothesis again, accepting it gives up early, and verification manages a symptom without diagnosing it.

questions.stem: A team's spend tripled with no change in the volume of work being done.
options: Look at what changed in the requests themselves
Assume prices rose and budget for the new level
Move to a cheaper tier to bring the spend back down
Cap usage until the spend returns to normal levels
questions.why: Constant volume with rising cost points at bigger requests or a changed configuration, and finding which is the whole fix.
questions.traps: Assuming a price change is untested, a tier move treats an unknown cause, and a cap hides the problem rather than solving it.

questions.stem: A shared Project is used by twelve people and one of them keeps changing the instructions.
options: Lock the instructions so that nobody can change them
Ask that one person to stop changing the instructions
Give each of the twelve their own copy of the Project
Agree who owns the instructions and how they change
questions.why: A shared setting needs a single agreed way of being changed, which is what stops one person's edits surprising eleven others.
questions.traps: Locking prevents improvement, asking one person to stop does not create a rule, and per-person copies end the sharing entirely.

questions.stem: An associate needs a colleague to use a result that changes as the inputs are adjusted.
options: Build it as something that recalculates on input
Produce a table covering the likely input values
Produce the result and rerun it whenever asked
Explain the calculation so the colleague can do it
questions.why: When the point is to vary the inputs, something that recomputes is what serves the need rather than a fixed answer.
questions.traps: A table covers only the values you guessed, rerunning makes you the bottleneck, and explaining the method delegates the work.

questions.stem: A team's cheaper tier matches the expensive one on 94% of the cases they tested.
options: Move to the cheaper tier, since 94% is a close match
Look at what the remaining six per cent have in common
Stay on the expensive tier, since 6% is a real gap
Use the cheaper tier and check a sample of outputs
questions.why: The disagreements are where the tiers actually differ, and their pattern tells you whether the cheaper tier is safe for this task.
questions.traps: Both tier decisions are made without looking at the failures, and sampling detects the gap rather than characterising it.

questions.stem: A non-technical lead wants colleagues to query a policy library without learning prompting.
options: Write prompts for the colleagues to copy and paste
Train the colleagues in how to write good prompts
Set up a Project they can simply ask questions of
Have the lead answer the questions on their behalf
questions.why: A Project turns the library into something you ask ordinary questions of, which removes the prompting skill from the path.
questions.traps: Copied prompts break when the question differs, training adds a barrier before any value, and routing through the lead does not scale.

questions.stem: A team's internal tool calls Claude on every keystroke and users find it laggy.
options: Move to a faster tier so each call returns sooner
Shorten the prompt so each call is cheaper to run
Show a loading indicator so the lag feels shorter
Call it when the user pauses rather than on each key
questions.why: The problem is the number of calls rather than the speed of any one, and triggering on a pause removes most of them.
questions.traps: A faster tier and a shorter prompt both optimise a call that should not be happening, and an indicator manages perception.

questions.stem: A team's task involves both mechanical extraction and difficult judgement in one prompt.
options: Use the strongest tier, since judgement is involved
Use a cheaper tier, since extraction dominates the work
Split it so each part can be matched to a tier
Keep it together, since splitting adds coordination
questions.why: Two different demands in one prompt force a single tier choice that is wrong for one of them, and splitting removes that compromise.
questions.traps: Either single-tier choice overpays or underperforms on half the work, and coordination cost is usually smaller than the mismatch.

questions.stem: A team is expanding a workflow to a region with different regulations and languages.
options: Expand it, since the underlying task is the same
Treat it as a new workflow to be validated afresh
Expand it and translate the prompts into the language
Do not expand it, since regulations differ by region
questions.why: Different rules and a different language change both what is correct and how well the model performs, which is a new validation rather than a rollout.
questions.traps: Task similarity hides the regulatory difference, translation addresses one of two changes, and refusing forgoes a legitimate expansion.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether a document belongs in Project knowledge or one chat.
options: Project if several conversations will need it
Project, since knowledge is where documents belong
Attach it, since attachments are always more precise
Both, so that it is available in either place
questions.why: The test is reuse: material that recurs across conversations belongs in the Project, and material for one belongs with it.
questions.traps: Neither blanket rule considers reuse, and doing both duplicates the content so that it competes with itself.

questions.stem: A team needs the model to always follow the company's approved wording for one answer.
options: Describe the approved position and let it phrase it
Supply the approved wording and require it verbatim
Instruct it to be careful about how it words this
Review each answer against the approved wording
questions.why: Where exact wording matters, providing the text and requiring it is the only thing that reliably produces it.
questions.traps: A described position gets rephrased, a care instruction has no target, and review catches the problem after the fact every time.

questions.stem: A team's costs come mostly from a small number of unusually long documents.
options: Move everything to a cheaper tier to reduce the total
Refuse documents over a certain length in the workflow
Handle the long documents differently from the rest
Accept it, since long documents genuinely cost more
questions.why: When a few inputs dominate the bill, they are the thing to treat specially rather than changing everything else.
questions.traps: A blanket tier change affects the many to fix the few, a length limit refuses valid work, and accepting it forgoes a targeted saving.

questions.stem: An associate with no coding background wants to automate reading and sorting emails.
options: Learn enough coding to build the automation themselves
Ask a developer to build the automation for them
Continue doing it by hand, since coding is required
Look for a route that needs no code before building
questions.why: Many automations of this shape are available without code, and checking that first avoids both the learning and the dependency.
questions.traps: Learning to code is a large detour, a developer creates a dependency, and assuming code is required is the untested premise.

questions.stem: A team's task is limited either by the model or by the quality of the information given.
options: Give better information first, since it is the cheaper test
Move to a stronger tier, since it is the faster test
Improve both at once for the largest improvement
Conclude it is the model, since the prompt seems fine
questions.why: Two hypotheses are separated by changing one, and improving what you supply is both cheaper and more often the actual cause.
questions.traps: Speed of testing is not the same as cost, changing both confounds the result, and judging the prompt by appearance is not a test.

questions.stem: A team's model errors turn out to be caused by inconsistent input formatting.
options: Move to a stronger tier that tolerates the variation
Add instructions describing every input format seen
Standardise the inputs, since the model was not the problem
Accept the errors, since input quality is outside the team
questions.why: A cause outside the model is fixed outside the model, and standardising removes the variation rather than paying to absorb it.
questions.traps: A stronger tier pays to tolerate a fixable problem, enumerating formats breaks on the next one, and input quality is usually within reach.

questions.stem: A team's workflow makes three sequential calls where each depends on the one before.
options: Run the three calls in parallel in order to save time
Nothing can be parallelised, so shorten each call instead
Merge all three of them into a single larger call
Accept the latency, since the dependency is unavoidable
questions.why: A genuine dependency chain cannot be parallelised, so the available time has to come out of each individual call.
questions.traps: Parallel execution is impossible when each input is the previous output, merging may lose the intermediate reasoning, and accepting it forgoes real gains.

questions.stem: A team must decide whether to let the model use tools or supply everything in the prompt.
options: Tools always, since they make the model more capable
Prompt always, since it is simpler and more predictable
Both, so the model can choose whichever it needs
Tools where the data moves, prompt where it is fixed
questions.why: A tool earns its complexity when the information changes between requests, and a fixed body of material is cheaper supplied directly.
questions.traps: Absolute answers ignore how the data behaves, and offering both leaves an unnecessary choice inside the request.

questions.stem: A workflow will be rolled out company-wide and was validated on one team's data.
options: Validate on data from the teams that differ the most
Roll it out, since one team's validation is evidence
Validate on a random sample from every single team
Roll it out team by team and fix problems as found
questions.why: The teams whose work differs most are where the workflow is most likely to break, which makes them the informative test.
questions.traps: One team's validation does not generalise, a random sample spends effort where it is least likely to find anything, and staged rollout finds problems in production.

questions.stem: An associate wants a preference about tone to hold across every future conversation.
options: State the preference at the start of each conversation
Put it where it applies without being restated
Ask the model to remember it for the next time
Correct the tone whenever an answer does not match
questions.why: A standing preference belongs in a setting that applies automatically, since anything requiring restatement will eventually be forgotten.
questions.traps: Per-conversation statement is the repetition being avoided, a request to remember does not persist, and correction never becomes a rule.

questions.stem: A team could spend more on a stronger tier or the same amount on better inputs.
options: Spend on the tier, since capability is the harder limit
Spend on inputs, since they are within the team's control
Compare them on the same task before deciding
Split the budget evenly between the two options
questions.why: Both are plausible and the return on each is measurable on this task, which makes the comparison the decision.
questions.traps: Either preference is a guess about where the limit sits, and splitting spends half on whichever turns out not to matter.

questions.stem: A team wants a conversation preserved so its approach can be reused by others later.
options: Keep the conversation and share a link to it later
Copy the conversation into a shared team document
Ask the model to summarise how the work was done
Extract the approach into something that is reusable
questions.why: A conversation records one instance, and what makes it reusable is separating the method from that instance.
questions.traps: A link and a copy both preserve the transcript rather than the technique, and a generated summary describes rather than packages it.

questions.stem: A first-pass screen flags anything needing attention and misses roughly one in fifty.
options: Ask what happens to the cases the screen misses
Accept it, since one in fifty is a good hit rate
Move to a stronger tier to reduce the miss rate
Have a person re-screen everything it did not flag
questions.why: A screen's miss rate only matters in light of what a missed case costs, and that determines whether one in fifty is fine or unacceptable.
questions.traps: A hit rate without consequence is meaningless, a stronger tier improves the number without pricing it, and re-screening everything defeats the screen.

questions.stem: A team's workflow costs two hundred a month and saves about eight hours of work.
options: Keep it, since eight hours clearly exceeds the cost
Drop it, since two hundred a month is a real expense
Compare it against what those eight hours are worth
Keep it and try to reduce the monthly cost further
questions.why: The comparison is between the money and the value of the time freed, and that value depends on what the eight hours now do.
questions.traps: Both quick verdicts assume a value for the hours, and optimising the cost skips the question of whether it is worth having.

questions.stem: A team needs output to arrive inside a system that accepts only one fixed layout.
options: Instruct the model to always use that exact layout
Fix the layout deterministically after generation
Change the receiving system to accept variation
Have a person reformat the output before it is sent
questions.why: A strict downstream contract needs a deterministic step, because generated text will vary however precisely it is instructed.
questions.traps: Instructions are followed most of the time rather than always, changing the receiving system is a heavier fix, and a person in the path defeats the automation.

questions.stem: A team's Claude spend is growing and finance wants a figure for next year.
options: Give a range with the assumptions that drive it
Extrapolate this year's growth into next year
Give this year's figure, since next year is unknown
Give the highest plausible figure just to be safe
questions.why: A forecast under genuine uncertainty is a range with its drivers named, which is what lets finance plan and revise it later.
questions.traps: Straight extrapolation assumes the growth continues, repeating this year ignores the trend, and a worst case misallocates budget.

questions.stem: A team must choose between a shared Project and a scheduled job for a weekly report.
options: Project, since the team can then ask follow-up questions
Scheduled, since a weekly report ought to be automatic
Both, so the report exists and can also be queried
Scheduled where it must happen, Project where it is asked for
questions.why: The distinction is whether the report has to appear without anyone acting, and that is what separates the two surfaces.
questions.traps: Follow-up questions and automation are each an advantage of one, and running both maintains two things where one is needed.

questions.stem: An associate keeps a Project for a piece of work that finished three months ago.
options: Archive it, since it no longer answers questions
Keep it, since the work may come back one day
Keep it and add the newer work into it as well
Delete the Project and all its documents entirely
questions.why: A Project earns its place by answering current questions, and finished work belongs out of the way rather than competing with live material.
questions.traps: Hypothetical revival is how Projects accumulate, mixing new work in dilutes both, and deleting loses material that may still be needed.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works for one person and they want the whole team using it.
options: Give everyone the workflow and let them start using it
Find out what that person supplies that others will not
Have that person train each colleague individually
Wait until more people ask for it before sharing it
questions.why: A working personal workflow usually carries unwritten context, and identifying it is what makes it survive the handover.
questions.traps: Handing it over unexamined exports the gaps, individual training does not scale, and waiting for demand delays a known benefit.

questions.stem: A team asks whether a stronger model will fix answers that are wrong because the data is old.
options: Yes — stronger models have more recent knowledge
Yes — stronger models are better at spotting staleness
No — the data being old is not a capability problem
No — but a stronger model would reduce the errors
questions.why: Stale information produces stale answers regardless of how capable the model is, because the problem is the input rather than the reasoning.
questions.traps: Recency of training does not track the team's own data, spotting staleness is not having current facts, and capability does not substitute for correct data.

questions.stem: An associate asks how they should compare two tiers for their own particular task.
options: Read the published benchmarks for the two tiers
Ask colleagues which of the tiers they prefer using
Use the more expensive one, since it should be better
Run both on the same cases and compare the results
questions.why: A tier's benefit is task-specific, so the only decisive comparison is on the cases the workflow actually meets.
questions.traps: Benchmarks measure other tasks, colleague preference is anecdote, and price is a proxy rather than a measurement.

questions.stem: A team wants an answer they can act on immediately and will not need again.
options: Ask directly and use the answer as it comes back
Build a repeatable workflow around the question
Document the question and answer for future use
Set the question up as a scheduled recurring task
questions.why: A single, immediate need is served by asking, and any structure around it costs more than it can return.
questions.traps: A workflow, documentation and a schedule all invest in a repetition that is never going to happen.

questions.stem: A team needs the model to work through a derivation where the intermediate steps matter.
options: Ask for the answer and check it independently after
Ask for the answer and then ask how it was reached
Use a setting that shows the working, not just the result
Break the derivation into separate small questions
questions.why: When the steps are what has to be checked, they have to be produced as part of the work rather than reconstructed afterwards.
questions.traps: Independent checking repeats the derivation, an after-the-fact explanation is a new output rather than a trace, and splitting loses the continuity.

questions.stem: An associate asks what it is that actually drives the cost of a single request.
options: How long the request takes to be answered fully
How much text goes in and how much comes back out
How difficult the question is to answer properly
How many times the request has been run before
questions.why: Cost tracks the volume of text in and out, which is why long context and long answers are what move the bill.
questions.traps: Time, difficulty and history all feel like cost drivers but are not what is actually measured.

questions.stem: A team wants new joiners to get consistent answers about their internal processes.
options: Have each new joiner ask an experienced colleague
Send new joiners the documents to read themselves
Write a list of frequently asked questions for them
Give them a Project holding the process documents
questions.why: A Project answers questions in the joiner's own words from the authoritative documents, which is what makes the answers consistent.
questions.traps: Colleagues give varying answers, unread documents help nobody, and a fixed FAQ only covers the questions someone anticipated.

questions.stem: A team's costs will rise with volume and they want to know when to start worrying.
options: Work out the cost per item and project it forward
Wait until the monthly bill becomes noticeable
Set a monthly cap and stop when it is reached
Assume the cost will stay roughly where it is now
questions.why: A per-item cost turns volume plans into a forecast, which is what lets the team see the problem before it arrives.
questions.traps: Waiting means reacting, a cap stops work rather than planning for it, and assuming stability ignores the growth they already expect.

questions.stem: A team's task is to sort tickets into twelve categories that are clearly documented.
options: The strongest tier, since twelve categories is a lot
A cheaper tier, tested against the documented categories
The strongest tier, since misclassification is costly
Whichever tier handles the highest volume fastest
questions.why: Well-documented classification is within reach of cheaper tiers, and testing against the definitions is what confirms it for this data.
questions.traps: Category count is not difficulty, cost of error argues for verification rather than the top tier, and speed is not the fit question.

questions.stem: An associate reports that a cheaper tier gives correct but noticeably blander answers.
options: Move back to the expensive tier, since quality dropped
Stay on the cheaper tier, since the answers are correct
Decide whether the blandness actually matters here
Add an instruction asking for more engaging answers
questions.why: Correctness and style are different requirements, and whether the style difference costs anything depends on who reads the output.
questions.traps: Both quick decisions assume an answer about the readers, and a style instruction treats a difference that may not need treating.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to compare two long contracts clause by clause against each other.
options: Provide one contract and describe the other one
Compare a few clauses at a time across many chats
Summarise both contracts and compare the summaries
Provide both contracts and ask for the comparison
questions.why: A clause-level comparison needs both texts present, since the differences live in the exact wording.
questions.traps: A description loses the wording, many small chats lose the overview, and summaries drop the very detail being compared.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to draft replies inside the support tool their agents already use.
options: Integrate it there, since that is where the work happens
Have agents copy the ticket into a separate window
Have agents write drafts separately and paste them back
Train agents to switch between the two tools quickly
questions.why: Putting the capability where the work already happens removes the copying that would otherwise be paid on every single ticket.
questions.traps: All three alternatives ask the agent to move data between tools on every ticket they handle.

questions.stem: A Project answers well on its documents and confidently wrong outside of them.
options: Add more documents so fewer questions fall outside
Instruct it to say when a question falls outside the documents
Tell users only to ask questions the documents cover
Accept it, since the Project is for those documents
questions.why: The failure is that out-of-scope questions get answered as if in scope, and telling it to flag them is what makes the boundary visible.
questions.traps: More documents move the boundary rather than marking it, instructing users relies on them knowing the contents, and accepting it leaves confident errors in place.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is being adopted by a second team with a slightly different goal.
options: Hand it over, since the workflow is already proven
Rebuild it for the second team entirely from scratch
Ask what their goal is before handing the workflow over
Have both teams share and maintain one workflow
questions.why: A slightly different goal often means slightly different correctness, and finding out is what determines how much can be reused.
questions.traps: Handing over unexamined exports the first team's assumptions, rebuilding discards proven work, and shared ownership decides before the fit is known.

questions.stem: A team's requests are cheap individually and their monthly bill is nonetheless large.
options: Reduce the per-request cost by shortening prompts
Move to a cheaper tier to reduce the unit price
Accept it, since each request is already cheap
Look at the volume rather than the per-request cost
questions.why: When unit cost is low and the total is high, volume is the driver, and that is where any reduction has to come from.
questions.traps: Prompt length and unit price both attack a cost that is already small, and per-request cheapness is what makes the total surprising.

questions.stem: A team's workflow fails specifically on inputs longer than about twenty pages.
options: Handle long inputs differently rather than changing tier
Move to a tier that handles longer inputs better
Reject inputs longer than twenty pages entirely
Truncate long inputs so they fit within the limit
questions.why: A failure that appears at a length threshold is about how long inputs are processed, and restructuring that is the direct fix.
questions.traps: A tier change may raise the threshold without removing it, rejecting refuses valid work, and truncation silently drops content.

questions.stem: A team is told the newest tier is better and their workflow is carefully tuned already.
options: Compare them as they are and take the better result
Switch to the newest tier, since it is an improvement
Retune before comparing, since tuning is tier-specific
Stay put, since retuning would cost more than it gains
questions.why: A prompt tuned for one tier can underperform on another, so comparing untuned against tuned measures the tuning rather than the tier.
questions.traps: An unfair comparison produces a wrong conclusion, switching on reputation skips the test, and assuming retuning is not worth it prejudges the gain.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to make the same twenty-step change across sixty files.
options: Do the twenty steps in a conversation for each file
Ask for instructions and apply them by hand to each
Do the first file carefully and copy the pattern across
Use a surface that can act on the files directly
questions.why: Sixty repetitions of a mechanical change is exactly the case for something that operates on the files rather than describing the change.
questions.traps: All three alternatives put a person in the loop sixty times over.

questions.stem: A team needs a one-page visual summary that stakeholders can look at in a meeting.
options: Produce a written description of what it should show
Produce something rendered rather than described
Produce the numbers and let stakeholders visualise them
Produce a detailed report the meeting can work from
questions.why: A visual summary has to be seen, so the deliverable is the rendered thing rather than an account of what it would contain.
questions.traps: A description, raw numbers and a report all leave the visualisation itself undone.

questions.stem: A team's Project answers are shaped by an instruction that nobody remembers adding.
options: Review the instructions and remove what is not wanted
Add a counter-instruction to offset the unwanted effect
Rebuild the Project from scratch without instructions
Accept it, since the answers are still broadly useful
questions.why: Instructions are a short, editable list, and reading them is the direct route to removing an effect nobody intended.
questions.traps: Counter-instructions stack rules that fight each other, rebuilding discards everything else, and accepting it leaves an unowned rule shaping answers.

questions.stem: A team's spend is fine and one workflow's latency is annoying its users daily.
options: Optimise cost, since it is easier to measure and reduce
Optimise both, since they usually move together anyway
Optimise the latency, since that is the live complaint
Accept the latency, since the spend is under control
questions.why: Effort belongs on the dimension that is actually hurting, and here the users have already identified which one that is.
questions.traps: Measurability is not importance, cost and latency often trade rather than move together, and a healthy budget does not address the complaint.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a task needs a more capable model or a better prompt.
options: Try a stronger tier with the current prompt first
Try both of the changes together in order to save time
Assume it is the prompt, since prompts usually are
Try a better prompt on the current tier first
questions.why: The prompt is the cheaper and faster variable to change, which makes it the sensible first test of two competing explanations.
questions.traps: Testing the tier first spends more to learn the same thing, changing both confounds the result, and assuming the answer skips the test.

questions.stem: A workflow will run in three countries and was designed around one country's rules.
options: Extend it and adjust wherever problems come up
Identify where the rules differ before extending it
Build a separate workflow for each of the countries
Extend it with a note that rules vary by country
questions.why: Rule differences determine what the workflow must do differently, and mapping them is what shows how much can be shared.
questions.traps: Fixing problems as they appear means being wrong first, three separate workflows assume no overlap, and a note does not change behaviour.

questions.stem: An associate finds their task performs about the same on every tier they have tried.
options: Use the cheapest, since capability is not the limit
Use the strongest anyway, in case inputs get harder
Keep testing until a difference eventually appears
Conclude the measurement must be wrong somewhere
questions.why: Equal performance means the task is not capability-limited, and the cheapest tier is then the rational choice.
questions.traps: Hypothetical future difficulty is not a current reason to pay, more testing repeats a settled result, and doubting the measurement without cause is unjustified.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to act on a schedule and produce a report without being asked.
options: Ask someone to run the report each time it is due
Set a calendar reminder for whoever is on duty
Run it whenever the report is next needed by someone
Use a surface that runs without a person triggering it
questions.why: The requirement is that it happens without human action, which only something self-triggering actually satisfies.
questions.traps: A person, a reminder and on-demand running all reintroduce the human step that was to be removed.

questions.stem: A team's Project is slow compared with a plain conversation and members are complaining.
options: Move the work back into plain conversations instead
Accept it, since Projects are inherently slower
Reduce what the Project has to search through
Move to a faster tier to compensate for the delay
questions.why: A Project's speed follows how much material it has to consider, so trimming it addresses the actual cause.
questions.traps: Abandoning the Project loses the grounding, "inherently slower" is not true of a well-curated Project, and a faster tier pays to search the same bloat.

questions.stem: A team's task needs both speed and careful reasoning and no tier offers both.
options: Choose the faster tier and accept weaker reasoning
Split the task so each part gets what it needs
Choose the stronger tier and accept a slower response
Wait for a tier that offers both characteristics
questions.why: When one step needs speed and another needs care, separating them lets each be served instead of compromising both at once.
questions.traps: Either single choice sacrifices a real requirement, and waiting defers the work indefinitely.

questions.stem: A consultant keeps one Project holding brand guidelines for all six of their clients.
options: Keep one Project and name the client in each question
Keep one Project and organise the files by client
One Project per client, so each answer sees only its own
