questions.traps: A walkthrough shows what without why. Shadowing transfers some knowledge informally, and rebuilding duplicates work already done.

questions.stem: A team measures their workflow's accuracy but not how long it takes people to use it.
options: Continue measuring accuracy, since that is the property that determines whether the workflow produces output the team can rely on for their work
Measure time instead of accuracy, since the accuracy has been stable for several months and the time cost is the variable that is currently unknown
Measure both, since a slow accurate workflow may still not be worth it
Ask people whether the workflow feels fast enough to them
questions.why: Value depends on accuracy and cost together. Measuring only one leaves the trade-off invisible.
questions.traps: Accuracy alone cannot show whether the workflow is worth using. Swapping the measure loses the other half, and perception is not measurement.

questions.stem: A workflow requires people to trust output they cannot easily verify, and several colleagues are uncomfortable doing so.
options: Explain how the model works so colleagues understand why the output can be relied upon in the kinds of cases this workflow is designed to handle
Give them a way to check, even a partial one
Point to the accuracy measurements the team has collected so far
Accept that some of the people will simply not adopt it
questions.why: Discomfort with unverifiable output is reasonable. Providing a means to check addresses the actual concern rather than arguing against it.
questions.traps: Explaining the mechanism does not let anyone check a specific output. Aggregate accuracy says nothing about the item in front of them, and accepting non-adoption forfeits the value.

questions.stem: An associate's integration calls Claude once per row of a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet has grown from 50 rows to 5,000.
options: Move to a faster tier so the five thousand individual calls complete more quickly than they currently do under the existing configuration
Run the integration overnight so that the time it takes does not affect anyone during the working day when they need the results
Split the spreadsheet and run several copies in parallel
Reconsider the per-row design at this volume
questions.why: A design that suited 50 rows may be wrong at 5,000. Revisiting the unit of work is the question the volume change raises.
questions.traps: A faster tier optimises within an unexamined design. Overnight running and parallelism both scale the same per-row pattern.

questions.stem: A team's workflow fails safely but produces no indication that anything went wrong, so people assume it ran.
options: Make success and failure both visible
Add an alert that fires when the workflow fails so that the team is notified promptly
Ask people to check whether the output was produced before they rely on it in their own work downstream of this particular process
Run the workflow more frequently so a failure is less consequential
questions.why: Silent success and silent failure are indistinguishable. Making both visible is what lets people tell the difference without checking.
questions.traps: A failure alert helps but leaves silence ambiguous when alerting itself fails. Manual checking is the burden being removed, and frequency does not address visibility.

questions.stem: A team wants to introduce Claude into a process where three of the seven steps are waiting for approvals from other departments.
options: Apply Claude to the four steps the team controls, since those are the parts where improvement can be delivered
Address the approval waits first, since they dominate elapsed time and no drafting gain reaches them
Ask the other departments to approve rather faster
Run the drafting steps in parallel with the approval waits so the total elapsed time is compressed
questions.why: Elapsed time sits in the approval queues, so improving the drafting steps produces work that waits in the same place. The constraint has to move first.
questions.traps: Improving the controllable steps feels productive but does not change throughput. Asking for speed is not a design change, and parallelism does not shorten the waits themselves.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has a review step that catches roughly one error a month, and reviewers spend four hours a week on it.
options: Remove the review step, since catching one error a month does not justify four hours of skilled reviewer time each and every week that the workflow operates
Reduce the review down to a sample of the total output
Weigh what those errors would have cost against sixteen hours of reviewer time a month
Keep the review, since any error reaching a customer is more costly than the reviewer time spent preventing it from happening in the first place
questions.why: Both quantities are known, so the decision is an explicit comparison. What the caught errors would have cost is the missing half of it.
questions.traps: Removing or keeping the step on principle decides without the consequence figure. Sampling reduces both cost and catch rate without reasoning about either.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to automate a step whose output is used as evidence in regulatory filings.
options: Automate it fully with a comprehensive audit trail so that every step of the process is recorded and can be reconstructed later if a regulator asks how a particular figure was produced
Automate it and have a person sign off on the filings monthly
Automate the routine filings and keep a person involved only for the ones that involve unusual circumstances or figures that fall outside the normal expected ranges
Keep a person accountable for what is filed, using Claude to prepare rather than to submit
questions.why: Regulatory filings carry personal accountability, which cannot sit with a system. Preparing rather than submitting keeps the benefit and the accountability in the right places.
questions.traps: An audit trail records what happened without making anyone accountable. Monthly sign-off follows the filing, and exception-only involvement still auto-files the majority.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on an external service that has been reliable for a year. There is no fallback if it becomes unavailable.
options: Decide in advance what the workflow does when the service is unavailable
Add monitoring so the team is alerted quickly if the external service becomes unavailable and can respond to the situation before it affects too much work
Choose a more reliable external service to depend upon
Accept the risk, since a year of reliable operation is reasonable evidence that the service is dependable enough for the workflow's purposes going forward
questions.why: A dependency with no defined behaviour on failure fails in an undefined way. Deciding the fallback in advance is what makes the outage survivable.
questions.traps: Monitoring tells you it broke without saying what to do. Switching services moves the dependency, and past uptime does not bound future outages.

questions.stem: A team's monthly workflow produced a different answer this month, and nobody kept a record of the prompt or data used last month.
options: Rerun last month's analysis using the current prompt to see whether the difference comes from the prompt or from the data that was used in each of the two months
Accept that some variation between the months is to be expected
Start recording the inputs and configuration for each run so differences become explainable
Ask the person who ran it last month whether they remember doing anything differently on that occasion than they have done this time around
questions.why: Without a record of what was run, a difference cannot be attributed to anything. Recording inputs is what makes future differences diagnosable.
questions.traps: Rerunning cannot recover last month's prompt. Accepting variation abandons comparability, and recollection is unreliable for exactly this kind of detail.

questions.stem: A team's workflow writes results into a shared document that several people edit at the same time.
options: Add a note at the top of the shared document asking people not to edit it
Write into a location the workflow owns, and let people copy from it
Run the workflow overnight when nobody is editing
Have the workflow check whether the document has been modified and skip writing if it has
questions.why: Automated writes and concurrent human editing conflict by design. Giving the workflow its own output location removes the contention entirely.
questions.traps: A request not to edit relies on compliance. Overnight running narrows the window without closing it, and skip-on-modification silently drops results.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether Claude has improved quality. They have no measure of quality from before it was introduced.
options: Compare the current quality against what the team believes the previous quality was
Use output volume as a proxy for quality since it is the measure that is actually available for both periods and shows a clear and substantial increase
Ask customers whether they have noticed an improvement in quality over the past few months since the new workflow was introduced
Say plainly that the before figure does not exist, and start measuring quality now
questions.why: An honest answer names the missing baseline and starts the measurement. That serves the question better than a reconstructed figure.
questions.traps: Recalled quality is unreliable. Volume is not quality, and customer recall over months is weak and confounded by everything else that changed.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is used enthusiastically by the people who helped design it and ignored by everyone else.
options: Involve the non-users in the next iteration rather than explaining the current one to them
Run a demonstration session showing the non-users how the workflow operates and what benefits the designers have seen from using it in their own daily work
Ask the designers to encourage their colleagues to take it up
Accept the split, since the people who designed it are the ones whose work it was designed around and others may have genuinely different needs
questions.why: Participation in design is what produces ownership, and that is the difference between the two groups. Involving non-users addresses the cause.
questions.traps: A demonstration explains a design made without them. Peer encouragement does not change the artefact, and accepting the split forfeits most of the value.

questions.stem: A workflow passes a document from Claude to a person, who often has to go back to the source to understand a claim in it.
options: Ask for a shorter document so the person has less material to work through when they are checking the claims that the workflow has produced for them
Require each claim to name where it came from, so the source is reachable from the document
Attach the source documents alongside the output that is produced
Ask the person to check only the claims that seem most important
questions.why: Repeated returns to the source mean the document lacks provenance. Naming the source per claim removes the lookup entirely.
questions.traps: Shortening reduces the material without adding traceability. Attaching sources still requires searching them, and checking selectively accepts unverified claims.

questions.stem: A team maps a process and finds that the same information is entered by hand three times in different systems.
options: Use Claude to speed up each of the three data entry steps
Combine the three systems into one single system
Address the duplicate entry, since it is waste that also creates three chances to introduce an error
Add a validation step that checks the three entries match
questions.why: Triple entry is waste and a triple error surface. Removing the duplication addresses both, which speeding it up does not.
questions.traps: Faster duplication is still duplication. System consolidation is a large project, and validation detects the errors the waste creates rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step where the correct behaviour differs between two jurisdictions and nobody has confirmed which rules apply where.
options: Establish the jurisdictional rules before automating anything
Automate using the stricter of the two jurisdictions' rules everywhere
Automate and add a jurisdiction field so the behaviour can be adjusted
Leave the step manual until the position is clear
questions.why: An unconfirmed rule cannot be automated correctly. Establishing the requirement is the prerequisite rather than something to work around.
questions.traps: The stricter rule may be wrong or costly in the other jurisdiction. A placeholder field automates before the rule exists, and leaving it manual defers rather than resolves.

questions.stem: A team wants a checkpoint but every candidate reviewer is already fully committed to other work.
options: Add the review to someone's workload anyway, since the control is necessary and the team will need to find a way to absorb the additional time it requires
Automate the review by adding a second Claude step to do it
Skip the review for now and add it later once capacity becomes available somewhere in the team for someone to take on the additional responsibility
Reduce what needs reviewing so the remaining volume fits the capacity that exists
questions.why: When review capacity is fixed, the scope of what is reviewed has to shrink to fit. Narrowing to the high-consequence subset is what makes the control real.
questions.traps: Adding unfunded work produces the rubber stamp. A second model step is not independent, and deferring leaves the control absent indefinitely.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow depends on a file arriving in a shared folder each morning, and occasionally it arrives late or not at all.
options: Make the workflow wait and report when the file has not arrived, rather than proceeding without it
Run the workflow later in the day so that the file has had more time to arrive before the process attempts to read it from the shared folder
Ask the team that produces the file to deliver it earlier and more reliably than they currently manage to do on most mornings
Use the previous day's file when the current one has not arrived
questions.why: A missing input should stop the workflow visibly rather than producing output from nothing or from stale data. Reporting is what makes the dependency's failure explicit.
questions.traps: A later run narrows the window without handling absence. Upstream reliability is outside the team's control, and falling back to yesterday's file produces confidently wrong output.

questions.stem: A team's workflow catches errors reliably but the person notified about them has no authority to fix the underlying cause.
options: Ask the notified person to escalate the errors they receive to the team that owns the underlying system
Log the errors to a file for later analysis by the team
Route the notification to whoever can actually address the cause
Ask the notified person to correct each error manually as it arises
questions.why: A control that notifies someone powerless produces a queue rather than a fix. Routing to the person who can act is what closes the loop.
questions.traps: Manual escalation adds a hop and depends on persistence. Logging defers, and manual correction treats symptoms indefinitely.

questions.stem: A team's workflow behaves differently for two people because each has different personal settings configured in their account.
options: Ask both people to align their personal settings so that the workflow behaves the same way
Move the workflow into shared configuration so personal settings do not affect it
Document the settings that the workflow requires to run
Have one person run the workflow for the whole team so that the settings in use are consistent across every run that the team relies on for its work
questions.why: Account-level settings are invisible inputs to every request. Moving the workflow into shared configuration removes the dependency on individual accounts.
questions.traps: Aligning settings by hand relies on both people maintaining them. Documentation records the requirement without enforcing it, and single-operator running creates a bottleneck.

questions.stem: A team's workflow demonstrably saves time, and the team has used the saved time to take on more of the same work.
options: Report the saving as realised, since the time was genuinely freed and the team has been able to use it productively on further work of the same kind
Report the saving as unrealised since headcount did not change
Measure the additional output produced and report that as the benefit instead of reporting the time saving that made the additional output possible in the first place
Check that the additional work is worth doing before counting the saving as a benefit
questions.why: A saving reinvested in more of the same work is only a benefit if that work has value. Checking that is what distinguishes real value from busier people.
questions.traps: Counting it as realised assumes the extra work is worthwhile. Calling it unrealised ignores real output, and measuring volume repeats the same assumption.

questions.stem: An associate's colleagues find the workflow useful but say they forget it exists when they are busy.
options: Put it where the work already happens so remembering is not required
Send periodic reminders about the workflow so that it stays in people's minds during the busy periods when they are most likely to forget that it is available
Add it to the team's written process documentation instead
Ask the team lead to mention it in team meetings so that colleagues are regularly reminded that the workflow exists and is available for them to use
questions.why: Forgetting under pressure is a placement problem. Putting the capability in the path of the work removes the need to remember it at all.
questions.traps: Reminders, documentation and meeting mentions all rely on recall at the moment of need, which is exactly what fails when people are busy.

questions.stem: A workflow has Claude produce a draft that a person finishes, but the person rewrites most of it because the draft is aimed at the wrong reader.
options: Ask the person to give feedback after each draft so that the prompt can be improved over time and future drafts require less rewriting than the current ones do
Ask for a shorter draft so that there is less of it to rewrite
Accept the rewriting as the normal division of labour between the model producing raw material and the person shaping it into something that suits the audience
Supply the reader and purpose as inputs so the draft starts in the right place
questions.why: A draft aimed at the wrong reader is missing an input rather than needing more polish. Supplying audience and purpose fixes it at the source.
questions.traps: Iterative feedback eventually converges but repeats the waste meanwhile. A shorter draft is less wasted work rather than better work, and accepting the rewriting normalises a fixable gap.

questions.stem: A team is asked to reduce a process from ten days to five and has identified Claude as the way to do it.
options: Apply Claude to every step that involves producing written material
Apply Claude to the single longest step in the process
Find where the ten days actually go before assuming drafting is the constraint
Set the five-day target as a goal and let each step's owner work out how to contribute to reaching it within their own part of the overall process
questions.why: A target without a breakdown of where the time goes cannot be planned against. Locating the ten days is the prerequisite to any intervention.
questions.traps: Filtering by activity type presumes the answer. The longest step may not be reducible, and devolving the target does not reveal where the time sits.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step, but the manual version currently produces a written record that an auditor relies on.
options: Automate the step and generate the record separately afterwards
Ensure the automated version produces an equivalent record before the manual one is removed
Ask the auditor whether the record is still needed
Automate the step and keep the manual version running in parallel for a period
questions.why: A manual step often produces artefacts other people depend on. Preserving the record as part of the automated design is what avoids breaking an obligation.
questions.traps: A separately generated record is a version of the right answer but sequenced after the removal. Asking the auditor is reasonable but does not itself preserve anything, and parallel running defers the problem.

questions.stem: A team's checkpoint is placed correctly but the person staffing it changes weekly, so standards vary noticeably.
options: Assign the checkpoint permanently to one person so that the standard applied to each item is consistent from one week to the next across the whole workflow
Rotate the reviewers rather less frequently than at present
Have two people staff the checkpoint together each week
Write down what the check must cover so the standard travels with the role
questions.why: Variation between reviewers means the standard lives in individuals rather than in the process. Documenting it is what makes the check reproducible regardless of who performs it.
questions.traps: A permanent assignment removes variation by removing rotation, at the cost of a single point of failure. Slower rotation and pairing both dilute the variation without defining the standard.

questions.stem: An associate wants to connect Claude to a system, and the only available access method returns far more data than the task needs.
options: Send the full response and rely on Claude to use only the parts of it that are relevant to the task it has been asked to perform on each occasion
Filter the data down to what the task needs before it is sent
Request a narrower access method from the system's owners
Accept the additional data since it costs little and may occasionally contain something useful that the task turns out to need at some point in the future
questions.why: Sending only what is needed limits both cost and exposure. Filtering at the boundary is the control that does not depend on the model ignoring what it receives.
questions.traps: Relying on the model to ignore data still transmits it. A narrower method may not exist, and accepting excess data ignores both the cost and the exposure.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has never failed, and the team has concluded that error handling would be unnecessary complexity.
options: Recognise that an untested failure path is a risk rather than an absent one
Add error handling only for the failure modes that have actually occurred
Accept the current design since it has proven reliable in practice over an extended period of real use and adding complexity would introduce its own risks
Add a general catch-all that stops the workflow on any unexpected condition
questions.why: Absence of observed failure is not absence of failure modes. Treating the untested path as a real risk is what makes the design honest.
questions.traps: Handling only past failures waits for each one to happen once. Inferring safety from an incident-free record is the trap, and a blanket stop is a reasonable tactic rather than the reasoning being tested.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good output but the quality depends on how carefully the person phrases their request each time.
options: Train the team to write better requests so that everyone reaches the standard the most careful person currently achieves when they use the workflow
Ask Claude to clarify any request that seems vague to it
Standardise the request so the variable input is data rather than phrasing
Accept that output quality will vary with the effort each person puts into their request
questions.why: Phrasing-dependent quality means the prompt is doing work that should be fixed in configuration. Standardising it removes the variable.
questions.traps: Training raises the floor without removing the dependency. Clarification adds a round trip, and accepting the variation forfeits repeatability.

questions.stem: A team wants to compare two versions of a workflow but can only run one at a time on real work.
options: Alternate between them over a period so both meet a comparable mix of work
Run the first version for a month and the second for the following month, then compare the results from the two months to see which performed better overall
Run both of the versions on historical cases instead
Ask the team which version they prefer after they have had a chance to use each of them for a reasonable period of time in their normal work
questions.why: Alternating within the same period balances the mix of work each version encounters, which sequential months do not.
questions.traps: Consecutive months confound the version with whatever else differed between them. Historical cases may not reflect current work, and preference is not measurement.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires a change that makes one person's job noticeably harder while making four people's jobs easier.
options: Proceed, since the workflow produces a net benefit across the team
Address the cost falling on that person rather than treating it as an acceptable trade
Ask that person to accept the change for the good of the team as a whole
Compensate that person with recognition for absorbing the additional difficulty that the change has created within their own part of the process
questions.why: Concentrated costs and diffuse benefits is the classic pattern that stalls adoption. Addressing the concentrated cost is what makes the change stick.
questions.traps: Net-benefit reasoning ignores who bears the cost. Appeals to team spirit and recognition both ask one person to absorb a fixable design problem.

questions.stem: A workflow's output is consumed by a downstream team who have never been asked what they need from it.
options: Send them the current output and ask for feedback so that improvements can be made
Design the output to include everything that might be useful
Ask them what they need before designing the output format any further
Ask the upstream team what they think the downstream team probably needs
questions.why: The consumer's requirements are the specification for the output. Asking is faster and more accurate than inferring or iterating toward it.
questions.traps: Feedback on a design made without them is slower. Including everything shifts filtering downstream, and second-hand assumptions are guesses.

questions.stem: A team's process includes a step that everyone agrees is unnecessary, but nobody knows why it was introduced.
options: Remove the step, since everyone involved in the process agrees that it serves no useful purpose in the work as it is currently carried out by the team
Keep the step, since it was presumably introduced for a reason and removing it might cause a problem that nobody currently anticipates happening
Automate the step so it costs less while remaining in place in case it turns out to serve some purpose that is not currently understood
Find out why it exists before removing it
questions.why: Steps usually exist for a reason that outlived its explanation. Finding the reason is what distinguishes safe removal from removing a control.
questions.traps: Removing on consensus risks deleting something load-bearing. Keeping it forever pays a permanent cost, and automating preserves the waste.

questions.stem: An associate proposes automating a step where the model would need to interpret tone in customer messages to decide how to route them.
options: Automate it, since tone is a well-understood property of text and language models are generally capable of assessing it accurately across a range of contexts
Route the tickets on keywords rather than on tone
Test how well tone interpretation performs before designing anything around it
Automate it and have a person review the routing decisions for the first month
questions.why: Whether tone routing works on this team's messages is an empirical question. Testing it is what determines whether the design is viable at all.
questions.traps: Assuming capability skips the test. Keyword routing is a different design chosen without evidence, and a review month tests in production.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers are asked to check accuracy but are given the output only in a format that makes checking slow and awkward.
options: Give reviewers the output in a form that makes the check practical
Ask reviewers to allow more time for each item so that the awkward format does not prevent them from completing the checks they are supposed to perform
Reduce the number of items that are reviewed each week
Ask Claude to produce a summary of the key claims alongside the output
questions.why: A check that is awkward to perform gets performed badly. Making it practical is the direct fix and costs less than the alternatives.
questions.traps: More time absorbs the friction rather than removing it. Reviewing fewer items weakens the control, and a model-generated claim list is not independent of the output.

questions.stem: A team's integration passes data to Claude and stores the response, but nothing records which version of the prompt produced each response.
options: Store the responses with a timestamp so that the approximate period each one was produced in can be identified later if questions arise about a particular result
Record the prompt version with each stored response so results stay interpretable
Keep a separate change log recording every prompt edit
Ask the person who maintains the prompt to note when they make significant changes so the team has some record of when the behaviour may have shifted
questions.why: Stored results are only interpretable against the configuration that produced them. Recording the version with the response is what preserves that link.
questions.traps: A timestamp requires correlating against a separate history. A change log and manual notes both leave the association to be reconstructed.

questions.stem: A workflow produces one wrong output in every two hundred, and the team has decided that rate is acceptable.
options: Continue, since a failure rate of one in two hundred is low by most standards and the effort to reduce it further would be substantial relative to the benefit
Reduce the failure rate further before doing anything else
Measure the rate more precisely so the team has a more accurate figure to base their acceptance decision on than the current approximate estimate
Check that the consequences of the wrong ones are also acceptable, not just the rate
questions.why: An acceptable rate depends entirely on what a failure does. The rate alone cannot support the judgement without the consequence.
questions.traps: Accepting on the rate skips the consequence. Reducing it further acts without knowing whether it matters, and a more precise rate is still only half the picture.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works when run against clean data and fails unpredictably when the data has small inconsistencies.
options: Validate and normalise the data before it enters the workflow
Add instructions telling Claude how to handle each of the inconsistencies the team has encountered so far in the data they have been working with
Ask the upstream team to send data that is already clean
Add a review step that checks the output whenever the input data contained inconsistencies
questions.why: Input variability handled at the boundary makes downstream behaviour predictable. Normalising is what turns unpredictable failure into a controlled path.
questions.traps: Per-case instructions grow indefinitely and miss new cases. Upstream cleanliness is outside the team's control, and reviewing afterwards catches rather than prevents.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has been running for a year and nobody has checked whether the problem it solves still exists.
options: Continue the workflow, since it has been running successfully for a year and there is no indication that anything has changed about the situation it addresses
Expand the workflow so that it covers more cases than now
Confirm the problem is still there before continuing to invest in solving it
Measure the workflow's performance more thoroughly so that the team has better evidence about how well it has been operating over the past twelve months
questions.why: Workflows outlive the problems that justified them. Confirming the problem still exists is the question that determines whether any of the other measurement matters.
questions.traps: Continuing on momentum is the pattern being tested. Expanding scales a possibly obsolete solution, and better performance data does not establish continued relevance.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow is adopted quickly but people use it for a different purpose than it was designed for.
options: Correct the misuse by explaining what the workflow was designed for and asking people to use it for that purpose
Redesign the workflow around the original purpose
Restrict the workflow so that it can only be used for the purpose it was originally designed to serve
Find out what problem they are actually solving with it
questions.why: Unprompted repurposing is strong evidence about where the real need is. Understanding it is more valuable than correcting it.
questions.traps: Correcting the usage discards the signal. Redesigning around the original purpose doubles down on it, and restricting removes value people are evidently getting.

questions.stem: A workflow requires the person receiving Claude's output to know context that was available upstream but is not passed along.
options: Ask the receiving person to request the context from the upstream team
Pass the context forward as part of the handoff
Have the receiving person sit with the upstream team
Ask Claude to include any context it used in its output so the receiving person has visibility of what informed the result they are being asked to work with
questions.why: Context a downstream step needs is part of what the handoff must carry. Passing it forward is the design fix.
questions.traps: Requesting it on demand adds delay and depends on knowing what is missing. Co-location is a heavy fix, and a model-reported context summary is not the upstream context.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to improve an existing process or redesign it, and the existing process was built around constraints that no longer apply.
options: Improve the existing process incrementally, since that is less disruptive to the people who work within it and delivers benefits sooner than a full redesign would
Redesign only those steps that are most affected by the change
Keep the existing process and add Claude to the steps where it fits most naturally
Redesign, since the current shape reflects constraints that have since disappeared
questions.why: A process built around removed constraints is optimised for a world that no longer exists. Incremental improvement preserves that shape.
questions.traps: Incremental improvement and partial redesign both keep the obsolete structure. Adding a tool to an obsolete process improves the wrong thing.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step and has established that the model performs it correctly 96% of the time.
options: Automate it, since 96% accuracy exceeds the rate that the manual process was achieving before the automation was proposed by the team
Ask what happens in the other 4% and whether that is detectable and recoverable
Automate the step and review a sample of the decisions
Improve the prompt until the accuracy is higher than 96% before automating the step
questions.why: The decision turns on what the 4% does and whether anyone will notice. An accuracy figure alone cannot support an automation decision.
questions.traps: Comparing to the manual rate ignores the failure's consequence. Sampling catches some, and chasing a higher rate defers the same unanswered question.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is designed so that a failure in one step stops everything downstream, including steps that do not depend on it.
options: Decouple the independent steps so an unrelated failure does not block them
Add error handling to the failing step so that it recovers automatically and the downstream steps are not blocked when a problem occurs during its execution
Run the independent steps first, before the one that fails
Accept the coupling since it is simpler to reason about a workflow where a failure anywhere stops the whole process
questions.why: Unnecessary coupling turns a local failure into a total one. Decoupling genuinely independent steps limits the blast radius.
questions.traps: Recovery in the failing step does not address the coupling. Reordering helps by accident, and accepting the coupling keeps the amplification.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow depends on a colleague manually triggering it each morning, and it is skipped whenever that colleague is away.
options: Ask the colleague to arrange cover with someone else whenever they are going to be away
Document the trigger procedure so that anyone on the team is able to run the workflow if the usual person happens to be unavailable on a given day
Schedule the trigger so the workflow does not depend on one person being present
Run the workflow twice as often on the days it does run
questions.why: A workflow that needs a specific person present each morning has an availability dependency that scheduling removes entirely.
questions.traps: Arranged cover and documentation both keep a human trigger that can be missed. Running more often on available days does not fill the gaps.

questions.stem: A team is designing a workflow and must decide whether the human checkpoint reviews every item or only the ones that meet certain conditions
options: Review everything, since conditions may not capture every case where an error would matter and full coverage is the only way to be certain nothing important is missed
Review a fixed proportion of the items that come through
Review whatever the reviewer has time for on any given day, adjusting the proportion up or down
Define conditions tied to what an error would cost, and review those items fully
questions.why: Conditional review tied to consequence concentrates the available attention where errors cost most, which is what makes limited review capacity effective.
questions.traps: Reviewing everything is the unsustainable pattern this question is about. A fixed proportion ignores stakes, and capacity-driven review lets workload set the control.

questions.stem: A team's process has one step that fails often and one step that fails rarely but catastrophically
options: Address the frequently failing step first, since it disrupts the process regularly and fixing it will produce the most visible improvement to how the process runs day to day
Weigh frequency against consequence rather than addressing whichever fails more often
Address the catastrophic step first because of its severity
Address both steps at the same time so that neither of the two problems is left outstanding
questions.why: Risk is frequency times consequence, and neither dimension alone determines priority. Weighing both is what produces a defensible ordering.
questions.traps: Prioritising by frequency ignores severity. Prioritising by severity ignores exposure, and doing both at once avoids the prioritisation the question is testing.

questions.stem: An associate is asked whether a step should be automated, and the step currently takes forty minutes a day across the team
options: Ask what the step's errors would cost before deciding on the time saving alone
Automate it, since forty minutes a day across a team is over three working weeks a year and that is a substantial saving to leave on the table indefinitely
Automate it if the automation can be built quickly enough
Leave it manual, since forty minutes spread across a team is a small amount per person and does not justify the effort of building and maintaining an automation
questions.why: Automation decisions weigh the saving against what automated errors would cost. The time figure is only half of the input.
questions.traps: Deciding on the time saving alone in either direction omits the risk side. Build speed is a cost consideration rather than a decision criterion.

questions.stem: A workflow's most likely failure is that the model produces plausible output from an input it did not fully receive
options: Add a review step that reads the output carefully to identify anything that looks as though it might have been produced from incomplete information during the run
Choose a stronger model so the problem occurs less often
Check that the input arrived complete before the output is produced or used
Ask Claude to state whether it received the complete input
questions.why: Truncated input producing plausible output is only caught by verifying the input, since the output gives no signal. That check has to be upstream.
questions.traps: Reviewing output cannot detect what was never there. A stronger model produces more plausible output from partial input, and self-reported completeness is unreliable.

questions.stem: A team wants their workflow to produce the same result if it is run again in six months with the same inputs
options: Pin the configuration and record it, since defaults and models change over time
Document the workflow thoroughly so that it can be reconstructed in six months if anyone needs to reproduce the result that was originally obtained from it
Save the output somewhere so it can be consulted later
Run the workflow again now and confirm that it produces the same result
questions.why: Reproducibility over time requires pinning what varies and recording it. Models and defaults change, so an unpinned workflow drifts.
questions.traps: Documentation describes without pinning. Saving output preserves a result rather than the ability to reproduce it, and a repeat run today says nothing about six months out.

questions.stem: A team's workflow reads from a system whose owners are planning a change to its data format next quarter
options: Wait until the change happens and fix the workflow at that point
Build the workflow so that it accepts both of the formats
Ask the system owners to delay their change until the team has had time to prepare the workflow for the new format they intend to introduce
Agree the change with them and adapt before it lands, rather than after
questions.why: A known upcoming change is something to coordinate around. Adapting before it lands avoids an outage that is entirely predictable.
questions.traps: Waiting guarantees a break. Accepting both formats adds permanent complexity for a transition, and asking others to delay is not within the team's control.

questions.stem: A team wants to demonstrate their workflow's value but the benefit is that a rare expensive mistake no longer happens
options: Report that the mistake has not occurred since the workflow was introduced
Express the value as the expected cost avoided, with the frequency and cost stated
Report the time saved by the workflow instead of the value
Wait until enough time has passed to show a statistically meaningful reduction in the rate at which the expensive mistake occurs across the organisation
questions.why: Prevention value is expressed as expected cost avoided, which makes both the frequency and the consequence explicit and lets a reader judge the estimate.
questions.traps: Absence over a short period is weak evidence for a rare event. Time saved measures something else, and waiting for statistical significance on a rare event takes years.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires people to trust it with work they consider high-stakes, and adoption has stalled at the low-stakes cases
options: Encourage people to try it on higher-stakes work so that they can see for themselves that it performs just as well there as it does on the simpler cases
Mandate its use on the high-stakes work as well as the rest
Treat the low-stakes adoption as the evidence base for extending upward
Accept the current split, since using it on low-stakes work
questions.why: Accumulated low-stakes performance is exactly the evidence that justifies extending scope. Using it deliberately turns caution into a staged rollout.
questions.traps: Encouragement without evidence asks for trust. Mandating removes the judgement, and accepting the split forgoes the value where it is largest.

questions.stem: A workflow's two steps are owned by different people who each optimise their own step, and the overall result has got worse
options: Measure and optimise the end-to-end result rather than each step separately
Ask both owners to coordinate their changes so that improvements to one step do not create problems for the other step in the sequence
Combine both of the steps under a single named owner
Add a third step that corrects whatever problems arise from the interaction between the first two steps in the workflow
questions.why: Local optimisation against local measures degrades the whole. Measuring end to end is what aligns the incentives with the outcome.
questions.traps: Coordination without a shared measure leaves both optimising locally. Single ownership is a reorganisation, and a corrective step treats the symptom.

questions.stem: An associate discovers that the process they are mapping is performed differently by each of the five people who do it
options: Standardise on the approach used by the most experienced person
Establish which variations are deliberate before standardising anything
Standardise on whichever of the variations is the fastest
Let each person keep their own variation and design the workflow to accommodate all five of the different approaches that are currently in use across the team
questions.why: Variation often encodes real differences in the cases each person handles. Distinguishing deliberate adaptation from drift is what makes standardisation safe.
questions.traps: Standardising on seniority or speed may discard necessary adaptations. Accommodating all five builds complexity around variation nobody has understood.

questions.stem: A team's workflow asks a person to approve output they did not request and have no context for
options: Ask the approver to request context from the person who initiated the work
Add a summary of the context to each item under review
Ask the approver to approve on the basis of whether the output looks internally consistent and well-formed
Give the approver the context, or move the approval to someone who has it
questions.why: An approval without context is a formality. Supplying context or relocating the approval is what makes it a real decision.
questions.traps: On-demand context requests add delay and depend on knowing what is missing. A generated summary is not independent, and approving on form alone concedes the point.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step, and doing so would mean nobody in the team understands how that part of the work is done any more
options: Automate it, since the point of automation is that people no longer need to concern themselves with the details of how the work is performed on a routine basis
Document the step in detail before automating any of it
Keep enough understanding in the team to supervise and change the step later
Rotate people through the manual version occasionally so that the knowledge does not disappear entirely from the team over the longer term
questions.why: Automating away all understanding leaves a step nobody can supervise, debug or modify. Retaining working knowledge is what keeps the team in control of it.
questions.traps: Treating opacity as the goal is the misconception. Documentation and rotation are both mechanisms for retaining understanding rather than alternatives to it.

questions.stem: A workflow retries automatically when a step fails, and a persistent failure now produces thousands of retries
options: Increase the interval between retries so that the volume of attempts is lower
Remove the retry logic so the workflow stops after one attempt
Ask someone to monitor the workflow so that persistent failures are noticed and the process can be stopped manually when this situation arises again
Cap the retries and escalate when the cap is reached
questions.why: Retries handle transient failures and must not run unbounded against a persistent one. A cap plus escalation distinguishes the two cases.
questions.traps: Longer intervals reduce the rate of a still-unbounded loop. Removing retries loses transient recovery, and manual monitoring is a person doing what a cap does automatically.

questions.stem: A team's workflow relies on a document that a colleague updates informally whenever they think of it
options: Ask the colleague to notify the team whenever they update the document
Establish a defined update cadence and owner for the document
Take a copy of the document for reference
Add a note to the workflow saying that the document may not be current
questions.why: An input that changes informally makes the workflow's behaviour unpredictable. Defining ownership and cadence is what makes the dependency reliable.
questions.traps: Notification depends on remembering. A copy goes stale immediately, and a caveat documents the problem without fixing it.

questions.stem: An associate's integration works but sends credentials in a way the security team has not reviewed
options: Have the security team review it before the integration goes into use
Proceed, since the integration is internal and the credentials do not leave the organisation's own systems at any point during its normal operation
Ask the security team to review it after launch
Use a different credential with fewer permissions so that the risk is lower even
questions.why: Credential handling is a security review matter and the review belongs before use. That is a governance boundary rather than a technical preference.
questions.traps: Internal scope does not exempt credential handling from review. Post-launch review accepts the exposure, and reducing permissions without review still bypasses the control.

questions.stem: A team's workflow shows a clear benefit in the pilot metrics but the people using it say it makes their work harder
options: Trust the metrics, since they measure the outcome objectively
Trust the user reports rather than the measured pilot figures
Investigate the discrepancy rather than choosing which signal to believe
Continue the workflow and monitor whether the user reports change over the coming months as people become more familiar with how it operates
questions.why: A gap between measured benefit and experienced burden usually means the metric misses a real cost. Investigating is what reconciles them.
questions.traps: Choosing either signal discards information. Waiting for familiarity assumes the complaint is an adjustment problem rather than a finding.

questions.stem: A team's workflow was designed by someone who has since left, and the current team does not know why it works the way it does
options: Reconstruct the reasoning before changing anything
Change whatever seems suboptimal, since the current team are the ones who use it and are best placed to judge what would work better for them now
Leave the workflow unchanged rather than risking a regression
Rebuild the workflow from scratch so that the current team fully understands every decision that has gone into the version they are working with
questions.why: Undocumented design decisions often encode constraints. Reconstructing the reasoning is what makes change safe rather than a gamble.
questions.traps: Changing what looks suboptimal risks removing something load-bearing. Freezing it forever is a permanent cost, and rebuilding discards a working system.

questions.stem: A workflow passes output to a system that silently truncates anything over a certain length
options: Ask Claude to produce shorter output so that the material it generates stays within the limit that the receiving system is able to accept
Increase the receiving system's length limit so nothing is cut
Enforce the length limit at the handoff so truncation cannot happen silently
Check the receiving system periodically to identify records that appear to have been truncated so they can be corrected when the problem is found
questions.why: Silent truncation at a boundary is a contract violation that must be caught where it occurs. Enforcing the limit makes the failure explicit.
questions.traps: Shorter output reduces the incidence without preventing it. Raising the limit may not be possible, and periodic checks find truncation after the data is already wrong.

questions.stem: A team wants to measure a process before changing it, but measuring would itself take three weeks of effort
options: Measure the process thoroughly, since a change made without a baseline cannot be evaluated afterwards and the three weeks is an investment in knowing whether it worked
Measure the one or two things the decision actually depends on
Skip the measurement and change the process
Measure after the change instead, since that will show how the new process performs and the old one is being replaced anyway so its performance matters less
questions.why: Measurement should be scoped to what the decision needs rather than to the process as a whole. That is what makes a baseline affordable.
questions.traps: Full measurement over-invests. Skipping it loses the baseline entirely, and measuring only afterwards leaves nothing to compare against.

questions.stem: A team is considering automating a step where the input occasionally contains something the model should refuse to process
options: Automate it and rely on the model to decline when it encounters material it should not process
Keep the step manual so that the incidental knowledge is retained
Automate it and add a review step that identifies any cases where the model processed something it should have declined to handle in the first place
Design the refusal path deliberately rather than leaving it to the model's judgement
questions.why: A refusal path that matters should be designed and tested rather than assumed. Defining what the workflow does with such input is part of the design.
questions.traps: Relying on default behaviour leaves the boundary undefined and untested. Manual handling forgoes the automation, and after-the-fact review catches failures rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: A team's workflow was designed around one failure mode and a different one has now occurred twice
options: Revisit the failure analysis, since the assumptions behind it have been shown incomplete
Add handling for the new failure mode alongside the existing handling
Increase the level of monitoring applied
Treat the two occurrences as unusual and continue with the current design
questions.why: Two occurrences of an unanticipated mode is evidence that the original analysis was incomplete. Revisiting it is what surfaces what else was missed.
questions.traps: Patching the new mode addresses this one and leaves the analysis unrevised. More monitoring watches without understanding, and dismissing two occurrences ignores the evidence.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives consistent results within a single session and different results across sessions
options: Accept the variation, since some difference between sessions is a normal property of working with a model and the results within any single session remain consistent
Run everything within a single session to avoid the variation entirely
Identify what differs between sessions, since something is varying that should not be
Average the results across several sessions so that the variation between them is smoothed out in the figure the team actually reports and uses
questions.why: Consistency within sessions and variation across them points at a session-scoped input such as accumulated context or configuration. That is findable.
questions.traps: Accepting it abandons a diagnosable problem. Forcing single sessions is a workaround, and averaging conceals rather than explains the variation.

questions.stem: An associate wants to integrate Claude into a process, and the integration would be the only automated part of an otherwise manual workflow
options: Build the integration, since automating any part of a manual process delivers a saving and the surrounding manual steps do not prevent that part from being faster
Check whether the manual steps around it would absorb the benefit
Automate the whole of the process rather than only this single step
Automate the step and measure whether the overall process time falls
questions.why: A single automated step inside a manual process often produces work that then waits. Checking whether the surrounding steps absorb the gain is the prior question.
questions.traps: Assuming the local saving reaches the outcome is the error. Full automation may not be feasible, and measuring afterwards spends the effort before asking.

questions.stem: A team's workflow reduces errors but the errors it prevents were previously caught by a downstream check that still runs
options: Report the error reduction, since fewer errors being produced is a genuine improvement
Remove the downstream check entirely now that errors are prevented upstream
Continue running both, since redundant checks provide additional assurance and the cost of the downstream check was already being incurred before the workflow was introduced
Check whether the downstream check can now be reduced, since otherwise the saving is not realised
questions.why: If a downstream check still absorbs the same cost, preventing errors upstream has not yet produced a saving. Whether the check can be reduced is what realises it.
questions.traps: Reporting the reduction claims a benefit that has not landed. Removing the check outright is premature, and keeping both indefinitely means the workflow pays for itself twice.

questions.stem: A team introduces a workflow and the people who use it most are the ones who were already most productive
options: Consider the rollout a success, since the workflow is being adopted and the people using it are getting value from it in their day-to-day work
Target the least productive users in the next phase of the rollout
Check whether the workflow is widening rather than closing the gap
Accept the pattern, since more capable users adopting new tools more readily is a common and expected outcome that does not require any particular intervention
questions.why: If a tool amplifies existing capability, the aggregate improves while the spread widens. Noticing that is what tells you whether the rollout met its goal.
questions.traps: Adoption by the already-productive is not the same as the intended outcome. Targeting others assumes the cause, and accepting the pattern skips the check.

questions.stem: A workflow's output includes a confidence indicator that the receiving person has learned to ignore because it is rarely informative
options: Explain to the receiving person what the confidence indicator means
Replace it with a numeric score
Keep it, since it costs nothing to produce and may occasionally be useful
Remove it or make it meaningful, since an ignored signal is worse than none
questions.why: A signal people have learned to ignore trains them to ignore signals generally. Either making it informative or removing it is the honest response.
questions.traps: Explaining an uninformative signal does not make it informative. A numeric version of the same weak signal is no better, and keeping it normalises ignoring indicators.

questions.stem: A team is asked to make a process faster, and the process is already faster than the downstream team can consume its output
options: Look downstream, since speeding up production ahead of consumption creates a queue
Speed up the process as requested, since that is what has been asked for and the downstream team's capacity is not within this team's control or responsibility
Slow the process down so it matches what the downstream team can take
Speed up the process and store the additional output until the downstream team is ready to consume it
questions.why: Producing faster than the next stage can absorb builds inventory rather than delivering value. The constraint is downstream.
questions.traps: Delivering the request as stated produces a growing queue. Slowing down is not the ask, and buffering output is inventory rather than throughput.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to automate a decision that is currently made by consensus between three people
options: Automate it using the position the three people usually converge on, since that represents the collective judgement they would have reached anyway in most cases
Establish whether the consensus encodes a rule or genuine disagreement
Keep the decision manual rather than automating any part of the step
Automate it and route to the three people only in the cases where the model is uncertain about which way the decision should go on the evidence available
questions.why: Consensus may be an agreed rule applied by three people or a genuine negotiation. Which it is determines whether the decision can be specified at all.
questions.traps: Encoding the usual outcome assumes a rule exists. Keeping it manual forgoes the analysis, and uncertainty routing presumes specifiability.

questions.stem: A workflow has good error handling for the failures the team anticipated and no handling for anything else
options: Add a defined behaviour for unanticipated failures rather than leaving them undefined
Extend the error handling to cover additional failure modes as the team identifies them through experience of running the workflow over time
Choose a stronger model so that the truncation problem happens less
Accept the current coverage, since the anticipated failures are the ones most likely to occur and handling every conceivable failure is not a realistic goal
questions.why: Unanticipated failures need a defined default such as stopping safely and escalating. That is what stops an unknown failure from becoming an undefined one.
questions.traps: Extending coverage case by case leaves each new mode undefined until it happens. A stronger model does not define behaviour, and accepting the gap leaves the workflow open-ended.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is run by four people and produces four noticeably different levels of quality
options: Train all four people to the standard achieved by whoever currently produces the best results
Have the best performing person run everything for the team
Standardise the parts that vary rather than training four people toward one standard
Accept the variation as the normal range of quality that different people produce when performing the same task in their own individual ways
questions.why: Person-dependent quality means the workflow leaves too much to the operator. Moving the variable parts into fixed configuration is what makes quality independent of who runs it.
questions.traps: Training toward a standard leaves the dependency in place. Single-operator running is a bottleneck, and accepting variation forfeits repeatability.

questions.stem: A team's integration works reliably but nobody has recorded what it does, and the person who built it has moved teams
options: Leave it alone, since it works reliably and there is no immediate need to spend time documenting something that is not currently causing any problems for anyone
Rebuild it so the current team understands it
Contact the person who built it whenever a question arises about how the integration works or what it is doing in a particular situation
Document what it does and who owns it now, before anything needs changing
questions.why: An undocumented, unowned integration is a problem the moment it needs changing or breaks. Documenting and assigning ownership now is cheap.
questions.traps: Leaving it works until it does not. Rebuilding discards a working system, and depending on someone in another team is a fragile arrangement.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is measured on how many items it processes, and the team has started routing easy items to it to improve the number
options: Ask the team to stop selecting easy items so that the throughput figure reflects the workflow's performance across a representative mix of the work
Change the measure, since it is driving behaviour that does not serve the goal
Keep the measure and add a quality measure alongside it
Accept the selection, since processing easy items through the workflow is still productive work
questions.why: A measure that can be gamed will be. Changing it so it aligns with the goal is what removes the incentive rather than policing it.
questions.traps: Asking people not to respond to an incentive rarely works. A second measure alongside a gameable one leaves the incentive, and accepting the selection accepts a meaningless figure.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires a small amount of setup per user, and half the team have not completed it
options: Do the setup for them, since a small barrier is stopping half the benefit
Send instructions explaining how to complete the setup so that the remaining team members can get themselves up and running when they have a moment
Remind people weekly until the setup is complete
Accept the partial adoption, since the people who completed the setup are presumably the ones who found the workflow most useful for their own work
questions.why: Small barriers stop adoption disproportionately. Removing the barrier entirely is cheaper than repeatedly asking people to cross it.
questions.traps: Instructions and reminders both leave the barrier in place. Inferring preference from an uncrossed barrier confuses friction with disinterest.

questions.stem: A workflow's steps are each fast, but work waits between them because each step runs on a different schedule
options: Speed up the individual steps so that the total processing time falls
Combine all of the steps together into one single larger step
Align the schedules or make the steps trigger each other
Run each step more frequently so that work waits a shorter time between the completion of one step and the start of the next one in the sequence
questions.why: Elapsed time is dominated by waiting between steps rather than by the steps themselves. Triggering removes the wait rather than shortening it.
questions.traps: Faster steps do not touch the waits. Combining steps is a larger change than needed, and more frequent runs reduce the wait without eliminating it.

questions.stem: A team maps their process and finds that half the steps produce output nobody downstream actually uses
options: Automate the production of the unused output with Claude
Ask downstream teams whether they might use it
Keep producing it, since somebody may have needed it at some point and stopping could cause a problem that is not currently visible to the team
Stop producing the unused output
questions.why: Work producing unused output is waste. Stopping it is a larger and simpler gain than making it cheaper to produce.
questions.traps: Automating waste entrenches it. Canvassing for hypothetical users looks for a reason to continue, and preserving it against an unknown need pays permanently.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step, and the person who currently performs it uses the time to notice patterns that inform other decisions
options: Automate the step, since noticing patterns is not the purpose of the step and the person will find other opportunities to observe the same information elsewhere
Identify what that noticing produces and preserve it deliberately
Leave the step manual and recruit a replacement person to be trained
Automate the step and ask the person to review the automated output periodically
questions.why: Manual work often produces incidental value nobody designed. Identifying it before automating is what stops a hidden benefit from disappearing silently.
questions.traps: Assuming the noticing will happen elsewhere is unfounded. Leaving it manual is more than needed, and periodic review of output is not the same as working through the material.

questions.stem: A workflow fails in a way that is obvious to the team but invisible to the customers who receive its output
options: Ask the team to check the output more carefully so that the failures they can recognise are caught before anything reaches the customers who would not notice them
Notify the customers whenever one of these failures actually occurs
Accept the situation, since the team notices the failures and can correct them when they are identified during the course of their normal work
Add detection at the point the customer would experience the problem
questions.why: A failure invisible to the person affected needs detection oriented to their experience rather than to the team's. That is where the control belongs.
questions.traps: More careful team checking still catches only what the team recognises. Notification follows detection, and relying on incidental team awareness leaves customers exposed.

questions.stem: A team wants their workflow to be usable by a different team with different data but the same underlying task
options: Separate the parts that are specific to this team's data from the general method
Give the other team a copy of the workflow and let them adjust whatever does not fit their own data and processes
Rebuild the workflow from scratch for the other team involved
Document the workflow in detail so the other team can understand how it works and decide for themselves what they need to change about it
questions.why: Reusability comes from separating the general method from the local specifics. That is what makes a second deployment a configuration exercise rather than a rebuild.
questions.traps: Handing over a copy to adapt distributes the same untangling work. Rebuilding duplicates effort, and documentation describes without separating.

questions.stem: A team is asked for the return on their workflow and the largest benefit is that a task can now be done at all
options: Estimate what the task would have cost to do manually and report that figure as the saving the workflow has delivered to the organisation
Report the cost figure without any benefit figure alongside
Describe the new capability rather than forcing it into a time-saved figure
Report the time saved on the other smaller tasks the workflow also performs
questions.why: A capability that did not previously exist is not a saving, and describing it as one distorts it. Naming it as new capability is the honest account.
questions.traps: A hypothetical manual cost invents a baseline that never existed. Reporting cost alone omits the benefit, and substituting a minor measurable benefit understates the main one.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works well and a colleague in another team wants to copy it for a task that is superficially similar
options: Share the workflow, since it works well and the colleague can adapt whatever does not fit their own situation
Check whether the underlying task is actually the same before copying it across
Advise the colleague to build their own version from scratch instead
Share the workflow and offer to help them set it up so that the transfer goes smoothly and they get the benefit as quickly as possible in their own team
questions.why: Superficial similarity often hides different requirements. Checking whether the tasks match is what determines whether copying will work at all.
questions.traps: Sharing on surface similarity risks a poor fit discovered later. Advising a rebuild forgoes reuse, and helping with setup accelerates a transfer that may be wrong.

questions.stem: A team is about to add Claude to a process and is deciding what they should do first.
options: Identify which steps Claude is best suited to
Ask the team which steps they find most tedious
Write down how the process actually runs today
Pilot Claude on one step and see what happens
questions.why: You cannot tell what a change did without a description of what was there before, and that description also shows where the change belongs.
questions.traps: Picking steps by suitability skips which steps matter, tedium is not the same as cost, and a pilot with no baseline produces no comparison.

questions.stem: A team is designing a workflow and asks where the human checkpoint should sit in it.
options: At the end of the workflow, after every step has run
At the start, so the input is checked before processing
At whichever step the team has capacity to staff
Before the point where the output has an effect
questions.why: A checkpoint exists to stop a bad output doing damage, so it belongs at the last moment before the output acts on anything.
questions.traps: The end of the workflow may already be past the point of effect, input checking catches different problems, and capacity determines staffing rather than placement.

questions.stem: A team is asked what should happen when their workflow receives an input it cannot handle.
options: Produce the best result it can from what it received
Stop and tell someone, rather than produce a result
Skip the input and carry on with the remaining ones
Retry the input until it eventually goes through
questions.why: An input the workflow cannot handle has no correct output, so the safe behaviour is to halt visibly and let a person deal with it.
questions.traps: A best effort on bad input is exactly the plausible-but-wrong failure, silent skipping loses work unnoticed, and retrying a structurally bad input never succeeds.

questions.stem: A team wants to show that their Claude workflow was worth the effort of building.
options: Compare the outcome it targets before and after
Report how many items the workflow has processed
Report how many people on the team now use it
Report how much time the team believes it saves
questions.why: Value is a change in the thing the workflow was meant to improve, and that requires a before and an after.
questions.traps: Volume measures activity, adoption measures uptake, and a believed saving is an impression rather than a measurement.

questions.stem: An associate is connecting Claude to a system and asks what data should be sent to it.
options: Everything the system holds, so nothing is missing
Only the fields the task itself actually requires
Everything except the fields marked as confidential
Whatever the system returns in its default response
questions.why: Sending only what the task requires limits both the exposure and the material the model has to work through.
questions.traps: Sending everything maximises both, excluding only marked fields leaves unmarked sensitive data, and a default response is not a decision about what is needed.

questions.stem: A team wants their monthly workflow to give the same answer if it is rerun next year.
options: Record the prompt, the inputs and the settings used
Record the output so it can be compared later on
Ask the same person to run it again next year
Write down the date on which the workflow was last run
questions.why: A run is reproducible when everything that determined it has been captured, which is the prompt, what went in, and how it was configured.
questions.traps: The output is the thing being reproduced, the same person cannot recall the settings, and a date records when rather than how.

questions.stem: A team lead wants to know why a carefully built workflow is not being used by anyone.
options: Improve the workflow further before promoting it again
Make the workflow mandatory for the affected task
Ask the people who are not using it what stops them
Send a reminder explaining the benefits once more
questions.why: The reason for non-adoption sits with the non-adopters, and asking them is the only way to find out what it is.
questions.traps: Improving it assumes quality is the barrier, mandating it forces use without removing the barrier, and a reminder repeats a message that has already failed.

questions.stem: A workflow passes Claude's output to a colleague who does not know what was asked for.
options: Ask the colleague to request context when they need it
Add a note to the output describing its general purpose
Have the colleague run the workflow themselves instead
Pass the original request along with the output
questions.why: A handoff works when the receiver has what they need to judge the work, and the request is what makes the output interpretable.
questions.traps: Asking on demand adds a round trip each time, a general note is not the specific request, and moving the work is a bigger change than the gap requires.

questions.stem: A team asks which steps of a process are the safest ones to automate first.
options: Steps whose output is checked further down anyway
Steps that take the longest for people to perform
Steps that the team finds the least interesting
Steps that involve the fewest people in the team
questions.why: A step whose result is verified downstream has a natural safety net, which makes it the cheapest place to be wrong while learning.
questions.traps: Duration, tedium and headcount all describe the cost of doing the step rather than the cost of getting it wrong.

questions.stem: An associate maps a process and finds two separate steps producing the same information.
options: Remove the later of the two duplicated steps found
Remove whichever of the two takes longer to perform
Find out why both exist before removing either one
Keep both, since duplication provides a cross-check
questions.why: Apparent duplication often turns out to serve two different purposes, and finding out which is what makes removal safe.
questions.traps: Position and duration are arbitrary grounds for choosing, and assuming a deliberate cross-check is the same guess in the opposite direction.

questions.stem: A team asks how they would know if their workflow had started to fail quietly.
options: Wait for someone downstream to report a problem
Decide now what a failure would actually look like
Check the outputs whenever there is spare capacity
Assume the workflow is failing if usage drops off
questions.why: You can only detect a failure you have described, and describing it in advance is what makes monitoring possible.
questions.traps: Downstream reports arrive after the damage, spare-capacity checking is not a schedule, and usage is not a quality signal.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether their workflow saves money, and what it actually saves is time.
options: Convert the saved hours into a monetary figure
Report the time saving without any further comment
Say that the workflow does not save money at all
Say what the saved time is now being spent on
questions.why: Saved time only becomes value when it goes somewhere, so what it is now used for is the answer to the question actually asked.
questions.traps: A monetary conversion asserts a saving that may not have been realised, an unqualified time figure leaves the question unanswered, and a flat denial ignores real value.

questions.stem: An associate's integration works and they are asked what happens when the model responds slowly.
options: Wait as long as it takes for a response to arrive
Retry the request immediately if it feels too slow
Decide how long to wait and what to do after that
Treat any slowness as a failure and stop the workflow
questions.why: A defined timeout with a defined action is what stops a slow response becoming a stuck workflow.
