questions.traps: Waiting indefinitely blocks everything behind it, immediate retries multiply the load, and treating any delay as failure discards work that would have completed.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step that is currently the only training opportunity for new joiners.
options: Automate it, since training is not the step's purpose
Automate it and build the training in somewhere else
Leave it manual so new joiners keep learning from it
Automate it only once new joiners have done it once
questions.why: The training value is real and separable, so the step can be automated as long as what it taught is deliberately replaced.
questions.traps: Dismissing training ignores a genuine cost, keeping the step preserves the training by paying for it forever, and one exposure does not replicate repeated practice.

questions.stem: A workflow hands work to a team who consistently return it asking for the same missing detail.
options: Ask the receiving team to be more specific in requests
Have the sending team add the detail on each return
Meet with the receiving team to agree ways of working
Add the missing detail to what the workflow produces
questions.why: A repeated request is a specification the handoff is missing, and putting it into the output fixes every future instance.
questions.traps: The receiving team has been specific enough to name it, adding it on return repeats the work, and a meeting discusses a fix that is already known.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces slightly different formatting each run and downstream automation breaks.
options: Fix the format at the point the output is consumed
Add a stronger formatting instruction to the prompt
Ask the downstream system to accept the variations
Have a person tidy the output before it is passed on
questions.why: Generated text will vary, so a deterministic step that shapes it into the required format is what makes the downstream contract reliable.
questions.traps: A stronger instruction reduces variation without eliminating it, changing the consumer moves the problem, and manual tidying puts a person into an automated path.

questions.stem: A workflow is used by the team that built it and ignored by the two teams it was built for.
options: Run training sessions for the two other teams
Find out what those two teams' work actually needs
Have the building team run the workflow for them
Ask leadership to require the two teams to adopt it
questions.why: A workflow built for someone else without their input usually misses their actual task, and finding out is what makes it adoptable.
questions.traps: Training teaches a tool that may not fit, running it for them removes their agency and scales badly, and a mandate produces compliance rather than use.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer approves 99% of outputs and the team wonders whether the step is worth keeping.
options: Remove the step, since almost everything is approved
Keep the step, since it is evidently catching something
Reduce the review to a sample of the outputs instead
Find out whether the 1% would have caused real harm
questions.why: The value of a checkpoint is what it prevents rather than how often it fires, so the caught cases are what decide whether to keep it.
questions.traps: A low rejection rate can mean the check is working, "catching something" does not say whether it matters, and sampling changes the depth before the value is known.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has an error path that has never once run in eighteen months of use.
options: Test it deliberately, since it has never been exercised
Remove it, since eighteen months suggests it is unused
Leave it, since it will work when it is finally needed
Rewrite it to handle a wider range of failures
questions.why: Untested behaviour is untested regardless of how long it has sat there, and the first real failure is a bad time to find out.
questions.traps: Absence of firing is not evidence it is unnecessary, assuming it works is the risk itself, and widening its scope adds more untested behaviour.

questions.stem: A team finds one step whose owner has left and whose purpose nobody can now explain.
options: Remove it, since nobody can explain why it exists
Keep it, since removing it might break something
Find out what depends on its output before touching it
Automate it as it stands so it costs less to run
questions.why: A step's purpose shows in what consumes its output, and tracing that is what turns an unknown into a decision.
questions.traps: Removing an unexplained step is how outages happen, keeping it forever institutionalises the unknown, and automating it preserves it without understanding it.

questions.stem: A team's pilot shows a large benefit and the wider rollout shows almost none at all.
options: Look at how the pilot group differed from everyone else
Conclude that the pilot result was measured incorrectly
Roll the workflow back, since the benefit did not reproduce
Extend the rollout period so the benefit has time to appear
questions.why: Pilots run with motivated people on selected work, and the difference between that group and the rest is usually the explanation.
questions.traps: Measurement error is one hypothesis among several, rolling back discards the question, and more time does not change who is using it.

questions.stem: An associate's integration sends one request per row and the file has grown to fifty thousand rows.
options: Run the same integration and simply allow it more time
Process only the rows that have changed recently
Split the file and run the integration several times
Batch the rows so that one request covers many of them
questions.why: Per-row calls scale linearly in cost and time, and batching changes the shape of that cost rather than just its schedule.
questions.traps: More time does not reduce the work, filtering to changed rows changes the task, and splitting the file runs the same number of requests.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step where the model is right 99% of the time and the error is silent.
options: Automate it, since 99% is better than people achieve
Automate it only with a way to detect the silent 1%
Do not automate it, since a silent error is unacceptable
Automate it and review a sample of outputs each week
questions.why: A silent error is one that reaches its destination unchallenged, so detection is the condition that makes the accuracy figure usable.
questions.traps: Comparing to human accuracy ignores that human errors are noisier, a blanket refusal forgoes a strong step, and weekly sampling may never find a rare silent failure.

questions.stem: Two teams disagree about the format of the output that one of them passes to the other.
options: Have the sending team choose, since they produce it
Have the receiving team choose, since they consume it
Write the format down as an agreement between them
Support both formats so neither team has to change
questions.why: The interface between two teams is a shared commitment, and writing it down is what stops it drifting each time either side changes.
questions.traps: Letting either side decide unilaterally recreates the dispute, and supporting both doubles the surface that has to keep working.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives good results for the person who wrote it and worse ones for everyone else.
options: Have that person run the workflow for the whole team
Write down what that person does that the others do not
Simplify the workflow until everyone gets the same result
Accept the difference, since experience ought to count
questions.why: The gap is knowledge that lives in one person's head, and capturing it is what turns a personal workflow into a team one.
questions.traps: Centralising on one person creates a bottleneck, simplifying may remove what makes it good, and accepting it leaves the workflow undocumented.

questions.stem: A team's approver is given the output and a deadline that makes real review impossible.
options: Keep the deadline, since approvals must not delay work
Ask the approver to review as much as they can manage
Move the approval to after the output has been sent
Change either the deadline or the scope of the review
questions.why: A review that cannot be done is not a control, so either the time available or the amount being reviewed has to give.
questions.traps: Protecting the deadline preserves the appearance of a control, partial review leaves the boundary undefined, and reviewing afterwards removes the point of approving.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on a service that has an announced maintenance window each month.
options: Plan the workflow's runs around the announced window
Run as normal and retry if the service is unavailable
Ask the service owner to move the maintenance window
Build a second integration to a different service
questions.why: A known, scheduled outage is the easiest kind to design around, and scheduling around it is cheaper than any technical mitigation.
questions.traps: Retrying wastes runs on a predictable outage, asking the owner treats a scheduled window as negotiable, and a second integration is a large answer to a known window.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step whose correct output differs depending on which client it is for.
options: Automate it once and let the model infer the client rules
Leave it manual, since the rules vary too much to encode
Automate it per client, with the rules stated for each
Automate the common case and handle clients by exception
questions.why: Client-specific rules are knowable and writable, so stating them per client is what makes the automation correct rather than approximately right.
questions.traps: Inference invents rules where they are not stated, refusing assumes variation cannot be encoded, and a common case plus exceptions hides which clients are which.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has clearly improved quality and the time the process takes has gone up.
options: Report the quality gain, since it is what matters most
Report the net effect as a single combined figure
Optimise the workflow until the time cost disappears
Report both and let the trade-off be decided openly
questions.why: A genuine trade-off is a decision for whoever owns the process, and presenting both sides is what lets them make it.
questions.traps: Reporting only the gain hides the cost, a combined figure buries the exchange rate in an assumption, and optimising first delays a decision that can be made now.

questions.stem: A workflow's output is used by a downstream team who have started quietly reworking it every time.
options: Tell them to use the output exactly as it is delivered
Ask what they rework and fold it into the workflow
Accept it, since the rework is their own choice to make
Add a review step before the output ever reaches them
questions.why: Silent rework is unmet requirements showing up as extra effort, and finding out what it is turns it into a fixable specification.
questions.traps: Instructing them to stop removes the workaround without meeting the need, treating it as their choice leaves the cost hidden, and another review checks against the wrong standard.

questions.stem: A team must choose between one thorough reviewer and three quick ones for the same volume.
options: Choose the thorough reviewer, since depth catches more
Choose the three, since more eyes catch more problems
Match the choice to whether errors are subtle or obvious
Choose the three and have them review each other's work
questions.why: Subtle errors need depth and obvious ones need coverage, so the kind of mistake the workflow makes is what decides the shape of the review.
questions.traps: Depth and coverage are each right for a different failure, and cross-review adds cost without addressing which failure is being caught.

questions.stem: A team's workflow must produce the same result for auditors and the wording varies between runs.
options: Fix the facts and the formats, and let the wording vary
Record each run's output so the exact text is preserved
Rerun the workflow until the wording matches a previous run
Replace the model step with a fixed template instead
questions.why: Auditors need the substance to be stable and reproducible, which is achievable even though the exact sentences are not.
questions.traps: Recording outputs preserves history without making runs reproducible, rerunning for a match chases something unavailable, and a fixed template gives up the model's contribution.

questions.stem: A team's most experienced member is the only person not using the workflow, and their work is the best.
options: Accept it, since their results are already the best
Find out what they do that the workflow does not
Require them to use it for consistency with the team
Ask them to train the others in their own method instead
questions.why: The best performer's objection is usually information about the workflow's limits, and extracting it improves the workflow for everyone.
questions.traps: Accepting it loses the information, mandating it trades their quality for uniformity, and having them teach their method sidesteps the workflow question.

questions.stem: An associate must choose between an integration that is quick to build and one that is easier to change.
options: Pick the quick one, since it delivers value sooner
Pick the flexible one, since requirements always change
Build the quick one and replace it with the flexible one
Pick by how often the surrounding process actually changes
questions.why: Flexibility is worth paying for in proportion to how much change it will actually absorb, and the process's history is the evidence for that.
questions.traps: Speed and flexibility are each right in different conditions, and planning to replace it later is a cost that usually never gets paid.

questions.stem: A team finds the bottleneck is a person's availability rather than the duration of any step.
options: Speed up the steps around it to absorb the waiting
Automate the step that the person currently performs
Address the availability rather than speeding up steps
Accept it, since people's time cannot really be scheduled
questions.why: Making the other steps faster leaves the queue unchanged, because the constraint is when the person is free rather than how long the work takes.
questions.traps: Speeding up non-constraints just moves the wait, automating their step may not be possible or wise, and availability is usually schedulable.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has two failure modes and fixing either one makes the other more likely.
options: Decide which failure the process can better tolerate
Fix the one that occurs more often in practice
Fix the one that is the cheaper of the two to fix
Fix both, since leaving either one is unacceptable
questions.why: When two failures trade against each other, the choice is which harm the process can absorb rather than which is easier or more frequent.
questions.traps: Frequency ignores severity, cost of fixing is unrelated to consequence, and fixing both is not available when they genuinely trade.

questions.stem: A team's workflow shows no measurable benefit and everyone who uses it says it is better.
options: Trust the measurement and discontinue the workflow
Trust the users and continue without any measurement
Measure it for longer until a difference shows up
Look for what they value that is not being measured
questions.why: A consistent gap between measures and experience usually means the measures miss something real, and identifying it is the informative move.
questions.traps: Discarding either side throws away evidence, and measuring longer repeats a measurement that may be looking at the wrong thing.

questions.stem: A step is performed correctly by people and the rare errors are caught by the next step anyway.
options: Automate it, since the downstream check already covers it
Leave it, since people already perform the step correctly
Automate it and add a check specific to the new step
Leave it, since automation would add a new failure mode
questions.why: An existing downstream check makes this the low-risk case for automation, since a new class of error would still be caught before it mattered.
questions.traps: Current correctness is not a reason to keep paying for it, a second check duplicates one that exists, and new failure modes are acceptable when they are already caught.

questions.stem: An associate's integration works and the security team asks who can see the data passing through it.
options: Answer from what the associate remembers configuring
Answer from the configuration rather than from memory
Refer the security team to the tool's own documentation
Say that only the workflow's users can see the data
questions.why: A question about access is answered by what is actually configured, since that is what determines the answer and what an auditor can check.
questions.traps: Memory is unreliable about configuration, vendor documentation describes defaults rather than this setup, and an unverified assurance may simply be wrong.

questions.stem: A team's checkpoint catches errors reliably and adds three days to a five-day process.
options: Remove it, since three days on five is too expensive
Keep it, since it reliably catches real errors
Move the checkpoint rather than removing or keeping it
Run it in parallel with the rest of the process
questions.why: A checkpoint that works but sits badly is a placement problem, and moving it earlier or narrowing what it covers keeps the catch at less cost.
questions.traps: Removing it loses a working control, keeping it accepts a cost that has alternatives, and parallel running means the output moves before the check completes.

questions.stem: A team is rolling a new workflow out to sixty people and asks how they should start.
options: Roll it out to everyone at once for consistency
Roll it out to the most enthusiastic people first
Roll it out department by department alphabetically
Start with a small group and learn from what they hit
questions.why: A small first group surfaces the problems while they are still cheap to fix, and what they learn shapes the wider rollout.
questions.traps: An all-at-once launch multiplies every unfixed problem, enthusiasts hide friction others will hit, and an arbitrary order learns nothing between waves.

questions.stem: A team changes a workflow's prompt and wants to be able to go back if it goes wrong.
options: Note what was changed so it can be typed back later
Keep the previous version before making the change
Test the change carefully so a rollback is not needed
Change it gradually so the effect can be observed
questions.why: A kept copy is what makes a rollback immediate, where a description of the change has to be reconstructed under pressure.
questions.traps: Notes are lossy and slow to apply, careful testing reduces the chance rather than the need, and gradual change still leaves nothing to return to.

questions.stem: An associate is asked what could go wrong with a workflow nobody has tested using bad input.
options: They cannot say, because it has not been tested
Nothing, since the workflow handles its inputs well
The same things that go wrong with good input
Only the failures that the designer thought about
questions.why: Untested behaviour is unknown behaviour, and saying so is more useful than an estimate that sounds like knowledge.
questions.traps: Success on good input says nothing about bad, failure modes differ by input, and the designer's list is the hypothesis rather than the answer.

questions.stem: A team wants to measure their workflow and can only pick one single thing to track.
options: The number of times the workflow is run each week
The satisfaction of the people who operate it
The outcome that the process exists to produce
The time the workflow itself takes to complete
questions.why: A single measure should be the thing the process is for, since everything else is only a means to it.
questions.traps: Run count measures activity, operator satisfaction measures experience, and runtime measures one step rather than the result.

questions.stem: A workflow's output goes to three different teams who each need something different from it.
options: Ask each team what they need before designing it
Produce one output covering everything all three need
Produce the output that the largest of the teams needs
Let each team extract what they need from the output
questions.why: Three consumers means three requirements, and collecting them is what lets the output be designed rather than guessed.
questions.traps: A union of everything buries each team's part, sizing by team ignores need, and pushing extraction downstream repeats the work three times.

questions.stem: A team's workflow reads from a system whose owners are about to change its data format.
options: Wait until the change happens and fix what breaks
Ask the owners to delay the change until later on
Copy the data out now so the format stops mattering
Agree a date and test against the new format first
questions.why: A known upcoming change is something to prepare for, and testing before the switch is what turns a breakage into a non-event.
questions.traps: Fixing after the break accepts an outage, asking for a delay postpones rather than solves, and a copy goes stale immediately.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether a task that is performed twice a year is worth automating.
options: Yes, since automation is always worth the investment
Usually not — the build effort will not be repaid
Yes, since twice a year is still a recurring task
No, since infrequent tasks are always done manually
questions.why: Automation pays back through repetition, and twice a year rarely returns the cost of building and maintaining it.
questions.traps: "Always worth it" ignores maintenance, recurrence alone does not settle the arithmetic, and an absolute rule ignores high-value exceptions.

questions.stem: An associate is told a process takes two days and finds that it is two days of waiting.
options: Report the two days as the process's duration
Reduce the working time to shorten the two days
Distinguish the working time from the waiting time
Ask the team to work faster during the two days
questions.why: Waiting and working are different problems with different fixes, and separating them is what shows where the time actually goes.
questions.traps: Reporting the total hides the structure, and speeding up work that is not the constraint leaves the waiting exactly where it was.

questions.stem: A team asks what makes a review step a real control rather than a formality.
options: The reviewer is senior enough to be accountable
The reviewer can and sometimes does reject things
The review is recorded so it can be audited later
The review happens before the output is released
questions.why: A control is real when it changes outcomes, and rejections are the evidence that it can.
questions.traps: Seniority, records and timing all describe the shape of a review that may still never change anything.

questions.stem: A team's workflow fails and nobody can tell which step it actually failed at.
options: Record which step each run reached before stopping
Rerun the workflow and watch it as it runs through
Add more detail to the workflow's final output
Ask whoever ran it what they saw at the time it failed
questions.why: Locating a failure requires a record of progress, and capturing the step reached turns every future failure into a diagnosis.
questions.traps: A watched rerun may not reproduce it, output detail describes success rather than failure, and recollection is not a record.

questions.stem: A team is asked for their workflow's cost and gives only the software licence fee.
options: Give the licence fee, since that is the direct cost
Include the cost of the systems it connects to
Include the salary of everyone who uses the workflow
Include the time spent building and maintaining it
questions.why: The real cost of a workflow is dominated by the human effort to build and keep it running, which the licence line never shows.
questions.traps: The licence is the visible fraction, connected systems exist regardless, and full salaries charge the workflow for work people would do anyway.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires each person to complete a setup step, and half of them have not.
options: Send a reminder asking people to complete the setup
Complete the setup on everyone's behalf centrally
Find out what makes the setup step hard to complete
Remove the feature that requires the setup step
questions.why: A step half the team has not done is usually harder or less clear than it looks, and finding out is what makes it completable.
questions.traps: A reminder repeats an instruction that has not worked, doing it centrally may be impossible for a personal setting, and dropping the feature discards its value.

questions.stem: A workflow's output arrives with the receiving person while they are away on leave.
options: Ask the person to check their messages while away
Route the output to a role rather than to a person
Hold the output until the person returns to work
Send the output to the whole team instead of one person
questions.why: Routing to a role means the handoff survives any individual's absence without anyone having to remember to redirect it.
questions.traps: Expecting work during leave is not a design, holding output stalls the process, and broadcasting to everyone means nobody owns it.

questions.stem: A team automated a step and the person who used to do it now checks the automation instead.
options: Accept it, since a person is still involved in the step
Remove the checking, since the automation is working
Automate the checking as well so the person is freed
Ask whether the checking costs less than the step did
questions.why: If checking costs as much as doing, the automation has moved the work rather than reduced it, and comparing the two shows which happened.
questions.traps: Human involvement is not the goal, removing the check before its value is known is premature, and automating a check produces something else to check.

questions.stem: A team has four similar workflows built by four different people and wants to consolidate them.
options: Pick the best of the four and have everyone use it
Build a fifth workflow that covers all four cases
Find what the four actually have in common first
Keep all four, since each was built for a reason
questions.why: Four workflows may share most of their substance or almost none, and knowing which decides whether consolidation is possible at all.
questions.traps: Picking one imposes its assumptions on three other jobs, a fifth adds to the sprawl before understanding it, and keeping all four accepts the duplication.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is measured on throughput and the team has started routing easy work to it.
options: Change the measure to something that cannot be gamed
Tell the team to stop routing the work selectively
Accept it, since throughput has genuinely increased
Measure the difficulty of the work as well as the volume
questions.why: A measure that rewards selection will be satisfied by selection, so the fix is a measure whose only route to improvement is the real one.
questions.traps: Instructing people not to respond to an incentive rarely holds, the increase is an artefact, and a second measure leaves the first one still pulling.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is adopted quickly and people use it for a purpose it was not designed for.
options: Redirect people back to the originally intended purpose
Block the unintended use so the original design holds
Look at whether the new use is better than the old one
Rebuild the workflow around the unintended use
questions.why: Users finding a better use is information, and evaluating it is what decides whether the design or the usage should change.
questions.traps: Redirecting and blocking both assume the original design was right, and rebuilding assumes the opposite without checking.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has run for a year without failing and they are asked for their recovery plan.
options: Write one, since a year of success is not a plan
Say the workflow has not needed one in a year
Write one only if the workflow starts failing
Rely on rebuilding it from scratch if it ever fails
questions.why: A recovery plan is written while nothing is broken, because the moment it is needed is the worst possible moment to design one.
questions.traps: A clean record is not a control, waiting for failure defers the work to the crisis, and rebuilding from scratch is a plan only if it has been costed.

questions.stem: An associate's integration works and the team wants a second one built the same way.
options: Copy the first integration and change what differs
Check whether the first one's choices suit the second
Build the second from scratch to avoid shared problems
Make the first one generic enough to serve both
questions.why: What made the first integration right may not hold for the second, and checking prevents an assumption being copied along with the design.
questions.traps: Copying carries the assumptions silently, building from scratch discards what was learned, and generalising early designs for a case not yet understood.

questions.stem: A workflow's two halves are owned by different teams and neither knows the other's constraints.
options: Move both halves into a single team's ownership
Have one team document their half for the other
Add a coordinator sitting between the two teams
Have each side state what it needs from the other
questions.why: A working interface needs both sides' requirements on the table, and stating them is the cheapest way to get there.
questions.traps: Reorganising is a heavy answer to a communication gap, one-sided documentation leaves the other side unstated, and a coordinator relays rather than resolves.

questions.stem: A team is told to speed up a process and finds the slowest step is also the most valuable.
options: Speed up the valuable step, since it is the slowest
Leave the process alone, since the value justifies it
Look for time elsewhere before touching that step
Split the valuable step so parts of it run in parallel
questions.why: Cutting time from the step that carries the value risks the outcome, so the cheaper time is found in the steps that carry less.
questions.traps: Targeting the slowest step ignores what it produces, refusing to change anything abandons the goal, and parallelising is a fix chosen before the search.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers see the output but never the input the workflow worked from.
options: Give the reviewers the input alongside the output
Ask reviewers to request the input when they need it
Have the workflow summarise its input in the output
Train reviewers to judge outputs on their own terms
questions.why: Judging whether an output is right requires knowing what it was meant to be about, which is what the input provides.
questions.traps: On-demand requests slow every review, a generated summary inherits the output's errors, and judging output alone checks style rather than correctness.

questions.stem: A team's workflow behaves differently for two people because of their personal settings.
options: Ask both people to align their personal settings
Have one of the two people run everything instead
Document the settings each person should be using
Move the settings that matter into the workflow itself
questions.why: A workflow that depends on personal configuration is not a shared workflow, and pulling the relevant settings into it removes the dependency.
questions.traps: Manual alignment drifts, a single operator is a bottleneck, and documentation relies on everyone applying it correctly.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a judgement that two experienced staff make differently from each other.
options: Automate whichever version is applied more often
Settle the judgement between them before automating
Automate both and let the workflow pick one of them
Leave it manual, since the experts genuinely disagree
questions.why: You cannot automate a rule that has not been agreed, so the disagreement is the thing to resolve first.
questions.traps: Frequency does not make a judgement right, encoding both defers the disagreement into the workflow, and leaving it manual preserves the inconsistency.

questions.stem: A team's workflow benefit is that a rare and expensive mistake now happens less often.
options: Report the expected cost avoided, and say it is expected
Report the number of mistakes since the workflow began
Wait until enough time has passed to show a difference
Report the benefit as unmeasurable in the short term
questions.why: A rare-event benefit is estimated rather than counted, and presenting it as an expectation is both usable and honest.
questions.traps: Counting rare events over a short window shows nothing, waiting delays a decision indefinitely, and calling it unmeasurable understates a real benefit.

questions.stem: A team's workflow calls a service that charges per request and the volume is growing.
options: Negotiate a better rate with the service provider
Cap the number of requests the workflow may make
Move to a cheaper service that does the same thing
Check whether requests are being made unnecessarily
questions.why: Growing volume often includes repeated or avoidable calls, and finding those reduces the bill without changing anything else.
questions.traps: Negotiating and switching both address the price rather than the usage, and a cap limits the workflow rather than its waste.

questions.stem: A team's workflow saves each person ten minutes a day and nobody has changed how they work.
options: Accept it, since the time saving is real regardless
Report the saving as ten minutes times the headcount
Ask what the ten minutes would need to be for
Add more to the workflow until the saving is noticeable
questions.why: Time saved in small slices often disappears rather than being redirected, and asking what it could enable is what turns it into value.
questions.traps: An unrealised saving is not a benefit, multiplying it up asserts value that has not appeared, and expanding scope assumes the saving is the problem.

questions.stem: A team maps a process, finds every step necessary, and the total time is still too long.
options: Accept the duration, since every step has been justified
Look at what happens between the steps rather than in them
Remove the least valuable step despite its necessity
Run several of the necessary steps at the same time
questions.why: When the steps themselves are all justified, the remaining time is in the gaps between them, which is usually where most of it sits.
questions.traps: Accepting it abandons the goal, removing a necessary step breaks the process, and parallelising is one possible fix chosen before the time has been located.

questions.stem: A team's approval step is staffed by someone who cannot evaluate the content they approve.
options: Train the current approver to evaluate the content
Give the approver a checklist to work through instead
Move the approval to someone who can evaluate it
Remove the step, since the approval means nothing
questions.why: An approval by someone who cannot judge the content is a signature rather than a control, and the fix is to put it where the judgement exists.
questions.traps: Training is slower than reassignment and may not be feasible, a checklist substitutes procedure for judgement, and removing it loses a control that should exist.

questions.stem: A team's workflow can fail loudly and stop, or fail quietly and continue with degraded output.
options: Choose by whether a wrong result or a stopped process costs more
Always fail loudly, since silent failures are dangerous
Always continue, since stopping disrupts everyone downstream
Fail loudly in testing and continue quietly in production
questions.why: Both behaviours are defensible and the right one depends on what the process can absorb, so the comparison of costs is the decision.
questions.traps: Absolute rules in either direction ignore the process, and behaving differently in production is exactly where the untested path lives.

questions.stem: A team's workflow moved work from an expensive team to a cheaper one and the total time rose.
options: Report it as a saving, since the cost has come down
Report it as a failure, since the process got slower
Move the work back, since the change made things worse
Ask whether the cost saving is worth the added delay
questions.why: Cost and speed have moved in opposite directions, so the question is which one the process is actually optimising for.
questions.traps: Reporting either figure alone hides the other, and reverting decides the trade-off without anyone having stated it.

questions.stem: A workflow passes a summary to a decision-maker, and it is accurate but omits an exception.
options: Include the exceptions so that nothing at all is omitted
Have the summary name what it has deliberately left out
Have the decision-maker read the source document instead
Accept it, since a summary has to leave things out
questions.why: A summary that states its own boundaries lets the reader know when to go further, which is what makes summarising safe.
questions.traps: Including everything stops it being a summary, sending them to the source removes its value, and accepting silent omission is the failure being described.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step, and doing so would leave nobody who understands how it works.
options: Automate it, since understanding is not needed to run it
Leave it manual so the understanding stays in the team
Automate it and rotate people through the manual version
Automate it and keep a written account of the reasoning
questions.why: The understanding is what allows the step to be changed or fixed later, and writing it down preserves it without paying for the manual work forever.
questions.traps: Understanding matters the moment something breaks, keeping the step manual is an expensive way to store knowledge, and rotation maintains a process solely as training.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives the same answer every time and that answer has been wrong for months.
options: Consistency was never evidence that it was correct
The consistency shows the workflow is working properly
The error must therefore have been introduced recently
Repeatability and correctness are really the same property
questions.why: A workflow reproduces whatever it does, including a mistake, so stability tells you about the process rather than about the answer.
questions.traps: Treating consistency as correctness is the misconception, recency is an assumption, and conflating the two properties is the same error stated directly.

questions.stem: An associate must decide whether the workflow should hold its own copy of reference data.
options: Always read it live, since a copy will go out of date
Always copy it, since the workflow then has no dependency
Copy it where staleness costs less than an outage would
Copy it and refresh the copy on a fixed schedule
questions.why: A local copy trades freshness for independence, and which of those the workflow can better afford is what decides.
questions.traps: Absolute rules ignore the trade, and a fixed refresh sets the staleness window before anyone has said what it should be.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is genuinely better and its users feel it makes their job smaller.
options: Explain that the workflow frees them for better work
Take the concern seriously as part of the design
Proceed, since the improvement is objectively real
Pause the rollout until people come to feel differently
questions.why: How a change lands on the people doing the work determines whether it survives, which makes it a design input rather than an objection to manage.
questions.traps: Explaining talks past the concern, proceeding on objective merit is how good tools get abandoned, and pausing waits for a feeling to change on its own.

questions.stem: A team's error rate is within the limit they agreed and the errors fall mostly on one customer group.
options: Accept it, since the overall rate is within the agreed limit
Reduce the overall rate until that group's share falls
Exclude that customer group from the workflow entirely
Look at the distribution, since an accepted rate can land unevenly
questions.why: An acceptable average can conceal one group bearing most of the harm, which is a different question from whether the rate is low.
questions.traps: The agreed limit was set on the average, lowering the overall rate need not change the distribution, and excluding the group denies them the service.

questions.stem: A team is asked for one number and the costs and benefits are genuinely different in kind.
options: Give a combined figure using the team's best conversion
Give the benefit figure, since that is what was asked about
Give the numbers separately and say why they do not combine
Decline to give any number until they can be compared
questions.why: Forcing incomparable things into one number hides the judgement inside it, and showing them separately keeps that judgement with the decision-maker.
questions.traps: A conversion smuggles in an assumption, reporting one side is incomplete, and refusing outright leaves the decision without information.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers approve polished output faster, and errors in polished output are the costly ones.
options: Ask reviewers to be more sceptical of polished output
Have reviewers check against the source rather than reading it
Have the workflow produce rather less polished output
Add a second reviewer for the most polished outputs
questions.why: Fluency is what defeats reading-based review, so anchoring the check to the source is what makes polish stop mattering.
questions.traps: Asking for scepticism relies on resisting a strong effect, degrading the output damages it for readers, and a second reader repeats the same vulnerable check.

questions.stem: An integration is the only automated access to a system and the team wants more built on it.
options: Ask what the system's owners expect before building further
Build on it, since the integration already works reliably
Build a separate integration for each new use case
Stop, since one integration should not carry several uses
questions.why: Being the only automated route makes it a dependency the system's owners have a stake in, and their expectations shape what can safely be built on it.
questions.traps: Working today is not permission, one integration per use multiplies the dependency, and refusing forgoes legitimate reuse.

questions.stem: A team has five processes they could improve and asks which one they should start with.
options: The one that would be the easiest to change quickly
The one where an improvement would matter the most
The one that the team already understands the best
The one that currently has the most steps in it
questions.why: Effort is finite, so it belongs where the improvement changes the most, and that is a question about impact rather than convenience.
questions.traps: Ease, familiarity and step count all describe how comfortable the work would be rather than what it would achieve.

questions.stem: An associate is asked what has to be true before a step can be automated at all.
options: The step is currently taking too long to perform
The step is performed by more than one person
The step's rules can be stated clearly enough
The team has the budget available for the work
questions.why: Automation encodes a rule, so a step whose rules cannot be written down cannot be automated however desirable it is.
questions.traps: Duration, headcount and budget describe whether it is worth doing rather than whether it can be done.

questions.stem: A team is asked what their workflow should do when a downstream system is unavailable.
options: Discard the work and let the sender resubmit it
Carry on and simply skip the unavailable system
Fail the whole run so the problem is made visible
Hold the work and retry once the system is back
questions.why: A temporary outage is recoverable, so holding the work preserves it until the system returns rather than losing or bypassing it.
questions.traps: Discarding pushes the cost onto the sender, skipping produces incomplete results, and failing the run treats a transient problem as permanent.

questions.stem: A team's workflow needs credentials to reach another system and asks where to keep them.
options: In the credential store the organisation provides
Written inside the workflow's own configuration file
With the person who originally set the integration up
In a shared document that the team can all reach
questions.why: A managed credential store is what makes access controllable, auditable and revocable without editing the workflow.
questions.traps: Configuration files get copied and shared, an individual becomes a dependency, and a shared document widens access to everyone who can open it.

questions.stem: A workflow's output is passed on and the receiving person cannot tell how recent it is.
options: Assume the recipient knows that it is current
Include the time at which the output was produced
Ask the recipient to check the date if it matters
Only send the output on the day it was produced
questions.why: Recency changes how an output should be used, so stating it is what lets the receiver judge.
questions.traps: Assuming knowledge is how stale data gets acted on, asking them to check pushes the work downstream, and a same-day rule constrains the process without answering.

questions.stem: A team asks whether a person needs to see every output or only some of them.
options: It depends on what a missed error would actually cost
Every output, since any of them could be wrong
Only a sample, since checking everything is slow
Only the outputs the workflow flags as uncertain
questions.why: Review is a cost paid against risk, so the consequence of an error getting through is what sets how much of it to do.
questions.traps: Reviewing everything and sampling are each right in different conditions, and self-flagged uncertainty is a signal the workflow may not produce reliably.

questions.stem: A new joiner asks how they are supposed to learn to use the team's workflow.
options: Sitting with whoever has used it for the longest
Working it out from the prompts themselves alone
Asking questions in the team channel as they arise
Written instructions kept alongside the workflow
questions.why: Instructions that live with the workflow are available to everyone at any time and survive the departure of whoever knows it best.
questions.traps: Shadowing depends on someone's availability, reverse-engineering is slow and error-prone, and channel questions repeat the same answers indefinitely.

questions.stem: A team is asked to prove their workflow works and offers a demonstration of it running.
options: A demonstration is sufficient evidence that it works
A demonstration is sufficient if it uses real data
A demonstration shows it runs, not that it works
A demonstration proves nothing at all about a workflow
questions.why: Running successfully once shows the mechanism functions, while working means it produces the right result across the inputs it will meet.
questions.traps: A single successful run is the weakest possible evidence, real data in one run is still one run, and dismissing demonstrations entirely overstates it.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works and only one person knows the order that the steps run in.
options: Have that person run the workflow every single time
Ask that person to explain it whenever it is needed
Trust that the order is obvious from the steps
Write the order down where the team can find it
questions.why: A workflow that depends on one person's memory stops working the day they are unavailable, and writing it down is the cheapest fix.
questions.traps: A single operator is a bottleneck and a risk, on-demand explanation depends on availability, and obviousness is what the situation already disproves.

questions.stem: An associate is mapping a process and two people describe the same step quite differently.
options: Watch the step being performed by each of them
Take the description from the more senior person
Combine the two descriptions into a single one
Take whichever of the two descriptions is more detailed
questions.why: Two descriptions of one step usually means it is genuinely performed two ways, and watching is what shows what actually happens.
questions.traps: Seniority, merging and detail all pick between accounts without checking either against the work itself.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces an empty result and downstream steps treat it as valid.
options: Have the downstream steps check for an empty result
Have the workflow produce a placeholder instead
Have the workflow reject an empty result outright
Have someone check the results before they are used
questions.why: An empty result is a failure at the point it is produced, and stopping there prevents every downstream step having to guard against it.
questions.traps: Downstream checking spreads the same guard everywhere, a placeholder disguises the failure, and manual checking puts a person into an automated path.

questions.stem: An associate is connecting two systems that identify the same customer differently.
options: Use the identifier from whichever system is larger
Agree how the two identifiers map to each other
Match customers on their name and address instead
Ask the model to work out which records correspond
questions.why: Two identifier schemes need an explicit mapping, and agreeing it is what makes every later join correct rather than approximate.
questions.traps: Picking one scheme leaves the other unmapped, name matching is unreliable, and asking the model to infer identity invents links.

questions.stem: A workflow passes work to a person who has to decide whether it needs their attention.
options: Have the workflow say why it was sent to them
Have the person read each item and decide for themselves
Send everything, since deciding is their job anyway
Send only the items the workflow is unsure about
questions.why: Telling the receiver why something reached them lets them triage in seconds rather than reconstructing the reason each time.
questions.traps: Reading everything is the cost being avoided, "deciding is their job" ignores the effort, and filtering by the workflow's uncertainty changes what they see.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step whose rules are clear and whose exceptions are numerous.
options: Automate all of it, including the exception handling
Leave it manual, since the exceptions dominate it
Automate the rule and route the exceptions to a person
Automate it and accept the exceptions being wrong
questions.why: A clear rule with messy exceptions is the classic split: encode what is stable and let judgement handle what is not.
questions.traps: Automating exceptions encodes rules that were never agreed, leaving it manual forgoes the stable majority, and accepting wrong exceptions is choosing to be wrong.

questions.stem: A team finds a step that exists only to work around another team's constraint.
options: Automate the workaround so it costs less to run
Remove the step and let the constraint bite instead
Keep it, since the constraint is outside their control
Take it up with the team whose constraint it is
questions.why: The step is a symptom of something owned elsewhere, and raising it is what can remove the cost rather than making it cheaper to bear.
questions.traps: Automating a workaround entrenches it, removing it breaks the process, and assuming another team's constraint is immovable is usually untested.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives different results depending on which day of the week it runs on.
options: Fix the workflow so that it runs on one day only
Look for what differs about the input on those days
Average the results across the whole week instead
Accept it, since some variation is unavoidable
questions.why: A pattern tied to the calendar almost always tracks something about the data arriving on those days, and finding it explains the difference.
questions.traps: Restricting the run day hides the effect, averaging blends a real difference away, and calling it unavoidable stops the investigation.

questions.stem: A workflow is used correctly by the people who were trained and incorrectly by everyone else.
options: Train everyone who has not yet been trained on it
Restrict the workflow to people who are trained
Put what the training covered into the workflow
Accept the difference, since training clearly works
questions.why: Knowledge that only exists in training is knowledge the workflow is missing, and building it in scales where training does not.
questions.traps: Training everyone repeats indefinitely as people join, restricting access shrinks the benefit, and accepting it makes training a permanent dependency.

questions.stem: A workflow's receiving team says the output arrives too late to be of any use to them.
options: Speed up every step so the output arrives sooner
Find out when they need it and work back from that
Send a partial output earlier and the rest later
Ask the receiving team to change their own schedule
questions.why: A deadline you have not been told is a requirement you cannot design to, and eliciting it is what makes the rest of the design possible.
questions.traps: Speeding everything up is expensive and may still miss, partial delivery is a design chosen too early, and asking them to move ignores their constraints.

questions.stem: A team's workflow asks a person to confirm something they have no way of checking.
options: Move the confirmation to where it can be checked
Keep it, since a confirmation step adds oversight
Remove the step and rely on the workflow instead
Give the person more time to make the confirmation
questions.why: A confirmation nobody can substantiate is theatre, and relocating it to someone with the means to check is what makes it a control.
questions.traps: Unverifiable oversight is not oversight, removing it loses a control that should exist somewhere, and more time does not create the ability to check.

questions.stem: An associate's integration works in testing and the live system returns extra fields.
options: Ask the system's owners to stop sending extra fields
Update the integration to expect those specific fields
Filter the response down to the fields seen in testing
Handle unexpected fields rather than assume the shape
questions.why: A live system's response will keep changing, so tolerating fields you did not expect is what stops the next change breaking it.
questions.traps: Asking owners to freeze their output is rarely available, expecting today's extras breaks on tomorrow's, and filtering to the tested set discards data silently.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is judged a success and nobody has asked the people it was built for.
options: Rely on the measurements, which are already positive
Ask them after the next round of improvements
Ask them, since they are the ones it has to serve
Assume silence means they are satisfied with it
questions.why: The people the workflow serves hold information no measurement captures, and asking them is what turns a metric into a judgement.
questions.traps: Positive metrics can coexist with an unusable tool, deferring means designing further without the input, and silence is not endorsement.

questions.stem: A team's workflow catches its own errors and notifies a mailbox that nobody owns.
options: Send notifications to a person who can act on them
Add more detail to the notifications that are sent
Assign the mailbox to whoever has capacity now
Reduce the notifications so the mailbox stays clear
questions.why: Detection only counts when it reaches somebody able to respond, so naming that person is what completes the control.
questions.traps: More detail improves messages nobody reads, capacity-based assignment does not confer authority, and fewer notifications makes an unread mailbox quieter.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step and the input arrives in a different format each time.
options: Automate it and let the model handle each format
Standardise the input before automating the step
Leave it manual, since the input is not consistent
Automate one format and do the others by hand
questions.why: Variable input is the thing making the step hard, and normalising it upstream is what makes the automation both possible and reliable.
questions.traps: Relying on the model to absorb arbitrary variation is the fragile path, refusing gives up on a fixable problem, and partial automation keeps the manual cost.

questions.stem: A team finds that the same data is keyed in twice by two different people.
options: Remove the second entry, since it duplicates the first
Automate the second entry from the first one's data
Keep both, since two entries reduce the error rate
Find out whether the second entry serves as a check
questions.why: Double entry is sometimes waste and sometimes a deliberate verification, and which it is here determines whether it can be removed.
questions.traps: Removing or automating it discards a control that may be real, and assuming it is a control is the same guess reversed.

questions.stem: A team's checkpoint is staffed by a different person each week and the standards vary.
options: Write down what the check is actually looking for
Assign the checkpoint to one permanent person
Have two people check each item to average it out
Accept the variation, since reviewers differ anyway
questions.why: A rotating role needs its standard written down, since that is what makes different people apply the same check.
questions.traps: A permanent owner is a bottleneck and a single point of failure, doubling reviewers doubles cost without defining the standard, and accepting variation accepts an undefined control.

questions.stem: A team wants another team to use their workflow on similar but not identical work.
options: Give them the workflow and let them adapt it themselves
Separate what is general from what is specific to them
Build a new workflow for the other team's work
Have both teams use it exactly as it stands today
questions.why: Reuse works when the general part is distinguishable from the team-specific part, and doing that separation is what makes it portable.
questions.traps: Handing it over unexamined exports hidden assumptions, building fresh discards the work, and forcing identical use ignores the real differences.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on an external service with no agreement about its availability.
options: Assume it will be available, as it has been so far
Build a second route to the same capability now
Find out what happens when the service is unavailable
Stop using the service until an agreement exists
questions.why: A dependency with no commitment behind it is a risk to be sized, and knowing the impact of an outage decides how much to spend on it.
questions.traps: Past availability is not a commitment, a second route is a costly mitigation chosen before sizing, and stopping forgoes a working capability.

questions.stem: A step is automatable and the person doing it is the only one who ever questions the input.
options: Automate it, since questioning input is not that step's job
Leave it manual so the questioning continues to happen
Automate it and ask that person to review the outputs
Automate it and make the questioning an explicit step
questions.why: The questioning is a real function being performed incidentally, so automating safely means naming it and giving it somewhere to live.
questions.traps: Dismissing it loses a control nobody recorded, keeping the step pays for a side effect with the whole job, and output review looks at the wrong end.

questions.stem: A team must choose between preventing a failure and detecting it quickly once it happens.
options: Prevent it, since a failure that never happens costs nothing
Detect it, since prevention can never really be complete
Compare the cost of prevention against the cost of the delay
Do both, since prevention and detection are complementary
questions.why: Prevention and detection buy different things at different prices, and which is worth more depends on what the failure costs while it goes undetected.
questions.traps: Absolute preferences ignore the price, and doing both is right only when the budget allows what nobody has costed.

questions.stem: A team's workflow improved one team's numbers and made another team's work harder.
options: Measure the process end to end rather than by team
Report the improvement, since it is real for that team
Report both teams' numbers and simply leave it there
Reverse the change, since it moved cost rather than removing it
questions.why: A gain in one team beside a loss in another is usually cost moving rather than value created, and only an end-to-end view shows which.
questions.traps: Reporting one team's gain is the error, reporting both without combining leaves the question open, and reversing assumes the answer.

questions.stem: A process is documented accurately and everyone does something slightly different in practice.
options: Enforce the documented process across the whole team
Treat the difference as information about the document
Update the document to match what people actually do
Accept both, since the outcome is the same anyway
questions.why: A gap between the document and practice usually means the document misses something real, and investigating it tells you which one to change.
questions.traps: Enforcing assumes the document is right, updating assumes practice is right, and accepting both leaves the process undefined.

questions.stem: A workflow's output is correct and the receiving team keeps escalating questions about it.
options: Answer the questions as they arrive each time
Tell the team the output has been verified as correct
Add a covering note explaining the output in general
Ask what the questions are, since they name the gap
questions.why: Repeated questions are an unmet information need, and collecting them is what turns the escalations into a change to the output.
questions.traps: Answering each one repeats forever, asserting correctness answers a question they did not ask, and a general note may miss the specific gap.

questions.stem: A team must decide whether to make their workflow reproducible or to make it faster.
options: Reproducible, since a result that cannot be repeated is weak
Reproducible where the result is defended, fast where it is not
Fast, since speed is what people actually notice
Both, since the two are not really in conflict at all
questions.why: Reproducibility costs time and earns its place where someone will have to justify the result, which is not true of every workflow.
questions.traps: Absolute answers ignore what the output is for, and denying the conflict avoids a trade the team has already run into.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is mandatory and people have quietly built their own alternatives to it.
options: Enforce the mandate and remove the alternatives
Withdraw the mandate and let people choose freely
Adopt the most popular alternative as the standard
Find out what the alternatives do that the workflow does not
questions.why: Shadow workflows are a specification written by the people doing the work, and reading it is the most useful thing available.
questions.traps: Enforcement drives them further underground, withdrawing the mandate abandons the standardisation, and popularity does not make an alternative correct.

questions.stem: An associate must decide whether the workflow calls a system directly or via a shared service.
options: Direct where the workflow owns the concern, shared where others do
Direct, since fewer layers means fewer things to break
Shared, since a common route is easier to govern
Direct now and move to the shared service later on
questions.why: A shared service earns its overhead when several consumers need the same guarantees, and a direct call is right when only this workflow cares.
questions.traps: Absolute preferences ignore who else depends on it, and deferring the move is a migration that usually never happens.

questions.stem: A reviewer is expected to catch both format errors and factual ones, and catches only format.
options: Ask the reviewer to focus more on factual accuracy
Automate the format check so attention is freed up
Split the two checks, since they need different attention
Accept it, since format errors are the more visible ones
questions.why: Scanning for format and verifying facts are different activities, and one person doing both in one pass reliably does the easier one.
questions.traps: Asking for more focus does not change the interference, freeing attention does not redirect it, and accepting it leaves the factual check undone.

questions.stem: A workflow has run for two years and nobody has checked whether the problem still exists.
options: Continue, since the workflow is running without incident
Check whether the original problem is still there
Retire the workflow, since two years is long enough
Measure the workflow's current performance instead
questions.why: A workflow solving a problem that has gone away is pure cost, and confirming the problem is the only thing that settles it.
questions.traps: Running smoothly says nothing about whether it is needed, retiring on age is arbitrary, and performance measures how well it does something possibly pointless.

questions.stem: A team's workflow degrades gradually rather than failing, and nobody noticed for weeks.
options: Check the outputs manually on a weekly schedule
Rebuild the workflow so that it fails cleanly instead
Accept it, since gradual degradation is hard to detect
Set a threshold that turns the drift into an alert
questions.why: Gradual degradation is only invisible until someone defines the level at which it counts, and that threshold is what makes it detectable.
questions.traps: Weekly manual checks are expensive and still subjective, forcing clean failure discards graceful behaviour, and accepting it leaves weeks of bad output.

questions.stem: A team is asked to map a process that three departments each describe as belonging to them.
options: Map it as it runs and let ownership follow from that
Ask leadership to assign ownership before mapping it
Map each department's version of the process separately
Map the version described by the largest department
questions.why: What actually happens is a fact that can be established, and it is usually what settles an ownership argument rather than the other way round.
questions.traps: Waiting for a decision blocks work that would inform it, three separate maps preserve the disagreement, and size is not a claim to ownership.

questions.stem: A step can be automated and the regulator expects a named person to have performed it.
options: Automate it and name the person who approved the workflow
Leave it manual, since the regulator's expectation is clear
Automate the preparation and leave the act to the person
Automate it and ask the regulator to accept the change
questions.why: Where a rule attaches the act to a person, assistance goes into everything around it while the act itself stays where the rule puts it.
questions.traps: Naming a workflow approver misdescribes who performed the act, leaving it wholly manual forgoes legitimate help, and seeking an exemption starts from the wrong place.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is built for people who are not comfortable with technical tools.
options: Provide training so that people become comfortable
Have a technical person operate it on their behalf
Simplify the technical steps as far as possible
Design it so that no technical step is required
questions.why: A workflow for non-technical users has to be usable without technical skill, which is a design constraint rather than a training problem.
questions.traps: Training shifts the burden to users, an operator makes them dependent, and simplifying a technical step leaves it technical.

questions.stem: A team's workflow failed last month and they are deciding what to do about it now.
options: Add a check that would have caught that failure
Rebuild the step that failed so it is more robust
Find out why it failed before changing anything
Move on, since the failure has not happened again
questions.why: A fix aimed at a cause you have not established is a guess, and the investigation is what makes the change land on the right thing.
questions.traps: A targeted check and a rebuild both assume the cause, and moving on leaves an unexplained failure in place.

questions.stem: A team is asked how long their workflow took to start delivering anything useful.
options: Measure from the start of the work, not the launch
Measure from the day the workflow first went live
Measure from the first successful run of the workflow
Measure from whichever point makes the figure best
questions.why: The time to value includes everything spent before it ran, which is what someone deciding whether to do this again needs to know.
questions.traps: Measuring from launch or first run hides the build entirely, and choosing the flattering starting point is not a measurement.

questions.stem: A team asks whether they should automate the whole process or just one step of it.
options: The whole process, since partial gains are small
One step, so that what changed can be identified
The whole process, since one change is less disruptive
One step, since automation should always be gradual
questions.why: Changing one thing at a time is what lets the effect be attributed, which is how the next decision gets made on evidence.
questions.traps: Dismissing partial gains ignores learning, a single big change is more disruptive rather than less, and "always gradual" is right by accident rather than for the reason.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow will run against ten times its current volume next quarter.
options: Run it as it is and watch for problems appearing
Add capacity when problems actually start to appear
Test it at the higher volume before the quarter starts
Assume it scales, since nothing in it is volume-specific
questions.why: Behaviour under load is a question that testing answers cheaply and production answers expensively.
questions.traps: Watching and reacting means users meet the problem first, and assuming linear scaling is precisely the assumption being tested.

questions.stem: A workflow's output goes to a person who forwards it unchanged to someone else.
options: Ask whether the middle step is needed at all here
Automate the forwarding so that it happens faster
Keep it, since the person may well be checking it
Send it to both of the people at the same time
questions.why: A step that passes work along unchanged may be adding nothing, and asking is what distinguishes a relay from a review.
questions.traps: Automating a pointless step makes it cheaper rather than gone, assuming a hidden check is a guess, and sending to both leaves the middle role undefined.

questions.stem: A team's output is consumed by another system and the team wants to change its format.
options: Make the change and fix whatever breaks afterwards
Tell the consuming team before making the change
Keep the old format alongside the new one forever
Make the change, since the format is theirs to set
questions.why: A format that something else depends on is a shared contract, and notice is what lets the other side prepare.
questions.traps: Breaking first is an outage by choice, keeping both forever doubles the maintenance, and owning the producer is not the same as owning the interface.

questions.stem: An associate finds one step whose output nobody downstream appears to use at all.
options: Remove the step, since nothing appears to use it
Keep it, since the output may be used occasionally
Automate the step so it costs less to keep running
Confirm that nothing uses it, then remove the step
questions.why: Confirming before removing is what separates a genuinely unused step from one whose consumer you simply have not found yet.
questions.traps: Removing on appearance risks a hidden dependency, keeping it on a hypothetical preserves waste, and automating it makes waste cheaper.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has two benefits and only one of the two can be measured.
options: Report only the benefit that can be measured properly
Estimate the unmeasurable benefit as a number
Report the measured one and describe the other
Report neither until both of them can be measured
questions.why: An unmeasured benefit is still information, and describing it keeps it in the decision without dressing it up as a measurement.
questions.traps: Dropping it understates the workflow, inventing a number overstates the evidence, and reporting nothing withholds what is known.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires people to change a habit they have had for years.
options: Expect it to take time and plan for the transition
Announce the change and expect immediate adoption
Keep the old way available so nobody has to change
Make the new way faster so the habit changes itself
questions.why: Habit change is slow and predictable, so planning for the period where both exist is what gets a rollout through it.
questions.traps: Expecting instant change is how rollouts fail, keeping the old way indefinitely means nobody moves, and speed alone rarely overcomes habit.

questions.stem: A team has one step that fails often and one that fails rarely but expensively.
options: Handle the frequent one, since it happens more often
Handle both, since frequency and cost are different risks
Handle the expensive one, since the cost is greater
Handle whichever is cheaper to build handling for
questions.why: Risk is frequency times consequence, so a common cheap failure and a rare expensive one can both be worth addressing.
questions.traps: Picking by frequency or by cost alone uses half the picture, and build cost is about the fix rather than about the risk.

questions.stem: A team's workflow uses a tool feature that the vendor has announced will be removed.
options: Wait until the feature has actually been removed
Ask the vendor to keep the feature available anyway
Move to a different tool that will not change
Plan the change now, while there is still time
questions.why: An announced removal has a known date, and using the notice period is what turns a breakage into a planned migration.
questions.traps: Waiting guarantees an outage, asking a vendor to reverse a deprecation rarely works, and switching tools is a large answer to one feature.

questions.stem: A team is asked what makes a step a bad candidate for automation in the first place.
options: Its correct output depends on judgement that varies
It is performed by only one person in the team
It has not been performed the same way twice yet
It takes only a small amount of time to perform
questions.why: Automation needs a rule, and a step whose right answer depends on case-by-case judgement does not have one to encode.
questions.traps: Headcount is unrelated, inconsistent performance may just need standardising, and small duration affects the payback rather than the possibility.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is used by everyone and half of them say that it does not help.
options: Accept it, since they are using it regardless
Remove the workflow, since half see no benefit
Find out what those people are actually using it for
Improve the workflow until they change their minds
questions.why: Use without benefit usually means the workflow is being applied to the wrong task, and finding out which is the informative step.
questions.traps: Use is not benefit, removing it discards value for the other half, and improving it assumes the workflow rather than the fit is wrong.

questions.stem: A team wants to compare two workflow designs and can only run one of them at a time.
options: Run one for a month, then the other for a month
Alternate them across comparable batches of work
Run whichever seems better and compare to history
Ask the team which of the designs they prefer using
questions.why: Alternating across batches spreads whatever changes over time across both designs, which is what makes the comparison fair.
questions.traps: Sequential months confound the design with everything else that changed, comparing to history has no control, and preference is not performance.

questions.stem: A team's workflow failed once and the team has added four new checks in response.
options: Keep all four, since more checking is always safer
Remove all four and investigate the cause properly
Keep whichever of the checks are cheapest to run
Ask whether each check would have caught that failure
questions.why: Checks added in the aftermath often address imagined causes, and testing each against the actual failure is what keeps the useful ones.
questions.traps: Keeping everything accumulates cost, removing everything discards checks that may be right, and cost does not indicate usefulness.

questions.stem: A team's process has a step whose duration varies from ten minutes to two days.
options: Plan around the two-day case in order to be safe
Find out what distinguishes the slow cases from the rest
Report the average duration of the step instead
Split the step into a fast path and a slow path
questions.why: A wide spread means there are two different situations inside one step, and identifying them is what makes either the planning or the split possible.
questions.traps: Planning for the worst case wastes capacity, an average describes neither case, and splitting is a fix chosen before the distinction is known.

questions.stem: A team's workflow calls a service and the team has no visibility of what it costs.
options: Attribute the cost to the workflow before it grows
Ask finance for the total bill at the end of each month
Estimate the cost from the number of runs made
Wait until the cost becomes large enough to notice
questions.why: Attributing cost to the workflow while it is small is what makes later growth visible and the trade-off decidable.
questions.traps: A total bill hides which workflow drives it, an estimate is not attribution, and waiting means the first signal is a surprise.

questions.stem: A reviewer rejects roughly a third of outputs and one problem causes most of the rejections.
options: Keep reviewing, since the step is clearly working
Add a second reviewer to handle all of the volume
Fix the cause so the reviewer stops seeing it
Lower the standard so fewer outputs are rejected
questions.why: A review that keeps catching one thing is telling you what to fix upstream, which is cheaper than catching it forever.
questions.traps: Working as designed is not the same as working well, more reviewers scale the symptom, and lowering the standard hides it.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces a report and last quarter's version cannot now be reproduced.
options: Store each report so the output is at least kept
Rerun the workflow and use the current result
Note that the older reports cannot be reproduced
Store the inputs and settings with each report
questions.why: Reproducing a past report requires what produced it, and storing that alongside the output is what makes each report defensible later.
questions.traps: Keeping the output preserves the answer without the working, a rerun answers a different question, and documenting the gap simply accepts it.

questions.stem: A workflow passes work between two teams and each thinks the other owns the failures.
