options: Add the document, since the tables are inside it
Extract the tables and add just those instead
Add the document and instruct it to use the tables
Add both the tables and the whole document as well
questions.why: The tables are what the questions reach for, and the surrounding prose only competes with them during retrieval.
questions.traps: Including the whole document is the bloat, an instruction does not remove the prose, and adding both duplicates the tables.

questions.stem: A Project instruction is followed on short questions and ignored on long ones.
options: Repeat the instruction at the end of the instructions
Shorten questions so the instruction is not crowded out
Accept it, since long questions are inherently harder
Check where the instruction sits relative to the question
questions.why: A long question can crowd out a standing rule, and knowing whether that is happening determines whether to shorten or restate it.
questions.traps: Repetition is a fix applied before diagnosis, constraining question length restricts the users, and accepting it forgoes a likely fix.

questions.stem: A team wants a Project shared with a partner and is unsure what the partner will see.
options: Share it and remove anything the partner mentions
Share only the documents rather than the Project
Check what sharing exposes before sharing anything
Assume they see the documents but not the instructions
questions.why: What a shared Project exposes is a fact to establish rather than assume, since the cost of guessing wrong is a disclosure.
questions.traps: Reacting to what the partner notices is already too late, sending documents separately answers a different question, and assumptions may be wrong.

questions.stem: A team's Project misses information that is definitely inside one of its documents.
options: Check how that document was processed on upload
Ask the question again using rather different wording
Add the document a second time to reinforce it
Add an instruction pointing directly at that document
questions.why: Content that is present but never retrieved usually did not survive processing, and checking that is the direct diagnosis.
questions.traps: Rewording and re-adding both work around an unknown cause, and an instruction cannot retrieve text that was never extracted.

questions.stem: A team's naming convention works and people abbreviate the names differently when searching.
options: Ask people to use the full names when searching
Change the convention to use abbreviations only
Include the common abbreviations in the names
Keep a list mapping abbreviations to full names
questions.why: Names that contain both forms are found either way, which fixes the problem without asking anyone to change their habits.
questions.traps: Asking people to change how they search rarely holds, abbreviation-only names lose clarity, and a mapping list is one more thing to consult.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether to include examples of good output in a Project.
options: Include them always, since examples clarify intent
Never include them, since they consume knowledge space
Include them only if the instructions are already short
Include them where the format is hard to describe
questions.why: An example earns its place when showing is clearer than telling, which is exactly the case for formats and register.
questions.traps: Universal inclusion adds material that description would handle, a blanket ban loses their clearest use, and instruction length is not the criterion.

questions.stem: A Project holds thorough documentation and users still ask questions it does not cover.
options: Add more documentation covering related areas
Collect those questions, since they show what is missing
Tell users the documentation already covers their area
Accept it, since no documentation covers everything
questions.why: The questions users actually ask are the specification for what the knowledge should contain, and collecting them costs nothing.
questions.traps: Guessing at related areas adds material nobody needed, contradicting users ignores evidence, and accepting it forgoes an easy improvement.

questions.stem: A Project has grown steadily, answers are still good, and nobody sees a reason to prune.
options: Prune anyway, since the cost appears only once it is late
Leave it, since the answers are demonstrably still good
Prune only when the answers actually begin to degrade
Set a maximum size and prune when it is reached
questions.why: Retrieval degrades gradually and the degradation is only obvious in hindsight, so pruning while things are good prevents it.
questions.traps: Current quality is what makes the risk invisible, waiting for degradation means users meet it first, and an arbitrary size limit is not about relevance.

questions.stem: Instructions were written by someone who has left and nobody understands one of the rules.
options: Remove it, since nobody can explain what it is for
Find out what it does before removing or keeping it
Keep it, since removing it might break something
Rewrite it in clearer language and keep the effect
questions.why: Testing what the rule actually changes turns an unknown into a decision, which neither removing nor keeping it blindly does.
questions.traps: Removing an unexplained rule is how regressions happen, keeping it institutionalises the unknown, and rewriting preserves an effect nobody has identified.

questions.stem: A team wants a Project's configuration shared with another team but not its documents.
options: Share the whole Project and ask them not to read the documents
Rebuild the Project for them without any documents in it
Share the instructions and let them supply their own knowledge
Describe the configuration and let them recreate it
questions.why: Instructions and knowledge are separable, so the configuration can travel while each team keeps its own material.
questions.traps: A request not to read is not a control, rebuilding is unnecessary work, and a description leaves them reconstructing what could simply be copied.

questions.stem: A Project holds an essential document that is far larger than everything else combined.
options: Keep it whole, since the whole document is essential
Summarise it and add the summary in its place
Move it out of the Project and attach it when needed
Split it so retrieval can reach the relevant part
questions.why: A single dominant document makes retrieval coarse, and splitting it into meaningful parts restores precision without losing any content.
questions.traps: Keeping it whole is the cause, a summary loses the detail, and attaching it per question repeats the cost every single time.

questions.stem: An associate must decide whether a Project should be broad enough to cover future work.
options: Build broadly, since adding scope later is disruptive
Build for current questions, since future ones are guesses
Build narrowly and create new Projects as needs arise
Build broadly, since a Project is cheap to maintain
questions.why: Speculative breadth costs precision on every question asked today in exchange for questions that may never actually come.
questions.traps: Anticipated disruption is usually smaller than the ongoing dilution, creating Projects per need is the consequence rather than the reason, and Projects are not cheap to maintain.

questions.stem: A team's Project is named clearly for them and means nothing to anyone outside the team.
options: Keep the name, since the team is who actually uses it
Keep the name and add a description alongside it
Rename it for the widest audience that will look for it
Rename it using a formal organisational code instead
questions.why: A name's job is to be recognised by whoever is searching, and that set is usually wider than the team that made it.
questions.traps: Current users are not the only future ones, a description is not what people search by, and a code is no more meaningful than jargon.

questions.stem: A Project answers well and nobody knows which of its twenty documents are load-bearing.
options: Find out, since curation is guesswork without it
Leave it, since the answers are good either way
Remove documents singly and observe the effect
Assume the largest documents carry the answers
questions.why: Knowing which documents the answers depend on is what makes every later addition or removal a decision rather than a gamble.
questions.traps: Good answers make the question feel unnecessary, one-at-a-time removal is slow and disruptive, and size is not a proxy for contribution.

questions.stem: A Project holds a document whose content is correct and that the team disagrees with.
options: Remove it, since the team does not agree with it
Keep it, since its content is factually correct
Add the team's own view alongside the document
Settle the disagreement, since the Project states a position
questions.why: A Project's knowledge speaks for the team that maintains it, so an internal disagreement has to be resolved rather than encoded.
questions.traps: Removing it suppresses a correct document, keeping it publishes a position the team rejects, and adding both makes the Project self-contradictory.

questions.stem: A Project instruction works for most questions and gives unhelpful answers for one kind.
options: Scope the instruction so it does not fire on that kind
Remove the instruction, since it fails on some questions
Keep it, since most questions are answered well
Add a second instruction covering the failing kind
questions.why: An instruction that is right in general and wrong in one case is a scoping problem, and narrowing it keeps the benefit without the failure.
questions.traps: Removing it loses the general benefit, keeping it accepts a known failure, and a counter-instruction leaves two rules competing.

questions.stem: A colleague uses a shared Project for questions it was never configured to answer.
options: Tell the colleague the Project is not for those questions
Decide whether to widen the Project or redirect the use
Widen the Project so it covers their questions too
Let them continue, since the answers seem acceptable
questions.why: An unanticipated use is either a gap worth filling or a misuse worth redirecting, and deciding which is the actual task here.
questions.traps: Redirecting without considering the need may waste a real signal, widening without deciding dilutes the Project, and unexamined use produces ungrounded answers.

questions.stem: A team's Project gives good answers and is noticeably slower than a plain conversation.
options: Move the work back to plain conversations for speed
Keep the Project, since grounded answers matter more
Ask whether the grounding is worth the extra time here
Reduce the knowledge until the speed difference goes
questions.why: Retrieval costs time and buys grounding, and whether that trade is worth it depends on how much the grounding matters for this work.
questions.traps: Both absolute choices decide the trade without pricing it, and cutting knowledge to chase speed sacrifices the very thing being paid for.

questions.stem: A team's Projects are well maintained and no new joiner can tell which one to use.
options: Have new joiners ask a colleague which one to use
Reduce the number of Projects until it is obvious
Give every Project a rather longer and fuller name
Describe each Project by the questions it answers
questions.why: A new joiner is choosing by what they need answered, so describing Projects that way is what makes the choice possible.
questions.traps: Asking colleagues does not scale, merging Projects damages them to fix a labelling problem, and a longer name is not a description of use.

questions.stem: An associate is setting up a Project for a team answering customer questions about three separate products.
options: Create a single Project containing all three products' material
Create a single Project and let each question name its product
Create one Project per product so each holds only its own material
Create one Project per team member rather than per product
questions.why: Projects work by narrowing what an answer draws on, so splitting by product keeps every answer grounded in the right material.
questions.traps: A combined Project makes each answer compete with two other products, naming the product in the question shifts the work to the asker, and splitting by person duplicates identical material.

questions.stem: A team's custom instruction says "be concise" and answers have started omitting steps the team needs.
options: Remove the instruction so that nothing constrains answer length now
Keep it and ask a follow-up whenever a step has been left out
Change it to "be detailed" so that the omissions stop happening
Replace it with an instruction naming what must always be included
questions.why: "Concise" names what to minimise but not what to protect, and naming the required content gives the instruction something it must preserve.
questions.traps: Removing it restores the verbosity it was written to fix, follow-ups repair each answer instead of the instruction, and "be detailed" swaps one vague direction for its opposite.

questions.stem: A Project holds both the current expenses policy and last year's version, and answers sometimes cite the old one.
options: Add an instruction telling the model to prefer the current version
Remove the superseded version from the Project
Rename the old file so its status is clear in any citation
Keep both so answers can explain what changed between them
questions.why: Two versions of one policy make every answer a guess about which applies, and the superseded one has no role in answering current questions.
questions.traps: A preference instruction leaves the wrong text available, renaming helps only a reader who checks the citation, and change-explanations are a rare need paid for on every common one.

questions.stem: An associate pastes a 200-page manual into a single conversation and the model's answers become vague.
options: Move the manual into a Project and ask questions against it
Paste the manual again to refresh it in the conversation
Break the manual into several conversations, one per section
Ask shorter questions so more room is left for the manual
questions.why: A Project retrieves the relevant part of a long document for each question, where pasting the whole manual forces everything to compete for attention at once.
questions.traps: Re-pasting adds a second copy of the problem, splitting by conversation makes cross-section questions impossible, and shorter questions do not reduce the pasted volume.

questions.stem: A team wants everyone to get consistent answers about their returns policy.
options: Circulate a prompt everyone is asked to paste before asking
Have one person ask and forward the answers to the others
Ask everyone to attach the policy to their own conversations
Put the policy in a shared Project the whole team uses
questions.why: A shared Project gives every member the same grounding without depending on anyone remembering a step.
questions.traps: A circulated prompt depends on each person using it correctly, routing through one person creates a bottleneck, and individual attachments drift as people keep different copies.

questions.stem: An associate has forty conversations named "Untitled" and cannot find last week's analysis.
options: Start a new conversation and redo the analysis from scratch
Rename conversations to describe what each one covers
Keep everything in one long conversation so nothing is lost
Search the conversations for a phrase the analysis likely used
questions.why: A descriptive name is what makes a conversation findable later, and naming as you go is what prevents the backlog in the first place.
questions.traps: Redoing the work discards it, one long conversation makes retrieval harder rather than easier, and search finds this one item without fixing the other thirty-nine.

questions.stem: A Project's knowledge holds a style guide and a set of past reports, and answers follow the reports' style rather than the guide.
options: Add an instruction stating the style guide governs where they differ
Remove the past reports so only the style guide remains
Rewrite the past reports to match the current style guide
Ask for the style guide to be applied in each request
questions.why: Two sources of style in one Project need a stated precedence, and the instruction is what tells the model which one wins.
questions.traps: Removing the reports loses their content, rewriting them is a large job for a rule that can be stated once, and per-request reminders depend on remembering them.

questions.stem: A team's instruction lists eight rules and the model reliably follows the first three.
options: Number the rules so each one is clearly separated from the others
Repeat the later rules at the end so they are seen again
Cut the list to the rules that actually matter for their work
Split the eight rules across two Projects used in turn
questions.why: Long instruction lists dilute one another, and deciding which rules genuinely matter is what makes the remaining ones stick.
questions.traps: Numbering changes presentation rather than the count, repetition lengthens the instruction further, and splitting across Projects means neither has the full rule set.

questions.stem: An associate notices a Project answer citing a document that the team retired two months ago.
options: Remove the retired document and check for others like it
Add the current document alongside the retired one
Note in the instructions that the retired document is out of date
Ask the model not to cite that document in future answers
questions.why: One stale citation usually means the Project was never pruned, so the fix is removal plus a check for the same problem elsewhere.
questions.traps: Adding the current version leaves both in play, an instructions note relies on the model weighing it correctly, and a per-answer request does not persist.

questions.stem: A long conversation about a contract starts producing answers that contradict what was agreed earlier in it.
options: Ask the model to re-read the earlier part of the conversation
Start a fresh conversation with the agreed points restated
Continue and correct each contradiction as it appears
Ask the model to summarise the conversation before continuing
questions.why: Once earlier detail has fallen out of a long conversation, restating what was agreed in a fresh one is what puts it back in reach.
questions.traps: The model cannot recover what is no longer available to it, correcting each contradiction treats symptoms, and a summary of a degraded conversation inherits its gaps.

questions.stem: A Project is being set up for onboarding questions and the team wants to include their entire internal wiki.
options: Include the whole wiki so no question can fall outside it
Include the whole wiki and instruct the model to focus on onboarding
Include a summary of the wiki instead of the pages themselves
Include the pages onboarding questions actually reach for
questions.why: Project knowledge earns its place by being used, and a whole wiki makes every onboarding answer compete with material about everything else.
questions.traps: Full coverage buys rare hits at the cost of common ones, a focus instruction does not reduce what is present, and a summary loses the detail the answers need.

questions.stem: Two associates share a Project and one keeps adding files that the other then removes.
options: Give one of them sole responsibility for adding and removing files
Keep both sets of files so neither person's work is lost
Agree what belongs in the Project before either one adds to it
Split it into a separate Project for each of the two
questions.why: The disagreement is about what the Project is for, and settling that is what stops the additions and removals from cycling.
questions.traps: Sole ownership decides who acts rather than what is right, keeping both sets is the bloat one of them objects to, and splitting ends the collaboration rather than the dispute.

questions.stem: An associate keeps one Project called "Work" holding material for four unrelated responsibilities.
options: Keep it and name each file by the responsibility it belongs to
Split it into one Project for each responsibility
Keep it and state the responsibility at the start of each question
Keep it and add instructions covering all four responsibilities
questions.why: A Project narrows what an answer draws on, and four unrelated bodies of material in one Project remove that narrowing.
questions.traps: File naming helps a person browsing rather than the retrieval, stating the responsibility each time relies on the asker, and four sets of instructions conflict with one another.

questions.stem: A team adds a 60-page appendix to a Project because one page of it is occasionally needed.
options: Add the whole appendix, since the needed page is inside it
Add the appendix and instruct the model to use only that page
Add a link to the appendix rather than the appendix itself
Add the page that is needed and leave the appendix out
questions.why: Project knowledge should hold what answers actually use, and fifty-nine unused pages compete with the one that matters.
questions.traps: Including the whole appendix for one page is the bloat itself, an instruction does not remove the other pages, and a link is not material the model can read.

questions.stem: A Project instruction requires a source citation for every claim, and the team finds answers to simple internal questions cluttered.
options: Keep the rule, since a uniform standard is easier to rely on
Drop the rule and ask for citations when they are wanted
Limit the citation rule to claims drawn from the Project's documents
Keep the rule and ask for shorter citations in the instruction
questions.why: The rule earns its cost on document-grounded claims and pays nothing on general ones, so scoping it to the case it protects keeps the benefit without the clutter.
questions.traps: Uniformity is defensible but pays the cost everywhere, dropping the rule loses the grounding the team wanted, and shorter citations reduce clutter without addressing where citations are unnecessary.

questions.stem: A Project holds a policy document and a FAQ that paraphrases it, and both are actively used by the team.
options: Keep the policy and drop the FAQ, redirecting its use to the policy
Keep both, since the FAQ answers questions the policy phrases formally
Keep the FAQ and drop the policy, since it is what people read
Keep both and mark the policy as the authority where they differ
questions.why: A paraphrase can drift from what it paraphrases, and keeping the authoritative text alone removes the possibility of the two disagreeing.
questions.traps: The FAQ's readability is real but does not survive divergence, dropping the policy discards the authority, and marking precedence manages a conflict the Project need not contain.

questions.stem: A Project's documents are all current, but three of them cover the same process from different departments' perspectives.
options: Keep the most detailed one, since it covers what the others say
Keep all three, since each department's process genuinely differs
Merge them into a single document covering the shared process
Split them into a separate Project for each department
questions.why: Overlap is not duplication when the underlying processes really differ, and collapsing them would lose distinctions the answers need.
questions.traps: The most detailed version may still omit another department's specifics, a merge assumes a shared process that does not exist, and separate Projects prevent the cross-department questions.

questions.stem: An associate must analyse a document that is longer than a single conversation can hold usefully.
options: Summarise it first and analyse the summary in a single pass
Put it in a Project and ask the analysis question against it
Analyse it in sections and then reason over the section findings
Analyse only the sections most likely to matter for the question
questions.why: Sectioned analysis keeps every part of the document in view at full detail, and reasoning over the findings is what recovers the whole-document conclusion.
questions.traps: Summarising first discards the detail the analysis needs, Project retrieval surfaces passages rather than reading everything, and choosing sections in advance assumes the answer's location.

questions.stem: A team shares a Project externally with a partner organisation and one document contains internal commentary.
options: Remove the commentary before the Project is shared
Share it and ask the partner to disregard the internal commentary
Share a copy of the Project with that document left out entirely
Keep the commentary but move it into the Project's instructions
questions.why: Sharing makes the commentary readable, and taking it out is what makes the rest of the document shareable.
questions.traps: A request to disregard does not unsee it, dropping the document loses content the partner needs, and instructions are shared along with everything else.

questions.stem: An associate's Projects are organised by client, and one piece of work spans three of those clients.
options: Create a fourth Project holding all three clients' material
Work in whichever client Project holds the most relevant material
Reorganise the Projects by type of work rather than by client
Work in each Project in turn and combine the three results
questions.why: A cross-client piece is an exception, and handling it as one keeps the per-client structure that serves the ordinary case.
questions.traps: A fourth Project duplicates material that will drift, working inside one client's Project silently omits the other two, and reorganising rebuilds everything around the exception.

questions.stem: A team debates whether to give their Project detailed instructions or to rely on well-written prompts.
options: Put everything in the instructions so no prompt has to carry it
Keep the instructions minimal and let each prompt carry its needs
Put the standing rules in the instructions and the specifics in prompts
Duplicate the standing rules in both so neither can be missed
questions.why: Instructions carry what is true of every request and prompts carry what is true of one, and the split follows from that difference.
questions.traps: Instructions holding everything cannot vary per request, minimal instructions push repeated rules onto every prompt, and duplication creates two places for a rule to go stale.

questions.stem: A Project instruction that worked well for six months starts producing answers the team considers off-key.
options: Rewrite the instruction, since it is no longer producing good answers
Check what changed in the work before changing the instruction
Remove the instruction and see whether the answers improve
Add a clause covering the cases the team is objecting to
questions.why: An instruction that was right for six months is more likely to be facing different work than to have become wrong, and knowing which it is determines the fix.
questions.traps: Rewriting assumes the instruction is the cause, removal tests that assumption destructively, and a new clause patches a symptom before the cause is known.

questions.stem: Two documents in a Project give different figures for the same metric, and both are current and correct.
options: Keep the one the team refers to more often in its work
Remove both and add a single document with the agreed figure
Ask the model to present both figures whenever the metric comes up
State in the instructions what each figure measures and when to use it
questions.why: Two correct figures mean two different measurements, and naming what each one measures is what lets an answer choose correctly.
questions.traps: Popularity does not make a measure right for a question, a single agreed figure discards a real distinction, and presenting both leaves the choice to the reader every time.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to remove "anything unnecessary" from a Project used by six people.
options: Ask the six what they use before removing anything
Remove what has not been cited in any recent answer
Remove what the associate does not personally use in their work
Remove nothing, since six people's needs cannot be known
questions.why: Necessity in a shared Project is defined by six people's use, and finding that out is what separates pruning from guessing.
questions.traps: Citation history misses material that is read rather than cited, personal use covers one of six, and refusing to prune leaves the bloat the request was about.

questions.stem: A conversation is nearing the point where early detail stops being reliably available.
options: Continue, since the model will retain whatever matters most
Restate the decisions made so far before continuing
Start a new conversation and link to the old one for reference
Ask the model whether it still has the early part in view
questions.why: Restating the decisions puts them back within reach at the point they would otherwise be lost, which is what keeps the thread coherent.
questions.traps: The model does not preserve by importance, a link is not something it can follow, and asking what it can still see invites an unreliable answer.

questions.stem: An associate shares a working Project and colleagues start editing its instructions in ways that conflict.
options: Lock the instructions so that nobody can change them at all
Let each colleague keep their own separate copy of the Project
Accept every change, since each was made for a real reason
Agree who owns the instructions and route changes through them
questions.why: Instructions are a single shared setting, so a shared Project needs a single point at which changes to them are decided.
questions.traps: Locking prevents legitimate improvement, per-person copies end the sharing, and accepting every change is what produced the conflict.

questions.stem: A team keeps finished work in the same Projects as active work and answers start drawing on completed jobs.
options: Add an instruction to ignore anything marked as finished
Keep it, since finished work is often a useful precedent
Move finished material out of the Projects that answer questions
Mark finished files with a date so their status is visible
questions.why: A Project answers from whatever it holds, so material that should not shape answers has to leave rather than be labelled.
questions.traps: An ignore instruction competes with retrieval, precedent value is real but does not justify contaminating current answers, and a date marks the file without excluding it.

questions.stem: An associate must choose between one Project with instructions for two audiences and two Projects with one audience each.
options: Use two Projects so each set of instructions has one audience
Use one Project and name the audience at the start of each request
Use one Project with instructions covering both audiences carefully
Use one Project and switch its instructions when the audience changes
questions.why: Instructions apply to everything in a Project, so two audiences in one Project means every request carries rules meant for the other.
questions.traps: Naming the audience per request depends on the asker, careful dual instructions still fire both sets, and switching instructions makes an error likely at every change.

questions.stem: An associate joining a team is asked what a Project's custom instructions are actually for.
options: The documents that answers in the Project should draw on
Rules that should apply to every conversation in the Project
A record of what the Project has been used for so far
The questions the Project is expected to be asked most often
questions.why: Instructions carry standing rules, which is what makes them apply without being restated in each conversation.
questions.traps: Documents are the Project's knowledge rather than its instructions, a usage record is not a setting, and anticipated questions are not rules.

questions.stem: A team asks whether adding more documents to a Project always improves its answers.
options: Yes — more material means fewer questions fall outside it
Yes — the model selects only the relevant parts regardless
No — unused documents compete with the ones answers need
No — but only because there is a limit on how much fits
questions.why: Retrieval has to choose among what is present, so material that no question uses makes that choice harder on every question.
questions.traps: Coverage is bought at the cost of precision, selection degrades as volume grows, and the ceiling is not the reason volume hurts.

questions.stem: An associate wants the same tone in every answer coming out of one Project.
options: State the tone in the Project's custom instructions
Ask for that tone at the start of every conversation
Add examples of the tone to the Project's knowledge
Correct the tone in each answer that does not match
questions.why: Instructions apply to every conversation in the Project, which is what makes a standing preference hold without restatement.
questions.traps: A per-conversation request depends on remembering it, examples in knowledge are retrieved rather than always applied, and per-answer correction never becomes a rule.

questions.stem: A team setting up a Project asks how often its documents should be reviewed for staleness.
options: Once a year, so that the review is never forgotten about
Only when an answer has been found to be wrong
Never, since documents added were correct when they were added
Whenever the material a document describes has changed
questions.why: A document goes stale when what it describes changes, so that change is the event that should trigger the review.
questions.traps: An annual cycle leaves a document wrong for up to a year, waiting for a wrong answer means the error reaches someone first, and correctness at the time of adding does not persist.

questions.stem: An associate notices long conversations losing earlier detail and asks a colleague why that happens.
options: The model deletes older messages in order to save storage
Only a limited amount of the conversation is in view at once
Earlier messages are summarised automatically as a chat grows
The model prioritises whatever the user marked as important
questions.why: A conversation is processed within a finite window, so the earliest content is what falls out of reach as the conversation grows.
questions.traps: Nothing is deleted for storage, automatic summarisation is not what happens, and there is no marking that pins content in place.

questions.stem: An associate wants to send a colleague both a question and the answer they received.
options: Retype the question and paste the answer into a message
Send the colleague the Project the answer came from
Share the conversation so the colleague sees both
Ask the colleague to run the same question themselves
questions.why: Sharing the conversation carries the exchange as it happened, including the wording that produced the answer.
questions.traps: Retyping risks transcription differences, the Project shows the material rather than the exchange, and a re-run can produce a differently worded answer.

questions.stem: A team wants to find which of their Projects holds the supplier contracts.
options: Name each Project after the material it actually holds
Keep one Project so nothing has to be located at all
Keep an external list mapping topics to Project names
Search each Project in turn until the contracts appear
questions.why: A descriptive name is what makes a Project findable without a second system to consult.
questions.traps: A single Project trades findability for precision, an external list is one more thing to maintain, and searching in turn repeats the cost every time.

questions.stem: A team's Project instruction contains a rule that applies only to one quarterly report.
options: Keep it in the instructions so it is never forgotten
Create a second Project used only for that report
Add a note to the rule explaining when it was written
Move the rule into the prompt used for that report
questions.why: Instructions apply to every conversation, so a rule that is true of one report belongs with that report rather than with all of them.
questions.traps: Never forgetting comes at the cost of firing on unrelated work, a second Project duplicates the shared material, and a dating note changes nothing about when the rule applies.

questions.stem: A Project is used both to draft customer emails and to analyse support ticket data.
options: Keep it, since both uses concern the same customers
Keep it and write instructions covering the two uses
Split it, since the two uses need different instructions
Keep it and add the analysis data as extra knowledge
questions.why: The two uses want different tone, format and material, and one set of instructions cannot serve both without compromising each.
questions.traps: A shared subject does not mean shared rules, dual instructions fire on both tasks, and adding data leaves the instruction conflict untouched.

questions.stem: An associate attaches five long documents to one question and the answer only reflects two of them.
options: Attach all five again and repeat the same question
Ask about the documents in two or three smaller groups
Ask the model to confirm it has read all five documents
Attach summaries of the five instead of the documents
questions.why: Five long documents in one question force them to compete, and smaller groups give each one room to be read properly.
questions.traps: Repeating the request reproduces the competition, a confirmation is not evidence, and summaries lose the detail the question needs.

questions.stem: A colleague reports getting a different answer from the shared Project than the associate did.
options: Compare the two prompts before assuming the Project changed
Assume the Project's knowledge was edited between the two runs
Re-run both questions and take whichever answer looks better
Add an instruction making answers more consistent across users
questions.why: Different wording is the most common reason two people get different answers from the same Project, so the prompts are what to check first.
questions.traps: An edit is possible but less likely than a wording difference, picking the better-looking answer skips the diagnosis, and a consistency instruction treats an unconfirmed cause.

questions.stem: An associate keeps their Project instructions in a separate document so the team can review them.
options: Delete the document, since the Project already holds the instructions
Keep both and let each be edited as convenient at the time
Paste the document into the Project's knowledge as well
Keep the document as the reviewed source and update the Project from it
questions.why: A reviewable copy is useful, but only one of the two can be authoritative, and naming the reviewed document as the source keeps them from diverging.
questions.traps: Deleting it loses the review trail, editing either freely is how the two drift apart, and adding it to knowledge puts the instructions where they will also be retrieved.

questions.stem: A team connects Claude to their Google Drive so it can answer questions about a shared folder.
options: Grant access to the whole Drive so nothing is ever missing
Check which folders the connection actually exposes to Claude
Assume the connection is read-only and needs no further review
Confirm the team is permitted to process that material
Disconnect it whenever the team is not actively asking questions
questions.why: A connector widens what Claude can reach, so the two things to establish are what it can now see and whether that material is permitted to be processed at all.
questions.traps: Read-only access still exposes content, whole-Drive access maximises exposure rather than limiting it, and disconnecting between uses controls nothing while it is connected.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to connect a shared mailbox to Claude or keep attaching files by hand.
options: Connect it and also attach the same files for redundancy
Keep attaching by hand where the need is genuinely one-off
Connect it where the same material is needed again and again
Always connect, since a connection is less work than attaching
Never connect, since attachments are always more precise
questions.why: A connection pays off through repeated use and carries a standing exposure, so how often the material is needed is what decides between the two.
questions.traps: "Always" ignores the standing access a connection creates, "never" forgoes a real saving, and doing both duplicates content that then competes for attention.

questions.stem: An associate connects a Drive folder and colleagues start getting answers from documents they cannot themselves open.
options: Review whether the connector's access matches each person's own
Tell colleagues to ignore answers about documents they cannot open
Accept it, since the connector was approved for the team
Raise it, since the connector may be widening effective access
Remove the connector and go back to manual attachments entirely
questions.why: A connector can let answers reach people who would not otherwise have access to the source, which is an access-control question rather than a convenience one.
questions.traps: Team-level approval does not settle individual entitlement, asking people to ignore what they have seen does not unsee it, and removing it discards a useful capability before the question is answered.

questions.stem: A team asks how a connected source differs from a document uploaded into a Project.
options: A connected source is always more accurate than an upload
Connected sources are reviewed by the platform before use
The connected source reflects changes made at the source
An upload can never be updated once it has been added
An uploaded copy stays as it was at the moment of upload
questions.why: A connection tracks the live source while an upload is a snapshot, and that difference is what decides which suits material that changes.
questions.traps: Currency is not the same as accuracy, uploads can be replaced, and connection does not imply any review of the content.

questions.stem: A team must decide what to connect for a Project answering questions about their current policies.
options: The archive of superseded policies, for historical context
Every folder the department owns, for maximum coverage
Nothing whose contents they are not permitted to process
The folder holding the approved current policies
Only sources somebody is responsible for keeping current
questions.why: A connection should reach current, permitted, owned material, because those three properties are what make the answers both correct and defensible.
questions.traps: Maximum coverage dilutes retrieval with material no question uses, and connecting the superseded archive reintroduces exactly the stale guidance the Project exists to replace.

questions.stem: An associate's connected folder is reorganised by its owner and Project answers quietly get worse.
options: Agree with the owner how changes will be communicated
Accept it, since connected sources are expected to change
Treat the connected source as a dependency with an owner
Re-upload the documents so the Project no longer depends on it
Ask the owner to stop reorganising the folder in future
questions.why: A live connection makes somebody else's housekeeping part of your Project, so the relationship with that owner is the thing to manage.
questions.traps: Re-uploading trades currency for stability without deciding which is wanted, asking the owner to freeze their folder is rarely available, and accepting silent degradation is the problem.

questions.stem: A team is setting up a Project and deciding what belongs in instructions rather than in knowledge.
options: Whatever the team wrote most recently goes in the instructions
Rules that should shape every answer go in the instructions
Anything long goes in knowledge and anything short in instructions
Material the answers should draw facts from goes in knowledge
Both should hold the same content so nothing can be missed
questions.why: Instructions shape how every answer is produced and knowledge supplies what is true, and the content's role is what decides where it belongs.
questions.traps: Length and recency describe the text rather than its function, and duplicating content across both makes it compete with itself.

questions.stem: An associate is asked what makes a Project worth creating rather than just using a conversation.
options: The documents involved are too large to attach to a chat
The task is important enough to deserve its own Project
Standing rules should apply without being restated each time
A Project is always preferable to a plain conversation
The same material is needed across many conversations
questions.why: A Project earns its setup cost through reuse of material and persistence of rules, which are the two things a conversation cannot give you.
questions.traps: Importance is not reuse, size is not the deciding factor, and a Project is overhead that a one-off question does not repay.

questions.stem: A team's Project answers are good and they are deciding what to add next.
options: Anything the department has produced in the last year
Documents that are hard to find anywhere else in the company
Material somebody is willing to keep current over time
Material that questions currently go unanswered without
Whatever is largest, since it covers the most ground
questions.why: Additions earn their place by answering real questions and by having someone to maintain them, because unmaintained material is what turns a good Project stale.
questions.traps: Recency, findability elsewhere and size all describe the document rather than whether any question needs it.

questions.stem: A team's Project instruction is long and the team wants to know what to cut.
options: Rules that no observed failure has ever depended on
Rules written in the longest and most detailed language
Rules that duplicate what a knowledge document already says
Rules that the newest team members do not understand
Rules that were added by people who have since left
questions.why: Instructions dilute one another, so what to cut is whatever earns nothing: rules preventing failures that do not occur, and rules restating the knowledge.
questions.traps: Authorship, length and familiarity all describe the rule's history or style rather than whether it is doing any work.

questions.stem: An associate wants a Project to behave differently for two kinds of request and has one instruction set.
options: Split it into two Projects, one per kind of request
Switch the instructions over whenever the kind changes
Write instructions covering both kinds and let the model choose
State the kind at the start of every single question asked
Accept that one instruction set applies to everything in it
questions.why: Instructions apply unconditionally to every conversation in a Project, so two behaviours genuinely need two Projects rather than one conditional rule set.
questions.traps: Dual instructions fire on both kinds, per-question labelling depends on the asker remembering, and switching invites an error at every changeover.

questions.stem: A team is reviewing a Project and asks which documents to remove.
options: The longest documents, since they crowd out the others
Documents written by people outside the immediate team
Documents nobody has opened in the last three months
Documents superseded by a newer version already present
Documents describing processes the team no longer follows
questions.why: Removal should target material that is wrong or redundant for current questions, which is what superseded and obsolete documents are.
questions.traps: Open counts, authorship and length are all proxies that would remove correct, load-bearing material along with the rest.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds documents that are each correct and collectively out of date as a set.
options: Establish which one describes how the work is done now
Add an instruction telling the model to prefer newer files
Record what changed, so the removal can be explained later
Keep them all, since each was accurate when it was written
Remove the ones describing processes that have been replaced
questions.why: Individually correct documents can still describe a process nobody follows, so the fix is to find the current one, remove what it replaced, and leave a trail.
questions.traps: Historic accuracy is not current applicability, and a preference instruction leaves the superseded text available to be retrieved anyway.

questions.stem: A team shares a Project widely and wants it to stay usable.
options: Name someone responsible for keeping it current
Give everyone permission to edit it as they see fit
Agree what may be added to it, and on what basis
Lock it so that nobody can change anything at all
Ask each person to keep their own copy up to date
questions.why: Shared material needs an owner and an agreed standard for additions, because those two things are what stop it decaying or bloating.
questions.traps: Unrestricted editing produces the bloat, locking prevents legitimate improvement, and per-person copies end the sharing altogether.

questions.stem: A second team wants the way a Project is set up without any of the first team's files.
options: Describe the setup and have them rebuild it from scratch
Share the whole Project and ask them not to open the files
Let the second team supply their own knowledge sources
Copy the documents across with the sensitive parts removed
Share the instructions, which carry the configuration
questions.why: Instructions and knowledge are separable, so the reusable part can travel while each team keeps its own material behind its own access controls.
questions.traps: A request not to open files is not a control, rebuilding from a description wastes work that could be copied, and redacted copies still move the material.

questions.stem: A team's Project is large and answers have become less precise than they were.
options: Precision is unrelated to how much a Project holds
Retrieval now has more material to choose between
Adding more documents will restore the lost precision
The model has become less capable since the Project grew
Cutting unused documents will sharpen the answers again
questions.why: Precision falls as retrieval has to select among more material, so the diagnosis and the fix are both about volume rather than capability.
questions.traps: The model has not changed, volume is exactly what drives the effect, and adding more compounds it.

questions.stem: A team's Projects are individually well run and nobody can find the right one.
options: Accept it, since each Project works well on its own
Keep a record of what exists and who owns each one
Describe each Project by the questions it answers
Rename them all using a stricter naming convention
Merge them into fewer Projects so there is less to search
questions.why: Findability at scale comes from describing Projects by use and keeping a register, neither of which requires damaging the Projects themselves.
questions.traps: Merging trades precision for findability, a stricter convention does not help someone who does not know what they are looking for, and individual quality is not organisational health.

questions.stem: An HR manager proposes using Claude to screen job applications and produce a shortlist for interview.
options: Applicant data being retained and used for training without candidates' consent
Consumption costs rising sharply as application volume peaks
The model's knowledge cutoff leaving it unaware of recent employment-law changes
Automated screening of people needs human accountability and a bias review before it is used
questions.why: Consequential automated decisions about individuals sit at the centre of this domain: they need an accountable person, a bias review and a route to recourse.
questions.traps: On commercial plans data is not used for training by default, so that is a policy point to confirm rather than the headline risk. Cost is a budget issue, and the cutoff applies to any use.

questions.stem: An associate wants to paste a customer list including names and account numbers into Claude to reformat it.
options: Paste it, since the task is internal and the output will not be shared externally
Remove or replace the identifying fields, since reformatting does not require real identifiers
Paste it and delete the conversation afterwards
Ask Claude not to retain the information
questions.why: Data minimisation is the control: a reformatting task needs the structure, not the identities. Substituting placeholders achieves the task without the disclosure.
questions.traps: Internal use does not exempt personal data from handling rules. Deleting afterwards does not undo the disclosure, and instructions do not govern retention.

questions.stem: A team wants to analyse customer complaints that contain personal details, and the organisation operates under data protection law.
options: Establish the lawful basis and what the privacy notice already told customers before doing anything
Anonymise the complaints and then proceed
Proceed, since analysing complaints improves service for those same customers
Ask the legal team to review the analysis once it has been produced
questions.why: Processing personal data needs a lawful basis and has to be consistent with what people were told. That determines what is permitted before any technical choice.
questions.traps: Anonymisation may be the right control but only once the basis is established. Beneficial purpose is not a lawful basis, and post-hoc legal review follows the processing.

questions.stem: A consultant wants to use one client's material as an example when working on another client's problem.
options: Use it since the two clients are not competitors
Use it with the client's name taken out
Treat the material as covered by the first client's confidentiality unless it is genuinely public
Ask Claude to generalise the example so it no longer resembles the original client's situation
questions.why: Client material is confidential regardless of who else sees the output. Whether it is genuinely public is what determines if it can be reused at all.
questions.traps: Non-competition does not release a confidentiality obligation. Name removal and generalisation both still derive from confidential material.

questions.stem: A team publishes a report drafted with Claude that contains an error, and a customer asks who is responsible.
options: The people who produced and approved the report, since accountability does not transfer to a tool
Claude, since the error originated in the generated text
Nobody in particular, since the error was not deliberate
The reviewer alone, since their role was to catch exactly this kind of problem
questions.why: Accountability attaches to the people who chose to use the tool and approved the output. It cannot be delegated to software.
questions.traps: Attributing responsibility to the tool is the misconception being tested. Diffusing it or narrowing it to one reviewer both misplace where the obligation sits.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to draft responses that are sent to customers under an employee's name.
options: Disclose it in every single message
Establish what the organisation's policy requires be disclosed, and follow it
Never disclose it, since the employee reviews and sends each message personally
Disclose it only when a customer asks whether a message was written by a person
questions.why: Whether and how to disclose is a policy question with legal and reputational dimensions. Establishing the organisation's position is what makes the practice defensible.
questions.traps: Blanket rules in either direction pre-empt a policy decision. Disclosing only on request treats a standing question as reactive.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to summarise performance reviews, and notices the summaries describe men and women differently.
options: Instruct the model to use neutral language in the summaries
Remove the names before summarising them
Investigate whether the difference originates in the reviews or in the summarisation
Accept the difference, since the summaries reflect what the original reviews actually said about each person
questions.why: A difference in output could come from the source reviews or be introduced during summarisation, and the response differs completely depending on which. Investigating is the first step.
questions.traps: Neutral language and name removal both treat the symptom before the cause is known. Assuming the source is faithful skips the investigation.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude for something they suspect breaches the organisation's acceptable use policy.
options: Proceed, since the request came from someone more senior
Proceed but keep a record of who asked
Ask Claude whether the use would be acceptable under a typical acceptable use policy
Check the policy and raise it before proceeding
questions.why: A suspected policy breach is checked against the policy and raised. Seniority of the requester does not change what the policy permits.
questions.traps: Following instructions does not transfer responsibility. A record documents rather than prevents, and the model cannot interpret your organisation's policy.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether they can use Claude-generated marketing copy commercially.
options: Assume they can, since the output was generated for them
Assume they cannot, since generated content has uncertain ownership
Check the terms that apply to their plan, since that is what governs the position
Ask Claude who owns the output it produces
questions.why: Rights in generated output are set by the terms of the plan being used. Reading them is what answers the question authoritatively.
questions.traps: Both assumptions guess at a documented position. Asking the model produces an unreliable account of a contractual matter.

questions.stem: A team wants to upload a spreadsheet for analysis, and three of its forty columns contain personal data the analysis does not use.
options: Remove the three columns before uploading, since the analysis does not need them
Upload it and instruct the model to ignore those columns
Upload it and delete it again afterwards
Upload it, since the analysis is legitimate and the personal data is incidental to the purpose
questions.why: Sending only what the task needs is the structural control. Columns that are never transmitted cannot be misused, which no instruction guarantees.
questions.traps: An ignore instruction does not prevent transmission. Deletion afterwards does not undo it, and incidental inclusion is still disclosure.

questions.stem: A lending team wants Claude to assess loan applications and produce a recommendation for each one.
options: Automate the recommendations and have a person approve them in bulk
Automate it and audit a monthly sample
Automate the straightforward approvals and route only the refusals to a person for review
Keep an accountable person deciding, with documented reasons that the applicant could be given
questions.why: Lending decisions affect individuals and usually carry a right to an explanation. An accountable decision-maker with documented reasons is what satisfies that.
questions.traps: Bulk approval is a rubber stamp. Sampling audits after the fact, and auto-approving while routing refusals still automates a consequential decision.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to identify which customers are most likely to leave, using their transaction history.
options: Proceed, since the data is already held by the organisation
Confirm the purpose is compatible with what the data was collected for
Anonymise the transaction history first
Ask customers for consent to the analysis
questions.why: Data collected for one purpose cannot automatically be used for another. Purpose compatibility is the question that determines whether the analysis is lawful.
questions.traps: Possession is not permission. Anonymisation may defeat the analysis, and consent is one possible basis rather than the first question.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude on documents covered by legal professional privilege.
options: Proceed, since the analysis is internal to the organisation
Proceed with the client's name removed
Ask the legal team to review the output once the analysis has been completed
Establish whether the disclosure would affect privilege before any material is shared
questions.why: Privilege can be affected by disclosure, and that is a legal question to settle before material is shared rather than after.
questions.traps: Internal use may still constitute disclosure. Name removal does not address privilege, and reviewing output follows the disclosure that matters.

questions.stem: A team is asked to sign off on Claude-generated analysis and is unsure what signing off commits them to.
options: Sign off, since another colleague has already reviewed the work
Sign off with a note that Claude was used in producing it
Establish what sign-off asserts, since it attaches their judgement to the content
Decline to sign off on anything that was produced with a generative tool
questions.why: Sign-off is an accountability act, and knowing what is being asserted determines what has to be checked before signing.
questions.traps: Relying on unspecified prior review is unfounded. A tool disclosure does not limit what is asserted, and refusing categorically forecloses legitimate work.

questions.stem: A team publishes research where Claude was used to analyse the data but not to write the conclusions.
options: Describe the tool's actual role, since readers judge methods by what was done
Do not mention it, since the conclusions are the authors' own
Mention it only in a closing appendix
State that the research was produced with AI assistance
questions.why: Method transparency means describing what the tool actually did, which is what lets a reader evaluate the work.
questions.traps: Omitting it hides part of the method. Burying it in an appendix understates it, and a vague acknowledgement does not tell readers what to evaluate.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted process produces outcomes that differ by postcode, and postcode correlates with ethnicity in their area.
options: Remove postcode from the model's inputs
Investigate whether the difference is justified by the process's legitimate criteria
Accept the difference, since postcode is not a protected characteristic
Add an instruction telling the model not to consider ethnicity in its assessments
questions.why: A proxy variable can produce discriminatory outcomes without the protected characteristic being used. Whether the difference is justified is the question that matters.
questions.traps: Removing postcode may not remove the correlation carried by other fields. The proxy argument is the misconception, and an instruction about ethnicity does not address the proxy.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to generate large volumes of reviews for their own product to post on a retail site.
options: Proceed, since the reviews describe the product accurately
Proceed but mark the reviews as company-written
Generate the reviews and have employees post them under their own accounts
Decline, since fabricated reviews presented as genuine are deceptive regardless of who writes them
questions.why: Fabricated reviews presented as independent customer feedback are deceptive, and that does not change because the content is accurate or because a person posts them.
questions.traps: Accuracy does not cure the misrepresentation of source. Marking them removes the deception but not the described practice, and employee posting compounds it.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to write copy in the distinctive style of a well-known author for a commercial campaign.
options: Proceed, since style itself is not protected
Proceed with an acknowledgement of the author
Consider whether the imitation would mislead or infringe before using it commercially
Ask Claude whether the copy would infringe the author's rights
questions.why: Commercial imitation raises questions of both infringement and misleading association. Considering those before use is what makes the decision informed.
questions.traps: The style argument is a partial truth that ignores passing off and endorsement implications. An acknowledgement may strengthen a false association, and the model cannot give a legal opinion.

questions.stem: A team is unsure whether a particular dataset counts as sensitive under their organisation's classification scheme.
options: Treat it as sensitive just to be safe
Check the classification scheme, since it is what determines the handling requirements
Treat it as non-sensitive since nobody has said otherwise
Ask the data owner for their view on how sensitive the material is
questions.why: The classification scheme is the authority, and consulting it produces the handling requirements directly rather than an estimate of them.
questions.traps: Defaulting either way guesses at a documented position. The data owner's view is useful input but the scheme is what governs.

questions.stem: A school wants Claude to help allocate places to applicants, with staff reviewing the output.
options: Ensure staff can see and change the reasoning, not just the outcome
Have staff approve the allocations as produced
Have staff review a sample of the allocations
Have staff review the allocations that fall outside the expected pattern
questions.why: Meaningful review of a consequential decision requires access to the reasoning, otherwise the review is an approval of an outcome nobody can interrogate.
questions.traps: Approving outputs without reasoning is a rubber stamp. Sampling and exception review both leave most decisions unexamined.

questions.stem: A team receives a request from an individual asking what personal data the organisation holds about them.
options: Ask Claude to search the organisation's systems for the individual's data
Reply that the data is held in systems that cannot easily be searched
Handle it under the organisation's existing process for such requests
Ask the individual to be more specific about what they are looking for
questions.why: Access requests have a defined legal process and timescale. Routing it there is what ensures the response is complete and compliant.
questions.traps: Using the model to search systems it cannot access does not answer the request. Difficulty is not a valid response, and narrowing the request does not discharge the obligation.

questions.stem: An associate wants to check a contract using Claude, and the contract contains a clause restricting disclosure to third parties.
options: Determine whether using the tool constitutes disclosure under that clause
Proceed, since the tool is not a third party in the ordinary sense
Proceed with the counterparty's name removed
Ask the counterparty for permission to use the tool on their contract
questions.why: Whether the clause is engaged is the question, and it turns on how disclosure is defined in that contract rather than on intuition about tools.
questions.traps: Assuming a tool is not a third party is the assumption to test. Name removal does not address the disclosure, and seeking permission presumes the clause applies without checking.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces an output that nobody in the team fully understands but which has been reliable so far.
options: Continue, since it has been reliable in practice over an extended period
Ensure someone can explain and defend it before it is relied on externally
Add a disclaimer to the output produced
Ask Claude to explain how the output was produced so the team has an account they can give
questions.why: Being able to explain and defend output is part of being accountable for it. Reliability does not substitute for understanding when the output is used externally.
questions.traps: A record of reliability does not equip anyone to answer a challenge. A disclaimer shifts risk, and a model-generated explanation is not an account the team can stand behind.

questions.stem: A team is asked by a customer whether AI was used in preparing the advice they received.
options: Say that a range of tools were used in preparing the advice
Decline to discuss internal processes
Explain that the adviser reviewed everything, without addressing the question that was asked
Answer honestly, since the customer has asked directly
questions.why: A direct question about how advice was produced is answered directly. Evasion damages trust more than the fact being disclosed.
questions.traps: Vague references to tools, refusal, and answering a different question are all forms of evasion of a question the customer is entitled to ask.

questions.stem: An associate notices Claude's suggestions for a job description use language that research associates with fewer applications from women.
options: Change the language, since the effect on applications is the outcome that matters
Keep it, since the wording was not chosen with any intent to exclude anyone
Ask Claude whether the wording is biased
Add a line encouraging applications from underrepresented groups
questions.why: Fairness is assessed on effect rather than intent, and the described effect is exactly what the wording change addresses.
questions.traps: Absence of intent does not remove the effect. Asking the model to assess its own wording is not independent, and an encouraging line does not offset language that suppresses applications.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to analyse publicly available social media posts to build profiles of individual customers.
options: Proceed, since the posts are publicly available
Consider whether compiling profiles from public posts is proportionate and permitted
Proceed but only for customers who have an existing relationship
Anonymise the profiles once they have been built
questions.why: Public availability of individual posts does not make aggregation into profiles permitted or proportionate. That is the question the scenario turns on.
questions.traps: The public-data argument is the misconception being tested. An existing relationship does not authorise profiling, and anonymising after building defeats the stated purpose.

questions.stem: A team wants to publish Claude-generated content under an individual employee's byline.
options: Publish it, since the employee directed and reviewed the work
Publish it with a note that AI was used
Consider whether the byline would misrepresent who created the content
Ask the employee whether they are comfortable with the byline
questions.why: A byline is a claim about authorship. Whether it misrepresents the actual creation process is the question that determines whether it is honest.
questions.traps: Direction and review may or may not amount to authorship, which is the point to consider. A note is one possible remedy, and the employee's comfort does not settle whether it misleads readers.

questions.stem: An associate is working on a task where using real data would be convenient and synthetic data would be sufficient.
options: Use real data, since it produces more realistic results
Use real data with the most sensitive fields removed
Use a small sample of real data rather than the full dataset
Use synthetic data, since it achieves the task without any exposure
questions.why: When synthetic data is sufficient, using it removes the exposure entirely. That is the strongest available control and it costs only convenience.
questions.traps: Realism is not needed when synthetic data suffices. Partial removal and sampling both reduce exposure without eliminating it.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to draft decisions about benefit eligibility, and applicants can appeal.
options: Give applicants the model's explanation of the decision
Ensure the reasons given to applicants reflect the actual basis for the decision
Tell applicants the decision was made using an automated process
Provide applicants with a standard set of reasons covering the common grounds for refusal
questions.why: An appeal depends on the reasons being the real basis for the decision. Ensuring that correspondence is what makes the appeal meaningful.
questions.traps: A model-generated explanation may not reflect the actual basis. Disclosure of automation and standard reason sets both fall short of giving the real grounds.

questions.stem: A team wants to keep conversation histories containing customer data indefinitely for future reference.
options: Apply the organisation's retention rules, since indefinite retention is rarely permitted
Keep them, since they may be useful and storage is inexpensive
Keep them but restrict who can access them
Keep them for a year and then review whether they are still needed
questions.why: Retention has to follow a defined policy tied to purpose. Indefinite retention of personal data is generally not permitted regardless of utility or storage cost.
questions.traps: Utility and cost are not retention criteria. Access restriction addresses a different risk, and an arbitrary year substitutes a guess for the policy.

questions.stem: An associate's team works for two clients who are direct competitors, using the same shared Project.
options: Keep one Project and instruct the model to keep the clients' material separate
Keep one Project and label each document with its client
Keep one Project and ask people to specify the client in each question
Separate the Projects, since shared context risks one client's material informing the other's work
questions.why: Isolation is structural: material that is not present cannot leak into another client's work. With competitors, that is the standard the situation requires.
questions.traps: Instructions, labels and per-question scoping all rely on correct selection every time, which is not an adequate control between competitors.

questions.stem: A team wants to know who should be accountable for a workflow that spans three departments.
options: Make all three departments jointly accountable
Make the department that initiated the workflow accountable
Name a single accountable owner, since responsibility spread across three departments diffuses
Make whichever department the output affects most accountable for the workflow overall
questions.why: Diffusion across departments is a recognised failure of shared controls. A named owner is what makes accountability real.
questions.traps: Joint accountability is the diffusion being described. Initiation and impact are both arbitrary bases when what matters is who can actually exercise control.

questions.stem: A team's proposal to a client was drafted with Claude, and the client's procurement rules require disclosure of subcontractors.
options: Establish whether the rules cover tool use, since they were written about subcontractors
Disclose it, since transparency is always the safer course
Do not disclose it, since a tool is not a subcontractor
Ask the client informally whether they would want to know about it
questions.why: Whether an obligation applies is determined by reading it. Procurement rules about subcontractors may or may not extend to tools, and that is establishable.
questions.traps: Disclosing reflexively and declining on a definitional argument both skip reading the rule. An informal enquiry does not establish the contractual position.

questions.stem: A team tests their Claude workflow for bias by checking whether it produces different outputs for names associated with different ethnicities.
options: Conclude the workflow is unbiased if the outputs match
Conclude the test is unnecessary since the model is designed to be fair
Recognise this is a useful test and check other attributes and proxies as well
Run the test occasionally rather than as part of the regular process
questions.why: Name-swapping is a genuine test but covers one attribute through one proxy. Extending it to other attributes and proxies is what makes the assessment meaningful.
questions.traps: Passing one narrow test does not establish general fairness. Assuming fairness by design skips testing, and occasional testing does not track changes.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to write messages that will be sent from accounts appearing to belong to different individuals.
options: Proceed, since the message content is accurate and not harmful
Proceed if the individuals have agreed to it
Proceed but keep a record of which messages were generated
Decline, since messages presented as coming from people who did not write them are deceptive
questions.why: Presenting messages as authored by people who did not write them misrepresents their source, which is the deception regardless of content.
questions.traps: Accurate content does not cure a false attribution. Individual agreement changes the situation materially and is worth distinguishing, but as stated the practice misrepresents authorship. A record does not address the deception.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to summarise a paid research report they subscribe to, and share the summary with colleagues who do not have access.
options: Share it, since a summary is not the original report
Check the subscription terms, since redistribution is what they typically restrict
Share it with attribution to the research provider
Ask the research provider whether they would object to the summary being shared
questions.why: Subscription terms typically govern redistribution and derivative use. Reading them is what determines whether internal sharing is permitted.
questions.traps: Summary status does not automatically escape the terms. Attribution does not grant redistribution rights, and an informal enquiry is weaker than the contract.

questions.stem: A team is asked to process a dataset and cannot determine who owns it or what restrictions apply.
options: Establish ownership and restrictions before processing anything
Process it, since it was provided to the team for that purpose
Process it and note the uncertainty in the output
Process a small sample to see whether anything sensitive appears in the data
questions.why: Unclear provenance and restrictions have to be resolved before processing, because the permitted handling is unknown until they are.
questions.traps: Being given the data does not establish what may be done with it. Noting uncertainty documents rather than resolves, and sampling does not reveal contractual restrictions.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to help decide which customers receive a service reduction, affecting several thousand people.
options: Automate it using the documented criteria
Automate it and notify affected customers of their right to complain
Document the criteria and keep a person accountable for applying them to individuals
Automate it for customers below a threshold and review the rest individually
questions.why: Decisions materially affecting thousands of individuals need documented criteria and an accountable person, so that each affected person has a real route to challenge the outcome.
questions.traps: Automating on documented criteria still removes the accountable decision. A complaints route follows the decision, and thresholding automates the majority.

questions.stem: A team member says they are not responsible for an error because Claude produced the text.
options: Accept the explanation, since the error genuinely originated in the generated text
