Write them and have a colleague verify the claims are accurate
Write them based on genuine feedback the company has received
Decline, since the reviews would misrepresent real customer experience
questions.why: A review asserts that a customer used the product and formed a view, so generating one misstates its source however the content is arrived at.
questions.traps: A generated label on a listing review still presents it as a review, accuracy does not repair a false source, and real feedback rewritten as a review attributes it to someone who did not write it.

questions.stem: An associate wants to summarise a contract that is held under a non-disclosure agreement with a customer.
options: Proceed, since a summary is not a disclosure of the contract
Proceed with the customer's name removed from the text first
Check what the agreement permits before putting the text in
Proceed and delete the conversation once the summary is done
questions.why: An NDA governs where the text may go, and the agreement is what settles whether this use sits inside its terms.
questions.traps: A summary is produced from the text, redacting the name leaves the substance, and deleting afterwards does not undo the processing.

questions.stem: A team publishes a research brief substantially drafted with Claude and asks whether to say so.
options: Say so where readers would reasonably expect to know
Say nothing, since the team reviewed and approved the content
Say so only if a reader asks how the brief was produced
Say so in every document regardless of how it was produced
questions.why: Disclosure is owed where the method would change how a reader weighs the work, and a research brief is such a case.
questions.traps: Review makes the content accountable but not the method visible, disclosure on request puts the burden on the reader, and a blanket statement everywhere loses the signal.

questions.stem: An associate uses Claude to help write an article and asks who may be named as its author.
options: Claude, since it produced most of the article's wording
The person responsible for the content and for its accuracy
Nobody, since authorship is unclear for assisted writing
The team as a whole rather than any one named individual
questions.why: Authorship attaches to the person who stands behind the work, which is what makes accountability for it meaningful.
questions.traps: A tool is not an author, declining to name anyone removes accountability, and a collective byline obscures who is answerable.

questions.stem: A hiring manager asks whether Claude can be used to reject applicants automatically.
options: No — a rejection decision needs a person who is accountable
Yes, provided the criteria used are documented in advance
Yes, provided rejected applicants can ask for a review
Yes, provided the model is checked for bias beforehand
questions.why: A hiring rejection materially affects a person, so the decision has to rest with someone who can be held to it.
questions.traps: Documented criteria, an appeal route and a bias check are all worth having, but none of them puts a person inside the decision.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to paste a spreadsheet of customer names and addresses into a conversation.
options: Paste it, since the task cannot be done without the data
Ask whether the personal data is needed for the task at all
Paste it once the customers have been notified afterwards
Paste it with the addresses removed and the names retained
questions.why: Data minimisation asks first whether the personal data is needed, because the safest handling of data is not to process it.
questions.traps: Necessity is the thing being assumed, notification after the fact does not authorise it, and half the identifiers is still personal data.

questions.stem: A team notices that a Claude-drafted job advert emphasises traits associated with one group of applicants.
options: Publish it, since the wording came from the role description
Publish it and monitor who applies over the first month
Ask for a version that appeals to a wider range of people
Rewrite the advert around the requirements of the role
questions.why: An advert should describe what the role requires, and returning to the requirements is what removes wording that filters applicants.
questions.traps: A source description does not launder the wording, monitoring measures the harm after it occurs, and appeal-broadening changes the framing without fixing the criteria.

questions.stem: An associate sends a Claude-drafted client email that contains an error, and the client complains.
options: Responsibility is shared between the associate and the tool
The tool is responsible, since it produced the wrong text
The associate is responsible, since they sent the email
Nobody is at fault, since the error was not intentional
questions.why: Responsibility follows the decision to send, which is a human act regardless of what drafted the text.
questions.traps: A tool cannot bear responsibility, sharing it with a tool is the same error stated softly, and lack of intent does not remove accountability.

questions.stem: A team wants to know which of their data warrants extra care before it is used with Claude.
options: Data that is stored in systems marked as internal only
Data that the team has not previously used with any tool
Data that is large enough to be difficult to review fully
Data that would cause harm if it were exposed or misused
questions.why: Sensitivity is defined by the consequence of exposure, which is what makes the classification useful for deciding handling.
questions.traps: Storage location is a proxy that misses sensitive data held elsewhere, novelty is not a risk property, and volume is a practical concern rather than a sensitivity one.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to write a message impersonating a supplier to test a colleague's vigilance.
options: Write it, since the purpose is to improve security awareness
Decline unless the organisation has authorised such a test
Write it and tell the colleague afterwards that it was a test
Write it but make the impersonation obvious enough to spot
questions.why: Phishing simulations are legitimate when an organisation runs them under authority, and what makes this one wrong is an individual deceiving a colleague on their own initiative.
questions.traps: A good motive does not create authority, a later reveal comes after the deception, and an easy version is still an unauthorised test.

questions.stem: An associate wants to share a Claude conversation that contains a colleague's performance feedback.
options: Share it, since the feedback was written to be acted upon
Share it with the colleague's name replaced by a role title
Do not share it beyond those already entitled to see it
Share it only with people in the same team as the colleague
questions.why: Performance feedback stays within the group already entitled to it, and sharing the conversation extends that group.
questions.traps: Being actionable does not widen the audience, a role title in a small team still identifies the person, and team membership is not the same as entitlement.

questions.stem: A customer asks whether they are talking to a person or to an assistant in a support chat.
options: Tell them plainly that they are talking to an assistant
Deflect, since the answer does not affect the help given
Say a person is available if they would prefer to wait
Answer only if the customer asks the question a second time
questions.why: A direct question about who is answering deserves a direct answer, and concealing it misleads the customer about the exchange.
questions.traps: The quality of help does not settle a question about identity, offering an alternative dodges what was asked, and requiring a repeat is evasion.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to reproduce several paragraphs from a published book for an internal deck.
options: Reproduce it, since the deck stays inside the organisation
Reproduce it with the author's name added at the end
Reproduce it reworded so the sentences are no longer identical
Use a short quotation with attribution instead of the passage
questions.why: Copying substantial text is a use of the work regardless of audience, and a short attributed quotation is what stays within fair use.
questions.traps: Internal use is still use, attribution does not license copying, and rewording a passage still takes its expression.

questions.stem: A team wants to use six months of customer support transcripts to find their most common complaints.
options: Strip the identifying details before the transcripts are analysed
Use them as they are, since the analysis is about complaints
Use only the transcripts from customers who have consented
Ask every customer for permission before any analysis happens
questions.why: The analysis needs the complaint content and not the identities, so removing what it does not need is what makes the use proportionate.
questions.traps: Analysing identified transcripts processes more than the purpose requires, consent-only selection biases the sample, and blanket permission-seeking is disproportionate once identifiers are gone.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to shortlist suppliers and finds the same three regions appearing every time.
options: Add a requirement that other regions must be represented
Check whether the criteria themselves favour those regions
Accept the outcome, since the criteria were applied evenly
Run the shortlist again to see whether the pattern repeats
questions.why: A repeated pattern points at the criteria, and examining them is what distinguishes a real signal from a built-in preference.
questions.traps: A representation quota changes the result without explaining it, even application of skewed criteria still produces skewed results, and a re-run confirms the pattern without diagnosing it.

questions.stem: A manager asks who should sign off on a Claude-assisted financial summary before it is issued.
options: The person who wrote the prompt that produced the summary
Anyone on the team, since the model did the calculation
Someone who can verify the figures against their source
The manager, since they requested the summary in the first place
questions.why: Sign-off means asserting the figures are right, which requires the ability to check them against what they came from.
questions.traps: Prompt authorship is not verification, delegating to the model is what sign-off exists to prevent, and requesting the work does not confer the ability to check it.

questions.stem: An associate needs to debug a problem using a log file that contains a handful of email addresses.
options: Use the log as it is, since only a handful are affected
Use the log and ask the model to ignore the addresses
Ask the log's owner whether the addresses may be included
Remove the addresses, since the debugging does not need them
questions.why: The debugging works on the log's structure rather than on who appears in it, so removing the identifiers costs nothing and removes the exposure.
questions.traps: A small number is still personal data, an instruction to ignore does not prevent processing, and asking permission is unnecessary when the data is not needed.

questions.stem: A credit team wants Claude to draft the reasoning that explains why an application was declined.
options: Draft it and let the decision follow from what it says
Draft the reasoning and the decision together in one step
Draft it from the decision a person has already made
Draft several possible reasonings and pick the best one
questions.why: The explanation must describe the decision that was actually made, which means the decision comes first and the drafting follows it.
questions.traps: Letting the text drive the decision inverts the order, producing both together makes the model the decider, and picking among reasonings selects a story rather than reporting one.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to draft legal advice for a client of the firm.
options: Draft it and send it with a note that it is not formal advice
Draft it for a qualified lawyer to review and take on
Decline, since legal drafting is outside what may be assisted
Draft it and cite the sources the reasoning relies upon
questions.why: Assistance with drafting is legitimate, and what makes advice advice is a qualified person taking responsibility for it.
questions.traps: A disclaimer does not change how the client will use it, declining refuses work that is properly assisted, and citations improve a draft without supplying the responsibility.

questions.stem: Two clients of the same firm are competitors, and one associate works on both accounts.
options: Keep each client's material in its own separate Project
Use one Project and take care not to mix the two clients
Use one Project, since the associate knows both accounts anyway
Use one Project and remove each client's files after the work
questions.why: Separate Projects make cross-contamination structurally impossible rather than dependent on care at every step.
questions.traps: Care is exactly what fails under pressure, personal knowledge is not the risk being managed, and deleting afterwards does not prevent mixing during the work.

questions.stem: A team's report includes a figure that Claude estimated because the real number was unavailable.
options: Remove the figure, since an estimate cannot be relied upon
Present it as a figure, since the report explains its method
Label the figure as an estimate and say how it was derived
Round the figure so that it clearly reads as an approximation
questions.why: An estimate is usable when a reader can see that it is one and judge the basis, which is what the label and the method provide.
questions.traps: Removing a useful estimate loses information, a method section elsewhere does not travel with the number, and rounding signals imprecision without disclosing the source.

questions.stem: An associate uses Claude to generate a product name and asks whether the name can be used.
options: Use it, since the name was generated rather than copied
Check whether the name is already in use before adopting it
Use it, since generated names cannot infringe existing marks
Use it and register it immediately to establish a claim
questions.why: A generated name can coincide with an existing mark, and the search is what establishes whether it is free to use.
questions.traps: Generation is not evidence of novelty, generated output has no immunity from prior rights, and registering before checking creates the conflict rather than avoiding it.

questions.stem: A team asks whether checking a model's outputs for bias once at setup is enough.
options: Yes — the model's behaviour does not change after setup
Yes — provided the check covered a large enough sample
No — but only if the model itself is later replaced
No — the inputs and the uses both change over time
questions.why: Bias shows up in the combination of model, inputs and use, and the last two keep changing after the check is done.
questions.traps: The surrounding system changes even where the model does not, sample size does not extend a check forward in time, and a model swap is one trigger among several.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether removing names is enough to make a customer dataset non-personal.
options: No — other fields can still identify a person in combination
Yes — a record without a name cannot identify anybody
Yes — provided no identification number is present either
No — but only where the dataset is small enough to search
questions.why: Identifiability comes from the combination of fields, so removing the name leaves postcode, date and role still pointing at someone.
questions.traps: Namelessness is not anonymity, removing ID numbers addresses one route among many, and small datasets are easier to re-identify but not the only ones.

questions.stem: A team wants a record of how a Claude-assisted decision was reached, for a later audit.
options: Record the conversation in full so nothing is left out
Record the final decision, since that is what was acted on
Record the inputs, the output and who approved it
Record the prompt, since it determined what came back
questions.why: An audit needs to see what went in, what came out and who took responsibility, which is what makes the decision reconstructible.
questions.traps: A full transcript buries the accountable facts, the decision alone loses its basis, and the prompt alone omits both the output and the approval.

questions.stem: A document is classified as internal and contains one paragraph of health information about an employee.
options: Handle it as internal, since that is its stated classification
Handle the document at the level the health paragraph requires
Handle it as internal but avoid quoting that paragraph
Remove the paragraph so the internal classification holds
questions.why: A document's handling follows its most sensitive content, which is what the single health paragraph sets here.
questions.traps: A stale classification does not describe the content, avoiding quotation does not change the processing, and deleting the paragraph destroys content to preserve a label.

questions.stem: A medical team wants Claude to draft patient letters explaining results a clinician has already interpreted.
options: Draft them, with the clinician reviewing before they are sent
Decline, since patient communication about results is clinical
Draft them and send those the clinician has pre-approved in form
Draft them and let the patient raise anything unclear afterwards
questions.why: The clinical judgement has been made and the letter communicates it, so drafting is assistance while the review keeps the clinician answerable for what reaches the patient.
questions.traps: Declining refuses legitimate assistance, template pre-approval does not cover what each letter says, and relying on the patient to catch problems moves the check to the wrong party.

questions.stem: A team removes gender from their applicant data and the shortlist's composition does not change.
options: Conclude the process is fair, since gender is no longer used
Remove more fields until the composition begins to change
Conclude the pattern simply reflects the applicant pool as it is
Look for fields that stand in for the one that was removed
questions.why: An unchanged outcome after removing a field suggests other fields carry the same information, and finding them is what tests the process.
questions.traps: Absence of the field is not absence of the signal, removing fields until the numbers move engineers an outcome, and a pool explanation is possible but untested.

questions.stem: An associate follows their team's approved prompt exactly and the output is wrong in a way nobody anticipated.
options: The associate is blameless, since the approved prompt was followed
The team revises the prompt and the associate stays answerable for sending
The team is at fault, since it approved the prompt in question
Nobody is at fault, since the failure could not be anticipated
questions.why: Following an approved process does not remove the duty to check what goes out, and an unanticipated failure is information the process should absorb.
questions.traps: Compliance with a process is not verification, blaming the approvers ignores the sender's check, and treating novelty as an excuse leaves the failure unaddressed.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to summarise a competitor's publicly posted product documentation.
options: Summarise it, since the documentation was published openly
Decline, since competitor material should not be processed
Summarise it only with the competitor's written permission
Summarise it but keep the summary out of any shared document
questions.why: Public documentation is published to be read, and summarising it to understand a market is ordinary competitive research.
questions.traps: A blanket refusal treats public material as off-limits, permission is not needed to read what was published, and restricting circulation manages a risk that is not present.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use a past client engagement as an example when drafting a proposal for a new client.
options: Use it with the client's name and identifying details removed
Use it, since the work belongs to the associate's own firm
Use it only in the form the client has agreed may be shared
Use it and inform the previous client after the proposal goes out
questions.why: What may be said about an engagement is set by the client agreement, and anonymisation does not by itself satisfy a confidentiality term.
questions.traps: Removing the name often leaves the engagement recognisable, firm ownership of the work product does not cover the client's information, and notice after circulation comes too late.

questions.stem: A team is asked to delete a customer's data and finds some of it inside past Claude conversations.
options: Delete the primary records, since conversations are working notes
Keep the conversations, since they document the work performed
Keep them but note that the customer has requested deletion
Delete the conversations along with the other copies of the data
questions.why: A deletion request covers the personal data wherever it is held, and a conversation containing it is one of the places it is held.
questions.traps: A working-notes distinction has no basis in the request, a work record is not an exemption, and annotating the data leaves it in place.

questions.stem: A team asks whether every internal email drafted with Claude needs to say that it was.
options: Yes — every use should be disclosed as a matter of policy
No — internal communications are outside disclosure entirely
No — routine internal drafting does not change how it is read
Yes — unless the sender has substantially rewritten the draft
questions.why: Disclosure matters where the method would change how someone weighs the content, and routine internal drafting does not meet that bar.
questions.traps: Universal disclosure buries the cases that matter, an internal exemption is too broad for consequential internal documents, and a rewriting threshold makes the test about effort rather than the reader.

questions.stem: A designer uses Claude to develop a tagline and the final line is largely their own edit.
options: Treat it as their work, since the final expression is theirs
Treat it as unattributable, since a tool contributed to it
Credit the tool alongside the designer for the final line
Treat it as the tool's output, since it produced the first draft
questions.why: Authorship follows the creative choices in the final expression, and substantial editing means those choices are the designer's.
questions.traps: Tool involvement does not void authorship, crediting a tool misstates what a byline means, and a first draft does not determine ownership of the final line.

questions.stem: A team wants to reuse a dataset collected for one purpose in a second, unrelated analysis.
options: Reuse it, since the data is already held by the organisation
Check whether the original basis for collection covers the new use
Reuse it with the personal identifiers stripped out first
Collect the data again specifically for the second analysis
questions.why: Data collected for one purpose is not automatically available for another, and the collection basis is what determines whether the new use sits inside it.
questions.traps: Possession is not permission, stripping identifiers helps but does not answer the purpose question, and re-collecting is disproportionate before the basis has been checked.

questions.stem: A school wants Claude to help identify students who may need additional academic support.
options: Use it to make the identification, since teachers lack the time
Decline, since decisions about students should not be assisted
Use it and confirm each identification with the student's parents
Use it to surface candidates that teachers then assess themselves
questions.why: Surfacing candidates is assistance and assessing them is judgement about a child, and keeping the second with teachers is what makes the use safe.
questions.traps: Time pressure does not justify delegating the judgement, a blanket refusal loses genuine help, and parental confirmation is not a substitute for professional assessment.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to write a Claude-drafted statement to be published under the chief executive's name.
options: Decline, since the words would not be the executive's own
Write it for the executive to approve and issue as their own
Write it but have it labelled as assisted in the publication
Write it only if the executive dictates the substance first
questions.why: A statement under an executive's name asserts their position rather than their authorship, and their approval is what makes the position theirs.
questions.traps: Personal authorship is not what such a statement claims, an assisted label misreads a long-standing convention, and dictation is one route to approval rather than a requirement.

questions.stem: A Claude-assisted process has produced correct results for eight months and nobody checks the outputs any more.
options: Continue without checks, since the record justifies the trust
Reintroduce checks on every output as was originally required
Reintroduce checks on a sample rather than on every output
Replace the checks with a review whenever someone complains
questions.why: A good record justifies reducing the check rather than dropping it, and sampling is what keeps a failure detectable at proportionate cost.
questions.traps: A clean record is evidence the checks worked rather than that they are unneeded, full checking ignores what the record shows, and complaint-driven review detects failures only after they land.

questions.stem: A team wants to know what "human in the loop" means in practice for their reporting work.
options: A person is available to answer questions about the output
A person wrote the prompt that produced the output
A person is named as the owner of the process overall
A person reviews the output before anything is acted upon
questions.why: The loop is the point at which a person's judgement can change what happens, which is the review before action.
questions.traps: Availability, prompt authorship and named ownership all describe people near the process rather than inside the decision.

questions.stem: An associate is about to paste a colleague's draft resignation letter into a conversation for editing.
options: Ask the colleague before using material about their employment
Proceed, since the associate was given the letter to help with
Proceed with the colleague's name removed from the letter
Proceed and delete the conversation once the editing is done
questions.why: The letter is the colleague's private employment matter, and their permission is what makes using it appropriate.
questions.traps: Being handed a document is not consent to process it elsewhere, a resignation letter identifies its author by content, and deletion afterwards does not create the permission.

questions.stem: A team asks how long they should keep conversations that contain customer data.
options: Indefinitely, since the conversations may be useful later
Until the customer relationship comes to an end
For a fixed period applied to all conversations equally
Only as long as the purpose that justified holding it requires
questions.why: Retention is bounded by the purpose that justified holding the data, which is what makes the period defensible.
questions.traps: Possible future usefulness is not a purpose, the relationship's end is unrelated to why the data was collected, and a uniform period ignores what each conversation was for.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to help draft a policy on how their own team may use it.
options: Not legitimate, since a tool should not shape the rules about itself
A legitimate use, since the policy is the team's own decision
Legitimate only if a compliance team writes the first draft
Not legitimate, since writing policy requires legal training
questions.why: Drafting assistance is ordinary work, and the team retains the decision about what the policy actually says.
questions.traps: Drafting is not deciding, a compliance first draft is a preference rather than a requirement, and policy drafting is not restricted to lawyers.

questions.stem: A team's support assistant gives an answer it is not confident about and states it as fact.
options: Have it decline to answer whenever its confidence is low
Have it add a general disclaimer to every answer it gives
Have it state plainly where the answer is uncertain
Have it give the answer and route the user to a person
questions.why: Telling the user where the answer is shaky lets them judge how far to rely on it, which is what the false confidence removed.
questions.traps: Refusing on low confidence loses useful partial answers, a blanket disclaimer carries no information about this answer, and routing to a person is heavier than the case needs.

questions.stem: An associate asks where bias in a Claude-assisted process most often originates.
options: In the data and the criteria the process is built around
In the model's wording choices when it writes an answer
In the individual user's intentions when they prompt it
In the number of examples supplied within the prompt
questions.why: A process inherits the skew in what it is given and what it is told to optimise, which is where most unfair outcomes begin.
questions.traps: Wording is a symptom, individual intent explains few systematic patterns, and example count affects quality rather than fairness.

questions.stem: A team asks whether anonymised data still needs handling controls of any kind.
options: No — anonymised data carries no meaningful risk at all
Yes — but only where the original data was regulated
Yes — re-identification and misuse are both still possible
No — provided the anonymisation was done carefully
questions.why: Anonymisation lowers risk without eliminating it, since combinations of fields and downstream uses can still cause harm.
questions.traps: Zero risk overstates what anonymisation achieves, the original regulatory status does not bound the residual risk, and care in the method does not make re-identification impossible.

questions.stem: A landlord wants to use Claude to decide which tenancy applications to accept.
options: Not appropriate — a housing decision needs human judgement
Appropriate if the criteria are applied to every applicant
Appropriate if unsuccessful applicants are given reasons
Appropriate if the landlord reviews a sample of decisions
questions.why: A tenancy decision materially affects someone's housing, which places it among the decisions a person must make.
questions.traps: Consistent criteria, stated reasons and sampled review all improve a process without putting a person into each decision.

questions.stem: An associate wants to translate another organisation's published article and post it on their company blog.
options: Translate it, since a translation is a new piece of writing
Translate it and credit the original author underneath it
Translate it for internal use rather than for publication
Check the article's licence before translating and publishing it
questions.why: Translation is a use of the original work, so what the licence permits determines whether it may be made and circulated.
questions.traps: A translation derives from the original, credit does not grant permission, and an internal audience answers a question that was not asked.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to keep evidence of how a Claude-assisted report was checked.
options: Note that the report was checked before it was issued
Note what was verified, by whom, and against what source
Save the conversation the report was generated from
Note the date on which the report was finally approved
questions.why: Evidence of a check has to say what was tested and against what, since that is what another person would need to repeat it.
questions.traps: A bare assertion of checking is not evidence, the generating conversation shows production rather than verification, and a date records timing only.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for help writing a complaint about a colleague to human resources.
options: Not legitimate, since it concerns a named colleague
Legitimate only if the colleague is told it was assisted
A legitimate use, since it is the associate's own complaint
Not legitimate, since HR matters should not be assisted
questions.why: Help with writing your own account of a workplace matter is ordinary drafting assistance.
questions.traps: Naming someone in your own complaint is unavoidable, disclosure to the subject is not required for a draft, and HR processes are not off-limits to drafting help.

questions.stem: A team asks whether they may discuss an unannounced product with Claude.
options: Yes, since the conversation is not a public disclosure
No, since unannounced products can never be discussed
Yes, provided the product's own name is not mentioned
Follow whatever their organisation's rules say about it
questions.why: Whether internal confidential material may go into a tool is set by the organisation's policy on that tool.
questions.traps: Non-publication is not the test, a blanket prohibition ignores that many organisations permit it, and omitting the name leaves the substance.

questions.stem: An associate receives a customer email containing personal details and wants help drafting a reply.
options: Include only the details the reply itself actually needs
Include the whole email so the context is complete
Include the whole email and then delete it afterwards
Include none of the email and describe it in general terms
questions.why: Using the minimum personal data needed for the task is what keeps the processing proportionate to the reply being written.
questions.traps: Full context includes details the reply does not use, deletion afterwards does not reduce what was processed, and describing everything second-hand loses accuracy for no privacy gain.

questions.stem: A Claude-assisted process fails and each person involved points at a different part of it.
options: Split responsibility across the people who touched it
Name a single owner for the process from end to end
Assign responsibility to whoever made the final change
Treat the failure as systemic rather than anybody's fault
questions.why: Diffuse responsibility is what allowed the gaps, and a single named owner is what makes the whole path answerable.
questions.traps: Splitting responsibility recreates the diffusion, the last person to touch it may not be the cause, and a systemic framing describes the problem without fixing the ownership.

questions.stem: A customer service team finds Claude's answers are consistently longer for some enquiry types than others.
options: Standardise the answer length across all enquiry types
Treat the difference as bias and adjust the prompt for it
Check whether the enquiry types genuinely differ in complexity
Ignore it, since answer length does not affect fairness
questions.why: A difference is only unfair if it is unwarranted, and comparing it against the complexity of each enquiry is what settles that.
questions.traps: Standardising hides the difference, calling it bias assumes what needs testing, and dismissing length ignores that service quality can vary with it.

questions.stem: An associate must send a document to Claude and one of its sections holds sensitive material.
options: Send the whole document, since the task concerns all of it
Send the whole document with the sensitive section redacted
Send a summary of the document rather than the document
Send the sections the task needs and hold back the rest
questions.why: Sending only what the task requires limits the exposure without weakening the work on the parts that matter.
questions.traps: Whole-document sending processes more than is needed, redaction still transmits the surrounding material and can be incomplete, and a summary loses the detail the task depends on.

questions.stem: A team asks whether they need a record of what personal data goes into Claude.
options: Yes — a record is what makes the processing accountable
No — the conversations themselves serve as the record
Yes — but only for data belonging to EU residents
No — records apply to storage rather than to processing
questions.why: Being able to say what personal data is processed and why is the basis of accountability, and that requires a record kept deliberately.
questions.traps: Conversations are the processing rather than a record of it, residency narrows a duty that is broader, and processing is exactly what records cover.

questions.stem: An insurer wants Claude to summarise claim files for the adjuster who decides them.
options: Not appropriate, since claims decisions affect policyholders
Appropriate, since the adjuster still makes the decision
Appropriate only if the summary is checked line by line
Not appropriate, since a summary can omit a material fact
questions.why: Summarising for a decider is assistance, and the adjuster's judgement is what keeps the consequential decision with a person.
questions.traps: Consequence rules out delegation rather than assistance, line-by-line checking defeats the point of a summary, and omission risk is managed by the adjuster's access to the file.

questions.stem: A team publishes a customer FAQ and one answer was drafted by Claude and then heavily edited.
options: Disclose it, since a tool contributed to that answer
Disclose it only for the answers that were not edited
No separate disclosure — the organisation publishes it as its own
Disclose the use of assistance across the FAQ as a whole
questions.why: An organisation publishing its own FAQ speaks in its own voice, and how it drafted its own words is not information a reader needs.
questions.traps: Tool involvement alone does not create a disclosure duty, an editing threshold makes the test about effort, and a page-level notice adds noise without informing a decision.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for a summary of a paywalled report their firm has legitimate access to.
options: Fine, since the firm has paid for access to the report
Not fine, since paywalled content cannot be processed
Fine, provided the summary is not shared with anyone
Fine for their own use, subject to the licence terms
questions.why: Access is granted on terms, and those terms are what determine what may be done with the content beyond reading it.
questions.traps: Payment does not define the permitted uses, a blanket prohibition ignores licences that permit this, and non-sharing addresses one term among several.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to write a reference for a former colleague they barely worked with.
options: Write it only if they can personally vouch for what it says
Write it, since the colleague asked them to do so
Write it from the colleague's own description of their work
Decline, since references should not be drafted with assistance
questions.why: A reference asserts the writer's own assessment, so the limit is what they can honestly attest rather than how it was drafted.
questions.traps: A request does not supply knowledge, writing from the subject's own account makes them the source of their own reference, and drafting assistance is not what makes a reference improper.

questions.stem: An associate's Project contains client material and they want a colleague to help with the work.
options: Share the Project, since the colleague is on the same team
Confirm the colleague is cleared for that client before sharing
Share the Project with the client's files temporarily removed
Send the colleague the answers rather than the Project itself
questions.why: Access to client material follows entitlement rather than proximity, and confirming it is what makes the sharing proper.
questions.traps: Team membership is not clearance, removing the files defeats the help being sought, and forwarding answers passes the same material along another route.

questions.stem: A team asks how much of their Claude-assisted work needs review before it is used.
options: In proportion to the consequences if it turned out wrong
All of it, since any output at all can contain an error
None of it, provided the prompt was carefully written
A fixed proportion of outputs sampled at random each week
questions.why: Review is a cost paid against risk, so its depth should follow what a mistake in that piece of work would actually cost.
questions.traps: Reviewing everything equally spends most effort where it matters least, prompt quality does not remove output risk, and a fixed random sample ignores which work is consequential.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted screening consistently favours candidates from a small set of universities.
options: Remove the university field from the data entirely
Weight candidates from other universities more heavily
Accept it, since those universities are genuinely selective
Ask whether the university is doing work the criteria should do
questions.why: The question is whether the institution is standing in for the skills that actually matter, and asking it is what separates a proxy from a signal.
questions.traps: Removing the field can leave proxies behind, reweighting corrects the count without examining the criteria, and selectivity is an assumption rather than a finding.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether a spreadsheet is sensitive and their team has no classification scheme.
options: Treat it as sensitive, since its status is unknown
Judge it by what harm its exposure would actually cause
Treat it as not sensitive, since nothing marks it as such
Ask a manager to classify it before doing anything at all
questions.why: Without a scheme the underlying test still applies, and the consequence of exposure is what that test measures.
questions.traps: Defaulting to sensitive stalls ordinary work, defaulting to open ignores the content, and escalating every unclassified file is disproportionate.

questions.stem: A customer asks what happens to the information they give a company's Claude-assisted support agent.
options: Tell them it is processed securely and is not shared
Direct them to the company's general privacy policy
Tell them how it is used and how long it is kept
Tell them the conversation is deleted after it ends
questions.why: A person asking about their own data is owed the specifics of use and retention, which is what lets them decide what to share.
questions.traps: A security assurance answers a different question, a general policy makes them find the answer themselves, and an unverified deletion claim risks being untrue.

questions.stem: A team asks whether their Claude-assisted process needs its own risk assessment or is covered by the department's.
options: It is covered, since the department's assessment covers the work
It needs one where the assistance changes what can go wrong
It needs one, since every use of a new tool requires its own
It is covered, provided the outputs are reviewed by a person
questions.why: A risk assessment tracks failure modes, so a new one is needed exactly where the assistance introduces failures the old one did not consider.
questions.traps: Coverage of the work is not coverage of the new failures, a blanket new-tool rule ignores uses that change nothing, and human review manages risk rather than identifying it.

questions.stem: A manager uses Claude to draft performance review text and edits it before the conversation with the employee.
options: Not acceptable, since performance assessment affects a person's job
Acceptable only if the employee is told the draft was assisted
Not acceptable, since the wording shapes how the review lands
Acceptable, since the assessment and the conversation are the manager's
questions.why: The judgement being communicated is the manager's own, and drafting help with expressing it does not move the decision anywhere.
questions.traps: Consequence rules out delegating the judgement rather than the drafting, disclosure of drafting method is not owed here, and wording influence is why the manager edits it.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to write copy claiming a product is "clinically proven" when no trial exists.
options: Decline the claim and offer copy describing what the product does
Decline the whole task, since the brief is asking for a falsehood
Write it with "clinically" removed so that only "proven" remains
Write it and flag the claim for the legal team to check
questions.why: The false claim is the problem rather than the copywriting, so removing the claim while doing the legitimate work is the proportionate response.
questions.traps: Refusing everything abandons work that is perfectly proper, weakening the wording keeps an unsupported claim, and passing it to legal delegates a judgement already clear.

questions.stem: A team's fairness check shows equal accuracy across groups but very different error types between them.
options: Accept it, since accuracy is equal across the two groups
Adjust the model until the error types also match up
Investigate, since equal accuracy can still hide unequal harm
Report the accuracy figure and note the difference
questions.why: A false positive and a false negative can cost a person very different things, so equal accuracy with different error mixes still distributes harm unevenly.
questions.traps: Equal accuracy is one measure among several, forcing error types to match assumes they should be, and reporting the difference stops short of examining it.

questions.stem: An associate learns confidential information in a meeting and later asks Claude a general question in that area.
options: Not fine, since their question is informed by what they learned
Fine, since a general question cannot disclose anything specific
Not fine until the information has been publicly announced
Fine, as long as the question does not carry the confidential detail
questions.why: Confidentiality restricts the information rather than the person's curiosity, so the test is what the question actually contains.
questions.traps: Being informed by knowledge is not disclosing it, general questions can still smuggle specifics, and waiting for an announcement is stricter than confidentiality requires.

questions.stem: A team operating in several countries asks which privacy rules apply to their use of Claude.
options: The rules covering the people whose data it is, wherever they are
The rules of the country in which the team is based
The strictest rules among all of the countries involved
The rules of the country in which the data is stored
questions.why: Data protection regimes generally attach to the individuals concerned, so the people the data is about determine which rules are engaged.
questions.traps: The team's location is one factor rather than the test, defaulting to the strictest is a policy choice rather than the legal position, and storage location does not decide whose rules apply.

questions.stem: A journalist asks a company whether an article on its site was written with AI assistance.
options: Decline, since drafting methods are internal matters
Answer the question truthfully as it was actually asked
Answer only if the article's accuracy is being questioned
Answer with a general statement about the company's practice
questions.why: A direct question from someone who will report the answer is answered directly, and evasion becomes the story instead.
questions.traps: Internal-matter framing invites the inference it is avoiding, conditioning on accuracy answers a question that was not asked, and a general statement dodges the specific article.

questions.stem: A team encrypts a file before sending it and asks whether that resolves the sensitivity question.
options: Yes — encrypted data cannot be read by anyone else
No — but only where the encryption strength is inadequate
No — it protects transit rather than what the use itself exposes
Yes — provided the key is held only by the recipient
questions.why: Encryption protects data on the way and at rest, while the question here is what the recipient is then permitted and able to do with it.
questions.traps: Unreadability in transit is not the exposure at issue, encryption strength is a different concern, and key custody addresses access rather than use.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-drafted marketing copy turns out to closely resemble a competitor's published tagline.
options: Use it, since it was generated rather than copied deliberately
Use it with a small alteration so the wording is not identical
Ask the competitor whether they object before publishing it
Change it, since the resemblance matters rather than how it arose
questions.why: A confusingly similar line creates the same problem whether it was copied or arrived at independently, so the resemblance itself is what has to go.
questions.traps: Intent does not cure similarity, minor alterations often leave the resemblance intact, and asking a competitor invites the dispute rather than avoiding it.

questions.stem: A charity wants Claude to help prioritise which applicants receive its limited emergency grants.
options: Use it to rank applicants, since the panel confirms the ranking
Decline, since need cannot be assessed with any tool at all
Use it to organise the applications and let a panel decide
Use it to reject the clearly ineligible and rank the remainder
questions.why: Organising the material helps the panel see it, while ranking by need is the judgement the panel exists to make.
questions.traps: Confirming a ranking anchors the panel to it, refusing all help wastes capacity that could reach more applicants, and screening plus ranking is the same delegation in two steps.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to analyse employee messages for signs of low morale.
options: Proceed, since the purpose is to improve employee wellbeing
Raise it, since monitoring private messages needs a separate basis
Proceed with the employees' names removed from the messages
Decline, since employee communications may never be analysed
questions.why: Reading employees' messages is surveillance whatever the motive, and whether it is permitted is a question for the organisation rather than the associate.
questions.traps: A benign purpose does not create the authority, anonymisation does not address the surveillance itself, and a flat refusal skips a question the organisation may have answered.

questions.stem: An external auditor asks a team to demonstrate that a Claude-assisted report was independently verified.
options: Show the source records the figures were actually checked against
Show the conversation in which the report was produced
Show the sign-off recording who approved the report
Show the prompt and instructions the team used for it
questions.why: Verification is demonstrated by the sources a figure was checked against, since that is what an auditor can independently re-test.
questions.traps: The generating conversation shows production, a sign-off records approval rather than checking, and the prompt shows intent rather than evidence.

questions.stem: A user tries to get Claude to bypass its safety guidelines by framing the request as fiction.
options: Comply, since a fictional framing removes the real-world risk
Comply, since the user is responsible for how they use the output
Refuse — the framing does not change the underlying request
Refuse only if the fictional scenario is unusually detailed
questions.why: What matters is what the output would enable, and wrapping a request in a story does not alter that.
questions.traps: Fiction does not neutralise instructions that work in reality, downstream responsibility does not license production, and detail is not what makes the request a problem.

questions.stem: An associate notices their team is using Claude in a way the organisation's policy prohibits.
options: Say nothing, since the team is more senior than they are
Raise it with the team and escalate if it continues
Stop using it themselves and leave the team to decide
Report it externally before raising it internally at all
questions.why: A policy breach is raised where it can be fixed, and escalation is what follows if raising it does not work.
questions.traps: Seniority does not remove the obligation, personal abstention leaves the breach running, and going outside first skips the internal route.

questions.stem: A team asks whether their prompts could reveal something sensitive even without pasting any data.
options: Yes — a question can disclose plans or problems by itself
No — only pasted documents can disclose anything at all
Yes — but only where names appear inside the question
No — questions are too short to carry sensitive content
questions.why: A question reveals what someone is working on, which can be as sensitive as the material behind it.
questions.traps: Disclosure is not limited to attachments, names are one form of sensitive content among many, and brevity has nothing to do with sensitivity.

questions.stem: A team asks whether their published policy should say which model they use.
options: Yes, since users deserve to know all technical details
No, since model choice is a purely internal decision
Yes, since naming the model establishes credibility
Only where the choice affects what readers rely on
questions.why: Transparency serves a reader's ability to judge, so a detail is worth publishing when it changes that judgement.
questions.traps: Exhaustive technical disclosure is not what transparency means, treating it as purely internal ignores cases where it matters, and using a name for credibility is marketing.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether telling Claude to "be unbiased" removes bias from an output.
options: No — the instruction does not change the underlying data
Yes — the instruction directs the model away from bias
No — but it helps where the topic is politically charged
Yes — provided the instruction is placed at the start
questions.why: Bias enters through the material and the criteria, and an instruction cannot see or correct either of them.
questions.traps: An instruction expresses intent rather than capability, topical charge is not where most process bias lives, and placement affects attention rather than the source.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether they need a lawful basis to process personal data with Claude.
options: No — the basis covers the original collection only
Yes — but only when the data leaves the organisation
Yes — the tool does not change the processing rules
No — using a tool is not a separate processing operation
questions.why: Using a tool on personal data is processing, and processing needs a basis regardless of which tool performs it.
questions.traps: A collection basis does not cover every later use, the organisational boundary is not what triggers the requirement, and tool use is exactly a processing operation.

questions.stem: A team asks whether output produced with Claude can be used commercially.
options: No — generated content cannot be commercially exploited
Yes — subject to the terms of use and to the law
Yes — without any conditions attached to the use
No — unless a person substantially rewrites it first
questions.why: Commercial use is permitted within the applicable terms, and those terms plus ordinary law are what bound it.
questions.traps: A blanket prohibition is wrong, unconditional use ignores the terms, and a rewriting threshold is not what governs commercial use.

questions.stem: A team asks what makes a decision "consequential" for the purposes of human oversight.
options: The number of people the decision applies to overall
The cost to the organisation if the decision is wrong
The amount of time the decision takes to be made
The size of the effect on the person it lands on
questions.why: Oversight rules exist to protect the person affected, so the weight of the effect on them is what triggers them.
questions.traps: Scale and organisational cost can both be low while the effect on one person is severe, and the time taken is unrelated to consequence.

questions.stem: An associate wants to check a Claude answer with a colleague who is outside the project.
options: Ask the question without the project's details in it
Share the full answer, since a colleague is internal
Share the answer with the project's name removed
Do not ask anyone outside the project for any help
questions.why: A colleague can help with the general point without receiving the project's confidential specifics.
questions.traps: Internal status is not entitlement, removing a name leaves identifying substance, and refusing all outside help is stricter than the duty requires.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether Claude may be used to help with their own university coursework.
options: Yes, since the coursework is the associate's own work
No, since coursework must be produced entirely unassisted
Follow the institution's own rules on assisted work
Yes, provided the assistance is not mentioned to anyone
questions.why: Academic integrity rules are set by the institution, and those rules are what determine what assistance is permitted.
questions.traps: Ownership of the assignment does not set the rules, a blanket prohibition ignores institutions that permit it, and concealment is the opposite of what integrity requires.

questions.stem: A team asks what to do when they cannot verify part of a Claude-generated output.
options: Remove the unverified part before passing it on
Say what could not be verified when passing it on
Pass it on, since the rest of the output checked out
Verify it later and pass the whole output on now
questions.why: A reader can weigh an unverified claim if they are told it is unverified, which is what makes the output honest to pass on.
questions.traps: Removing it may drop something important, partial verification does not extend to the rest, and verifying afterwards leaves the reader unwarned in the meantime.

questions.stem: A team asks whether the same care applies to data about their own staff as to customer data.
options: No — internal data carries less risk than external data
Yes — but only for payroll and health information
No — employment consent covers processing of staff data
Yes — employees have the same interests in their data
questions.why: Employees are people whose data can harm them if exposed, which is the same basis on which customer data is protected.
questions.traps: Internal circulation does not reduce the harm, sensitivity is not confined to two categories, and employment does not carry blanket consent.

questions.stem: A customer asks a company for a copy of the personal data it holds about them.
options: Provide it, including data held in working systems
Provide only the data held in the main customer record
Provide it once the customer explains why they want it
Decline, since working files are not a formal record
questions.why: A subject access request reaches the personal data an organisation holds, not only the tidy copy in the main system.
questions.traps: Restricting to the main record omits data held elsewhere, a reason is not a precondition, and informality does not exempt data from the request.

questions.stem: A team asks whether their Claude use needs recording when the outputs are only internal drafts.
options: Record every use, since all of it may later be queried
Record it where the drafts feed decisions that matter
Record none of it, since drafts are not final outputs
Record it only if someone raises a concern about it
questions.why: A record earns its cost where the work influences something consequential, and internal drafts often do exactly that.
questions.traps: Recording everything is disproportionate, treating drafts as inconsequential ignores what they feed, and waiting for a concern means the record is missing when it is needed.

questions.stem: A user's request is legitimate but the wording resembles an attempt to extract restricted content.
options: Refuse, since the wording resembles a restricted request
Answer but omit the parts that seemed most sensitive
Ask the user to rephrase before answering anything at all
Answer the legitimate request as it was plainly meant
questions.why: Resemblance is not intent, and the legitimate reading is what should be answered when it is the plain one.
questions.traps: Refusing on resemblance denies ordinary help, arbitrary omission produces a worse answer, and demanding a rephrase penalises the user for wording.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted process performs noticeably worse for users writing in a second language.
options: Treat it as a language problem outside the fairness scope
Ask affected users to write in their strongest language
Treat it as a fairness problem and address the gap
Accept it, since no system performs equally for everyone
questions.why: A systematic disadvantage tied to who the user is falls squarely inside fairness, whatever mechanism produces it.
questions.traps: A technical framing does not remove the disparate effect, shifting the burden to users is not a fix, and universal imperfection does not excuse a patterned gap.

questions.stem: A benefits office wants Claude to draft the letters explaining decisions caseworkers have made.
options: Fine, since the decision was made before any drafting
Fine, provided the caseworker checks each letter
Not fine, since benefits decisions affect vulnerable people
Fine, provided a sample of the letters is checked weekly
questions.why: Drafting after a human decision is assistance, and checking each letter is what keeps the explanation faithful to the decision made.
questions.traps: A prior decision does not guarantee the letter describes it, vulnerability calls for care rather than refusal, and sampling leaves unchecked letters reaching claimants.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether a document's age reduces how carefully it has to be handled.
options: Yes — older material is less sensitive than current material
No — sensitivity never changes once it has been assigned
Yes — provided the document is more than a year old
Sometimes — it depends on what the content still exposes
questions.why: Some information decays in sensitivity and some does not, so the current exposure the content creates is what decides.
questions.traps: Age as a general rule is wrong, permanent classification ignores information that genuinely stops mattering, and a fixed threshold is arbitrary.

questions.stem: A contractor working for a company wants to use their own Claude account for the company's work.
options: Fine, since the contractor is doing the company's own work
Not fine, since contractors may not use assistance at all
Check the company's rules before using a personal account
Fine, provided the contractor deletes the work afterwards
questions.why: Where company material may be processed is the company's decision, and a personal account is a different place from a company one.
questions.traps: Doing the work does not settle where it may be done, a blanket ban on assistance is not the issue, and deletion afterwards does not address the account.

questions.stem: A team asks whether they can claim copyright in text that Claude produced for them.
options: It depends on the human contribution to the final text
Yes — the person who wrote the prompt holds the copyright
No — generated text can never attract copyright at all
Yes — copyright follows whoever publishes the text first
questions.why: Protection generally tracks human authorship, so how much of the final expression is a person's own choice is what matters.
questions.traps: Prompting alone is a weak claim to authorship, a flat denial ignores substantially edited work, and publication does not create authorship.

questions.stem: A team wants to send customer data to Claude and their privacy notice does not mention such tools.
options: Proceed, since the notice covers processing generally
Update the notice before the processing begins
Proceed and update the notice at the next review cycle
Proceed, since specific tools are not named in notices
questions.why: A privacy notice has to describe the processing that actually happens, so it is updated before the new processing rather than after it.
questions.traps: General wording does not cover a materially new use, deferring to a review cycle processes first and tells later, and notices routinely describe categories of recipient.

questions.stem: A team asks whether labelling a report "AI-generated" is enough disclosure on its own.
options: Only if a reader also knows what was and was not checked
Yes — the label tells the reader everything they need
No — the model and its version must always be named too
Yes — provided the label appears near the top of the page
questions.why: The label tells a reader how the text was produced, and what they actually need is whether its claims were verified.
questions.traps: The label alone leaves reliability unaddressed, naming the model adds detail without answering the question, and placement affects visibility rather than content.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to check a Claude-drafted policy for bias and does not know where to start.
options: Read it for wording that seems loaded or one-sided
Ask Claude to review its own draft for any bias in it
Ask who the policy affects and how it affects each group
Compare it against a policy from another organisation
questions.why: Bias in a policy lives in its effects on different groups, so mapping who it touches is what makes the review substantive.
questions.traps: Loaded wording is a surface symptom, self-review reproduces the same blind spots, and a comparison inherits another organisation's problems.

questions.stem: A Claude output cites a source and the associate cannot find that source anywhere.
options: Keep it, since the claim itself appears to be correct
Keep it and note that the source could not be located
Replace it with a source that supports the same claim
Remove the citation and verify the claim independently
questions.why: An unlocatable citation may be fabricated, so it comes out and the claim stands or falls on its own verification.
questions.traps: A plausible claim does not validate the citation, noting the failure publishes the problem rather than fixing it, and substituting a source retrofits evidence to a claim.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to help write a grant application describing their team's work.
options: Fine, since grant writing is a standard drafting task
Not fine, since applications must be written unaided
Fine, provided the application describes real work
Fine, provided the funder permits assisted applications
questions.why: The integrity question in a grant application is whether its claims are true, and drafting help does not affect that.
questions.traps: Calling it standard skips the accuracy point, an unaided requirement is not a general rule, and funder permission matters only where the funder has spoken.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to flag which customer complaints look most serious so staff can triage them.
options: Fine — staff still read and decide on each complaint
Fine — triage is administrative rather than a real decision
Not fine — a missed serious complaint could cause harm
Fine — provided the flagging is reviewed each quarter
questions.why: Ordering work for people who still make the decisions is assistance, and staff reading each complaint is what keeps it so.
questions.traps: Triage does affect outcomes, harm potential argues for oversight rather than refusal, and quarterly review does not cover today's complaints.

questions.stem: An associate is confident in a Claude output but cannot explain how it reached its conclusion.
options: Do not use it, since unexplained conclusions cannot be trusted
Verify the conclusion rather than the reasoning behind it
Ask the model to explain its reasoning and rely on that
Use it, since confidence after a review is what matters
questions.why: What can be checked is whether the conclusion is right against its sources, and a stated rationale is not evidence of how it was produced.
questions.traps: Refusing all unexplained output discards useful work, a generated explanation is another output rather than a trace, and confidence is not verification.

questions.stem: A team is asked to prove their Claude-assisted process is fair before it goes live.
options: Show that the model was not given any protected attributes
Show that outcomes are equal across the groups involved
Show that the process was reviewed by a diverse group
Define what fairness means here, then measure against it
questions.why: Fairness has several incompatible definitions, so naming which one the process claims is what makes any measurement meaningful.
questions.traps: Excluded attributes leave proxies behind, equal outcomes is one definition among several, and a diverse review is process rather than evidence.

questions.stem: A team wants to keep conversations for quality improvement and their retention rule says thirty days.
options: Keep them longer, since quality improvement is a valid purpose
Keep them longer and anonymise them after thirty days
Extend the rule deliberately or work within the thirty days
Keep them indefinitely, since the rule covers customer data only
questions.why: A retention rule is changed openly if a new purpose justifies it, rather than treated as flexible whenever a good reason appears.
questions.traps: A valid purpose does not override an existing rule silently, late anonymisation has already exceeded the period, and reinterpreting the rule's scope is the same evasion.

questions.stem: A hospital wants Claude to draft discharge summaries from clinical notes, which a doctor then signs.
options: Not acceptable, since discharge summaries are clinical records
Acceptable — the doctor's signature carries the judgement
Acceptable only where the doctor also wrote the original notes
Not acceptable, since a summary can omit a clinical detail
questions.why: The doctor reads and signs, which places the clinical judgement with a person while the drafting remains genuine assistance.
questions.traps: Record status does not bar assistance, common authorship of the notes is unrelated to the check, and omission risk is what the signing review addresses.

questions.stem: An associate finds a way to make Claude produce content it would normally decline.
options: Report it rather than use it or share the method
Use it, since the content itself is not harmful to anyone
Share the method internally so colleagues can avoid it
Ignore it, since one person's finding is not significant
questions.why: A bypass is a safety defect, and reporting it is what gets it fixed rather than propagated.
questions.traps: A harmless instance does not make the bypass harmless, internal sharing spreads the method, and dismissing it leaves the defect in place.

questions.stem: A team must decide whether an aggregated statistic derived from sensitive records is itself sensitive.
options: No — aggregation removes the sensitivity of the sources
Yes — anything derived from sensitive data stays sensitive
No — provided the aggregate covers more than ten records
It depends on whether the aggregate can single anyone out
questions.why: Aggregation reduces identifiability, and whether it removes it depends on whether small groups let an individual be inferred.
questions.traps: Aggregation is not automatically safe, inherited sensitivity would make all analysis impossible, and a fixed group size is a rule of thumb rather than the test.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to summarise a document that was sent to them by mistake.
options: Summarise it, since it was received legitimately enough
Tell the sender and do not use the document at all
Summarise it and delete the document straight afterwards
Summarise it but do not act on anything it contains
questions.why: A document received in error was never meant for them, and using it is the disclosure the mistake would otherwise not have caused.
questions.traps: Accidental receipt is not authorisation, deletion afterwards follows the use, and reading without acting is still the access that was not intended.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted report quotes three sentences from a competitor's white paper with attribution.
options: Fine — a short attributed quotation is ordinary use
Not fine, since the source is a competitor's own material
Not fine, since any quotation requires the owner's permission
Fine, provided the competitor is told about the quotation
questions.why: Short attributed quotation for commentary or analysis is a normal and permitted use regardless of who published the original.
questions.traps: Competitor authorship does not change the rules, permission is not needed for a short attributed quotation, and notification is a courtesy rather than a condition.

questions.stem: A team is asked to explain to customers how their Claude-assisted pricing actually works.
options: Publish the full formula so the process is entirely transparent
Decline, since pricing methodology is commercially sensitive
Explain the factors and who decides, without the internal formula
Explain that a model is used and that the prices are fair
questions.why: Customers need to understand what drives their price and who is accountable, which is achievable without publishing a commercially sensitive formula.
questions.traps: Full publication trades a legitimate interest for transparency customers do not need, a refusal leaves them unable to judge, and an assurance of fairness explains nothing.

questions.stem: Two teams share a Claude-assisted workflow and each assumes the other one checks the outputs.
options: Have both teams check everything so nothing is missed
Move the whole workflow into one team's ownership
Add an automated check so neither team has to do it
Write down which team checks what, and at which point
questions.why: The gap is an unstated assumption, and making the responsibility explicit is what closes it without adding work.
questions.traps: Duplicated checking wastes effort and still diffuses responsibility, restructuring teams is heavier than the problem requires, and an automated check does not replace the judgement.

questions.stem: A Claude-assisted process is fairer than the manual process it replaced but still shows a gap.
options: Adopt it, since it is an improvement on what came before
Revert to the manual process until the gap has closed
Keep improving it — the old process is not the standard
Adopt it and publish the comparison with the old process
questions.why: The benchmark is what the process should achieve rather than what it replaced, so an improvement is a step rather than a finish.
questions.traps: Relative improvement sets the bar at the old failure, reverting gives up a real gain, and publishing the comparison advertises the same relative standard.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether their organisation may use Claude to help write its regulatory submission.
options: No, since submissions to a regulator must be unassisted
Yes — the organisation still signs and stands behind it
Yes, provided the regulator is told assistance was used
No, unless the regulator has published rules permitting it
questions.why: A submission is the organisation's own statement, and drafting assistance does not change who is asserting it or who answers for it.
questions.traps: An unassisted requirement is not a general rule, unprompted disclosure is not usually required, and waiting for explicit permission inverts the default.

questions.stem: An associate pastes a client document into Claude and then realises the client's policy forbids it.
options: Report it under the organisation's incident process
Delete the conversation and say nothing about it
Note it privately in case it is asked about later
Continue, since no harm appears to have resulted
questions.why: A breach of a client's terms is an incident the organisation has to know about, since only it can decide what the client is told.
questions.traps: Quiet deletion conceals it, a private note leaves the organisation unaware, and the absence of visible harm is not the test.

questions.stem: A team wants an image generated in the style of a named living artist for a campaign.
options: Name the artist, since a style itself is not protected
Name the artist and credit them in the campaign
Name the artist but alter the output afterwards
Avoid naming the artist and brief the look they want
questions.why: Invoking a living artist's name to imitate them trades on their identity, and describing the desired look achieves the brief without doing that.
questions.traps: Style may not be protected but the association is still traded on, crediting does not create permission, and altering the output does not undo how it was produced.

questions.stem: A user asks a company's assistant whether it can see their previous conversations.
options: Answer accurately according to what it can actually do
Say it can, since that is what users generally expect
Say it cannot, since that is the safer thing to claim
Avoid the question and offer to help with the task
questions.why: A user's question about the system's capabilities deserves the true answer, since they will act on what they are told.
questions.traps: Expectation does not define capability, a reflexively cautious claim can be false, and deflection leaves them acting on a guess.

questions.stem: A team wants to test a new workflow and plans to use real customer records to do it.
options: Use real records, since the test must be realistic
Use real records from customers who have left
Use synthetic or masked records for the testing
Use real records but with a much smaller sample
questions.why: A test exercises the workflow rather than the identities, so records that behave like the real ones carry the same value without the exposure.
questions.traps: Realism is achievable without real people, former customers retain their data rights, and a smaller sample reduces the count rather than the kind of risk.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether a person's work email address counts as personal data.
options: No — it belongs to the employer rather than the person
Yes — it identifies a particular individual person
Yes — but only if their name appears within it
No — business contact details are outside the rules
questions.why: Personal data is information relating to an identifiable person, and a work address routinely points at one.
questions.traps: Employer ownership of the account does not change who it identifies, name format is one route to identification among several, and business context does not create an exemption.

questions.stem: A team asks whether simply including more data will make their Claude-assisted process fairer.
options: Yes — larger samples correct for individual outliers
Yes — provided the additional data is recent enough
No — sample size has no bearing on fairness at all
Not by itself — more of a skewed sample stays skewed
questions.why: Fairness depends on what the data represents, so adding more of the same imbalance leaves the imbalance in place.
questions.traps: Volume reduces noise rather than bias, recency addresses staleness rather than skew, and denying any link at all overstates the point.

questions.stem: Someone outside the team uses a Claude-assisted output for a decision the team knew nothing about.
options: The team that originally produced that output for itself
Whoever decided to act on the output in their own work
