questions.traps: Dismissing the observation discards a finding. Longer prompts and longer answers both keep the attention split.

questions.stem: A team wants reproducible results and is currently regenerating the output each time it is needed.
options: Regenerate each time and compare against the previous version
Accept the variation between the generated versions
Generate once, validate, and reuse the validated output
Average across several generations of the same output
questions.why: When the same output is needed repeatedly, generating once and reusing a validated result is both reproducible and cheaper than regenerating.
questions.traps: Comparing every regeneration is ongoing work for no gain. Accepting variation defeats the requirement, and averaging is not meaningful for text.

questions.stem: A team's prompt occasionally produces a response declining part of the request while completing the rest.
options: Look at which part is being declined and why
Regenerate the response so that a complete answer is produced
Split the request into parts and submit them separately
Remove the part of the request that is being declined
questions.why: Understanding which element triggers the decline is what determines whether the request should be reframed or reconsidered.
questions.traps: Regenerating hopes the decline does not recur. Splitting and removing both act before understanding what is being objected to.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt has grown because each addition seemed small at the time.
options: Remove the most recent additions, since those are the ones that pushed the prompt to its current length and are most likely to be the least necessary of them
Review the whole prompt against what the task needs
Move to a cheaper tier so the longer prompt costs less
Accept the current length as the cost of the additions
questions.why: Incremental growth is only visible against the task's actual requirements. Reviewing the whole prompt against those is what identifies what to cut.
questions.traps: Removing by recency assumes newer means less necessary. A cheaper tier pays less for the same bloat, and accepting it forgoes the saving.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good output that their reviewers consistently find unusable.
options: Improve the output quality further so that it meets the standard the reviewers are applying when they assess whether the material is usable for their purposes
Change the reviewers for people with different standards
Find out what the reviewers need that the output does not provide
Ask the reviewers to be rather less demanding
questions.why: Output judged unusable despite being good is missing something specific to the reviewers' need. Finding out what is the direct route.
questions.traps: Improving general quality without knowing the gap is undirected. Changing or pressuring reviewers avoids a legitimate requirement.

questions.stem: A prompt produces the right answer but always adds an unnecessary preamble.
options: Say that the response should begin with the answer and contain no preamble
Ask for shorter responses so that the preamble is compressed along with the rest of the content the model produces in reply to the request
Delete the preamble manually from each response produced
Ask the model to stop being conversational
questions.why: A specific unwanted element is removed by naming it and stating what should replace it. That is the direct instruction.
questions.traps: Shortening compresses the answer too. Manual deletion repeats forever, and a vague instruction about tone is less precise than naming the element.

questions.stem: A team's workflow supplies a document and a set of instructions, and the model follows the document's own instructions instead.
options: Shorten the document so that its own instructional content is less prominent within the material supplied alongside the actual task instructions
Remove the document so its instructions cannot be followed
Repeat the task instructions after the document as well
Make clear which text is the task and which is material to be worked on
questions.why: Documents containing instructions can be read as directives unless the boundary is marked. Making the distinction explicit is what resolves it.
questions.traps: Shortening reduces the surface without marking the boundary. Removing the document loses the material, and repetition competes rather than clarifies.

questions.stem: An associate's results changed after the model was updated and they had not been tracking versions.
options: Rebuild the prompt against the new version so that it is tuned for the current model
Start recording which version produced which results
Revert to the previous model version and stay there
Accept that updates change behaviour
questions.why: Recording versions is what makes future changes attributable. Without it, every update produces an unexplained shift.
questions.traps: Rebuilding may be needed but leaves the same blind spot. Reverting is temporary, and accepting change without tracking it forgoes the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A team wants to know why the model sometimes says it is uncertain and sometimes does not, on similar questions.
options: Ask the model to always state its confidence so that the signal is available consistently across every response the team receives from the workflow
Verify only the answers where uncertainty was expressed
Treat expressed uncertainty as informative when present and uninformative when absent
Ask the question in a consistent way each time
questions.why: Expressed uncertainty is asymmetric: present it means something, absent it means nothing. That asymmetry is the point.
questions.traps: Mandating a confidence statement does not create the missing knowledge. Verifying only flagged answers misses confident errors, and consistent phrasing does not change the asymmetry.

questions.stem: A team's workflow could be made cheaper, faster or more accurate, and they cannot have all three.
options: Improve all three incrementally so that the workflow gets somewhat better on each of the dimensions
Decide which constraint actually binds for this workload
Optimise for accuracy since correctness matters most here
Optimise for cost since the budget is under pressure
questions.why: Optimisation requires knowing which dimension is binding. Identifying that is what makes the trade-off deliberate.
questions.traps: Spreading effort across three dimensions improves none meaningfully. Choosing accuracy or cost by default ignores which one is actually constrained.

questions.stem: An associate has a theory about why their workflow fails and has not tested it.
options: Act on the theory, since it is the most plausible explanation available and testing would take time that could be spent implementing the fix instead
Ask a colleague whether the theory sounds right
Implement a fix that would work regardless of the cause
Test the theory before acting on it
questions.why: An untested theory is a hypothesis. Testing it is usually quick and prevents effort going into a fix for the wrong cause.
questions.traps: Acting untested risks fixing nothing. A colleague's view is opinion, and a cause-agnostic fix is usually a workaround rather than a resolution.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works reliably except when the input it receives is unusually short, where it fails.
options: Handle the short-input case explicitly
Add a general instruction about handling inputs of varying length
Reject short inputs so the failure cannot occur at all
Pad short inputs until they reach a workable length
questions.why: A failure tied to an identifiable input property is addressed by handling that property. The pattern points at the fix.
questions.traps: A general instruction has no specific target. Rejecting short inputs refuses valid work, and padding fabricates content.

questions.stem: An associate supplies a glossary with their prompt and the model still misuses two of the terms.
options: Supply the glossary again in a different format so that the definitions are presented more clearly than they are in the current version being used
Remove the glossary since it is not resolving the terms
Ask the model to confirm it has read the glossary
Check whether those two terms are defined clearly enough in the glossary
questions.why: Two specific terms failing while the rest work points at those definitions rather than at the glossary mechanism. Checking them is the direct step.
questions.traps: Reformatting addresses presentation rather than the definitions. Removing the glossary loses the rest, and a confirmation adds a round trip.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives one answer when run alone and a different one when run after other work in the same conversation.
options: Run it in a fresh context so prior conversation does not influence it
Ask the model to disregard the earlier conversation when it answers the question that the workflow puts to it during the course of the session
Accept the difference between the two ways of running it
Run it twice and compare the two sets of results
questions.why: Accumulated conversation is an input that changes the result. Isolating the workflow in a fresh context removes that influence.
questions.traps: An instruction to disregard context competes with the context itself. Accepting the difference abandons reproducibility, and comparing measures rather than removes it.

questions.stem: A team finds the model produces a shorter answer than requested when the topic is sensitive.
options: Ask again more forcefully for the full length that was originally specified in the request
Split the request into parts and submit each separately
Consider whether the topic warrants the caution before pressing for length
Move to a different tier that may respond more fully
questions.why: Reduced output on a sensitive topic often reflects a substantive judgement. Considering whether it is warranted comes before pressing past it.
questions.traps: Pressing, splitting and switching tiers are all attempts to get around a response rather than to understand it.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow costs little per run and runs far more often than anyone realised.
options: Reduce the cost per run so that the total falls in proportion to the saving achieved on each individual execution of the workflow
Look at the total, since frequency matters as much as unit cost
Accept the cost since each individual run is inexpensive
Move to a cheaper tier so the frequent runs cost less
questions.why: Total cost is unit cost times frequency, and an unnoticed frequency is the variable that has been overlooked. Examining the total is what reveals it.
questions.traps: Optimising unit cost ignores the frequency that caused the surprise. Accepting it forgoes the finding, and a cheaper tier is one lever chosen before understanding the driver.

questions.stem: A team's workflow began failing after a colleague made an undocumented change.
options: Rebuild the workflow so that its current state is understood by everyone
Revert everything to the last known working backup
Find out what changed, since the timing points directly at it
Add monitoring so future failures are detected sooner
questions.why: A change immediately preceding a failure is the obvious first suspect. Establishing what it was is the fastest route to the cause.
questions.traps: Rebuilding and reverting both act without knowing what changed. Monitoring watches for future problems rather than explaining this one.

questions.stem: A team's instruction to avoid jargon has made the output vague rather than accessible.
options: Ask for simpler language in addition to the existing instruction
Remove the jargon instruction so precision can return
Ask for definitions of any jargon used
Give a list of terms that remain acceptable so precision survives
questions.why: A blanket ban removes vocabulary without supplying replacements, so the model reaches for imprecision. An allowed list keeps the words that carry meaning.
questions.traps: Adding a simplicity instruction compounds the problem. Removing the instruction abandons the goal, and inline definitions are a different technique.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt includes an example that is now inconsistent with the current requirements.
options: Add an instruction explaining that the example is out of date and should not be followed exactly as it is written in the prompt
Update the example, since it demonstrates the pattern the model will follow
Remove all the examples so none of them can mislead
Add a newer example alongside the outdated one
questions.why: Examples demonstrate the target and are followed. An inconsistent one actively teaches the wrong pattern, so it has to be corrected.
questions.traps: A correction note competes with the demonstration. Removing all examples loses the technique, and a second example creates a conflict.

questions.stem: A team measured their workflow at 91% and again at 94% on the same fifty cases a month apart.
options: Treat the difference as within the noise of a fifty-case sample
Conclude that the workflow has improved and record the higher figure as the current level of performance the team can expect from it
Investigate what improved between the two measurements
Average the two figures and report the combined result
questions.why: A three-point difference on fifty cases is well within ordinary variation. Recognising that prevents acting on noise.
questions.traps: Recording the higher figure and investigating an improvement both treat noise as signal. Averaging produces a number without addressing the imprecision.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on the model doing something it does reliably today and may not always.
options: Document the dependency so that the team knows what the workflow relies on if problems arise at some point in the future with the behaviour it depends on
Accept the risk since the behaviour is reliable today
Design the workflow so a change in behaviour is detected rather than silent
Test the behaviour periodically to confirm it still holds
questions.why: A dependency on unguaranteed behaviour needs detection, so that a change surfaces as a clear failure rather than as degraded output nobody notices.
questions.traps: Documentation records without detecting. Accepting the risk leaves it silent, and periodic testing is a partial form of the right answer without continuous coverage.

questions.stem: An associate wants to cut cost and the only lever they have considered is the model tier.
options: Move to the cheapest tier that produces acceptable results for the workload
Look at the prompt, the output length and the call pattern as well
Accept the current cost as the price of the workflow
Reduce how much the team uses the workflow each month
questions.why: Cost is driven by tier, input size, output size and frequency. Considering only one lever leaves most of the available saving untouched.
questions.traps: Optimising tier alone is the narrow view being tested. Accepting the cost and cutting usage both forgo capability rather than waste.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good results that arrive too late to be useful.
options: Treat timeliness as part of the requirement rather than a separate concern
Improve the output quality further so that the results are more valuable when they do arrive and better justify the time taken to produce them
Accept the delay since the output quality is high
Reduce the scope so the workflow completes sooner
questions.why: Output that arrives after it is needed has failed regardless of quality. Recognising timeliness as part of the requirement is the reframing.
questions.traps: Improving quality optimises the wrong dimension. Accepting the delay leaves the output useless, and scope reduction is a remedy chosen before the reframing.

questions.stem: A team's prompt asks the model to be thorough and the output has become repetitive.
options: Ask for shorter output so that the repetition is reduced along with the overall length of the response the model produces
Ask for less thorough output to reduce the repetition
Remove the repetitive passages manually
Replace the vague instruction with a specific requirement about coverage
questions.why: Thoroughness without a defined target is satisfied by length, which produces repetition. Specifying what must be covered replaces volume with substance.
questions.traps: Shortening compresses the repetition rather than removing it. Asking for less abandons the goal, and manual editing repeats forever.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow supplies context that is correct but written for a different purpose.
options: Supply additional context explaining the current purpose
Rewrite the context around what this task actually needs
Remove the mismatched context from the prompt entirely
Ask more specific questions so the context matters less
questions.why: Context assembled for a different purpose emphasises the wrong things. Rewriting it around the current task is what makes it useful.
questions.traps: Layering explanation on mismatched material adds volume. Removing it loses the information, and specific questions work around the mismatch.

questions.stem: A team's outputs vary and they have never checked whether their inputs vary in the same way.
options: Add an instruction asking for consistent output so that the responses become more uniform across the different runs of the workflow
Accept the variation as inherent to generated output
Run each input several times and compare the results
Check the inputs first, since output variation often traces to input variation
questions.why: Input variation is the most common and most checkable explanation for output variation. Ruling it in or out comes first.
questions.traps: An instruction cannot make varied inputs produce uniform outputs. Accepting the variation skips the check, and repeated runs measure without explaining.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a limitation they have hit is about the task or about how they framed it.
options: Try the same framing again to see whether the limitation appears consistently across repeated attempts at the request they are making
Move to a stronger tier so the limitation is not hit
Try a materially different framing of the same task
Ask the model whether the limitation is about the framing
questions.why: Testing a different framing distinguishes a task limitation from a framing one, which determines whether a workaround exists.
questions.traps: Repeating the same framing tests stability rather than the hypothesis. A stronger tier changes a different variable, and self-report is unreliable.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow runs nightly and the results are read once a week.
options: Run it weekly, matching the schedule to how the output is used
Keep the nightly schedule so that the most recent results are always available
Move to a cheaper tier so the nightly runs cost less
Shorten the outputs so each nightly run costs less
questions.why: Six of seven runs produce output nobody reads. Matching the schedule to consumption removes the waste entirely.
questions.traps: Availability arguments justify six wasted runs. A cheaper tier and shorter outputs both reduce the cost of work that should not happen.

questions.stem: A team fixed a recurring problem in their workflow and the same problem returned three weeks later.
options: Apply the same fix again since it resolved the problem last time and can be expected to resolve it again on this occasion as well
Add monitoring so the next recurrence is noticed sooner
Escalate to a stronger tier so the problem stops recurring
Establish whether the original fix addressed the cause or a symptom
questions.why: Recurrence suggests the fix addressed a symptom. Establishing whether the cause was ever found is what breaks the cycle.
questions.traps: Reapplying a symptomatic fix guarantees another recurrence. Monitoring detects the next one, and a tier change is unrelated.

questions.stem: A team's prompt contains two instructions that pull in opposite directions and the output satisfies neither well.
options: Strengthen both instructions so that the model gives more weight to each of them when it produces its response to the request being made
Decide which takes priority and say so
Remove both of the conflicting instructions entirely
Alternate between the two instructions across runs
questions.why: A genuine conflict cannot be resolved by emphasis. Stating the priority is what lets the model trade them off deliberately.
questions.traps: Strengthening both intensifies the conflict. Removing both loses two real requirements, and alternating produces inconsistent behaviour.

questions.stem: An associate finds the model performs better when they describe the situation before asking the question.
options: Treat it as coincidence, since the order in which information appears in a prompt should not affect the quality of the answer that is produced
Describe the situation in rather more detail
Adopt it as a technique and apply it deliberately
Ask the question first and then describe the situation
questions.why: Establishing the situation before the question gives the model context to interpret it against, and an observed improvement is worth applying deliberately.
questions.traps: Dismissing the observation discards a working technique. More detail and reversed ordering both change the technique rather than adopting it.

questions.stem: A team's workflow behaves differently for two inputs that look identical to them.
options: Compare the two inputs precisely rather than by eye
Run both inputs several times to establish whether the difference is consistent or whether it is just ordinary variation between individual runs
Accept the difference between the two apparently identical inputs
Combine the two inputs so they are processed together
questions.why: Inputs that look identical often differ in whitespace, encoding or hidden characters. A precise comparison finds what inspection misses.
questions.traps: Repeated runs establish that the difference is real without explaining it. Accepting it abandons the diagnosis, and combining changes the task.

questions.stem: A team's request is partially completed with a note explaining why the rest was not.
options: Regenerate the request so that a complete response is produced
Read the explanation and decide whether the remaining part should be pursued
Split the request so each part is submitted on its own
Rephrase the part that was not completed
questions.why: The note explains the limitation, and reading it is what tells you whether the remainder is worth pursuing and how.
questions.traps: Regenerating and rephrasing both try to get past an explanation without reading it. Splitting acts before understanding the cause.

questions.stem: An associate has optimised their prompt heavily and further changes make no measurable difference.
options: Continue optimising the prompt since further improvements will eventually be found through additional refinement of the wording and structure
Revert to an earlier version of the optimised prompt
Move to a stronger tier so the plateau is pushed higher
Accept the plateau and look at other parts of the workflow
questions.why: A plateau signals that the remaining gains are elsewhere. Redirecting effort to other parts of the workflow is what makes further progress.
questions.traps: Continued refinement is the sunk-cost path. Reverting rediscovers the same ceiling, and a tier change is a spend chosen without evidence.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has three possible causes for a failure and testing each takes about an hour.
options: Test all three at once so that the answer is found in a single hour
Test them in the order they occur in the workflow
Test the cheapest and most likely cause first
Ask Claude which cause is most likely
questions.why: Ordering diagnostic tests by likelihood and cost is what minimises the expected time to find the cause.
questions.traps: Testing all three simultaneously loses attribution. Workflow order is arbitrary, and the model cannot diagnose a system it cannot observe.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works and nobody knows which parts of it are doing the work.
options: Remove parts one at a time and observe what changes
Leave it alone, since the prompt works and investigating risks breaking something that is currently producing acceptable results for the team
Rewrite it more concisely so the working parts are clearer
Document what each part of it is intended to do
questions.why: Ablation identifies which parts carry the load, which makes the prompt maintainable and often shorter.
questions.traps: Leaving it unexamined accepts unmaintainability. A concise rewrite guesses at what matters, and documenting intent is not the same as testing effect.

questions.stem: An associate gets an answer that is accurate but far too formal for their audience.
options: Ask for the same answer written rather less formally
State in the prompt who the audience actually is
Rewrite the answer by hand into the right register
Add a note asking for the tone to be adjusted somewhat
questions.why: Register follows from the reader, so naming the audience is what makes the model choose the level rather than be told it.
questions.traps: Asking for "less formal" gives a direction without a target, hand-rewriting fixes one answer, and a note about tone repeats the vagueness.

questions.stem: A prompt asks for "a short summary" and the results vary from two lines to two pages.
options: Ask for a short summary in a more emphatic way
Cut anything over the intended length by hand
State the length wanted in words or in sentences
Run the prompt twice and take the shorter result
questions.why: "Short" is relative and a number is not, so giving the length explicitly is what removes the variation.
questions.traps: Emphasis does not define a quantity, hand-trimming repairs each output, and picking the shorter of two still leaves both undefined.

questions.stem: An associate repeats the same six-line preamble at the start of every conversation.
options: Shorten the preamble so retyping it costs less
Keep a copy of the preamble to paste in each time
Ask the model to remember the preamble for later
Move the preamble into the Project's instructions
questions.why: Instructions apply automatically to every conversation in a Project, which is exactly what a repeated preamble is trying to achieve.
questions.traps: A shorter preamble is still retyped, pasting from a copy is the same manual step, and a request to remember does not persist across conversations.

questions.stem: Claude declines a request and the associate believes the refusal is a misunderstanding.
options: Explain the actual purpose of the request and ask again
Repeat the request in exactly the same words again
Break the request into parts to get around it
Try a different phrasing until one is accepted
questions.why: A refusal often reflects how the request read, and supplying the real context is what lets it be assessed properly.
questions.traps: An identical repeat gives nothing new, splitting a request to evade a refusal is circumvention, and rephrasing until it passes tests wording rather than legitimacy.

questions.stem: An associate refers to "the document" and the model answers about a different one.
options: Ask the model which document it actually used
Remove the other documents from the conversation
Name the specific document that is being referred to
Repeat the question with more emphasis placed on it
questions.why: An ambiguous reference is resolved by naming what is meant, which removes the guess entirely.
questions.traps: Asking which one it used diagnoses without fixing, removing documents loses material the work may need, and emphasis does not disambiguate.

questions.stem: An associate runs the same prompt three times and gets three differently structured answers.
options: Run it several times and pick the best structure
Accept it, since the content is the same each time
Ask for the structure to be kept more consistent
Specify the structure the answer should follow
questions.why: Structure that is not specified is left to the model, so stating it is what makes it repeatable.
questions.traps: Picking the best of several repeats the cost each time, equivalent content still costs the reader, and asking for consistency does not say consistent with what.

questions.stem: An associate asks a broad question and gets a broad answer they then call unhelpful.
options: Ask the same question and request more detail in it
Ask the narrower question they actually wanted answered
Ask the same question with a longer answer requested
Ask several follow-up questions after the broad answer
questions.why: A broad question is answered broadly, so narrowing the question is what narrows the answer.
questions.traps: More detail on a broad question broadens it further, length is not specificity, and follow-ups get there eventually at more cost.

questions.stem: A prompt contains two instructions that pull against each other and the output satisfies neither.
options: Decide which instruction should win and say so
Restate both instructions more forcefully in the prompt
Put the more important instruction first in the prompt
Split the task into two separate prompts entirely
questions.why: A conflict has to be resolved by the author, and stating the precedence is what tells the model how to resolve it.
questions.traps: Force does not settle a contradiction, ordering is a weak signal of priority, and splitting produces two outputs that still conflict.

questions.stem: A team runs the same analysis on twenty documents and writes a fresh prompt each time.
options: Combine all twenty documents into a single prompt
Write one prompt and reuse it across the twenty
Write shorter prompts so each one costs less to write
Analyse only the documents most likely to matter
questions.why: A repeated task wants one stable prompt applied twenty times, which also makes the twenty results comparable.
questions.traps: One combined prompt makes the documents compete, shorter prompts still vary between runs, and skipping documents changes the task.

questions.stem: An answer is well written but omits a constraint the associate stated in the prompt.
options: Restate the constraint at the end of the prompt
Ask the model to apply the constraint it missed
Check where in the prompt the constraint appears
Add stronger emphasis to the constraint's wording
questions.why: A constraint buried inside a long prompt competes with everything around it, so where it sits is the first thing to look at.
questions.traps: Moving it to the end without knowing the cause is a guess, a follow-up repairs one output, and emphasis is a fallback rather than a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A model's answer contradicts a fact that was stated earlier in a long working session.
options: Point out the contradiction and ask for a correction
Start again in a new conversation from scratch
Ask the model to check its own earlier statements
Restate the fact at the point where it is needed
questions.why: A fact that has drifted out of reach is restored by restating it where the work needs it, which is cheaper than starting over.
questions.traps: Flagging the contradiction fixes one answer, starting over discards useful work, and asking it to check what it can no longer see does not help.

questions.stem: Two colleagues use the same Project and get answers with different levels of detail.
options: Compare their prompts before changing the Project
Add a detail-level instruction to the Project itself
Ask both of them to use identical wording every time
Accept it, since detail preference varies by person
questions.why: Two people asking differently is the most likely cause, and comparing the prompts is what distinguishes that from a Project problem.
questions.traps: A Project-level instruction treats an unconfirmed cause, identical wording is impractical, and accepting it assumes the difference was intended.

questions.stem: A model says it cannot verify a claim and the associate needs that claim checked.
options: Ask the model again with the claim rephrased slightly
Ask the model how confident it is in the claim
Check the claim against a reliable source themselves
Treat the claim as false since it was not verified
questions.why: A statement that it cannot verify something is accurate information, and verification then belongs to a source the person can consult.
questions.traps: Rephrasing does not create access, a confidence score is another generated statement, and unverified is not the same as false.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works well but takes three exchanges to reach a usable answer every time.
options: Accept it, since three exchanges is not a large cost
Fold what those exchanges add into the first prompt
Ask the model to skip straight to the final answer
Save the third answer and reuse it as a template
questions.why: The exchanges are supplying information the first prompt omitted, and putting it there is what removes the round trips.
questions.traps: Repeated cost adds up across a team, asking it to skip ahead does not supply the missing information, and reusing an old answer stops it being about the new input.

questions.stem: A prompt gives three examples and the output copies their subject matter rather than their form.
options: Replace the examples with ones on other subjects
Reduce the number of examples from three to one
Describe the desired form instead of showing it
State explicitly what the examples are demonstrating
questions.why: Examples are ambiguous about which of their properties matter, and naming the property is what makes them read as form rather than content.
questions.traps: Varying the subjects can help but leaves the intent unstated, fewer examples weakens the pattern, and dropping examples loses their value.

questions.stem: An output is right in substance but the associate cannot tell where its figures came from.
options: Ask for each figure to be tied to its own source
Ask for the answer to be produced again more carefully
Check every figure against the source documents
Ask whether the figures came from the attached files
questions.why: Requiring each figure to name its source makes checking possible and shows immediately where a figure has no basis.
questions.traps: A more careful re-run does not add traceability, checking everything by hand is the cost the request avoids, and a yes-or-no question about provenance is not a trace.

questions.stem: An associate attaches a spreadsheet and the model's numbers do not match what the file contains.
options: Ask the model to recalculate the figures more carefully
Retype the relevant numbers into the prompt directly
Convert the spreadsheet into a different file format
Check how the file was read before trusting the numbers
questions.why: A mismatch between a file and the answer usually means the file was not read as expected, and confirming that comes before any recalculation.
questions.traps: Recalculating from a bad reading repeats the error, retyping works around the cause without finding it, and reformatting is a guess at the mechanism.

questions.stem: A team wants identical output from identical prompts and finds small differences always remain.
options: Keep refining the prompt until the outputs match exactly
Constrain what matters and accept variation elsewhere
Accept the differences, since the meaning is unchanged
Post-process the outputs into a single fixed format
questions.why: Generation is not deterministic, so the practical target is that the parts you depend on are fixed while the wording around them varies.
questions.traps: Chasing exact matching pursues something unavailable, blanket acceptance ignores fields that must be stable, and post-processing formats output without controlling its content.

questions.stem: A prompt performs well on typical inputs and poorly on the unusual ones a team cares about.
options: Rewrite the prompt around the unusual cases instead
Handle the unusual cases manually outside the prompt
Add the unusual cases to the prompt as examples
Add an instruction to take extra care with edge cases
questions.why: Examples of the hard cases show the model what they look like and how they should be handled, without giving up performance on the common ones.
questions.traps: Rewriting around the exceptions degrades the typical case, manual handling forgoes the automation, and an instruction to take care names no case.

questions.stem: A team's prompt is long and detailed, and shortening it makes some of the outputs worse.
options: Cut the parts that no observed failure depended on
Keep it as it is, since every part earns its place
Cut it in half and accept the quality difference
Split it into a short version and a long version
questions.why: Length is worth paying where it prevents a failure that actually occurs, so the parts to cut are the ones no observed failure needed.
questions.traps: Assuming every part earns its place forgoes the saving, arbitrary halving trades quality blindly, and two versions double the maintenance without deciding anything.

questions.stem: A model gives a partial answer and says it cannot complete the rest of the request.
options: Rephrase the request until the whole thing is answered
Discard the partial answer as unreliable in its entirety
Take the partial answer and source the rest elsewhere
Ask it to complete the rest to the best of its ability
questions.why: A stated limit is useful information, and combining what it could do with another source for the rest is the efficient response.
questions.traps: Rephrasing to defeat a limit tests wording rather than capability, discarding good work overreacts, and pressing for a best effort invites a fabricated completion.

questions.stem: An associate cannot tell whether an output is wrong or whether they misunderstood the task.
options: Ask the model to explain what task it understood
Restate the task and check the output against it
Ask a colleague whether the output looks right
Rerun the prompt and compare the two outputs given
questions.why: Writing down what the task actually requires is what makes it possible to say whether the output meets it.
questions.traps: A model's account of the task is another output, a colleague faces the same ambiguity, and a second run tests stability rather than fit.

questions.stem: A Project answers well on recent documents and poorly on the older ones it also holds.
options: Remove the older documents from the Project entirely
Add an instruction to weight older documents equally
Accept it, since recent documents matter more anyway
Check whether the older documents are still readable
questions.why: A systematic difference by document age often points at how those files were prepared, and checking their readability is what finds it.
questions.traps: Removing them assumes they are unwanted, an equal-weighting instruction cannot repair unreadable material, and accepting the pattern leaves real content unusable.

questions.stem: A team's outputs are consistent within a day and drift noticeably over several weeks.
options: Check what has changed in their inputs and prompts
Assume the model changed and adjust the prompt for it
Freeze the prompt so that nothing can change at all
Accept drift as unavoidable in any generative system
questions.why: Slow drift usually tracks changes in the material or the prompts around it, and finding what moved is what makes the drift explainable.
questions.traps: Blaming the model is the least testable explanation, freezing the prompt does not freeze the inputs, and calling it unavoidable stops the investigation.

questions.stem: A team must choose between one prompt that does three things and three prompts that each do one.
options: Keep one prompt, since fewer steps means less work
Split them, since smaller prompts are always better
Keep one prompt and add checks at the end of it
Split them where the three parts fail independently
questions.why: Splitting pays where the parts fail for different reasons, because each piece can then be diagnosed and fixed on its own.
questions.traps: Step count is not the cost that matters, "always better" ignores the overhead of three runs, and end-of-prompt checks do not isolate the failures.

questions.stem: A prompt produces good content in the wrong format every single time.
options: Show the format wanted as a small worked example
Describe the format in more words than before
Reformat each answer by hand after it comes back
Ask for the format to be followed more closely
questions.why: A format is easier to show than to describe, and a small example removes the ambiguity a description leaves behind.
questions.traps: More description restates the same ambiguity, hand-reformatting repeats every time, and asking for closer adherence names no target.

questions.stem: An answer includes a confident statement the associate knows to be wrong.
options: Correct that statement and use the rest as it is
Correct it and check the rest of the answer too
Discard the entire answer and start the task again
Ask the model whether the statement is correct
questions.why: One confident error suggests others may be present, so the rest of the answer is now something to check rather than something to trust.
questions.traps: Fixing one error and trusting the rest assumes it was isolated, discarding everything wastes usable work, and asking the model to grade itself is not a check.

questions.stem: An associate spends more time editing outputs than they would have spent writing from scratch.
options: Stop using the model for that particular task
Accept the editing as the cost of using a model
Put what they keep editing into the prompt itself
Ask for shorter outputs so there is less to edit
questions.why: Repeated edits are a specification the prompt is missing, and moving them into it is what stops them recurring.
questions.traps: Abandoning the task gives up a fixable problem, treating editing as unavoidable ignores the pattern, and shorter outputs cut volume rather than the mismatch.

questions.stem: A conversation started about one project and has gradually drifted onto a second one.
options: Continue, since both projects are the associate's work
Start a separate conversation for the second project
Say clearly which project each question is about
Summarise the first project before moving on to it
questions.why: Two projects in one conversation make every answer draw on both, and separating them restores the narrower context each needs.
questions.traps: Shared ownership is not shared context, labelling each question depends on remembering it, and a summary does not remove the other project's material.

questions.stem: An associate's outputs are consistent with each other but consistently miss one required element.
options: Add the missing element by hand after each output
Ask the model why the element keeps being left out
Accept it, since the rest of the output is right
Add that element to the prompt as a requirement
questions.why: A consistently missing element was never asked for, and adding it to the prompt is what makes it appear every time.
questions.traps: Manual addition repeats forever, asking the model to explain its omission produces a story rather than a fix, and accepting it leaves the output incomplete.

questions.stem: An associate asks for something the model says it does not have access to.
options: Supply the information the model cannot reach
Ask again in case the answer comes out different
Ask the model to estimate the missing information
Treat the task as impossible and abandon it now
questions.why: A tool that cannot reach something can still use it once it is provided, which turns the limit into an input step.
questions.traps: Re-asking does not create access, an estimate substitutes invention for data, and abandoning the task gives up on a solvable gap.

questions.stem: The model produces a good answer to a question the associate did not actually ask.
options: Ask the question again in a much more direct way
Explain that the answer was not what was wanted
Read the prompt back and see what it actually asked
Add more context so the intent becomes clearer
questions.why: An answer to the wrong question usually means the prompt asked that question, and reading it back is what shows where.
questions.traps: Re-asking may reproduce the same wording, saying it was wrong does not identify the cause, and more context around an unclear ask leaves the ask unclear.

questions.stem: A prompt asks the model to "review" a document and the output comes back as a summary.
options: Use the word "review" more emphatically in the prompt
State what the review is supposed to look for
Ask for a review rather than a summary explicitly
Provide the document in a different format entirely
questions.why: "Review" covers many things, and naming what to look for is what turns it into a specific task.
questions.traps: Emphasis does not narrow a broad word, contrasting it with "summary" says what it is not, and format is unrelated to the ambiguity.

questions.stem: A team's process runs Claude twice, once to draft and once to check the draft.
options: Keep both, since the check catches real errors
Merge them, since a single pass can do both jobs
Drop the check, since it doubles the work involved
Drop the draft and check human writing instead
questions.why: A separate check looks at the draft as something to evaluate rather than something to continue, which is why it finds what the first pass missed.
questions.traps: Merging returns to a single pass that grades itself, dropping the check removes the safeguard, and checking human writing solves a different problem.

questions.stem: An associate finds their long conversation has become slow and noticeably less accurate.
options: Continue, since the conversation holds the history
Delete the earlier messages from the conversation
Ask the model to be more accurate from now on
Move the remaining work into a fresh conversation
questions.why: A conversation that has grown too long is best restarted with the conclusions carried across, since the length is itself the cause.
questions.traps: The history is what is causing the problem, deleting messages loses the record, and an instruction cannot recover context that is out of reach.

questions.stem: Two runs of the same prompt classify the same borderline item differently each time.
options: Run it three times and take the majority answer
Treat borderline items as needing human review
Define what makes the borderline case fall each way
Accept the variation, since the case is genuinely unclear
questions.why: A borderline case varies because the criteria do not reach it, and extending them is what makes the classification decidable.
questions.traps: Majority voting hides the ambiguity behind repetition, routing all borderline cases to a person forgoes an easy criterion, and accepting it leaves the boundary undefined.

questions.stem: A model produces an answer and then adds that its information may be out of date.
options: Ignore the caveat, since the answer looked complete
Ask the model for the most recent information it has
Remove the caveat before passing the answer on
Check the point against a current source of information
questions.why: A staleness caveat is a specific warning about a specific claim, and confirming it against something current is what resolves it.
questions.traps: Ignoring the warning is exactly what it exists to prevent, asking for its most recent information does not add anything newer, and removing the caveat hides the uncertainty.

questions.stem: A prompt works for one associate and produces noticeably worse results for a colleague.
options: Compare what each of them supplies alongside it
Rewrite the prompt to be clearer for both of them
Have the first associate run all of the requests
Accept it, since prompting skill varies between people
questions.why: The same prompt with different inputs is the likely difference, and comparing what each person supplies is what identifies it.
questions.traps: Rewriting treats an unconfirmed cause, routing work through one person creates a bottleneck, and attributing it to skill assumes the conclusion.

questions.stem: An associate cannot tell whether an output's weakness is the prompt or the source material.
options: Rewrite the prompt and see whether the output improves
Ask the model which of the two is the problem
Run the same prompt on material known to be good
Improve both the prompt and the material together
questions.why: Holding the prompt fixed and changing the material isolates which one carries the fault, which is what makes the next fix targeted.
questions.traps: Changing the prompt tests one hypothesis while leaving the other confounded, the model has no view of its inputs' quality, and changing both leaves the cause unknown.

questions.stem: A team is asked to reduce how much they paste into each prompt without losing quality.
options: Cut the longest of the documents from every prompt
Cut the material that has never changed an answer
Summarise all of the material before pasting it in
Cut the material added most recently to the prompt
questions.why: Volume is worth paying for where it changes the answer, so the material to cut is what has demonstrably never made a difference.
questions.traps: Length is not a measure of contribution, summarising everything loses detail indiscriminately, and recency says nothing about usefulness.

questions.stem: An associate provides background and the model keeps repeating it back in every answer.
options: Say the background is context rather than content
Remove the background from the prompt entirely
Ask for shorter answers so the repetition shrinks
Move the background down to the end of the prompt
questions.why: The model cannot tell what to use from what to reproduce unless it is told, and labelling the role of the material is what settles it.
questions.traps: Removing it loses the grounding, shorter answers compress the repetition without removing it, and position does not communicate purpose.

questions.stem: An output is worse than usual and the associate changed three things in the prompt at once.
options: Undo all three and go back to the original prompt
Keep the changes and adjust until it improves
Undo the changes and reapply them one at a time
Ask the model which of the changes hurt the output
questions.why: Three simultaneous changes make the cause unrecoverable, and reapplying them singly is what identifies which one did the damage.
questions.traps: Reverting entirely loses whatever the changes improved, adjusting blindly compounds the confusion, and the model cannot see the prompt's history.

questions.stem: A classification prompt agrees with human reviewers 92% of the time and the team wants higher.
options: Add more examples to the prompt until it improves
Accept 92%, since it is close to human agreement itself
Route every disagreement to a human reviewer instead
Look at the 8% for a pattern before changing anything
questions.why: The disagreements are the only evidence about what is failing, and finding their pattern is what makes the next change targeted.
questions.traps: Adding examples is a guess without knowing the failure, accepting the number assumes the errors are random, and routing everything to a human forgoes the gain.

questions.stem: A team can either improve their prompt or improve the documents that it reads.
options: Improve the prompt, since it is quicker to change
Improve whichever the observed failures point at
Improve the documents, since they last much longer
Improve both together for the largest total gain
questions.why: Effort belongs where the evidence says the problem is, and the pattern of failures is the only thing that says which.
questions.traps: Speed of change is not the same as value, durability is not the same as need, and doing both spends twice without learning which mattered.

questions.stem: A model declines part of a request and the associate is under time pressure to deliver.
options: Find a phrasing that gets the whole request answered
Deliver the covered part without mentioning the gap
Deliver what is covered and flag the part that is not
Miss the deadline rather than deliver a partial answer
questions.why: A partial delivery with the gap named is honest and useful, and it leaves the recipient able to decide what to do about the remainder.
questions.traps: Rephrasing to defeat a refusal is circumvention, a silent gap misleads the recipient, and missing the deadline discards work that was ready.

questions.stem: A team's prompt has grown by one clause each time something went wrong and is now unwieldy.
options: Rebuild it around the failures that still occur
Keep it, since each clause was added for a reason
Remove the oldest clauses, since they are least relevant
Split it into several prompts run one after another
questions.why: Clauses accumulate against failures that may no longer happen, so rebuilding around the current ones restores the prompt without losing protection.
questions.traps: Historic justification does not prove current need, age does not indicate irrelevance, and splitting carries the same clauses across several prompts.

questions.stem: A Project retrieves the right documents but the answers still miss the key details in them.
options: Add the documents a second time to reinforce them
Ask more specific questions so the detail is requested
Move the key details into the Project's instructions
Check whether the detail survives how the file was stored
questions.why: Correct retrieval with missing detail points at the document itself, so how the file was prepared and stored is where to look.
questions.traps: Duplicating documents does not repair their content, more specific questions cannot retrieve what is not there, and moving details into instructions works around a broken document.

questions.stem: An associate's outputs improve when they add "think carefully" and they want to know why.
options: Keep the phrase, since the outputs are visibly better
Treat the improvement as untested until it is measured
Add similar phrases to strengthen the effect further
Remove it, since such phrases have no real effect
questions.why: An impression from a handful of outputs is not evidence, and comparing with and without on the same inputs is what turns it into a finding.
questions.traps: Visible improvement is exactly what small-sample impressions produce, stacking phrases compounds an unverified effect, and dismissing it in advance is the same error reversed.

questions.stem: A team gets consistent outputs in testing and inconsistent ones once real users are involved.
options: Add more test cases until the tests catch the problem
Constrain the prompt further so users can vary less
Accept it, since real use is always messier than testing
Compare the real inputs against the tested inputs
questions.why: The variable that changed is the input, and comparing the real ones with the tested ones is what shows what the testing left out.
questions.traps: More test cases without knowing what is missing is a guess, constraining users treats the symptom, and accepting it abandons the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A team must decide whether to keep tuning a prompt that is already good enough for its purpose.
options: Keep tuning, since improvement is always worthwhile
Stop, and spend the effort where output still fails
Stop permanently, since the prompt is now finished
Keep tuning until further changes stop helping at all
questions.why: Effort is worth more where the work is failing, and a prompt that meets its purpose has stopped being the constraint.
questions.traps: Endless improvement ignores opportunity cost, calling it finished forgets that inputs change, and tuning to exhaustion is the same over-investment stated as a rule.

questions.stem: An associate gets a list when they wanted prose, and their prompt did not say which.
options: State in the prompt what form the answer should take
Ask for the list to be converted into prose afterwards
Accept the list, since the content is all there
Provide an example of prose from a previous answer
questions.why: Output form is chosen by the model when the prompt is silent, so saying which form is wanted removes the choice.
questions.traps: Converting afterwards is an extra step every time, accepting the list ignores that form matters to the reader, and an old example is indirect where a direct statement works.

questions.stem: An associate asks about "last quarter" and the answer covers the wrong three months.
options: Ask the model which quarter it actually interpreted
Ask the question again using the same wording
Give the actual dates rather than the relative period
Add the current date to the top of the prompt
questions.why: A relative period depends on a reference point the model does not reliably share, and explicit dates remove that dependency.
questions.traps: Asking what it assumed diagnoses without fixing, repeating the wording repeats the ambiguity, and today's date still leaves the quarter boundary to interpretation.

questions.stem: A team pastes the same reference table into every one of a hundred prompts.
options: Put the table in a Project the prompts run against
Paste a shorter version of the table each time
Paste the table once at the start of each conversation
Ask the model to memorise the table for later use
questions.why: Material used by every prompt belongs in the Project, where it is available without being resupplied each time.
questions.traps: A shorter table loses rows, once per conversation is still a hundred pastes across a hundred conversations, and memorisation across conversations does not happen.

questions.stem: A prompt describes a task in three paragraphs and the model does only the first part.
options: Repeat the later parts at the end of the prompt
Break the task down into explicitly numbered steps
Write the three paragraphs in a more forceful tone
Send the three paragraphs as three separate prompts
questions.why: Multi-part tasks buried in prose lose their later parts, and numbering makes each one a visible requirement.
questions.traps: Repetition lengthens the prompt, tone does not create structure, and three prompts lose the connection between the parts.

questions.stem: A model states it cannot browse the internet and the associate needs current figures.
options: Ask the model for its best guess at the figures
Ask the model to try browsing anyway just in case
Use older figures, since current ones are unavailable
Provide the current figures inside the prompt itself
questions.why: A stated capability limit is resolved by supplying what the tool cannot fetch, which keeps the analysis current.
questions.traps: A guess at figures is fabrication, asking it to try anyway ignores a clear statement, and old figures answer a different question.

questions.stem: An associate wants every answer from a Project to end with the same three-line footer.
options: Add the footer by hand to each answer produced
Ask for the footer at the end of every single prompt
Put the footer text in the Project's instructions
Ask the model to remember the footer for next time
questions.why: A requirement that holds for every answer belongs in the instructions, which is where it applies without being repeated.
questions.traps: Manual addition repeats forever, asking in each prompt is the repetition being avoided, and memory does not carry across conversations.

questions.stem: An answer misreads a term that means something specific in the associate's industry.
options: Avoid the term and describe the concept instead
Define the term where it is used in the prompt
Ask the model what it understood the term to mean
Add the industry name at the start of the prompt
questions.why: A term with a specialised meaning needs that meaning supplied, since the general reading is otherwise the reasonable one.
questions.traps: Avoiding the term loses precision, asking what it understood diagnoses without fixing, and naming the industry is an indirect hint.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a scanned document and the answers reference text that is not in it.
options: Ask the model to read the document more carefully
Upload the same scan a second time to be sure
Check whether the scan's text was actually readable
Ask the model to describe what it can see in it
questions.why: Invented references from a scan usually mean the text was never extracted, and checking that is what identifies the cause.
questions.traps: A careful re-read cannot recover text that is not there, re-uploading repeats the same extraction, and a description is another output rather than a check.

questions.stem: A team's daily report takes four prompts and they want it down to one.
options: Combine all four regardless of what they each use
Keep four, since each step has a single purpose
Automate the four prompts to run one after another
Combine the steps that draw on the same material
questions.why: Steps that draw on the same material can share one pass, while steps that do not would only compete inside a combined prompt.
questions.traps: Combining everything makes unrelated material compete, keeping four accepts the cost without testing it, and automating four runs does not reduce them.

questions.stem: A prompt asking for "the top three risks" returns three risks that are all the same kind.
options: Ask for the risks to come from different categories
Ask for five risks and select three from those
Ask for the top three risks rather more specifically
Run the prompt twice and merge the two lists together
questions.why: "Top three" ranks without requiring spread, so asking for coverage across categories is what produces a varied list.
questions.traps: Asking for more and selecting shifts the work to the reader, restating the same phrase changes nothing, and merging two similar lists produces a longer similar list.

questions.stem: A team's outputs are consistent for one associate and vary for everyone else on the team.
options: Have that associate write the prompt for everyone
Look at what that one associate does differently
Add more constraints to the prompt for the others
Accept it, since individual style always differs
questions.why: One person getting stable results means something in their approach is working, and finding out what is the fastest route to spreading it.
questions.traps: Having one person write prompts does not transfer the practice, more constraints guess at the difference, and accepting it discards a working example.

questions.stem: A model gives an answer with a caveat and the associate strips it out before sending.
options: Verify the point, and keep the caveat until it is
Strip it, since caveats undermine the reader's confidence
Strip it and verify the point some time afterwards
Replace it with a general disclaimer on the document
questions.why: A caveat marks where an answer is uncertain, so it comes out when the uncertainty is resolved rather than when it is inconvenient.
questions.traps: Reader confidence is not worth a false impression, verifying afterwards sends an unqualified claim first, and a general disclaimer does not locate the specific issue.

questions.stem: A prompt gets a good answer that ignores the most recent of three attached files.
options: Ask the model to include the third file's content
Attach the third file on its own in a new prompt
Reorder the files so the newest one comes first
Check whether the third file was actually attached
questions.why: An entirely ignored file often was not read at all, so confirming it arrived comes before any change to the prompt.
questions.traps: Asking for its content assumes it is available, a separate prompt works around the question, and reordering guesses at attention when the cause may be absence.

questions.stem: A team's answers improve when they attach fewer documents and they want to know which to drop.
options: Drop the longest documents from the attachment set
Drop the oldest documents from the attachment set
Drop the ones that no answer has ever drawn on
Drop documents until the answers stop improving
questions.why: A document earns its place by being used, so the ones that have never contributed are the ones that can go without loss.
questions.traps: Length and age are proxies that can remove heavily used material, and dropping until improvement stops finds a point without knowing what was lost.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know whether a longer prompt is always a better prompt.
options: Yes — more instruction gives the model more to work with
No — shorter prompts are more reliable in general
Yes — provided the extra length is well organised
No — length helps only where it removes ambiguity
questions.why: What improves a prompt is resolving what was unclear, and words that do not do that compete with the ones that do.
questions.traps: More instruction can dilute rather than help, blanket brevity is the same rule in reverse, and organisation improves readability rather than content.

questions.stem: A team wants to check whether a change to their prompt actually improved anything.
options: Run the new version and see whether it looks better
Run both versions on the very same set of inputs
Ask the team whether the outputs feel improved now
Run the new version several times for consistency
questions.why: Comparing versions on identical inputs is what separates a real improvement from the ordinary variation between runs.
questions.traps: Judging the new version alone has nothing to compare against, impressions are what a comparison is meant to replace, and repeated runs measure stability rather than improvement.

questions.stem: A team adds an instruction that fixes one failure and introduces a different one.
options: Scope the instruction to the case it was written for
Remove the instruction and accept the original failure
Add a second instruction to counter the new failure
Keep both failures, since neither one is severe
questions.why: A broad instruction fires everywhere, so limiting it to the situation it was meant for keeps the fix without the side effect.
questions.traps: Removing it restores the first problem, countering with another instruction builds a stack of interacting rules, and accepting both gives up on a solvable conflict.

questions.stem: An associate has a prompt that fails roughly one time in twenty and cannot reproduce the failure.
options: Change the prompt and watch whether failures stop
Run the prompt repeatedly until a failure occurs
Collect the failing cases until a pattern appears
Accept a one-in-twenty rate as the cost of the tool
questions.why: An intermittent failure is diagnosed from its instances, and gathering enough of them is what turns randomness into a pattern.
questions.traps: Changing the prompt without a hypothesis tests nothing, brute-force repetition produces a case without context, and accepting the rate ignores what the failures cost.

questions.stem: A team must choose between a fast prompt that is occasionally wrong and a slow one that is not.
options: Match the choice to what an error would cost here
Choose the fast one, since speed compounds across volume
Choose the slow one, since accuracy is always the priority
Use the fast one and check its output with the slow one
questions.why: Speed and accuracy trade against each other, and the cost of being wrong in this particular use is what settles the exchange rate.
questions.traps: Volume arguments ignore the error cost, an absolute priority on accuracy over-pays where errors are cheap, and running both spends the slow prompt's cost anyway.

questions.stem: A Project's answers are good but the associate cannot tell which document each one came from.
options: Reduce the Project to fewer documents so it is obvious
Ask for the source document to be named in the answer
Read the documents afterwards to work out the source
Ask the same question of each document separately
questions.why: Requiring the source in the answer makes provenance part of the output rather than something reconstructed afterwards.
questions.traps: Shrinking the Project loses material, reading afterwards is the cost being avoided, and per-document questioning multiplies the runs.

questions.stem: A prompt produces stable output until the team add one more example, after which it varies.
options: Remove the new example and return to the stable set
Add further examples until the stability returns
Accept it, since more examples should mean more variety
Check whether the new example conflicts with the others
questions.why: An example that pulls against the existing ones gives the model two patterns to follow, and finding the conflict explains the instability.
questions.traps: Removing it loses whatever it was added for, adding more compounds an unexamined conflict, and treating variety as expected misreads what examples are for.

questions.stem: A model consistently declines a legitimate task and no amount of rephrasing helps.
options: Keep rephrasing until some version is accepted
Split the task so each part looks unobjectionable
Find another way to do the part it will not do
Abandon the whole task, including the parts it will do
questions.why: A persistent refusal is a boundary rather than a wording problem, so the work is routed around it rather than pushed through it.
questions.traps: Persistent rephrasing is an attempt to defeat the boundary, disguised splitting is the same thing done more carefully, and abandoning everything gives up the parts that work.

questions.stem: Two prompts produce equally good outputs and a team must standardise on one of them.
options: Keep the one whose failures are easier to interpret
Keep whichever of the two prompts is the shorter one
Keep the one whose author is more readily available
Keep both and let each person choose between them
questions.why: Equal quality makes maintainability the tiebreak, and a prompt whose failures are easy to interpret is cheaper to keep working.
questions.traps: Brevity is not maintainability, author availability is temporary, and keeping both is a decision not to standardise at all.

questions.stem: A team's prompt library has thirty prompts and nobody knows which of them are still used.
options: Keep all thirty, since deleting one may break something
Keep the ones used in the last month and drop the rest
Ask everyone to review all thirty and vote on them
Keep the ones with a current owner and a current use
questions.why: A prompt survives if someone depends on it and someone maintains it, and those two facts are what the audit needs to establish.
questions.traps: Keeping everything preserves the confusion, recency misses seasonal work, and a vote measures opinion rather than use.

questions.stem: An associate must decide whether to give the model a summary or the full document.
options: Give the summary, since it is easier for the model to use
Give the full document where its detail is what matters
Give the full document, since more context is always better
Give both so the model can choose which to rely on
questions.why: The choice follows the task: analysis that turns on specifics needs the specifics, while a question about the gist does not.
questions.traps: Ease of use is not the criterion, "always better" ignores the cost of volume, and supplying both makes them compete for attention.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to confirm a fact and it says that it is not certain.
options: Press it for a definite answer one way or the other
Take the uncertainty as meaning the fact is false
Treat the stated uncertainty as useful information
Ask a differently worded question to get certainty
questions.why: An admission of uncertainty is more useful than a confident guess, because it tells you exactly where checking is needed.
questions.traps: Pressing for certainty invites a fabricated one, uncertainty is not falsity, and rewording to remove a caveat changes the presentation rather than the knowledge.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt gives the model a role and nothing else about the task.
options: Give a more senior-sounding role in the prompt
Describe the actual task alongside the role given
Describe the role itself in much greater detail
Give two roles so more perspectives are covered
questions.why: A role shapes tone and framing while the task is what the model is being asked to do, and the task is what was missing.
questions.traps: Seniority in a role label does not add task detail, elaborating the role adds more of what is already there, and two roles multiply framing without a task.

questions.stem: A team's answers use different terms for the same thing across a single report.
options: Standardise the terms by hand after each draft
Ask for terminology to be kept consistent throughout
Accept it, since the meaning is clear either way
Give the preferred term for each concept in the prompt
questions.why: Terminology that is not specified varies between passages, and naming the preferred term is what fixes it.
questions.traps: Hand-standardising repeats every time, asking for consistency does not say which term wins, and inconsistent terms in one report undermine it.

questions.stem: An associate needs the model to use a definition from a document rather than the common one.
options: Quote the definition directly in the prompt itself
Attach the document and mention it in passing
Ask the model to use the document's definitions
Say that the common definition should not be used
questions.why: A definition the answer depends on is worth putting where it cannot be missed, which is directly in the prompt.
questions.traps: A passing mention relies on retrieval finding it, a general instruction does not supply the wording, and forbidding the common meaning leaves no replacement.

questions.stem: A team wants to know when a task is worth automating with a prompt at all.
options: When it takes a long time to do by hand each time
When several people in the team have to do it
When it recurs and its output can be checked easily
When the team has a prompt that nearly works already
questions.why: Repetition is what makes the investment pay back, and checkability is what makes the result usable.
questions.traps: Duration alone does not justify it for a one-off, headcount is a form of repetition already covered, and an existing prompt is a starting point rather than a reason.

questions.stem: An answer is correct but the associate wanted to know how confident to be in it.
options: Ask what the answer depends on for it to be true
Ask the model how confident it is in the answer
Ask for the answer to be produced a second time
Ask for the answer with more supporting detail
questions.why: Confidence in an answer comes from seeing its assumptions, since those are what a reader can check independently.
questions.traps: A stated confidence level is another generated claim, a second run tests stability rather than truth, and more detail can be equally unfounded.

questions.stem: A model says it cannot open a link the associate has pasted into the prompt.
options: Paste the same link again in a different format
Paste the relevant content instead of the link
Ask the model to describe what the link contains
Ask the model to try opening the link one more time
questions.why: If the tool cannot fetch a page, supplying its content directly is what makes the material available.
questions.traps: Reformatting a link does not create access, a description of an unopened page would be invented, and retrying ignores a stated limit.

questions.stem: A prompt produces an answer that is right but assumes knowledge the reader will not have.
options: Ask for the answer to be written rather more simply
Explain the missing background to the reader yourself
Ask for technical terms to be avoided in the answer
Say in the prompt who will actually read the answer
questions.why: The reader determines how much has to be explained, so naming them is what sets the level throughout.
questions.traps: "More simply" is a direction without a target, explaining afterwards is work repeated each time, and avoiding terms treats vocabulary rather than assumed knowledge.

questions.stem: An associate asks the same question twice and gets answers that differ in emphasis.
options: Treat the difference as an error to be reported
Always run the question twice and compare the answers
Expect some variation and specify what must be fixed
Use only the first answer to avoid the confusion
questions.why: Wording varies between runs by design, so the practical response is to pin down whatever the work depends on.
questions.traps: Variation is not a defect, running twice doubles the cost as a routine, and taking the first answer avoids the question rather than answering it.

questions.stem: A team's Project has grown to two hundred documents and answers have become vaguer.
options: Keep it, since a larger Project covers more ground
Split it into Projects by the questions people ask
Add instructions telling the model where to look
Remove the two hundredth document and reassess
questions.why: Vagueness at scale is retrieval competing across too much material, and splitting by question type is what restores the narrowing.
questions.traps: Coverage is what is causing the vagueness, an instruction does not reduce what is present, and removing one document out of two hundred changes nothing.

questions.stem: An associate needs an answer the model can only partly support and the deadline is today.
options: Send what is supported and say what part is not
Send the whole answer and verify it afterwards
Send nothing until the whole answer is supported
Send the whole answer with a general disclaimer
questions.why: Distinguishing the supported part from the unsupported one gives the recipient something usable and an accurate picture of its limits.
questions.traps: Verifying after sending leaves the reader exposed in the meantime, withholding everything discards usable work, and a general disclaimer does not say which part is weak.

questions.stem: A prompt tells the model what not to do and the output still does it occasionally.
options: Repeat the prohibition twice within the prompt
Make the prohibition considerably more strongly worded
Remove the prohibition, since it is not working
State what to do instead of the thing forbidden
questions.why: A prohibition leaves the alternative unspecified, and naming what should happen instead gives the model something to do.
questions.traps: Repetition and stronger wording restate the same negative, and removing it gives up without offering any replacement.

questions.stem: An associate has an output they are unsure about and no source to check it against.
options: Run the same prompt again and compare the answers
Ask the model to justify its answer more fully
Identify what would have to be true for it to hold
Accept it, since no check is available to be made
questions.why: Naming the answer's dependencies turns an unverifiable whole into specific claims that can each be pursued.
questions.traps: A second run tests stability rather than truth, a fuller justification is more of the same output, and accepting it because checking is hard is how errors travel.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce the number of prompts in a workflow without losing any checks.
options: Merge everything, including the checking steps
Merge the work steps and keep the checks separate
Keep every step, since each has its own purpose
Remove the checks that have never found anything
