questions.why: Work steps can share a pass while a check needs its own, since a pass that grades itself is not a check.
questions.traps: Merging the checks in removes their independence, keeping everything forgoes the saving, and a check that has found nothing may be preventing failures.

questions.stem: Two people write prompts for the same task and get outputs neither of them can compare.
options: Have one person write both of the prompts instead
Compare the outputs and pick whichever looks better
Agree the output's format before either writes a prompt
Standardise the wording of the two prompts themselves
questions.why: Comparability comes from a shared output shape, and agreeing that first is what makes two different approaches measurable against each other.
questions.traps: One author removes the comparison, picking the better-looking output judges without a standard, and matching prompt wording removes the difference being tested.

questions.stem: An associate's question depends on information they gave three days ago in another conversation.
options: Restate the information in the current conversation
Ask the model to recall the earlier conversation
Link the earlier conversation in the new prompt
Continue the earlier conversation rather than a new one
questions.why: Conversations do not share context, so information the question needs now has to be present now.
questions.traps: There is nothing to recall across conversations, a link is not something the model can follow, and reviving an old conversation carries its accumulated length as well.

questions.stem: A team's prompt is being used for a task slightly different from the one it was written for.
options: Extend the original so that it handles both tasks
Use the original as it is and edit the outputs
Write a wholly new prompt for the second task
Fork it rather than bend the original to cover both
questions.why: A forked copy keeps each prompt focused on its own task while preserving the work already proven in the original.
questions.traps: Extending it makes one prompt serve two masters, editing outputs repeats the cost, and starting from scratch discards what already works.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know how to tell a capability limit from a policy refusal.
options: A limit is permanent and a refusal is temporary
A refusal explains itself and a limit does not
A limit says it cannot, a refusal says it will not
There is no useful difference between the two
questions.why: The distinction matters because a limit is worked around by supplying what is missing, while a refusal is not addressed by rewording it.
questions.traps: Permanence does not separate them, explanations accompany both, and collapsing the distinction leads to the wrong response in each case.

questions.stem: A team's outputs score well on every measure they check and users still complain.
options: Add more measures until the complaints are explained
Ask users what they are judging that the measures miss
Tell users what the measures show about the quality
Treat the complaints as unrepresentative of most users
questions.why: A gap between measures and satisfaction means the measures are missing something users care about, and only users can say what that is.
questions.traps: More measures chosen internally repeat the blind spot, telling users the numbers argues with their experience, and dismissing them assumes the answer.

questions.stem: A prompt runs faster after a team removes its examples, and quality drops only on rare inputs.
options: Keep the faster version, since most inputs are fine
Restore the examples, since quality dropped at all
Keep both versions and choose per input as it arrives
Decide whether those rare inputs are ones they care about
questions.why: The trade is speed against the rare cases, so what those cases cost when they go wrong is what decides it.
questions.traps: Majority performance ignores the tail, treating any drop as unacceptable over-pays where the tail is harmless, and per-input choosing needs the judgement being avoided.

questions.stem: A team standardises on one prompt and two people say their own version worked better.
options: Test all three on the same inputs before standardising
Standardise anyway, since consistency is the goal
Let each person keep whichever version they prefer
Merge the three versions into one combined prompt
questions.why: Three candidate prompts and a shared test set is exactly the situation a comparison settles, and standardising first discards possible improvements.
questions.traps: Standardising first assumes the chosen prompt is best, letting everyone differ abandons the goal, and merging combines three approaches without testing any of them.

questions.stem: An associate can either put reference material in a Project or paste it into each prompt.
options: Always use the Project, since it avoids repeated pasting
Always paste it, since the model then certainly sees it
Project for material reused across questions, prompt for the rest
Do both so the material is available either way
questions.why: A Project retrieves what a question needs from a shared body, while pasting guarantees that one specific item is present for one specific question.
questions.traps: Always using the Project relies on retrieval for material that must be present, always pasting repeats work for shared material, and doing both duplicates content that then competes.

questions.stem: A team's output quality drops after they switch to a shorter, cleaner version of their prompt.
options: Restore the old prompt and keep it exactly as it was
Keep the shorter prompt and accept the lower quality
Shorten it further, since the direction seemed right
Find what the removed text was doing before restoring it
questions.why: Something in the removed text was earning its place, and identifying it is what lets the prompt stay clean while recovering the quality.
questions.traps: A wholesale revert loses the clean-up, accepting lower quality gives up the reason for the change, and shortening further compounds an unexamined loss.

questions.stem: A model completes a task but notes that it is outside what it can do reliably.
options: Discard the output, since the model has disclaimed it
Treat the note as a reason to check the output closely
Use the output, since the model completed the task
Ask the model whether the note was really necessary
questions.why: A reliability note tells you where the risk is concentrated, which is guidance about how much checking the output needs.
questions.traps: Discarding it wastes work that may be correct, using it unchecked ignores a specific warning, and asking the model to reconsider its caveat invites it to withdraw useful information.

questions.stem: A team must justify the time they spend maintaining prompts to a sceptical manager.
options: Show the work the prompts do and what failure would cost
Show how many prompts the team has written so far
Show how much faster the prompts are than working by hand
Show that other teams maintain their prompts as well
questions.why: Maintenance is justified by what the prompts are relied on for and what breaks without them, which is the case a manager is actually asking for.
questions.traps: A count measures activity, a speed comparison ignores the maintenance question itself, and pointing at other teams is not an argument about this one.

questions.stem: An associate gets a poor output and wants to work out what to change first.
options: Move to a more capable model group straight away
Change the prompt and see whether things improve
Ask the model to explain what went wrong for it
Read the prompt back to see what it actually asked
Check whether the inputs were what they intended
questions.why: Diagnosis starts by establishing what was actually asked and what was actually supplied, because both are cheaper to check than to guess at.
questions.traps: Changing things without a hypothesis tests nothing, a model change is the expensive guess, and a self-explanation is another output rather than a trace.

questions.stem: An associate changed three things in a prompt at once and the output became worse.
options: Keep the changes and adjust until it improves again
Undo them and then reapply them one at a time
Revert everything and return to the original prompt
Ask the model which of the three changes hurt it
Recognise that the cause is currently unrecoverable
questions.why: Simultaneous changes make attribution impossible, so the only route back to a cause is reapplying them singly.
questions.traps: A full revert discards whatever improved, blind adjustment compounds the confusion, and the model cannot see the prompt's history.

questions.stem: A result looks off and the associate cannot say whether the brief or the output is at fault.
options: Check the output against that written statement
Rerun the prompt and compare the two outputs given
Ask the model to explain what task it understood
Ask a colleague whether the output looks about right
Write down what the task itself actually requires
questions.why: Stating the requirement explicitly is what makes it possible to say whether the output meets it, which is otherwise a comparison against an unstated standard.
questions.traps: A model's account of the task is another output, a colleague faces the same ambiguity, and a second run tests stability rather than fit.

questions.stem: A prompt asking for a brief overview returns anything between a paragraph and several pages.
options: Run it twice and keep the shorter of the results
Trim anything over the intended length by hand
Ask for a short summary rather more emphatically
State the length wanted in words or sentences
Replace the relative term with a concrete number
questions.why: "Short" is relative and a number is not, so replacing the vague term with a quantity is what removes the variation.
questions.traps: Emphasis does not define a quantity, hand-trimming repairs each output, and picking the shorter of two leaves both undefined.

questions.stem: A prompt demands exhaustive detail and a strict word limit, and the output satisfies neither.
options: Put the more important instruction first in the prompt
Decide which instruction should take precedence
Split the task into two entirely separate prompts
State that precedence explicitly in the prompt
Restate both instructions more forcefully than before
questions.why: A contradiction has to be resolved by the author, and stating which rule wins is what tells the model how to resolve it.
questions.traps: Force does not settle a contradiction, ordering is a weak signal of priority, and splitting produces two outputs that still conflict.

questions.stem: A rule added to stop over-long answers has started truncating the ones that need length.
options: Add a second instruction countering the new failure
Recognise a broad instruction as firing everywhere
Remove it and accept the original failure returning
Scope the instruction to the case it was written for
Keep both failures, since neither one is severe
questions.why: An instruction that is right in one case and wrong in another is a scoping problem, so narrowing it keeps the fix without the side effect.
questions.traps: Removing it restores the first problem, a counter-instruction builds a stack of interacting rules, and accepting both gives up on a solvable conflict.

questions.stem: An associate says "the spreadsheet" with three attached and gets an answer about the wrong one.
options: Name the specific document that is being referred to
Ask the model which document it actually used
Repeat the question with rather more emphasis
Remove the other documents from the conversation
Remove the ambiguity rather than diagnosing it
questions.why: An ambiguous reference is resolved by naming what is meant, which removes the guess instead of investigating it.
questions.traps: Asking what it used diagnoses without fixing, removing documents loses material the work may need, and emphasis does not disambiguate.

questions.stem: A long working session starts producing answers that contradict what was agreed earlier.
options: Ask for a summary before continuing the session
Ask the model to re-read the earlier conversation
Correct each contradiction as and when it appears
Recognise that early detail has fallen out of reach
Restate the agreed points in a fresh conversation
questions.why: Once earlier detail is out of reach, restating it in a fresh conversation is what puts it back, because nothing can recover what is no longer available.
questions.traps: The model cannot re-read what it cannot see, correcting each contradiction treats symptoms, and a summary of a degraded thread inherits its gaps.

questions.stem: A Project surfaces the correct file every time and the specifics inside it never appear.
options: Ask more specific questions so the detail is requested
Add the documents a second time to reinforce them
Recognise correct retrieval as pointing at the document
Check whether the detail survived how the file was stored
Move the key details into the Project's instructions
questions.why: Correct retrieval with missing detail points at the document itself, so how it was prepared and stored is where the fault lies.
questions.traps: Duplicating documents does not repair their content, specific questions cannot retrieve what is absent, and moving details into instructions works around a broken file.

questions.stem: A weekly report comes back laid out differently each week from an unchanged prompt.
options: Accept it, since the content is the same each time
Ask for the structure to be kept more consistent
Specify the structure that the answer must follow
Check each output against that specified structure
Run it several times and pick the best structure
questions.why: Structure that is not specified is chosen afresh each run, so stating it and verifying it is what makes the shape repeatable.
questions.traps: Asking for consistency does not say consistent with what, picking the best repeats the cost, and varying structure breaks anything downstream.

questions.stem: A team needs two runs of the same prompt to match and the wording never quite does.
options: Keep refining until the outputs match exactly
Constrain the parts the work actually depends on
Accept all the differences, since meaning is unchanged
Post-process everything into one fixed format
Accept variation in the wording around those parts
questions.why: Generation is not deterministic, so the workable target is fixing what is depended upon while letting the surrounding wording vary.
questions.traps: Chasing exact matching pursues something unavailable, blanket acceptance ignores fields that must be stable, and post-processing formats without controlling content.

questions.stem: An associate opens every session by pasting the same paragraph of standing context.
options: Put standing content where it applies automatically
Keep a copy of it to paste in on each occasion
Move the preamble into the Project's instructions
Ask the model to remember it for the next time
Shorten the preamble so retyping it costs less
questions.why: Content that should apply to every conversation belongs in the instructions, which is what makes it apply without being resupplied.
questions.traps: A shorter preamble is still retyped, pasting is the same manual step, and a request to remember does not persist across conversations.

questions.stem: A team's bill is driven by a reference document attached to every single call they make.
options: Recognise identical repeated content as the cost driver
Accept the cost, since the guide improves the output
Move the guide somewhere it is not resent each time
Send the guide only on the first request of a session
Shorten the guide until the cost becomes acceptable
questions.why: Material identical on every request should live outside the request, because that is precisely what is being paid for repeatedly.
questions.traps: Shortening loses guidance, first-request-only leaves later requests without it, and accepting the cost forgoes an easy saving.

questions.stem: Part of a request comes back unanswered and the deliverable is due within the hour.
options: Deliver the covered part without mentioning the gap
Find a phrasing that gets the whole thing answered
Miss the deadline rather than deliver it partially
Deliver what is covered and flag the part that is not
Let the recipient decide what to do about the gap
questions.why: A partial delivery with the gap named is honest and usable, and it leaves the decision about the remainder with the person who needs it.
questions.traps: Rephrasing to defeat a refusal is circumvention, a silent gap misleads the recipient, and missing the deadline discards work that was ready.
